News.title: Top chef who became youngest in UK to win Michelin star dies – as tributes pour in for ‘inspiration & gent’
News.content:
'INCREDIBLE LEGACY Top chef who became youngest in UK to win Michelin star dies – as tributes pour in for ‘inspiration & gent’







Next

CHEF Ian McAndrew, known for being the youngest UK chef to lead a restaurant to a Michelin star has died.

After more than five decades in hospitality, Ian is remembered for his “exemplary” commitment to British cooking.

His death was announced by The Master Chefs of Great Britain on social media.

Several top chefs worked under Ian including Phil Vickery, Michael Deane and Paul Kitching.





He was described by Tom Kerridge as an “outstanding chef and a wonderful man”.

Ian started out with Anton Mosimann at the Dorchester in London in the late 1970s.

He then became executive chef of Eastwell Manor in Kent where he led the venue to a Michelin star in 1982.

Three years later he again won the award for his own restaurant, Seventy Four in Canterbury.



Ian also spent time at 116 Knightsbridge in London and the Boathouse Brasserie in Hythe.

News.title: Rider who died in plunge from rollercoaster ‘captured falling in chilling souvenir pic after hitting ride 3 times’
News.content:
Next

A THEME park visitor who plunged to his death from a towering rollercoaster was reportedly captured in a chilling souvenir photograph during the tragedy.

The man allegedly struck the ride three times as he fell, with horrified witnesses describing the terrifying moments before he hit the ground.



The tragedy unfolded on Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia, where the victim fell from the Goliath rollercoaster, the tallest in the state.

One witness claimed the man’s horrifying fall was captured in a souvenir picture taken during the ride.



“He fell and hit the car three different times,” the witness told 11Alive reporter Cody Alcorn.

The photograph has not been publicly verified, and it remains unclear exactly what it shows.

Read more on Six Flags LAST RIDE World-famous rollercoaster shut down for good after 100 'brain injury' complaints



Several other people were reportedly injured during the incident, which sparked a major emergency response and forced officials to evacuate the theme park.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as riders returned to the station, with one person allegedly screaming that the passenger sitting beside him had fallen out.

A Reddit user who claimed to have been waiting in line for the rollercoaster described the disturbing aftermath.

“The train pulled into the station, all the riders were distressed and a man who was sitting next to the person who was died was screaming that whoever was sitting next to him fell out,” the person wrote.



The witness described the experience as “very sad and surreal.”

Meanwhile, other thrillseekers were left stranded on the rollercoaster after the ride was shut down.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show passengers stuck on an incline as workers scrambled to bring them to safety.

Riders were reportedly evacuated four at a time, with staff helping them out of their seats and onto a staircase alongside the tracks.

The victim has not yet been publicly identified, and investigators have not established what caused him to fall.



Six Flags confirmed the tragedy in a statement.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” a spokesperson told the Daily Mail.

“Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”



“We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” the spokesperson added.

The company said park staff and local authorities responded immediately and were cooperating with the investigation.

“Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”

Mableton Mayor Michael Owens also expressed his condolences following the deadly incident.

“Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the individual’s family, friends and loved ones during this difficult time,” he said.



Owens confirmed that Mableton Public Safety Director Dr Kerry Stalling was working alongside Cobb County police and park security.

“We are grateful to the personnel responding to this incident, and we will continue to support coordination with the appropriate authorities,” he added.

“Out of respect for the family and the ongoing investigation, we will refrain from commenting further at this time.”

The Goliath rollercoaster has been one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s major attractions since opening in 2006.

Manufactured by Bolliger & Mabillard, the giant ride stands 200 feet tall and reaches speeds of up to 70mph.

News.title: Bomb threat on flight from New York to Israel sparks evacuation weeks after axe attack on hijacked plane
News.content:
PLANE CHAOS Bomb threat on flight from New York to Israel sparks evacuation weeks after axe attack on hijacked plane







Next

A PASSENGER plane arriving in Tel Aviv had to be evacuated at a remote runway after a bomb threat, it is reported.

The Delta Air Lines flight travelling from New York had already landed at Ben-Gurion Airport on Tuesday when a chilling message was received.



According to Israeli outlet Ynet, the message claimed an explosive device was on board the packed flight.

Panicked passengers were rushed off the plane and taken to a terminal while the aircraft was removed from the main airport.



Security teams carried out extensive checks but found nothing unusual, the outlet reports.

The security scare comes less than two weeks after an attempted hijacking on a separate passenger plane bound for Tel Aviv.

Omani co-pilot, Hamam al- Hammami, 29, allegedly attacked his captain Smit Machchhar with an onboard crash axe as he tried to take control of a flydubai passenger jet.

Israeli sources have since claimed that al-Hammami was plotting to crash into Ben-Gurion Airport – the country’s main international gateway.



Heroic passengers and crew grappled with the co-pilot to regain control of the plane after it dropped a terrifying 14,000ft in just 29 seconds.

A preliminary investigation has now found al-Hammami was inspired by the 9/11 attacks.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the September 11, 2001 attacks after four commercial planes were hijacked and crashed in the United States.

In a statement the United Arab Emirates’ Attorney General said “carrying out a similar operation” was firmly “established in his mind”.

The co-pilot wanted to carry out “a premeditated plot with a terrorist objective” to cause “the greatest possible number of casualties”, the statement said.



In preparation for the attack al-Hammami reportedly prepared by visiting Tel Aviv on previous flights, preliminary findings revealed.

He took part in two flights to Ben Gurion Airport to become familiar with the route and airport, investigators said.

Two posts made to a LinkedIn profile bearing the name Hamam al-Hammami were published in quick succession nine hours after the incident.



It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance.

One included a video featuring a photo of Ayman al-Zawahiri, who led al Qaeda after the death of Osama Bin Laden.

This was followed with an image of Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi, who killed nine people, including seven American CIA officers, in a 2009 suicide bombing.

The latest incident also comes just weeks after Delta resumed its nonstop service between New York and Tel Aviv.

In September the US carrier restarted daily flights from JFK to Ben-Gurion Airport following a review of the security situation in the region.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

At the time, Delta said the safety and security of its customers and employees remained its “top priority”.

It would continue to monitor developments alongside government and aviation authorities, the statement added.

News.title: Newly released Christa Pike 911 call reveals confused response after botched execution – & why it was treated as fake
News.content:
Next

EMERGENCY responders were left scrambling after killer Christa Pike survived her execution – with a desperate call for help initially dismissed as a hoax.

Newly released 911 records reveal the chaotic scenes that unfolded as officials struggled to establish whether the shocking emergency was real, delaying potentially life-saving treatment.



The confusion began when a caller from Tennessee’s Riverbend Maximum Security Institution reported that Pike, 50, was still alive despite receiving two doses of a lethal injection drug.

But the caller was unable to provide a verification code used by agencies to confirm that emergency requests are genuine, prompting dispatchers to question whether they were being targeted by a prank.



The first call came at 8.40pm on September 30, just over an hour after prison officials began attempting to execute Pike for the brutal 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer.

“We’ve been carrying out an execution tonight. We’ve administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased,” the caller said, according to a transcript.



The caller, whose identity and job were redacted, reported that Pike was unconscious and not breathing normally.

But when dispatchers contacted the prison’s Central Control to verify the emergency, officials reportedly insisted they had not made the call.

By 9.03pm, dispatchers had concluded that the request was fake.

“Per supervisors here at the DEC (Department of Emergency Communications) we have been informed it is a false call,” one dispatcher said.



“There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison.”

However, the terrifying situation was very real.

Just minutes later, a first responder reported that someone claiming to be a state official was outside the prison gates, desperately demanding that emergency crews be allowed inside.

“Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people.”

At around 9.08pm, one of Pike’s attorneys, Kelly Gleason, also called emergency services pleading for urgent medical assistance.



“My client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care,” Gleason said.

It was not until around 9.11pm – roughly 31 minutes after the first call – that prison officials confirmed the emergency was genuine and responders were cleared to enter.

The confusion continued even as medics prepared to transport Pike to hospital.



At 9.34pm, one responder asked dispatchers to ensure prison officials knew where the inmate was being taken.

“Just ‘cause there’s been so much other confusion, I want to make sure they are aware of this,” the responder said.

The extraordinary sequence of events was revealed in emergency dispatch recordings obtained by the Associated Press through a public records request.

Audio of the initial 911 call was withheld under state law, although a written transcript was released.

Pike was rushed to hospital and placed on a ventilator for several days, with her lawyers at one stage fearing she would not survive.



However, she regained consciousness last Tuesday and began speaking in a limited capacity and walking with assistance.

Her attorneys confirmed Saturday that she had been discharged and returned to the women’s prison where she had spent around 30 years behind bars.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” they said.

Pike was just 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, brutally murdered 19-year-old Slemmer at a job training camp in 1995.

Prosecutors said Pike believed Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend and lured the teenager into a wooded area.



There, she tortured the victim with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt before Shipp carved a pentagram into her body.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shipp, who was 17 at the time, received a life sentence with the possibility of parole, while Pike was sentenced to death.

It remains unclear whether Tennessee officials will attempt to execute her again.

News.title: Multiple fatalities including children feared in Waterford fire with gardai at scene amid locals’ ‘absolute heartbreak’
News.content:
'DISTURBING SITUATION' Multiple fatalities including children feared in Waterford fire with gardai at scene amid locals’ ‘absolute heartbreak’







Next

MULTIPLE people, including children, are feared dead in a serious house fire in Waterford city.

Gardai and emergency services remain at the scene of the “evolving incident” at a home in the Birchwood estate, Kilcohan, around 3km from Waterford city centre.

Hearses have been seen leaving the scene of the fire.

The alarm was raised at 5.13am this morning, a spokesperson for Waterford Fire Service said.





Taoiseach Micheal Martin described the blaze as a “deeply disturbing situation”.

He said: “Our thoughts and prayers are with anybody who has lost their lives and all who are affected.

“We thank the first responders who are at the scene.

“We say to everyone to give space to the first responders, to the gardaí to deal with what clearly is a very worrying and deeply disturbing situation.”



A number of units from local fire stations rushed to the scene earlier this morning and on arrival found a well-developed fire.

Firefighting operations began immediately and a number of casualties were removed from the two-storey house.

It is understood that there are multiple fatalities, including children.

The fire was extinguished and the scene handed over to gardai.



A large cordon remains in place, sealing off the area.

Sinn Fein TD David Cullinane told RTE’s Morning Ireland that he knew the family and that the news is devastating.

He said: “Obviously there is shock, but people will know the family and there is absolute heartbreak when you have children involved as well. So it’s obviously very emotional.

“I knew the family very well. In fact, I only met him very recently, so I’m in shock myself still and my heart is broke.

“Obviously for the family, we don’t know the number of fatalities, but we do know it’s very high.



“And obviously if anybody does survive, we wish them our best wishes.”

Local Fianna Fail councillor Jason Murphy described hearing sirens “screeching” past his house this morning and “knowing something terrible was after happening”.

He told the Irish Sun: “It’s awful. People have lost their lives and there is a feeling of just helplessness that there’s nothing we can do, only pray for these people.

“Our thoughts are with the emergency services as well, sometimes we can forget them.”

He added: “It will take a long time to get over this for people in that area. It’s a very tight-knit community up there.”



Bishop of Waterford and Lismore Alphonsus Cullinan told RTE’s Today with David McCullagh: “It’s not something natural. It’s something totally unnatural to lose one, to lose several lives in this way and it’s just an unspeakable tragedy.”

Waterford City and County Council has set up a support hub for those affected by the fire at the Butler Community Centre in St John’s Park.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Garda spokesperson said: “An Garda Siochana and other emergency services are currently at the scene of a fire at a domestic residence in Waterford City.

“As this is an ongoing evolving incident An Garda Siochana is not in a position to provide any further detail.”

News.title: Ship sinks after two vessels hit by drones off coast of Bulgaria in ANOTHER attack as rescue operation underway
News.content:
SEA BLITZ Ship sinks after two vessels hit by drones off coast of Bulgaria in ANOTHER attack as rescue operation underway







Next

TWO ships have been blasted off Bulgaria’s coast, a week after a similar strike blitzed two boats in the Black Sea.

One ship was sunk after the drone attack in the early hours of Tuesday, Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev said.



Three drones blasted one ship, the Malta-flagged Chelsea 3, at around 1.30am, as it sailed 18 nautical miles off the Bulgaria’s coast.

All 15 crew members of the Ukrainian-owned boat were rescued, five of them injured in the strike.



The Chelsea 3’s crew was made up of seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis.

A second ship was blitzed and sunk 17miles east of Krapets, the Bulgarian PM said.



He added that one crew member had been rescued from the boat but did not say whether others on board had survived the strike.

Radev slammed the attacks in a national address, saying: “This is absolutely unacceptable another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters.

“I am due to speak with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte.”

He said he did not have clear evidence pointing to a perpetrator of the attacks but summoned Russia‘s ambassador to Bulgaria “for a conversation”.



Radev said “the outcome benefits the Russian Federation”.



He said: “Bulgaria continues to seek support for an investigation into the attacks to determine the country of origin of the drones.

“We are also seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and enhance our response capabilities.”

Although Bulgaria does not border Russia or Ukraine, all three countries have strategic ports on their Black Sea coastlines.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha blamed Russia for the strikes and slammed what he called Vladimir Putin’s “deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.”

He said: “The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage.”



European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the Black Sea “has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine”.

She condemned the strikes as “unacceptable”, adding: “Those responsible should be held accountable.”

It comes a week after a similar strike sunk one boat and blasted another inside the Nato member’s Exclusive Economic Zone – not part of the nation’s sovereign territory.

One cargo ship was engulfed in flames and sunk after the attack.

No trace of the crew onboard had been found when Bulgaria called off the search for the sailors last week.



All 18 members of the crew of the Able, which was also badly damaged in the attack, were rescued.

The 11 Turkish and seven Indian seafarers were saved by Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria.

Two of them were hospitalised after the blast, with one suffering burns and another a head injury.

Radev described the strikes as a “flagrant attack on maritime law”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “Such an attack within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable.



“Two merchant vessels were attacked by sea and air drones.”

News.title: Man, 47, arrested on suspicion of murder after ‘sudden death’ of woman
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MURDER PROBE Man, 47, arrested on suspicion of murder after ‘sudden death’ of woman







Next

A MAN, aged 47, has been arrested on suspicion of murder after the “sudden death” of a woman.

Police launched an investigation after paramedics found the woman dead at the scene at a house in Newcastle-Under-Lyme yesterday morning.

The 47-year-old man, from Stoke-on-Trent remains in custody,

The woman’s next of kin have been informed.





A spokesperson for Staffordshire Police said: “We have launched a murder investigation after a woman died in Newcastle-under-Lyme.

“We were called by West Midlands Ambulance Service at 11.15am this morning (Monday 12 October), who attended Clayton Lane following reports of the sudden death of a woman.

“Officers attended and, sadly, a woman was pronounced dead at the scene.

“The woman’s next of kin has been informed.

“A 47-year-old man, from Stoke-on-Trent, has been arrested on suspicion of murder. He remains in custody.”

News.title: Andy Burnham puts foot in it leaving Government scrambling to clean up his Brexit mess
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham seems to be picking up a dangerous habit of putting his foot in it.

The Prime Minister left his government scrambling around after declaring the 2016 Brexit vote had been interfered with by Moscow.



He claims he was told it was “clear” that Moscow had rigged the vote.

Several hours later, Foreign Minister Stephen Doughty was sent out on the airwaves to clear up the mess.



Then, at the daily briefing with journalists, it had to be squeezed out of Downing Street that the result was legitimate.

Avid readers will be aware that the in-out result was clear and the result was accepted.

It was a decisive 52-48 per cent vote in favour of Leave which was finally enacted after Boris Johnson‘s Get Brexit Done election in 2019.

But for Number 10, this is becoming an all too familiar pattern.

The Manchester City scandal has seen Number 10 change its position following comments by the PM on the cheating row.

The public should place great trust in what politicians say.



It’s clearly time that some in government think twice before speaking.

Meanwhile, here in Bangkok, Chancellor John Healey will arrive in Bangkok tomorrow to meet world finance leaders.

The International Monetary Fund, meeting in Thailand for their annual meeting, have warned that Britain faces an growth downgrade for next year.

As the Budget approaches, they also warn the Treasury to go on an unfunded spending splurge.

Any cost-of-living measures should be used “sparingly” and targeted.



Energy bills on average could rise by £276 at the turn of the year but financial help is only likely to be on the way to those most in need.

The UK’s sluggish economy coupled with high debt and borrowing costs simply can’t go any further.

News.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but energy prices and rates to hit in 2027
News.content:
The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.

The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.

Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".

Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.

Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.

Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.

But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.

"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.

The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031.

Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".

The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.

While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events.

News.title: Chris Mason: Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
News.content:
With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.

He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.

Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.

First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.

Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.

In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.

"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.

Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.

"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, external, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.

The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.

Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.

And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.

"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.

In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.

His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt â calling the prime minister "a liar."

The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary, external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

News.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
News.content:
The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.

Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.

This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.

Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.

Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.

Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.

News.title: Hundreds more prisoners to be freed in second phase of early release scheme
News.content:
About 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales early on Tuesday in the second phase of the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis.

The group will include offenders serving up to two and a half years for crimes.

Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half.

The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload.

Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

Tuesday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.

Napo, the probation service union, said the releases have put enormous strain on its members, who are charged with monitoring the offenders in the community.

Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.

On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.

The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a Â£700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.

News.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
News.content:
Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government.

Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed.

With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.

But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect.

Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition".

In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.

The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need.

News.title: Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
News.content:
One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest.

Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won.

Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors.

The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture.

Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him".

Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court".

The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky.

Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields.

Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously.

Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge.

Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London.

At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about Â£1bn.

But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares.

News.title: NHS staff get 'landmark' payout over nitrous oxide exposure
News.content:
NHS maternity staff who were exposed to excessive levels of nitrous oxide have received "landmark" payouts totalling Â£735,000, a union said.

Basildon Hospital in Essex settled claims from 121 staff, including 85 midwives, who took legal action after reporting fatigue, anxiety, headaches and "brain fog" after the gas levels breached safety limits.

The Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust said it had apologised to staff.

The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said it was the largest group legal action ever brought by midwives in the UK.

The gas, also known as Entonox, is used to provide temporary pain relief for women giving birth.

The staff members behind the claims were found to have breathed it in over long shifts for months and years.

According to an internal report from Basildon Hospital, some members of staff were exposed to levels up to 30 times higher than the legal workplace exposure limit between 2021 and 2023.

They were also not told for 16 months about test results commissioned by the trust that showed their exposure had breached safety thresholds.

The legal action was first revealed by the BBC in May.

The trust settled the claims after admitting its staff had been exposed to dangerously high levels of the gas.

News.title: Cut screen time in classrooms to avoid long-term health issues, government urged
News.content:
The amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health", a group of more than 150 clinicians has warned.

GPs, paediatricians and other specialists said in an open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper that tablets and laptops are being used without a full understanding of their long-term health impacts, including on eye health.

The clinicians said they are prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

The government said it was consulting on screen time guidance for children aged five to 18 but that technology could be a powerful learning tool if used properly.

The group of clinicians said nearly one million children are using screens in most lessons, despite studies suggesting a rise in short-sightedness.

They pointed to an analysis of 276 studies covering 5.4 million participants around the world.

That analysis, they claimed, found a rise in short-sightedness among children and adolescents from around 24% in 1990 to almost 36% by 2023, warning the condition is associated with an increased risk of a range of eye health problems.

Many children now spend longer on screens in the classroom than is recommended in a 24-hour period, the letter said, adding: "As a country, we need to wake up to this now, and start rolling back screen use in schools before the damage compounds further."

One of its signatories was, Dr Becky Foljambe NHS GP and founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme parents had not been given the chance to "opt out" of the "excessive" use of screens in schools, which risks children "just not thriving" in education.

She said an "explosion" in short-sightedness "cannot be put down to genetics alone".

Foljambe said it was a "lazy argument" to advocate for screen use to prepare children for a digital work, adding: "They also need their sleep, their eyesight, they need rest, they need ability to critically think and appraise."

"We are conscious that some of this evidence is still surfacing but the direction of travel is consistent across multiple, independent, and in some cases very large, bodies of research," the letter continued.

It also warned that children with special educational needs are "disproportionately" directed to screen-based learning.

A Department for Education spokesperson said the government was developing new screen-time guidance for children aged five to 18, and will consult on the safety of artificial intelligence and educational technology in schools.

They said: "Used well, technology can be a powerful tool to support learners who need it and free up teachers to deliver the excellent education every child deserves."

It comes after a ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

News.title: Lockerbie bombing suspect seized from Libya in 'cloak and dagger' operation
News.content:
A Lockerbie bombing suspect has claimed he was illegally removed from Libya to stand trial in the United States after "a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the dead of night".

Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has alleged he was abducted by armed men and handed over "hooded and bound" to FBI agents, who had a plane waiting to fly him out of the country.

Al-Marimi, also known as Mas'ud, has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people.

The Libyan argues he was the victim of an unlawful rendition and has asked a judge in Washington DC to throw the case out of court.

In response, the US Department of Justice said, under American law, the manner of his removal should not stop his thrice-postponed trial from finally getting underway in January.

Al-Marimi's version of what happened is detailed for the first time in papers lodged with the court by his legal team.

News.title: I've woken from endometriosis operations to find the surgery hasn't been done
News.content:
Earlier this year Cardiff and Vale health board added their specialist endometriosis centre to their risk register, citing that changes by the BSGE could cause its closure unless changes were made to meet accreditation criteria.

Lutfi Shamsuddin, one of the team of endometriosis surgeons at the centre, told the cross-party meeting the issues centred around allocating dedicated time for a multi-disciplinary team to be involved in complex cases, and ensuring surgeons performed a minimum number of operations per year.

He said limited access to sufficient theatre time meant individual surgeons may be unable to carry out the volume of work required to meet the threshold for BSGE accreditation.

In addition, all accredited centres must have named gynaecologists, specialist nurses, colorectal surgeons, urologists and radiologists with time dedicated in their rota for endometriosis care at least six times a year.

However, he said his own centre relied on "the goodwill" of a radiologist or urologist when required, rather than having those roles planned into the endometriosis service.

It is estimated about one in 10 women have endometriosis. Shamsuddin said about 60% of patients can have their care managed by GPs in the community, however 40% are referred to hospital gynaecology teams.

For cases deemed to be "deep infiltrating endometriosis" which affects other organs such as the bladder and bowel, women in south Wales will be referred to one of two BSGE accredited centres. Cases in north Wales are sent to hospitals in Liverpool or Chester.

Cardiff and Vale also considers referrals from Cwm Taf Morgannwg, while Swansea Bay will receive referrals from Hywel Dda. Aneurin Bevan is understood to be seeking accreditation, and will consider referrals from Powys.

Gynaecologists told the meeting that the acute challenges in Cardiff "could easily be replicated by other centres in Wales".

Shamsuddin warned that losing accreditation would mean patients would be sent for care in England, at a higher cost to NHS Wales.

Abigail Holmes, clinical board director for women and children at the health board, told the meeting they were "working incredibly hard to make sure our service does not collapse".

She said "the only way the service can survive" was for it to be a nationally commissioned service by NHS Wales' joint commissioning committee (JCC).

The meeting heard representations have been made to the JCC by the gynaecology clinical improvement network, which is part of NHS performance and improvement, pressing the need for a pan-Wales approach.

Endometriosis services were discussed in June 2024 as a possible area to be commissioned by the JCC, however as no new investment was made available for 2026-27, national services were not established.

A spokesperson said it recognised the concern, but responsibility currently remains with individual health boards. It said it would continue to work with the Welsh government, health boards and others to support discussions.

The concerns about the future of the centre at Cardiff and Vale health board have prompted a petition, which has already reached more than 11,000 signatures.

David Fluck, executive medical director at the health board, said: "We recognise the importance of BSGE accreditation and are actively working towards reaccreditation when our current accredited period expires.

"We want to reassure patients that our endometriosis service is a core-funded health board service. We are working towards longer-term service sustainability and improvement in line with the women's health plan, with the needs of our patients at the heart of these discussions."

Swansea Bay University Health Board has not placed its service on a risk register, however it too has challenges around theatre capacity, workforce and sustainable multidisciplinary support for complex surgery.

News.title: Chronic UTIs made MP 'feel like a drug user'
News.content:
Warning: This story contains reference to suicide

An MP says she was left "feeling like a drug user" while trying desperately to find pain relief for chronic urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Labour MP Dr Allison Gardner has been living with the "searing pain" of recurrent infections for about 10 years, after first experiencing symptoms with perimenopause.

According to the Chronic Urinary Tract Campaign (CUTIC), more than 1.6 million women in the UK suffer from chronic lower urinary tract symptoms, but there is no official medical definition of the condition.

That is something Gardner is trying to change, with the support of a cross party group of MPs in Parliament.

Gardner told the BBC how a lack of consensus on what constituted a chronic UTI left her feeling sidelined by doctors, who did not always understand the condition and were limited in the length of antibiotic courses they could prescribe.

"You end up hunting for a decent length of antibiotic courses that will give you some relief," she said.

UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra, external. As women have a shorter urethra than men, bacteria are more likely to reach the bladder or kidneys and cause an infection.

Chronic UTIs are infections where symptoms do not go away, and do not clear with a short course of antibiotics. They can also be difficult to diagnose, due to a lower level of bacteria shown in urine samples.

News.title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
News.content:
Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.

Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.

She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals.

It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Kerry is alleged to have carried out research on prominent targets over a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."

She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016.

"We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.

The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".

Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.

In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action."

Reform has in recent months accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".

Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.

There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough.

"We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.

According to data released to the BBC in April, the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.

MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.

In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

News.title: Barbells and beats: This is the new student night out
News.content:
From pecs to decks, students in Nottingham are trying a new workout that turns a gym into a club night.

There's no alcohol involved... just high-energy drinks and pure adrenaline.

Friends Phoebe Constanta and Ella Birkwood, second-year students at Nottingham Trent University, are among those trying the new night that combines pumping iron with pumping tunes.

They said they were looking for "a new gym to try out" and decided to go along to Castle After Dark, a new alcohol-free student event at a city centre gym.

Phoebe, 20, said: "We found it really interesting that it's a night event, but it's not based around alcohol and the club. It's about wellbeing and interacting with people your age."

Ella added: "I'm loving it."

News.title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
News.content:
The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.

Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".

Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.

The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.

Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.

It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.

The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.

Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.

So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.

Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers â about a dozen B-1s from the base â back to their home stations on American soil.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

News.title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths
News.content:
A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025.

Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood."

Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while he carried out his attack.

Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his extremist mindset but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue.

It took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews.

Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue.

"On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men â Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby â lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured.

"What happened that day must be fully understood. So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby.

"This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court."

News.title: Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100
News.content:
World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100.

Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings, arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day.

He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment".

A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met."

Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him.

"I've had a super lifetime," he said.

When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do."

News.title: I’m a travel expert. Here are five cheap European city breaks this autumn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As winter approaches and the days begin to get colder, the autumn ‘shoulder season’ is an ideal time to explore some of Europe’s most beautiful cities at a gentler pace.

During October, visitor numbers tend to fall, allowing travellers to secure significant savings during a much quieter time of year.

“The prices of flights and hotels can drop quite significantly this time of year,” says Laura Carden-Lovell, travel expert and head of operations at travel resale marketplace Transfer Travel.

Nonetheless, she encourages off-peak holidaymakers to factor in additional costs that can quickly mount up.

“It’s important to also think about transportation within the city you want to visit and to find out how much this might cost,” recommends Carden-Lovell. “Walkable cities are great if you're planning on going on a quick city break, as you will be able to see a lot of places for free on foot.

“Car rental prices also typically fall during shoulder season periods compared to peak summer seasons.”

Many hidden gems in Europe, particularly in the Balkans, have seen a surge in interest driven by social media.

“Social media provides travellers with a snapshot of what to see and do in a particular destination, so platforms like TikTok and Instagram can be a great source of inspiration for holiday planning,” says Carden-Lovell.

For anyone who has been patiently waiting for the perfect last-minute city getaway, here are five budget-friendly destinations to consider:

1. Tirana in Albania

“Tirana in Albania is bright, colourful, and is full of history,” says Carden-Lovell.

“Albania is one of the largest, fastest-growing tourism markets in Europe, so its capital Tirana has become increasingly popular.”

The city encompasses many distinct and interesting areas to explore that blend a vibrant modern culture with a unique communist and Ottoman history.

“I would recommend starting exploring at Skanderbeg Square [the main plaza in the centre of Tirana], which costs nothing to explore,” advises Carden-Lovell. “Then head into Blloku, a lively neighbourhood where you can go café hopping.”

open image in gallery Tirana has become increasingly popular ( Alamy/PA )

To get the best picturesque views of Tirana, hop on the Dajti Ekspres, a cable car that takes you directly from the edge of Tirana up to the edge of Dajti Mountain National Park.

“It’s the longest leisure cable car in the Balkans and costs around £15 for a return trip,” says Carden-Lovell. “The national park itself is also completely free to explore.”

2. Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina

“Sarajevo is something a little bit different and is a great affordable option for an autumnal city break,” says Carden-Lovell.

It’s also regarded as an incredibly good city for mooching.

“In the Old Town there are lots of traditional market stalls, lots of local crafts, some really good food shops and some historic mosques to look around,” says Carden-Lovell.

open image in gallery A walking tour can be a great way to explore Sarajevo ( Alamy/PA )

“It has also got the famous Pigeon Square [officially known as Baščaršija Square], which is centred around the iconic wooden Sebilj fountain, so there’s a lot of history packed into this small city.”

A walking tour can be a great way to explore the highlights of the city.

“Most walking tours are free and are a great way to learn about what the city has to offer. You can book a lot of these online,” says Carden-Lovell.

3. Sofia in Bulgaria

“Bulgaria is another great place to visit on a budget,” says Carden-Lovell. “Its capital, Sofia, has got some really nice cathedrals which are very pretty both inside and out.”

The capital of Bulgaria is filled with reminders of its extensive history.

open image in gallery You may get some real steals on flights to Sofia ( Alamy/PA )

“You could join a walking tour to look around some of the Roman ruins or churches, and the historic Roman thermal baths are also worth seeing if you have time,” says Carden-Lovell.

This delightful city has an efficient, affordable public transport network, so it’s very easy to get around.

“Sofia has a really cheap tram system, so you don’t necessarily have to walk everywhere if you don’t want to,” says Carden-Lovell.

4. Tallinn in Estonia

“I’d also recommend visiting Tallinn in Estonia – this one is really popular on TikTok,” says Carden-Lovell.

“Stay in the heart of the old town, which is UNESCO-listed. It has wonderful fairytale streets and colourful buildings.”

After you’ve wandered around the charming old town, check out Telliskivi Creative City, the creative hotspot of Tallinn.

open image in gallery The Patkuli Viewing Platform offers a panoramic view of Tallinn’s medieval Old Town ( Alamy/PA )

“It’s a bit more modern than the old town and there are lots of independent cafes, local artists, street art and bars to explore here,” says Carden-Lovell.

She also suggests relaxing in one of the city’s public saunas.

“Saunas are a big part of the culture in Estonia, so I definitely recommend going to a sauna somewhere, especially in the colder shoulder season,” recommends Carden-Lovell.

5. Riga in Latvia

“Another great city to visit in shoulder season is Riga in Latvia,” says Carden-Lovell. “You can explore the medieval town on foot, and soak up all the history.

“Transportation is also super-cheap and there are loads of independent coffee shops to pop into.”

Make sure you visit St. Peter’s Church, which is one of the most recognisable landmarks in the city.

open image in gallery St. Peter’s Church is one of the most recognisable landmarks in Riga ( Alamy/PA )

“On the observation tower of St. Peter’s Church you get a great 360-degree view of the city,” says Carden-Lovell.

It usually costs around €3 to look inside the church, but if you want to go to the observation tower it costs €9, according to Tripadvisor.

Riga also has a vibrant and growing food scene.

“I would really recommend trying Latvian honey cake here,” recommends Carden-Lovell.

News.title: Second man who chopped down Sycamore Gap tree released from prison
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

The second of two men who chopped down the Sycamore Gap tree has been released from prison.

Daniel Graham, 41, was sentenced to four years and three months for causing criminal damage to the famous tree beside Hadrian’s Wall, Northumberland, when he was jailed in July last year alongside Adam Carruthers.

Carruthers was released in April and now Graham has also been freed on licence after serving 16 months plus the time he served on remand, as first reported in The Mirror.

Mrs Justice Lambert told the pair they would serve 40% of the sentence behind bars, with the remainder being served on licence in the community.

Ministry of Justice spokesman said in a statement on Monday: “The felling of the Sycamore Gap tree was a disgraceful crime.

“Offenders released on licence are subject to strict conditions and can be returned to prison immediately if they breach them.”

Daniel Graham, 41, was sentenced to four years and three months for causing criminal damage to the famous tree beside Hadrian’s Wall, Northumberland, when he was jailed in July last year alongside Adam Carruthers ( PA Archive )

Former friends Graham and Carruthers were convicted of criminal damage to the much-loved tree, which had stood for more than 100 years in a fold in the Northumberland landscape.

They were also convicted of criminal damage to Hadrian’s Wall, caused when the sycamore fell on the ancient monument in September 2023.

During their trial, Newcastle Crown Court heard the two engaged in a “moronic mission” to cut down the landmark, travelling for more than 40 minutes from their homes in Cumbria, then carrying their equipment across pitch-black moorland during a storm in September 2023.

They took a wedge from the tree as a trophy that has never been recovered, and revelled in the media coverage as news of the vandalism caused national and international headlines.

Mrs Justice Lambert was sure that Carruthers cut the tree down while Graham drove him there and filmed it on his phone. Its destruction took less than three minutes.

The Sycamore Gap tree had stood for over a century in a dip next to Hadrian’s Wall in the Northumberland National Park, becoming a sacred place in the region for marriage proposals, scattering of ashes and birthdays.

The tree was a symbol of Northumberland and featured in the Kevin Costner and Morgan Freeman film Robin Hood: Prince Of Thieves.

News.title: UK braced for 70mph winds as Met Office issues weather warning
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A yellow weather warning has been issued by the Met Office as parts of the country are set to face up to 70mph winds on Wednesday.

Parts of the Scottish highlands and Outer Hebrides (Na h-Eileanan Siar) have a yellow warning for wind from 10am to 7pm on Wednesday.

The region could be hit with strong winds that are likely to cause road, air and ferry transport delays. Some short-term loss of power and other services is possible.

The Met Office has forecast gusts of 50 to 60 mph, with some exposed coastal and hilly locations predicted to see gusts of around 70 mph late morning and early afternoon.

Forecasters said the winds will ease over the afternoon and into the weekend.

Heavy rain is forecast to move into northwest Scotland later in the day.

The rest of the UK is set to see sunny spells and patchy cloud, while the north of England and coastal areas are set to see winds.

This is a breaking story – more to follow...

News.title: Black Sea drone attack on two ships condemned as ‘unacceptable’ escalation of Russian war
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has condemned drone attacks on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's coast on Tuesday, calling for those responsible to face justice.

Two ships were hit in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, sinking one and prompting emergency rescues, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

Rescuers pulled all 15 crew from the Ukrainian-owned "Chelsea 3", sailing under Maltese flag, with five treated for minor injuries, Radev confirmed via social media.

"The Black Sea ‌has become ‌another front of ⁠escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable," Ms von der ‌Leyen said ​on X. "Those ‌responsible ⁠should be ⁠held accountable."

open image in gallery Ursula von der Leyen condemned the drone attacks on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's coast on Tuesday, calling for those responsible to face justice. ( AP )

The crew, comprising seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, said three aerial drones struck the vessel's deck and hull.

One person from the sunken vessel was saved, Radev added, without giving details regarding others aboard. The strikes occurred 18 and 17 miles (29 and 27.5 kilometres) from the Bulgarian coast.

During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking Nato and European Union assistance.

While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “logic, as I have already stated, indicates that the result is in favor of the Russian Federation,” Radev said.

open image in gallery Some rescued crew members were taken away in an ambulance. ( Reuters )

The attacks come exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew from a Pulau-flagged vessel.

Ukraine’s military did not conduct any operations near the locations of last week's drone strikes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who pointed the finger at Russia.

A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said.

Russia did not immediately comment on Tuesday's incident.

Radev said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation Tuesday.

Additional reporting by Reuters.

News.title: 90s star admits he hated being recognised for breakout role for years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Devon Sawa admitted that he spent years resenting questions about Casper, the 1995 fantasy film that made him a familiar face to a generation of young cinemagoers.

Casper follows teenager Kat Harvey (Christina Ricci) and her father James (Bill Pullman) as they move into a haunted mansion inhabited by a friendly young ghost and his three mischievous uncles.

Directed by Brad Silberling and written by Sherri Stoner and Deanna Oliver, the movie also stars Cathy Moriarty and Eric Idle, with Sawa appearing as Casper’s human form in the closing sequence.

While Sawa’s appearance was brief, it went on to become one of the film’s most enduring scenes, with Casper asking Kat the now-iconic question: “Can I keep you?”

open image in gallery Devon Sawa and Christina Ricci in ‘Casper' ( Universal Pictures )

Sawa said that it didn’t matter how many projects he ended up doing, he could never escape Casper.

“Doesn’t matter what I do nowadays. It doesn’t matter how cool the project is, I will always have to say, ‘Can I keep you?’ to somebody at some point,” he told People. “There will always be Casper stuff.”

“There was a time in my life I was like, ‘I don’t wanna talk about Casper. How dare you? I am a thespian,’ you know?” he continued. “But I gotta embrace it. It’s why I’m here. It’s what got me here.”

In 2022, Sawa spoke to The Independent about taking on markedly different roles to escape his Casper character.

“I had to smoke pot in movies and I had to be in a hip-hop video. That is what I felt like I had to do to get away from ‘Can I keep you?’,” Sawa laughed and said at the time. “Everybody wanted to hear, ‘Can I keep you?’ It drove me nuts.”

open image in gallery Devon Sawa said he spent years resenting questions about Casper ( Universal Pictures )

Casper grossed $288m worldwide during its original theatrical run in 1995 and returned to 1,100 US cinemas in October 2025 to mark its 30th anniversary, making a further $1.84m.

After Casper, Sawa became a teenage heartthrob, starring alongside Ricci again in the coming-of-age drama Now and Then (1995) and appearing in the family adventure film Wild America (1997) opposite Jonathan Taylor Thomas. He later took on darker roles, playing a punk rocker in SLC Punk! (1998) and a teenager whose hand becomes possessed by the devil in the horror comedy Idle Hands (1999), before starring as Alex Browning in the 2000 supernatural horror film Final Destination.

That same year, he played the obsessive fan in Eminem’s music video for “Stan”, directed by Dr Dre, which became another defining role in his career.

Sawa is lately enjoying a career resurgence. He played a younger man spending a night with Jean Smart’s veteran comedian Deborah Vance in HBO’s Emmy-winning comedy Hacks and portrayed different characters in the horror series Chucky across its run from 2021 to 2024.

open image in gallery Devon Sawa is enjoying a career resurgence with roles in ‘Hacks’ and ‘Chucky’ ( Karen Ballard/HBO Max )

Sawa is now starring in Disney’s supernatural teen drama Coven Academy, in which he plays Mr Cole, a charismatic warlock professor at an elite magical boarding school in New Orleans.

Created by Tim Federle, the show follows teenage witches and their warlock classmates as they navigate supernatural rivalries, forbidden romances and a threat to their city.

Sawa appears alongside Tiffani Thiessen, who plays the school’s head, Miss Graves, and Malina Pauli Weissman, Malachi Barton, and Jordan Leftwich.

“I think it is going to be one of those that hopefully in 20 years, people will be like, ‘Oh, Mr Cole.’ And I won’t be able to shake that either,” he said, meaning Coven Academy, currently streaming on Disney+.

News.title: Surge in Isa millionaires as estimated total reaches 7,730
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The number of Isa millionaires has surged by more than 50% in a year – to reach around 7,730, according to figures obtained by a money app.

Plum obtained the figure, which was rounded to the nearest 10, from HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), following a freedom of information (FOI) request.

HMRC said that, as at April 5 2024, the estimated number of individuals with total Isa holdings of £1 million or more was 7,730.

The figure marks a 52% jump – or 2,660 new members of the Isa millionaires club – compared with 5,070 Isa millionaires that HMRC previously said were recorded by April 2023.

According to HMRC’s latest response to Plum, the average Isa millionaire was sitting on a pot worth around £1,348,000 in April 2024.

The mean average market value of the top 25 Isa millionaire holdings was £11,928,000, rounded to the nearest £1,000.

The majority of Isa millionaires, at around 7,300, were sitting on amounts worth £1,000,000 to £1,999,999 in April 2024.

Meanwhile around 60 had pots worth £4,000,000-plus. The average value of holdings among this group was £7,708,000.
