Sports.title: Viking’s two head coaches on Champions League adventure: ‘For us, it’s the best team in the world’
Sports.content:
“When we recruit players, we say something bold.” The morning’s training session at Lyse Arena has finished and, over lunch, Morten Jensen is explaining how he and Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim have propelled Viking Stavanger from mediocrity to an implausible place among Europe’s elite. “We always tell them: ‘If you come to Viking and play for us, we’re going to be the best coaches you ever had.’”

It is a story more than a decade in the making for Jensen and Aarsheim, who were appointed joint head coaches in November 2020. On Tuesday they will oversee the club’s first home Champions League game, against Bayern Munich, the latest step in a journey that has brought shared success in every sense.

“We were talking on the phone one evening, it must have been around 2012 or 2013,” Aarsheim says, sitting across the table and recalling one of countless conversations between close friends who had first met on the semi-professional scene. “I worked in a bank, he was in the oil and gas industry, we both had local teams part-time. And I remember we said: ‘Hey, we should take a team together one day.’”

They are outwardly an odd couple. Aarsheim had played almost 300 games for Viking during the 1990s and 2000s. He cemented club legend status as a classy midfielder and captain, combining modest league successes with a handful of short Uefa Cup runs before starting to coach at Randaberg. Jensen’s attempts to forge a playing career at Viking had been stalled by injury; he had played college soccer in the United States before landing back in Norway’s lower divisions and managing tiny Havørn.

“He’s always calm, collected, analytical,” says Jensen of Aarsheim, five years his senior at 51. “His personality is not to be stubborn, but find solutions, so he’s always interested and seeking to learn new things. He can explode and be aggressive when he needs to, but it’s at the right time and there needs to be a reason.”

It is Aarsheim’s style to weigh words deliberately, a dash of swearing added for effect. The rhetoric falls to Jensen. “What’s impressive with Morten is how big he thinks and that he dares to tell it out loud,” Aarsheim says. “He talks about winning the league, the Champions League, everything, while I’m thinking: ‘Let’s just get a good team first.’ But it transmits. We put dreams to the players and put that flame inside for them to dream bigger. We don’t want players simply to be satisfied to play here.”

Viking have become an outstanding side themselves under Aarsheim and Jensen. “I think we have shown many players, young and a little bit older, that we see potential and can develop them,” Jensen says.

View image in fullscreen Viking’s CEO, Eirik Bjørnø (left), and the sporting director, Erik Nevland, have helped change the Stavanger club off the pitch. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

Their paths had converged, becoming assistants to the previous Viking head coach, Bjarne Berntsen, before both were due to be interviewed for his replacement. “They gave us the tasks independently,” Jensen remembers. “And we said: ‘What if we just come together? Would you fancy that?’”

“I’m sat there thinking: ‘Jesus, are we really going for this?’” remembers Eirik Bjørnø, who was 29 and newly promoted to Viking’s chief executive officer position, when Aarsheim and Jensen turned up for their interview. The pair had everything planned, down to a 120-page dossier on how their team should play. At Jensen’s instigation, they had also prepared a special slide.

“Suddenly there’s this photo of a bunch of sheep,” Bjørnø says. “They had a big spiel about all the sheep, everyone following the main sheep. Then up pop these two wolves on the photo.” The sheep were, quite plainly, Viking’s competitors. As Jensen tells it: “We said: ‘Are you going to hire these two badass wolves? We’re going to eat up all the sheep.’”

Bjørnø and Viking’s sporting director, the former Manchester United and Fulham striker Erik Nevland, were persuaded. “We were at a place in history where we needed to do something different to become better,” says Nevland, who played for Viking across three stints and scored twice in a Uefa Cup win against Chelsea. “It was kind of: ‘Let’s go for it.’ It just made sense. It was a bit of a gamble but we were in a position where we could do that.”

Joint managers are vanishingly rare at the highest level. “It comes up all the time,” Nevland says. “When I talk to sporting directors from other countries it’s not Viking any more, it’s: ‘Oh, you’re the club with two head coaches.’ It’s something different but it’s a dynamic thing; it’s not like we will necessarily do it this way whenever they move on. It’s special, but why change something that works?”

Their efforts bore spectacular fruit last year, beating a previously imperious Bodø/Glimt to the Eliteserien title. Viking had been a dominant force in Norway during the 1970s but had not been champions since 1991. They had even been relegated in 2017. “In the first two years we learned a lot of things that we’ll never do again,” says Jensen. Finishing 11th in 2022 brought a keener focus on developing local players; those who, like their managers and the similarly homespun Bjørnø‑Nevland double act, know what it entails to represent this mountain-fringed port city in Norway’s south-west.

View image in fullscreen Zlatko Tripic is Viking’s captain and talisman. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

“We’ve done it with a lot of people that care for each other,” Bjørnø says. “We’re trying to enjoy the ride together, and that makes us a lot stronger. When you have success together, it makes such a big difference when you actually feel that you’re friends.”

Nevland sees more benefits from such an intense local flavour. “It just gives us a feeling that everything we do means more,” he says. “The decisions you make are a little bit more thorough because it’s so important for the region and everyone you know. If it’s for my brother or my neighbour, you know all the decisions impact them in some kind of way.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Stavanger, enriched hugely by the discovery of oil 200 miles off shore in 1969, can adore its football team again. “There had been something underlying that was missing for the people here,” Jensen says. “We wanted to play entertaining football and move our people. And maybe that’s the most fun part: it’s not the Champions League or the title win, it’s seeing how many kids are running around with Viking jerseys around the city and in the schools. A decade ago you would only see Manchester United and Liverpool shirts. That’s the one thing I am most proud of.”

A video meeting longer than 10 minutes would risk losing the players’ attention. This one earlier in the day has focused on ways to exploit the high press of SK Brann, fierce rivals from up the coast who Viking must visit for an awkward test four days before facing Bayern. “They killed us last year out there, remember that,” Jensen tells the squad, assembled in a television room next to the changing areas, shortly before it winds up. “We thought we were going to be there, but they ran over us, they challenged us, they had more energy.”

Aarsheim generally oversees Viking’s defensive drills; Jensen focuses on attack. They have shown Viking’s players 10 short clips, selected by a six-strong staff during a coaches’ meeting that started at 8.30am. All bets are off in these highly charged derbies against Brann. The focus is on how Viking can impose their style and minimise the effect of an intense, raucous environment. “We’re going to be better in the first duel, we’re going to be better than them in the second-ball phase, it’s going to be important,” Aarsheim says.

It is raining lightly by the time training starts. Aarsheim clenches his fists on the touchline when one of the crossfield switches Viking have been practising finishes with a tap-in. In the centre circle, Jensen is telling their forwards how to escape the Brann press. Later in the session, they watch side-by-side from seats in the stand.

The tone is businesslike, positive, collaborative. But who gets to play good or bad cop if necessary? “I think we mix it up and sometimes we plan it,” Aarsheim says. “Yeah, we do that as a tool sometimes,” Jensen continues. “But we don’t believe in shouting and yelling at them. It’s not going to make them better footballers. So we try to develop their football intelligence, but also the people. I think our strongest asset is in man-managing.”

View image in fullscreen The English-born New Zealand midfielder Joe Bell (centre) last season helped Viking to a first Eliteserien title since 1991. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

They are often asked what happens if they disagree over, for example, a selection issue. “Then we’ll discuss, loudly sometimes, with the rest of our staff in the coaching room and will both have to defend our choices and reasoning to them,” Jensen says. “We’ll all discuss it until we have an agreement. But 99% of the time we are pretty agreed in terms of who to use in a particular game so it’s very seldom we waste time over that.”

Aarsheim takes over. “I can read Morten in one second. If he really wants something from his stomach then I sense it: ‘OK, let’s go with that.’ It’s never been a problem.”

The fit is instinctive and has become second nature to Viking’s team, too. “You can see the respect and loyalty they have to each other,” says Zlatko Tripic, the long‑serving captain, speaking under calmer skies after the session. “They give a lot of responsibility to the players and let us discuss things. If you ask everyone in the dressing room, there is huge respect for how they deal with things and have given us this comfort and confidence.”

It is a self-assuredness Viking hope can help them trouble Bayern. Nothing appears off limits in Norwegian football’s recent run of fairytales. “This should be the best period of their lives,” says Jensen of a squad that, 72 hours later, heed the warnings and win 2-0 in Bergen. “It’s our job to make them do the best they can,” Aarsheim says. “For us, Viking is Barcelona. The players have to understand that we see Viking as more than a club. In our heads, it’s the best team in the world.”

Sports.title: Coventry land long-awaited home win as Mfuni seals rout of Newcastle
Sports.content:
If ever validation is needed for attack being the best form of defence, Frank Lampard can call this game up on Wyscout. Coventry climbed out of the relegation zone to the heady heights of 14th place after their second successive win showcased the benefits of their manager’s willingness to balance risk with reward.

Jack Rudoni’s early penalty underscored a sense of positivity that was enhanced by an even quicker goal at the start of the second half from Sidiki Cherif and not unduly dimmed by Sven Botman’s howitzer making it 2-1.

Late goals from the substitutes Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni allowed promoted Coventry to pull away from a Newcastle side who, after a strong start to the season, also lost their last away game at Leeds by this scoreline.

Newcastle could have gone fourth in the Premier League with victory but despite missing several chances they could not argue with the defeat. As their manager, Matthias Jaissle, said: “There were elements in both boxes where we need to step up and do better. Those fine margins can make all the difference.”

Even when Botman had reduced the deficit with 20 minutes remaining and Newcastle threatened to take charge, Coventry left two or three players up on the halfway line. It could be perceived as a bold and brave move and Lampard, who wants supporters to be entertained throughout this first season back in the elite since 2000/01, deserves credit. On other days they might come unstuck but here it was a case of he who dares wins.

Not that he was ready to take the plaudits. “It probably means I didn’t manage to scream well enough to tell one or two of them to get back,” the Coventry manager said. “But at times we do certainly leave one or two players up the pitch because I think it will occupy their defenders. And in this [kind of] game of transition, sometimes you can defend with eight players.”

View image in fullscreen Frank Lampard is delighted by Coventry’s win. Photograph: Chris Radburn/Reuters

It was 25 years since John Hartson had last scored a home Premier League goal for Coventry. So there was a momentous feel to the occasion when Rudoni stepped up to take his penalty in the sixth minute.

After three weeks of international football had left Sky Blues fans longing for more following their victory at Nottingham Forest, the atmosphere went up another notch when Lukas Hornicek, hesitant when coming out to palm the ball away from Ephron Mason-Clark, brought Cherif down as they contested the loose ball.

Coventry, for all their summer signings, feel very united after 18 successful months under Lampard, culminating in their Championship triumph. This sense of community was underlined as Rudoni lifted his shirt to show the message “Get well soon Nan” after scoring his penalty.

Rudoni’s grandmother is in hospital after suffering a heart attack. “He’s such a great lad,” Lampard said. “I’ve been there for him. He’s so close with his family. So I’m pleased he could have that moment for them.”

Newcastle had plenty of space and ball just about every time they attacked. But the risk-and-reward strategy meant Coventry were dangerous in the extreme on the transition.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They had Bobby Thomas to thank for denying Newcastle twice shortly before the interval. Firstly the centre-back headed off the line after Jacob Murphy turned Harvey Barnes’s superb cross past Carl Rushworth.

Then when Matias Fernandez-Pardo raced clear, rounded Rushworth and shot goalwards, Thomas had recovered sufficiently to clear. On his first Premier League start since signing from Fenerbahce for £21m in the summer, Cherif deputised for the suspended Taiwo Awoniyi.

The 19-year-old forward is evidently not the finished product but he has raw attributes from which Coventry can build. When Malick Thiaw headed out a long throw-in, Cherif swivelled to strike a crisp drive that swished through four pairs of plum-coloured stockings and beyond Hornicek’s grasping fingers.

View image in fullscreen Sidiki Cherif doubles Coventry’s lead with a rocket. Photograph: Chris Radburn/Reuters

Then Cherif should have made the game safe. Botman miscued Brandon Thomas-Asante’s cross but unmarked from six yards out Cherif clunked his shot wide. That miss briefly appeared crucial as Botman was allowed to wander forwards unchallenged before belting a shot into the top corner of Rushworth’s goal.

Simms made it 3-1 in the 81st minute, however, after the excellent Thomas-Asante nicked the ball on the edge of the area for the striker to shoot home. There was still time for Thomas-Asante to fire against a post before victory was emphatically sealed when Mfuni twinkle-toed his way into the penalty area to strike in left-footed.

Sports.title: Fresh concerns over 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia after missile strikes in Riyadh
Sports.content:
Asia’s elite men’s footballers are on edge as they prepare to travel to conflict-affected Saudi Arabia for January’s Asian Cup.

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport in recent days have killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds.

Five of the continental tournament’s eight venues are in Riyadh, and the hosts will meet Palestine in the tournament opener on 7 January. In total, 31 matches will be held in the capital, including the final on 5 February.

The eastern parts of Saudi Arabia have also been threatened during the Iran-US conflict this year, including the city of Al Khobar in the Persian Gulf which will host seven matches including Australia v Singapore on 9 January.

Consternation is building across Asia about the safety of those travelling to Saudi Arabia. The Japanese Football Association withdrew from the FIFAe video game World Cup due to be held in Saudi Arabia later this month, “following a comprehensive assessment of the current situation in the host country and the available information regarding safety and security”.

A statement from Beau Busch, president of Fifpro Asia/Oceania, said his organisation’s thoughts are with all people impacted by the conflict in the region, but he acknowledged players’ concerns about the coming tournament.

“The safety of players, fans and staff must be the priority and the central consideration in the planning and delivery of the AFC Asian Cup,” he said.

Ange Postecoglou’s Riyadh-based Al-Nassr, who have Cristiano Ronaldo in their ranks, had an Asian Champions League match delayed by an hour on Monday. A Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh.

Busch is also chief executive of Australian players’ union, Professional Footballers Australia. The Socceroos are also due to travel to the region in the November international window for matches against Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman.

“Through the PFA and Fifpro, the global players’ union, we have continued to monitor the situation and engage closely with Football Australia and external experts,” he said.

“Risk assessments are conducted before all camps and will continue to be critically important ahead of the Asian Cup with the ever changing security situation in the region,” he said.

“We will continue working with all stakeholders to ensure player safety, wellbeing and welfare remain the priority ahead of January and the upcoming November friendlies in the region.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Football Desk Australia 

A statement from Football Australia said it was “closely monitoring the situation in Saudi Arabia”, that “the safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and supporters remains paramount” and that risk assessment will be a “key focus” ahead of January.

“We remain in regular contact with Professional Footballers Australia and will continue our dialogue with the Asian Football Confederation regarding its plans for the tournament, guided by the advice of the Australian government,” a spokesperson said.

The Australian government’s Smartraveller website was last updated on Monday. “We continue to advise reconsider your need to travel overall due to the security situation in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

The Asian Football Confederation declined to comment on Tuesday despite the players’ concerns.

The organisation has signed up an array of Saudi Arabia-based sponsors for the tournament including Aramco, Alrajhi Bank and NEOM.

Fifa awarded the right to host the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia three years ago in an abbreviated process that was a surprise to observers.

Sports.title: Burnham’s meeting with City’s al-Mubarak and other contact with club disclosed
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham had a formal meeting with Manchester City’s chair, ­Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at an investment summit, chatted to him in the stands at a star player’s testimonial game and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits.

Details of the prime minister’s contacts with the scandal-hit club and its Abu Dhabi owners during his time as Greater Manchester mayor were released by the combined authority. Burnham old MPs that “all of my dealings” with Manchester City’s owners would be published.

A Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) spokesperson said: “In October 2021 Andy Burnham, in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester, had a formal meeting with Khaldoon al-Mubarak at the UK government’s global investment summit arranged by the Department for International Trade.

“In his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions, including attending Vincent Kompany’s testimonial match in September 2019, where he met the chairman informally in the stands. These have been declared in the usual way.

“Also during his time as mayor, representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would routinely join business delegations as part of mayoral international visits.

“This included representatives from Manchester United travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and Manchester City staff supporting visits to China and Japan.”

City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club maintain their innocence and appealed against the verdict.

Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”. Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment is serious and that, where wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the consequences.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The shadow sports minister, Louie French, said the disclosure of Burnham’s meetings was “far from the full transparency that football fans deserve”. French said: “Burnham cannot hide behind the GMCA – he must take responsibility for this himself. We have been given precious little information about these meetings, what was discussed and what may have been agreed.

“If Burnham has nothing to hide, why is he being so tight-lipped? His bizarre intervention in defence of Man City’s owners has raised serious concerns among fans. It’s time for the prime minister to come clean about his relationship with City Football Group so the public can make their own conclusions.”

Sports.title: Football regulator to recommend cost controls in landmark report with 94% of clubs making loss
Sports.content:
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) is to recommend clubs introduce greater cost controls in its long-awaited State of the Game report, to be published on Tuesday.

The 250-page draft report, with a final version to follow in the spring after an eight-week public consultation beginning this week, will paint a damning picture of the financial state of English men’s football, including the stark finding that 94% of the top 116 clubs are loss-making.

The report will include a series of recommendations for the regulator and clubs to improve sustainability, with the IFR chair, David Kogan, and chief executive, Richard Monks, to provide more details at a press ­conference in Manchester on Tuesday.

That event is likely to be dominated by questions about whether the regulator could force the sale of Manchester City if the mass guilty verdicts of an independent commission are upheld on appeal.

As administrators of an enhanced owners, directors and senior executives test the IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners and executives “where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals”.

The State of the Game report sprung out of the Football Governance Act, which created the IFR, which has taken almost 18 months to produce the most detailed study ever of the football industry and its finances.

EFL clubs have been waiting for the report in the hope that it will give them greater impetus as they continue to negotiate with the Premier League over a new financial ­settlement, although it may not ­necessarily do so given details that may emerge of extravagant and unsustainable spending by many lower-division clubs.

The Premier League has offered a new deal to the EFL worth £180m a year over 10 years, a significant increase from the current £150m figure, but the EFL wants £207m a year and the option to renegotiate after five years.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The EFL has also proposed the creation of a new so-called “lifeboat fund” for clubs in financial distress.

The IFR has powers to impose a settlement on the leagues if they cannot agree themselves. Both sides are likely to seize on elements of the report to bolster their arguments.

Sports.title: Six questions facing England as they target next year’s Women’s World Cup
Sports.content:
England have two jobs to do on Tuesday. The first, avoiding an almighty upset and progressing past Greece on aggregate in their Women’s World Cup playoff to reach a final tie, should be a formality for one of the world’s best-resourced teams. The second, honing their style to play like contenders for next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, is a far trickier but crucial challenge.

Friday’s relatively uninspiring 3-1 first-leg victory in Crete left room for improvement and England had plenty to work on as they trained at St George’s Park on Monday under gloomy-looking clouds. More broadly, over the next eight months, there are six questions facing the European champions.

Can England defend well enough to win a world title?

England had 58 touches in Greece’s box and turned that into three goals, whereas Greece had two touches in England’s box but managed to score and hit the crossbar. Sarina Wiegman said she was not happy her team had conceded. Their defending in June’s 4-0 defeat by Spain also left much to be desired, and it feels as if England are not yet certain about who should partner the captain, Leah Williamson, at centre-back. Wiegman mentioned on Monday that stopping counterattacks was something they must fix – they also struggled defending quick breaks in April 2025 when losing in Belgium. That year, they found a way to win the Euros but they must tighten up defensively if they want to win a first world title in the Maracanã in July.

Why are the forwards not clicking?

England were wasteful in the final third in Greece and not for the first time in recent months. In the World Cup qualifying group England were 1-0 and 2-0 winners over Iceland in games where they should have scored more. A ruthless Spain, the world’s No 1 side, secured 6-1 and 3-0 wins over Iceland. On Monday Wiegman was asked what one element of Friday’s performance she would most like to improve and replied: “The execution in the final third. We got in good positions but then it’s [about] staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time, and deciding what cross or cutback you’re going to choose.”

View image in fullscreen England preparing for the second leg against Greece on Tuesday. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

Who should start in attacking midfield?

For the past year, it has repeatedly felt as if Wiegman does not know who should start as the No 10, with Jess Park, Lucia Kendall and Laura Blindkilde Brown given chances along with Lauren James. Dropping – and recalling – Ella Toone, plus the late addition of Grace Clinton to this squad, adds mystery. Erica Meg Parkinson’s debut on Friday adds another youngster into the mix, and Beth Mead can also play as a 10. Asked on Friday whether the No 10 position had the most question marks surrounding it, Wiegman said: “There’s a lot of competition on that position, where we have a lot of options, which also means, tactically, we can do different things. You can call it a ‘question mark’ – I call it many options.”

What about the right wing?

England’s left-wing starting position feels nailed on for Lauren Hemp, who has been in tremendous form for Manchester City. The right side, however, looks uncertain, not least because Chloe Kelly has been left out. James, England’s most technically gifted player, would be the first choice for many, but she can also play centrally, and the uncapped Freya Godfrey has impressed for London City Lionesses. On Friday, Blindkilde Brown started on the right before being replaced at half-time by Mead. Whoever starts, there are only a handful of matches before next summer to build fluidity.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Laura Blindkilde Brown started at right wing in the first leg against Greece. Photograph: InTime Sports/AP

Which youngsters should be given a chance?

There have been growing calls for the 20-year-old Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter to be handed her debut and the 21-year-old Godfrey could be in line for her debut on Tuesday. If England held a greater first-leg advantage, England would surely be more likely to experiment in Leicester, although Wiegman confirmed she would make changes. Keira Walsh said of her Chelsea teammate Potter that it was “a really good thing that she’s finally being appreciated for how good she is”, and added: “Her intelligence gives me confidence, knowing that she’s perfectly capable of stopping the counter.” There has also been praise for Parkinson, with Esme Morgan, who has played against Parkinson in the NWSL, describing the 18-year-old as a “smart player, really tidy on the ball, with incredibly good movement”. It remains to be seen whether Wiegman will opt for youth or experience as the season progresses.

Do England need clarity over Wiegman’s future?

Off the pitch, the biggest unknown facing England is the future of Wiegman, whose contract runs until the end of the World Cup. There have been no reasons to suspect the squad are unsettled by the uncertainty, but the topic is likely to be mentioned in every England press conference until there is clarity. Walsh said on Monday: “Obviously I’d want her to stay. I think everyone in England would love her to stay. I really appreciate her as a manager but it’s her decision.” Wiegman did not wish to discuss the matter, saying: “We’re only focused on Greece and I don’t want to talk about me.”

Sports.title: Carrick promises Manchester United will ‘come out fighting’ after sticky start
Sports.content:
Manchester United have endured their worst league start in 40 years but Michael Carrick insists he is “loving it”. United arrived in Madrid without Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw, who both picked up knocks in the draw against Tottenham at the weekend, and with the coach admitting that his team are in “a spot”, but he vowed that they would “come out fighting”.

Despite collecting just six points in the Premier League so far, Carrick claimed he did not feel under pressure and backed his captain, Bruno Fernandes, who he revealed was still “carrying something”, to rediscover his form. As he talked about building, there was a reminder too of the fact that Arsenal, the champions, finished “seventh or eighth” in Mikel Arteta’s first two seasons.

“To do something good, to do something great, you have got to be able to do something difficult,” said Carrick, whose side take on Atlético Madrid at the Metropolitano Stadium in the second round of games in the Champions League league phase on Tuesday.

“We hoped for a lot more, we expected a lot more, and we are where we are,” Carrick added. “I was aware that, winning as many as we had [last season], it was going to get more challenging, stickier. I understand that when it is not going well there is a real clamour and a feeling that it’s a disaster, that it’s all wrong and that everything needs to be changed. I kind of get that, but that’s not our mindset and it’s certainly not mine. You have to deal with things and overcome them. That is what I did throughout my career. We have to accept reality but we are building and you can’t lose sight of the journey.”

On the pressure he is under, Carrick said: “It depends on how you define ‘pressure’. There is our own expectation: we know what we want, what we are capable of and that comes from us. I don’t look outside. I don’t feel the pressure from that at all.

“I’m pretty good at shutting off, to be honest; closing off and living a little bit in my bubble. And I think that’s what we do as a group. We look after each other, we all know what’s out there and it’s about managing it, controlling it and staying focused on what we can do. It is about us wanting to succeed, to win. That’s the drive. There is no negativity. It’s also fine lines sometimes. We are hugely confident and we have confidence in each other. I have the utmost confidence in the boys that we can win a lot of games.

“[That’s] because I know them, I know how much they care, I know how strong the group is. And, anyway, you’ve got no choice: that’s why we’re here. We’re here to test ourselves and that’s the opportunity that’s in front of us. If you haven’t got that little bit in you where maybe it’s a little bit crazy times but you actually love the challenge and really want to dig deep to find the answers, then this is not the place for you.”

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick backed Bruno Fernandes to rediscover his form from last season. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

Despite the poor domestic start, which also included exiting the Carabao Cup against Brighton at Old Trafford, Carrick’s side did win their Champions League opener convincingly against Sabah last month.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We need to do something about it now and accept the reality,” Carrick said. “I love this part of it: sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there. You see within the group, the squad, the club, who’s really there and who wants to be there for the long term, [who] is really attached to it and [for whom it] really means something. The supporters are there: they know what they want, they’re desperate for it, and we’ve got to give them something. You have to embrace the challenge. I totally believe that we’ll work through it.”

Asked if he believed that Fernandes could recover his form, Carrick said: “I think it’s pretty obvious to say that he can, yeah. I mean, he’s a top player, Bruno. Sometimes things don’t quite go for you, but he’s done some incredible things for this football club and he will do the same in the future, there’s no doubt about that. I’ve seen that a lot was made of [his fitness]. He was carrying something.

“People don’t maybe realise it, but it happens a lot: players play with issues. I probably played 80% of the games with some sort of issue. It’s not ideal, but it’s manageable. Bruno was able to play the games; that’s the commitment he that he has. He’s pretty much over it. It’s not a major deal, he’s in good shape and he was really bright [in training] this morning, looking forward to the game.”

Sports.title: Hincapié and Zubimendi out after warm-down injuries but Arsenal get Saliba boost
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has admitted frustration after Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi sustained ankle injuries during the warm-down after Arsenal’s win against Leeds on Saturday.

Both are due to have scans on Monday to determine the extent of the damage, although Arteta said they would miss the Champions League game at home to Lille on Tuesday and that Hincapié’s injury “looks a little bit more serious”.

“We had a training session planned after the game for the players,” the manager said. “They didn’t have enough minutes to get everybody in the right rhythm and in two very unfortunate actions, we lost two players.”

Arteta described it as “far from ideal” but dismissed suggestions he would change the post-match routine. “When they have to play, they have no rhythm, and when you ask them to play, they’re going to have no impact in the game,” he said. “That could happen at the Emirates; it never happened in the seven years I was here. It could happen the next day in the training session, and that has happened before, and hopefully it happens now and doesn’t happen again. What can you do? If I knew I had a crystal ball clear, I’d say: ‘Guys, go in the Jacuzzi, everybody, I’ll see you tomorrow.’”

Hincapié and Zubimendi were expected to feature against Lille having not started in the Premier League this season. Arteta seemed disappointed with Illan Meslier and his staff after the reserve goalkeeper gave Hincapié a piggyback off the pitch rather than waiting for a stretcher.

“That’s something else not to discuss here,” he said. “Today they’re going to have a further scan and probably tomorrow we’ll know more and then we’ll see how they’re going to go. Piero’s one looks a little bit more serious, I think, but we’ll have to wait and see.”

There was better news for Arsenal as William Saliba has resumed training on his own as he recovers from a back injury sustained at the World Cup. Arteta would not be drawn on when the France defender could be back and is determined not to rush his recovery. “We’re still talking about weeks,” he said.

Gabriel Magalhães is likely to be partnered by Ezri Konsa again against the Brazil defender’s former club on Tuesday. Gabriel insisted he would not hesitate to take another penalty in a shootout despite missing the crucial spot-kick in the Champions League final against Paris Saint-Germain. “I was sad, and I didn’t want to miss a penalty, but I have learned from this and if I have another opportunity, I will be ready to take it,” he said.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta has challenged Bukayo Saka to score more goals after the forward found the net five times in his past four England appearances and revealed that they had been working on rotating him into more central areas to finish moves.

“He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins,” he said. “That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well. He could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know. When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he … He needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals.”

Sports.title: 'Michael Carrick told me: "Management's not for me"': Nicky Butt's damning revelations on private conversations with Man United boss as he becomes second-favourite for the sack
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United star Nicky Butt has bizarrely claimed Michael Carrick told him 'management's not for me' before he took the job at Old Trafford.

Carrick, 45, returned to the club where he earned legendary status as a player in January in the aftermath of Ruben Amorim's sacking.

Despite a strong end to last season where he guided United to third place, Carrick already finds himself under pressure this time around after picking up six points from six matches.

Such has been his side's difficult start that Carrick is second favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave at 5/2 with Paddy Power, just behind 2/1 favourite Alvaro Arbeloa.

The former midfielder was heavily criticised after United's 1-1 draw with ten-man Tottenham at the weekend, and Butt revealed some of their private conversations about his coaching ambitions.

'I was with Michael before he got the Man United job and spoke to him about management,' Butt told The Good, The Bad & The Football podcast.

Nicky Butt has bizarrely claimed Michael Carrick told him 'management's not for me'

The Man United boss is under pressure after a difficult start to the season for the Red Devils

'He went "no it's not for me, it's too much, my head's all over the show, I'd only do it for the big job. The big job is Man United."

'So because that club's gone to him he's naturally going to go and do it. I think when he's gone through that door, put aside last year because like Scholesy said that's totally different to this year, I think he's realised he's gone into a club that's different to the club that he knew and was at.

'But these lads won't turn down Man United. Ole Gunnar (Solskjaer) wouldn't turn it down.

'Roy Keane might never turn that down. When that club comes calling and you've been at that football club, you don't turn it down.'

The comments from Butt, who didn't play with Carrick at Old Trafford but came across him during his time as a coach at the club, are hugely unhelpful for the United boss.

One win in the first six Premier League games marks United's worst start to a campaign in 40 years, but Carrick came out fighting ahead of Tuesday's Champions League clash at Atletico Madrid.

He said: 'I love this part of sometimes when it's not quite going for you, you see who's really there in the group, players, the squad, who's really there and who wants to be there in the long-term.

'[You see who is] really attached to it and [who it] really means something [to].

'The supporters are there, they’re desperate for it, and we’ve got to give them something.

'I think you’ve got to embrace the challenges to get to where you want to be. We’re right there now in the middle of it, but I totally believe that we’ll work through it.'

Butt added that the opportunity of the United job was too good for Carrick to ever turn down

When questioned on whether he is under pressure, Carrick added: 'It depends how you define pressure. There's our own expectation.

'We know what we're capable of doing as a team, what we expect as a group and as a football club. That comes from us.

'I certainly don't look outside or elsewhere of what it should look like. I know fine well what it should look like. I've felt it and I've felt the ups and I've felt the downs. I don't feel the pressure from that at all.'

After the Atletico match, United face Leeds, Bournemouth, Chelsea and Aston Villa in the Premier League before the November international break, while they also take on Como and Roma in Europe.

Sports.title: How Carlo Ancelotti's son became more than a 'nepo-baby' manager: Lille boss Davide recites Greek mythology, bonded with Duncan Ferguson and was caught in Neymar controversy - now, he is looking to spring a shock on Arsenal
Sports.content:
The apple doesn’t fall far from the tree at casa Ancelotti.

Talk to people in football about Davide, son of Carlo, and their responses might as well be about his dad. Amiable. Unflappable. Intelligent. Tactically flexible. Good man-manager. Tale padre, tale figlio, as they say in Milan. Like father, like son.

Where Davide diverges from Carlo is a lack of experience — more specifically the absence of a trophy cabinet full to the point of bursting.

While Carlo has won the European Cup seven times as a player and manager, the younger Ancelotti will be managing in just his second game in the competition at Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium on Tuesday night. Work to do, too, after his Champions League debut saw his Lille side twice blow a lead at home to Real Betis.

Another point of difference: Davide’s love of all things Ancient Greece. Davide is a prodigious reader of Greek mythology and unafraid to reference tales of Theseus and Odysseus in team talks delivered to what you suspect are a few dozen blank faces in the Lille dressing room.

Asked recently which mythological character he would compare himself to, Ancelotti’s answer was revealing. Heracles would have made sense — a son of Zeus who forges a fearsome reputation of his own — but he opted for Prometheus, a Titan who stole fire from the Gods to gift to humanity.

Carlo Ancelotti's son Davide has become more than a 'nepo-baby' manager (pictured in 2024)

Davide's Lille are flying high in Ligue 1 ahead of Tuesday's Champions League clash at Arsenal

‘I identify with his human side,’ said Davide. ‘He helped humanity a lot after creation. He stole from the Gods and always stayed on humanity’s side. I also believe strongly in human relationships, so I choose him.’

On Tuesday, stealing three points from Mikel Arteta would suffice.

So what can Arsenal fans expect from the ‘nepo baby’ taking his first few steps out of his father’s shadow?

Well, first and foremost, a difficult evening. Lille are second in Ligue 1, just one point off the top and three points ahead of reigning European champions Paris Saint-Germain. Ancelotti held PSG to a draw in his second game in charge, two goals in stoppage time denying his side a famous win.

‘We are playing direct football this season,’ Lille supporter and host of the Simplement Dogues podcast Dimitri Favorinus told Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s very, very modern and a big difference to our previous managers’ style of play.

‘Under them, Lille were a possession-based team, we wanted to have the ball and took our time building attacks. Davide’s team is more pragmatic, more adaptable. When there is a direct solution, the team will take it.’

That directness is helped by an old-school No9. On Tuesday it will be either former Arsenal frontman Olivier Giroud or, more likely, Japan international Ayase Ueda, who has hit the ground running since signing from Feyenoord in August.

The wingers are key to the Ancelotti system, although he will be without the suspended Ethan Mbappe — yes, Kylian’s brother — at the Emirates after he elbowed a Betis player in the face in the previous round. Living up to a famous name in football, it ain’t easy.

Davide is doing an admirable job of it, mind you. Unable to make the grade as a player at AC Milan, he cut his losses early and started coaching aged 23.

He followed his father first to PSG, then Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, Napoli, Everton, back to Real and Brazil. This after obtaining a degree in sports science.

Davide assisted his father at teams including Real Madrid (above), before leaving to take charge of Botafogo in 2025 and later Lille at the start of the summer

Lille will hope to mount a shock at the Emirates as Mikel Arteta's side prepare for a tricky test

At Everton — having been welcomed to the club by Duncan Ferguson via a whisky-fuelled evening at a Liverpool jazz bar where both Ancelottis hummed along to a rendition of Nessun Dorma — Davide did much of the hard work on the training pitch.

He formed close bonds with the players, and impressed staff behind the scenes with a lack of ego. Davide and his wife Ana based their young family on Merseyside and were popular figures in the community.

Things became difficult when the health of Davide’s mother, Luisa, seriously deteriorated. He was forced to miss training sessions as he flew back to visit her in Italy, but his work ethic was beyond reproach. Luisa passed away in May 2021, just before the Ancelottis returned to Madrid.

Lille played Everton in a pre-season friendly this summer and it felt significant that Davide spoke to the club’s in-house TV channel after the game. Many inside and outside Finch Farm would be pleased to see him return to the club as No1 some day.

Despite holding face-to-face talks with Rangers, Davide’s first role sans Carlo came at Brazilian side Botafogo last year. It was to last just five months.

‘He was well-liked and adapted quickly to the country,’ said one source in Brazil. ‘But his training routine with the players was intense and he did not get a lot of good results.’

His time as assistant to the national team brought with it some controversy. He appeared to shake his head in frustration when his father sent for Neymar to come on in a World Cup group-stage win over Scotland.

Slighting Neymar carries a death sentence in Brazil and Ana received some ugly abuse on social media. ‘Do you know that you are interpreting an imagine in a completely wrong way, with no relation to reality, and that because of this I have been receiving countless insults,’ she posted online. ‘We are the ones who want Brazil to win.’

Former Arsenal striker Olivier Giroud could start at No 9 in Lille's pragmatic and adaptable XI

During the Ancelottis' time at Everton, Davide (left) was welcomed to the club by Duncan Ferguson (right) via a whisky-fuelled evening at a Liverpool jazz bar

Another statement from Davide nipped the outcry in the bud. He later earned praise for fronting up and giving the first TV interview after Brazil’s shock elimination by Norway in the last 16. That interview was in Portuguese — one of six languages he speaks fluently.

For now, though, it is back to French. With a Greek twist.

‘He’s a very cultured coach,’ Giroud, who at 40 is three years older than his manager, has said. ‘He always tries to communicate with us through metaphors or stories from Greek mythology, which he’s passionate about. These are powerful messages.

‘He is open-minded. He tries to learn from great quotes and figures and draws inspiration from great coaches.’

Ancelotti cites Pep Guardiola, Jurgen Klopp, Roberto De Zerbi, Diego Simeone and Arrigo Sacchi as influences — as well as former basketball coach Phil Jackson. And papa of course. Ancelotti Snr still calls his son after every game.

Davide has studied Arsenal closely in the past — having come up against them with Real in the 2025 quarter-finals, and used the Gunners’ 0-0 draw at the Etihad as the blueprint for Real’s defensive masterclass at the same ground a year earlier.

Expect Lille to defend in a 4-4-2 or 4-4-1-1 out of possession, be cautious with their pressing and try to hit Arsenal on the counter, with former Spurs man Nabil Bentaleb playing long passes from midfield.

A result at the English champions would be the best achievement of Ancelotti’s fledgling career as his own man.

His appointment at Lille came at the behest of club president Olivier Letang, an old ally of Carlo’s, and led to speculation Davide was a soft touch who Letang could mould to his whim. So far, Davide is doing a good job of proving those doubters wrong.

‘He’s a lovely guy,’ added Favorinus. ‘Very close with his players, and very accessible in the media. He’s young, and has a freshness to him. He’s a new face, using new words. I’m excited to see what he can do in the Champions League.’

Sports.title: Corinthians in MELTDOWN: How ex-Man United star Memphis Depay and new coach Clarence Seedorf are being blamed for 'trying to destroy' the Brazilian giants
Sports.content:
Former Man United star Memphis Depay has been labelled the 'main culprit' for Corinthians' problems with the Brazilian giants fighting to avoid relegation.

Corinthians, whose squad also includes Jesse Lingard, are currently 16th in the Brazilian top flight after a run of eight straight defeats.

The latest defeat came on Sunday with the club losing 4-1 to second-placed Palmeiras.

It was announced ahead of the match that legendary Dutch midfielder Clarence Seedorf will take charge of the team, replacing Fernando Diniz, who was sacked last week.

Seedorf's last coaching role came seven years ago with the Cameroon national team, while he previously had underwhelming spells at his former club AC Milan, as well as Shenzhen FC and Deportivo La Coruna.

According to Brazilian newspaper Globo, Corinthians' owners sought the approval of Depay before confirming Seedorf's appointment as manager.

Memphis Depay has come under fire with Corinthians battling to avoid relegation

The club were reported to have turned to the Dutchman after being rejected by several coaches.

Depay has been one of Corinthians' key players since joining in 2024, with the forward scoring 12 times and providing 10 assists last season as the club won the Copa do Brasil and the Supercopa do Brasil.

The Dutchman, however, has contributed just one goal and two assists in 23 appearances this season, and has been seen by one of the club's former players as one of the main reasons for their struggles.

Craque Neto, who scored 80 goals in 228 games for the club, claimed Depay and the club's ownership are at risk of destroying the club.

'For me, he [Depay] is the biggest incompetent and he'll stay that way,' he said on Radio Craque Neto.

'It's unbelievable what he's doing to Corinthians.

'It hurts, it makes you want to cry to see the prestige he has, he's set the club on fire.'

Depay has been labelled as 'one of the main culprits' and accused of 'trying to destroy' the club by one of its former players

Concerns have also been raised over the appointment of Clarence Seedorf, who will take up his first coaching job in seven years as the club battles to avoid relegation

The former forward turned radio commentator was also critical of the appointment of Seedorf after his long spell out of coaching.

'Now they've hired Clarence Seedorf, who's also Dutch. This company, whose name I don't even know, has hired Seedorf,' he added.

'They're going to destroy Corinthians, they're all opportunists, that's what's happening.

'For me, Memphis is the main culprit for what's currently happening at Corinthians.'

Corinthians director of football Marcelo Paz has defended the appointment of Seedorf, who has joined until the end of the season.

'A name like Seedorf's transcends,' he said.

'It's not that he arrived somehow, it's a name we had access to, we identified him as a leader, a winner, a guy who decided to resume his coaching career.

'He was decided for next year, but the invitation from Corinthians came up and he wanted to come here. It's important for us to have someone who has the desire, and he wanted to.

'We understand that he's a guy who will arrive with a lot of energy, spirit, and knowledge.

'It's very clear to him in our initial conversations what we need at this moment: pragmatism, winning games, scoring points, and finishing the year with a good score, already thinking about next year.'

Seedorf will take charge of his first match when Corinthians host Vitoria next Monday.

With eight matches to go, Corinthians are only out of the relegation zone due to having more wins than Internacional, with both teams having 32 points.

Sports.title: Coventry 4-1 Newcastle: Sky Blues show Man City what a win built on honesty and grit looks like, writes CRAIG HOPE - as Frank Lampard's men secure their first home Premier League win in 25 years against leaderless Magpies
Sports.content:
Now here was a Sky Blue victory built on honesty and decades of endurance - unlike the one at Anfield 24 hours earlier. Coventry City are not Manchester City, be that on the pitch or off it. During the years when Manchester City cheated their way to Premier League and European titles, Coventry were playing in all three divisions of the Football League. Their ascent to the top tier has not been particularly pretty, and neither at times was this first home win of the season. It lacked, for the large part, the silk and skill of Manchester City’s dismantling of Liverpool. But Frank Lampard’s side have different qualities - and Newcastle were no match for that hard work, grit and collective will. This win was pure, never to be contested in a court of law or the court of public opinion. The goal that confirmed elevation to 14th did not arrive until the 81st minute - on the back of a nervy period in which Newcastle threatened to steal a point - but when it did it was entirely deserved. ‘An outstanding performance,’ said Lampard. ‘We were really good at the basics - second balls, duels. Those actions are critical to the modern Premier League. It’s not all pretty patterns. Coventry secured back-to-back Premier League wins by earning a 4-1 victory over Newcastle Sidiki Cherif scored the pick of Coventry's goals with a driven effort from outside the box Matthias Jaissle has seen his Newcastle side concede four times in their last two away games ‘And yes, it's big thing coming out of the bottom three. We have to tap into that in a humble way. It’s the balance of confidence to over confidence now.' It was substitute Ellis Simms who slammed into the bottom corner after an error from Joelinton for 3-1. Then, to give the scoreline a better reflection of Coventry’s superiority, fellow substitute Stephen Mfuni lashed home another belter four minutes from time. ‘You’ve seen the City, now **** off home’ chorused the home crowd, and a chunk of the away end soon heeded that advice. Newcastle have more problems than their opponents right now - a lack of leaders and identity, for starters. This was a second straight 4-1 defeat on the road and, beyond long balls that invariably come back, it is hard to determine what Matthias Jaissle is trying to achieve with his team. PLAYER RATINGS COVENTRY (4-3–2-1): Rushworth 7; Van Ewijk 7, Pinnock 6, Thomas 7, Dasilva 7; Yirenkyi 7 (Onyeka 78, 6), Grimes 7 (Torp 83), Rudoni 7 (Mfuni 83, 7); Cherif 8 (Simms 78, 7), Mason-Clark 6 (Sakamoto 61, 6); Thomas-Asante 7 Subs: Bentley, Latibeaudiere, Hamer, Gboho Manager: Frank Lampard 8 NEWCASTLE (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 4; Miley 5 (Dedic 59, 5), Thiaw 5, Botman 6, Hall5; Gonzalez 5, Willock 5 (Joelinton 59, 4); Murphy 4 (Toure 59, 5), Wissa 4 (Osula 78), Barnes 5; Fernandez-Pardo 3 Subs: Pope, Schar, Bamba, Steur, Burn Manager: Matthias Jaissle 4 Referee: John Brooks 7 ‘We can only apologise to the fans that took the journey,’ said Jaissle. ‘We need to analysis it clearly, especially in the box, at both ends. The desire and hunger to score, to finish the attacks, that was missing. We conceded the goals too easily and didn’t finish our chances.’ Even before kick-off, this did not feel like a stadium that had witnessed two defeats without a goal on their team’s return to the Premier League, such was the noise. The 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest before the break had clearly restored belief. But there is nothing quite like a home goal to raise spirits - and the volume - still further. Twenty-five years on from Coventry’s last, and just six minutes in, Jack Rudoni brought relief to that particular quest. The midfielder had Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek to thank for the opportunity to score his first Premier League goal from the penalty spot. The Czech looked like he was gathering a bar of soap when Ephron Mason-Clark’s low shot ran through bodies and into - and out of - his grasp. Hornicek should have cut his losses but instead chased redemption. His team were soon chasing the game when his recovery dive sent Sidiki Cherif skyward at the expense of the spot-kick. Coventry missed a couple of chances to extend their advantage - a lack of composure was their undoing - but that was also the case at the other end, and preservation of the lead was always Lampard’s chief concern. Jack Rudoni opened the scoring for Coventry from the penalty spot in the early stages Jaissle’s concern should be his £51million forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who does not look or play yet like a Premier League striker Sven Botman had given Newcastle some barely deserved hope with a rocket into the top corner Ellis Simms, pictured, and Stephen Mfuni came off the bench to score and seal Coventry's win Jaissle’s concern, meanwhile, should be his £51million forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo. The young Belgian wants to play as striker and he used that desire as part of his bargaining when agreeing to join from Lille last month. Except, he does not look nor play like a Premier League centre-forward. At least not yet. And so, in the short term, the head coach needs to ignore the wishes of the player and pick a better option in such a key position. The second half began as badly as the first for Jaissle’s side. Milan van Ewijk’s long throw-in was headed only as far as the edge of the penalty area by defender Malick Thiaw and, when the efforts to close down Cherif were slow, the Guinean teenager very quickly blasted back into the bottom corner. Sven Botman gave Newcastle some barely warranted hope with a 20-yard rocket into the top corner, but it was short-lived. Coventry’s stay in the Premier League, you suspect, might not be.’
