World.title: Tinubu’s Achievements: Delta Deputy Gov, Diaspora Nigerians Disagree in Atlanta
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Delta State Deputy Governor, Sir Monday Onyeme, has clashed with Nigerian community leaders in Atlanta, United States, over President Bola Tinubu’s performance, with the deputy governor defending the administration’s economic reforms and infrastructure projects while his audience challenged their impact on ordinary Nigerians.

The disagreement, which occurred during Onyeme’s recent working visit to Georgia, exposed a sharp divide over whether the federal government’s policies are delivering the promised transformation or worsening the economic hardship confronting millions of citizens.

While Onyeme described Tinubu as a once-in-a-generation leader whose decisions were repositioning Nigeria for sustainable growth, some members of the audience cited the high cost of living, persistent insecurity, deteriorating highways and alleged irregularities in public procurement as evidence that the administration had fallen short of expectations.

The exchanges became particularly pointed when community leaders Raymond Ekuerhare and Chief Emeka Chimekwene rejected the deputy governor’s glowing assessment, insisting that Nigerians abroad were not relying on social media alone to evaluate developments at home.

Onyeme had accused Nigerians of using social media to spread misinformation, disinformation and half-truths about the achievements of Tinubu’s administration and the government of Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori.

He argued that such narratives were damaging Nigeria’s international image and preventing citizens abroad from appreciating what he described as the transformative impact of the President’s eight-point Renewed Hope Agenda.

“I have been around for a while, both as a private citizen and now in government. There is no Nigerian leader that even comes close to President Tinubu in terms of achievement, in making tough choices that will set the country apart, now and in the near future,” he said.

The deputy governor, who identified himself as a professional accountant, maintained that the administration’s policies were laying the foundation for long-term economic stability, improved governance and accelerated development.

But Ekuerhare, a business and community leader, who said he travelled to Nigeria almost every other month, disputed that assessment, pointing to the gap between government claims and the realities confronting citizens.

He specifically cited the condition of the Benin-Asaba, Ore-Benin, Benin-Warri and Warri-Ughelli-Bomadi roads, arguing that the state of the highways undermined claims of impressive infrastructure development.

“The eight-point Renewed Hope Agenda is only good on paper but not affecting people’s lives for good,” he said.

Ekuerhare also questioned the administration’s record on security, arguing that insecurity and kidnappings continued to undermine the freedom of movement and economic activities of Nigerians.

Chimekwene, another Delta State community leader in Atlanta, raised concerns over public procurement, particularly contracts he alleged had been awarded without competitive bidding to the Chagoury Group.

He argued that allegations of non-competitive contract awards raised questions about transparency and accountability, insisting that a government seeking to transform the country must demonstrate that public resources are being managed responsibly.

“We don’t depend on social media for serious matters of the state. We have family members at home; their lives and living conditions have not improved under President Tinubu,” he said.

Chimekwene also challenged Onyeme’s economic assessment, arguing that the hardship experienced by households made it difficult to describe the administration’s record as transformational.

He, however, expressed greater confidence in Onyeme’s account of the impact of Governor Oborevwori’s MORE Agenda in Delta State, saying members of the Diaspora could more readily verify some of the state government’s projects during visits home.

Responding to the criticisms, Onyeme insisted that the federal government’s policies had created the conditions enabling state and local governments to pursue development programmes more effectively.

He placed particular emphasis on local government autonomy, describing the Supreme Court’s July 2024 judgment on the financial independence of local councils as a landmark step towards strengthening grassroots governance and advancing true federalism.

The judgment followed the Federal Government’s legal action seeking to protect local governments’ constitutional rights, including their access to funds without unlawful interference by state governments.

Onyeme said successive administrations had failed to fully realise local government autonomy despite reforms introduced in 1976 under the military administration of General Murtala Muhammed and continued under General Olusegun Obasanjo.

He argued that the Tinubu administration had placed the issue at the centre of governance, enabling the country’s 774 local government areas to take greater responsibility for services directly affecting citizens.

According to him, local councils are now better positioned to undertake projects in road construction, primary healthcare, community education, sanitation, waste management and local security.

He also defended the removal of the petrol subsidy, foreign exchange reforms, tax changes and electricity sector reforms, arguing that the measures were designed to eliminate structural weaknesses, improve government revenue and create a more sustainable economic environment.

The deputy governor maintained that the reforms were beginning to produce results, pointing to economic growth in 2025 and 2026, increased emphasis on non-oil activities and improved investor confidence.

However, he acknowledged that the policies had imposed difficulties on households, insisting that the sacrifices would eventually yield long-term benefits.

Infrastructure development became another major point of contention, with Onyeme citing the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano dual carriageway and the proposed Akwanga-Bauchi-Gombe-Biu-Maiduguri Superhighway as evidence of the administration’s development ambitions.

The projects are intended to improve connectivity, facilitate trade and strengthen economic links between different parts of the country.

But Chimekwene challenged the presentation of the projects as major achievements, arguing that many remained at relatively early stages of completion.

Onyeme acknowledged concerns over the pace of construction, attributing delays in some cases to the technology being deployed for road development.

He nevertheless maintained that the projects represented an important investment in Nigeria’s long-term transport infrastructure.

The disagreement in Atlanta comes against the backdrop of far-reaching economic changes introduced by Tinubu since assuming office in May 2023.

The removal of the petrol subsidy and the unification of the foreign exchange market were among the administration’s earliest major policy decisions, intended to reduce fiscal pressures, improve market efficiency and attract investment.

However, the reforms also contributed to immediate cost pressures, particularly through higher transport and production expenses, while the depreciation of the naira and increases in food prices intensified concerns about household purchasing power.

The administration has subsequently pursued tax reforms, investment initiatives and infrastructure projects as part of its broader economic agenda. Yet the extent to which the resulting growth and government revenue gains translate into better living conditions remains central to the debate over its performance.

Insecurity, including kidnapping and attacks in parts of the country, has also continued to feature prominently in public criticism of government performance.

Against this background, the Atlanta encounter illustrated the difficulty of reconciling the government’s emphasis on macroeconomic reforms and long-term infrastructure investment with citizens’ demands for immediate relief, safer communities and functioning public infrastructure.

Onyeme urged Nigerians in the Diaspora to help correct what he considered misleading narratives about the country and to project Nigeria positively through their words and actions.

The meeting was hosted by Chief Collins Odinjor and his wife, Alero, with support from Mr Kingsley Dike and his wife, Tilda, and Mr Frederick Ogodo and his wife, Henrietta.

Others present included former Super Eagles coach Samson Siasia and his wife, Eunice; Professor Nuru Akinyemi of Kennesaw State University; Dr Dave Ogwu; Mr Felix Ochei; Pastor Orlando Scott; Attorney Ani Alumona Oluku; Mr Henry Nketeh; Ekuerhare; Chimekwene; Mr Ken Eze; and Mrs Ndidi Ogwu, who moderated the question-and-answer session.

World.title: Stop Dividing South-east for Selfish Political Interests, Ebonyi Group Tackles Umahi
World.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

The Association of Ebonyi Indigenes Socio-Cultural in the Diaspora (AEISCID) has warned the Minister of Works, David Umahi, to stop dividing the South-east for selfish political interests.

The group was reacting to a viral video in which Umahi said Ebonyi leaders were being attacked for refusing to support the presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi in the 2027 presidential election.

Umahi had in the video said: “You are calling out people like us because we said we will not vote for him and we tell our people not to vote for him, and you are insulting us,” while challenging Obi to mention any Ebonyi indigene he appointed when he was governor of Anambra State.

The minister also waded into Ebonyi State’s 2027 governorship zoning debate, saying: “Just like it’s not the turn of the South East and Peter Obi to be president of Nigeria, it’s not the turn of Ebonyi South to be governor of Ebonyi State.”

He added he would meet with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate, Ifeanyi Odii, to ask him to step down.

However, the President AEISCID, Paschal Oluchukwu, in a statement issued yesterday described Umahi’s comments as “shameful, uncivil, uncouth and unbecoming” of a former governor and serving minister.

The group said Umahi had appointed himself an “unofficial spokesperson” of Ndi Igbo and accused him of attempting to pitch Ebonyi people against Anambra and the rest of the Igbo nation.

Oluchukwu noted: “We wish to vehemently condemn these statements as they are shameful, uncivil, uncouth and terribly unbecoming of a leader at the level of Umahi.”

The group noted that it was troubled by what it called Umahi’s “senseless and relentless attacks” on Obi and other Igbo politicians for exercising their constitutional right to contest elections.

The Diaspora body also accused Umahi of hypocrisy on the zoning principle, recalling that he refused to step down in 2015 when his predecessor, Martin Elechi, anointed Prof. Onyebuchi Chukwu from the same Ebonyi South zone.

According to the group, Umahi’s current zoning advocacy is a ploy to perpetuate his political influence in Ebonyi through Governor Francis Nwifuru, whom it described as his puppet.

It alleged that Umahi single-handedly nominated his son, Osborn Umahi, as Chairman of Ohaozara LGA and is positioning him for higher offices, including the governorship in 2039.

The group urged the PDP governorship candidate, Odii to ignore Umahi’s call to step down and continue to offer alternative ideas to Ebonyians, insisting that “Ebonyi voters, not Umahi, will decide the 2027 election.”

It claimed that the Nwifuru administration has recorded no significant development project in nearly four years due to godfatherism.

To this end, the group gave Umahi 72 hours to recant his divisive statements and apologise to Obi, Odii, Ebonyi people and Ndigbo at large, or face legal action.

The group also urged President Bola Tinubu to call the minister to order, saying his role as a member of the Federal Executive Council should be to preach peace and unity, not incite hate.

Elections Campaign ‘ll Be Issue-based, Says APC’s PCC Women Directorate

Jonathan Eze

The Director of Women Mobilisation of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), Dr Betta Edu, yesterday declared that the 2027 presidential campaign would be issue-based, expressing confidence that the achievements of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration will provide compelling evidence for his re-election.

Edu, who stated that in Abuja, said Nigerian women were increasingly recognising the direction of the Tinubu administration and had intensified grassroots mobilisation across communities, households, and voting constituencies to secure another mandate for the president and sustain the implementation of his policies and development programmes.

She maintained that the APC would approach the forthcoming election with a clear message anchored on its record in government, ongoing infrastructure projects, economic reforms, educational opportunities, and initiatives designed to improve the livelihoods of Nigerians.

According to her, the party has substantial achievements to present to the electorate and would campaign on policies, programmes, and measurable results rather than empty promises or personality-driven rhetoric.

Edu expressed profound gratitude to President Tinubu for his leadership and commitment to the Renewed Hope Agenda, as well as the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, for her consistent advocacy for women, families, and national development.

She also appreciated Vice President Kashim Shettima and his wife, Nana Shettima; the Senate President and his wife; the Speaker of the House of Representatives and his wife; the Director-General of the Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari; the Secretary of the APC Presidential Campaign Council; and Chairman of the Progressives Governors Forum, Governor Hope Uzodinma; APC governors and other party leaders, governors, stakeholders, and members of the APC leadership for their contributions to strengthen the women’s grassroots mobilisation and advance the administration’s agenda.

The APC PCC women mobilisation director also expressed appreciation to the various women’s groups, associations, support organisations, and political structures within the party for their unwavering commitment, solidarity, and continued support for the administration and the party’s mobilisation efforts.

She acknowledged the contributions of wives of governors, women leaders, and grassroots organisers whose activities across states, local government areas, and communities have continued to strengthen the APC’s engagement with women and expand its political reach.

Edu said their commitment, organisational capacity, and willingness to work collectively would remain indispensable to the party’s preparations for the 2027 general election.

According to her, women remain a formidable force in Nigeria’s electoral process, not only because of their numerical strength but also because of their influence within families, community associations, markets, professional bodies and local political structures.

She stressed that the APC’s mobilisation strategy would go beyond rallies and public declarations to sustained engagement, political education, and direct communication with voters, as well as election-day voters’ sensitisation and mobilisation.

Edu said the objective was to ensure that Nigerians understood the administration’s policies, assessed their impact on their lives, and made informed decisions about the country’s future.

The director identified the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) as one of the significant initiatives through which the Tinubu administration was expanding access to higher education and creating opportunities for young Nigerians to pursue their academic ambitions.

She noted that the student loan programme was helping to address financial barriers that could prevent eligible students from accessing or completing tertiary education while offering families additional support in meeting the cost of education.

According to her, “NELFUND reflects the administration’s recognition that investment in education is essential to human capital development, economic productivity, and the long-term prosperity of the country.”

She said the programme, alongside ongoing infrastructure development, economic reforms, and other sectoral interventions, formed part of the administration’s record that the APC would present to Nigerians during the election campaign.

Edu further maintained that the party would communicate these achievements in clear and practical terms, enabling citizens to understand the policies, opportunities, and reforms available to them.

She added that the 2027 election would provide an opportunity for Nigerians to evaluate the administration, of which we can proudly say that the president has performed well. “The reforms were demanding, but now is time for prosperity,” she said.

For the Women Mobilisation Directorate, she said the immediate priority was to consolidate existing structures, strengthen coordination among women’s groups, and ensure that the party’s message reached voters in both rural and urban communities.

She urged APC women to remain united, organised and committed to the party’s objectives, stressing that their collective contributions would be vital to presenting the administration’s achievements to Nigerians and consolidating support ahead of the 2027 general election.

The group noted that Umahi failed to deliver his own polling unit and ward for the APC in the 2023 presidential election and lost his senatorial bid even in his Uburu village.

World.title: Shettima to North: You Have Nothing to Fear over Tinubu’s Second Term
World.content:
Idris says Tinubu’s reforms yielding results despite high living costs

Lists falling inflation, $55bn reserves, student loans as key achievements

•Science minister defends reforms, seeks president’s re-election

Iyobosa Uwugiaren, Deji Elumoye in Abuja and Emmanuel Ugwu-Nwogo in Enugu

Vice President Kashim Shettima yesterday mounted a fresh campaign to win the North over for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, assuring the region that it had nothing to fear from another four years of the administration and insisting that it stood to benefit even more if the president secured a second term in 2027.



With the battle for 2027 gathering momentum, Shettima urged northern political leaders and citizens to close ranks behind Tinubu, arguing that the region had already benefited from the administration’s appointments, agricultural interventions and infrastructure projects.

The vice president spoke at the State House, Abuja, when he received a delegation of Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A), a northern-based political group campaigning for Tinubu’s re-election, urging the region not to view another Tinubu presidency with apprehension but as an opportunity to consolidate the gains he said the region had recorded under the administration.



Also, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, yesterday said Nigeria’s economic reforms under Tinubu were beginning to produce measurable results, citing declining inflation, rising foreign exchange reserves, improved oil production and increased investment in infrastructure and social programmes.



In the same vein, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh (SAN) has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years in Aso Rock to complete his ‘bold’ economic reforms.



Shettima urged political leaders and citizens across the region to unite behind the administration, arguing that the North had benefited from its policies, appointments and development projects and stood to gain more if Tinubu secured another term.



According to him, the administration’s commitment to the region’s development and the welfare of its people should encourage northern stakeholders to support its continuation beyond 2027.



“Let’s unite as a people and work for the development of our region and the progress of our people through the re-election of this administration. We are benefiting and we stand to benefit more from this government in many ways,” the vice president said.



He cited the Bank of Agriculture’s disbursement of N450 billion to 700,000 smallholder farmers across the country, saying about 70 per cent of the beneficiaries were from the North.



“The Bank of Agriculture has disbursed N450 billion to 700,000 smallholder farmers in Nigeria and about 70 per cent of the beneficiaries are from the North,” he said.



Shettima also pointed to major infrastructure projects being undertaken by the administration, assuring the delegation that Tinubu remained committed to the region.



“The present administration is working towards completing landmark and groundbreaking projects in parts of the country. I can assure you that the president loves the North and the president will work for the North,” he said.



The vice president thanked the organisation for its support for Tinubu and urged its members to intensify mobilisation across wards, communities and local government areas in the region ahead of the 2027 presidential election.



Earlier, the Director General of Arewa for Asiwaju and former Jigawa State Governor, Abubakar Badaru, said the group would sustain its mobilisation efforts until Tinubu was re-elected.



Badaru disclosed that the organisation planned to engage religious leaders, including Muslim and Christian clerics, as well as other prominent Nigerians, to drum up support for the Tinubu-Shettima ticket.



“On discussions with the high profile, we have gone far. We have met them several times and the BoT is meeting them again to consolidate our gains and to tell them why there is a need to support this ticket,” he said.



He added that the group was also working with the Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), while concentrating on grassroots mobilisation to complement the council’s broader activities.



Also speaking, Chairman of the organisation’s Board of Trustees (BoT) and former Kano State Governor, Ibrahim Shekarau, said the group, which supported Tinubu’s election in 2023, was determined to repeat the feat in 2027.



Shekarau said the organisation had been engaging northern governors and other stakeholders to compare notes and identify areas of collaboration towards securing the president’s re-election.



He disclosed that the group had concluded plans to establish a fully fledged secretariat to coordinate its activities, with offices for directors and state coordinators who would collate reports, analyse developments and issue directives to members.



The former governor also formally invited Shettima to inaugurate the organisation’s office complex on Saturday, October 17, 2026.



Among those present at the meeting were former Plateau State governors Joshua Dariye and Simon Lalong; former Taraba State Governor, Jolly Nyame; former Kogi State Governor, Yahaya Bello; former Katsina State Governor Ibrahim Shema; former Bauchi State Governor Isa Yuguda; the President’s Special Adviser on Policy and Coordination, Hadiza Bala Usman; and Chairman of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, Buba Marwa.

Idris Lists Tinubu’s Achievements, Says Reforms Yielding Results



Also yesterday, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, said Nigeria’s economic reforms under Tinubu were beginning to produce measurable results, citing declining inflation, rising foreign exchange reserves, improved oil production and increased investment in infrastructure and social programmes.



However, Idris acknowledged that many Nigerian households continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures, stressing that the federal government’s priority is to ensure that improvements in the country’s economic indicators translate into more affordable essential goods and services, increased purchasing power and better living conditions.



Also, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh (SAN) has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years in Aso Rock to complete his ‘bold’ economic reforms.



Idris spoke during a media chat with senior editors at Radio House, Abuja, where he outlined the administration’s economic performance, security interventions, social investments and implementation of its Renewed Hope Agenda.



He maintained that the government’s economic reforms were strengthening the country’s fundamentals and restoring investor confidence, while conceding that more work was required to ensure that the benefits reached households across the country.



“Our task now is to ensure that this clear macroeconomic recovery is felt even more widely in the lives and households of Nigerians,” the minister said.

He identified food prices, market transactions, transport and household spending as areas where citizens needed to experience tangible improvements.

The minister recalled that the economy is projected to grow above 4 per cent, saying the nation’s economy was on course to grow by more than 4 per cent in 2026, while the country’s external position and foreign exchange market had improved.



He reiterated that Nigeria recorded a current account surplus of $12 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, stressing that inflation declined from approximately 27 per cent in January 2025 to around 15 per cent at the time of the briefing.

He described the development as an encouraging sign for household budgets but said the government’s ultimate objective remained to bring inflation into single digits.



According to him, external reserves exceeded $54 billion in September, representing their highest level in almost two decades, adding that the foreign exchange market had stabilised sufficiently to enable businesses and investors to make longer-term plans with greater confidence.



He explained that recent economic reporting has also documented the increase in Nigeria’s external reserves. Recent reports indicate that reserves stood at approximately $55.07 billion on October 8, citing Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) data.



The World Bank, meanwhile, projected average annual economic growth of 4.4 per cent through 2028, subject to continued reforms and improvements in public service delivery. The minister further disclosed that Nigeria earned more than $6 billion from non-oil exports in 2025, describing the figure as the highest in the country’s history.



He said the earnings supported businesses and entrepreneurs across agriculture, mining, petrochemicals, manufacturing, processing, transportation and logistics.



Idris argued that the combination of stronger external reserves, increased non-oil exports, improved oil production and a more stable foreign exchange market was creating opportunities for domestic investment and economic diversification.



Nevertheless, he emphasised that improved macroeconomic indicators must be accompanied by practical benefits for Nigerians, particularly those struggling with food, transportation, energy and other household expenses.



The minister identified infrastructure development as one of the principal channels through which the administration intends to translate economic recovery into employment and increased economic activity.



He explained that road construction projects generate income for contractors, suppliers, engineers, artisans, transport operators and food vendors, while completed roads improve connectivity, facilitate the movement of agricultural produce and increase access to markets.



According to Idris, the administration’s four legacy projects collectively cover approximately 3,000 kilometres across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones. He said the projects formed part of a wider portfolio of road, rail, port, electricity, healthcare and education investments being implemented across the country.

The minister also highlighted the recently approved highway project valued at approximately N1.5 trillion in Niger State, describing it as an investment expected to improve connectivity along an important agricultural and commercial corridor. He maintained that the projects were intended not only to improve transportation but also to stimulate economic activity in communities along their routes.



The expected benefits, he said, include faster transportation of goods, improved access to commercial centres, increased business opportunities and stronger links between rural producers and urban markets.



Speaking on food security in the country, the minister said Tinubu places food security at the centre of national economic policy, with government interventions focused on increasing domestic agricultural production and improving farmers’ incomes.



He listed mechanisation, improved access to agricultural inputs, irrigation development and agricultural financing among the measures being pursued to strengthen the sector.



According to the minister, these interventions are designed to increase food supplies, improve productivity and make food more affordable for Nigerian households. He argued that higher agricultural output would also strengthen rural economies by supporting farmers, processors, transporters and other businesses involved in the food supply chain.



The minister’s remarks come as the administration faces pressure to demonstrate that economic stabilisation is producing meaningful improvements in the affordability of basic commodities.



Although Idris described falling inflation as encouraging, he acknowledged that the government still needed to ensure that the improvement was reflected in the daily experiences of ordinary Nigerians.

The minister also outlined investments in healthcare and education, describing them as central to the administration’s efforts to improve living standards and expand access to essential services.



He disclosed that the federal government had recently commissioned two additional cancer treatment centres, bringing the number commissioned under the initiative to five following the earlier commissioning of three.



The administration, he said, was working towards making a total of 10 cancer treatment centres available to Nigerians.

Idris added that the government was also pursuing the revitalisation of primary healthcare facilities to expand access to medical services and strengthen the national health system.



On education, he said the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) had supported more than 1.6 million students, with over N192 billion paid in institutional fees and approximately N180 billion provided as upkeep allowances.



The programme, according to the minister, is intended to reduce the financial burden of tertiary education on students, parents and guardians. Idris said the intervention was part of the government’s broader social investment programme, which seeks to reduce financial barriers to education and support access to higher learning.



He also highlighted the Three Million Technical Talent programme, which aims to expand young Nigerians’ access to digital skills in software development, data science, cybersecurity and other emerging technologies.



The minister said investment in technical training, innovation and digital capabilities was intended to prepare young people for employment opportunities while supporting the country’s wider economic diversification objectives.



He added that renewed attention to domestic refining, solid minerals, industrial production and innovation was expected to support sustainable employment and reduce dependence on traditional sources of foreign exchange.



Idris said the Presidential Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and Electric Vehicle Initiative had attracted approximately $2.5 billion in private investment, alongside about N250 billion in government funding and commitments.



He disclosed that more than 120,000 vehicles had been converted under the initiative, while the country had established more than 400 certified conversion centres. According to him, Nigeria also had more than 90 refuelling stations, with approximately 180 additional stations under development.

Idris said the growing network of conversion centres and refuelling infrastructure was generating business opportunities and employment in host communities.



He also linked the programme to the administration’s wider response to rising energy costs, arguing that affordable alternatives and stronger domestic production could contribute to easing pressure on households and businesses.



The minister disclosed that the Federal Government had issued a N758 billion bond to settle pension arrears dating back as far as 2007, with almost one million pensioners expected to benefit.



He described the intervention as part of the administration’s effort to address inherited financial obligations and improve the welfare of retired workers.

Idris also announced that the government had issued N1.2 trillion in bonds to settle inherited debts owed to electricity generation and gas companies. He said clearing these obligations would help lay the foundation for new investments in the power sector, where outstanding payments and financing constraints have remained significant concerns.



The minister further disclosed that the National Social Register was directing support to more than 10 million households, while the Consumer Credit Corporation was helping working Nigerians spread the cost of essential purchases.



On national security, Idris said the protection of lives and property remained the first responsibility of the government and a central priority He said the federal government had strengthened the operational capabilities of the Armed Forces, intelligence services and other security agencies through improved coordination, equipment, logistics and support for personnel deployed to the frontlines.



According to the minister, security operations across several theatres had recorded successes against terrorists, bandits, kidnappers and other criminal groups. He said terrorist commanders and criminal kingpins had been neutralised, insurgent networks disrupted, hostages rescued and criminal enclaves dismantled.



Idris also highlighted operations in the Niger Delta targeting crude oil theft, illegal refining and pipeline vandalism, saying the measures had contributed to improved oil production and the protection of national revenue.



He said the government was encouraged by efforts to restore access to communities and economic activities in areas affected by insecurity.

Addressing fuel prices, the minister acknowledged that rising energy costs were placing pressure on households, businesses and the wider economy. He said governments across the world were adopting different measures to protect their economies and cushion the effects of higher energy costs on citizens.

Idris maintained that Tinubu remained committed to the economic reforms introduced by his administration while recognising the need to protect public welfare.



According to him, the government’s approach includes expanding affordable energy alternatives, strengthening domestic production and creating conditions for sustainable reductions in the cost of living.

Science Minister: President Deserves Second Term



Meanwhile, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Udeh, has defended Tinubu’s quest for a second term in office, maintaining that the president deserves to stay for another four years to complete his economic reforms.



Udeh, who is a member of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, while appearing on Arise News Prime Time, insisted that Tinubu has the capability to lead Nigeria out of the woods.



He backed the position that the presidency remains in the southern part of the country till 203, in line with power rotation arrangement.

Alluding to the challenges that Tinubu is getting from fellow southerners who are flying the presidential banners of opposition parties, the minister said that the South-west should retain it given that he is from that zone.



Udeh acknowledged that the South-east region has not produced Nigeria’s elected president but stated that he believed that it would eventually happen at a time in the future. However, he added that winning the presidency would ultimately depend on engagements across Nigeria’s regions, and winning votes from across Nigeria.



When asked what argument the ruling APC was advancing for Tinubu’s re-election, Udeh said the president, who is still in his first term, had initiated reforms that were beginning to produce positive results.



“Well, (the argument) is that Mr. President is in his first term, and has started reforms that are beginning to make a positive impact in the lives of Nigerians. It is not yet fully realised, but you can even tell that we are no longer as bad as we were in 2023, 2024,” he added.



To buttress his argument the minister cited statistics on Nigeria’s economic growth, saying the country has moved from about 2 per cent growth in 2023 to about 4 per cent presently. He also argued that increased revenue available to sub-national governments was creating opportunities for states and local governments to undertake development projects.



Referencing Enugu State, Udeh stated that developments recorded in the Coal City State so far in infrastructure and transportation have been unprecedented.



On the argument that the economic growth that the government is pointing to had not necessarily translated into improved living standards for ordinary Nigerians, Udeh acknowledged that inflation and hardship were yet to abate.



“We know that there’s inflation. We know that there’s still hardship. But we also know that Nigeria has been put on the track for development, to come out from economic hardship,” the minister said.

World.title: Obi: Fuel Subsidy Removal, Naira Floating, Tax Reforms Reasons for Nation’s Hardship
World.content:
ª Says FG’s petrol discount covers less than 4% of filling stations

Chuks Okocha in Abuja





Presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, yesterday, blamed President Bola Tinubu’s major reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidy, floating of the naira, and tax reforms for the worsening hardship in the country.

Obi said implementation of the different reforms had contributed to rising prices, business closures, unemployment, and declining living standards.

He also criticised the federal government’s 30-day petrol discount, stating that the initiative covers less than four per cent of the filling stations nationwide and offered inadequate relief to Nigerians struggling with high living costs.

Obi, in a statement, maintained that the government should focus on policies capable of reducing the cost of living rather than introducing short-term measures that would expire without resolving the underlying problems.

The former governor of Anambra State also reiterated his position that fuel subsidy should be restored alongside support for agriculture, healthcare, education, and infrastructure.

He said such interventions should operate under a transparent and accountable framework to ensure that public resources benefitted Nigerians rather than being diverted through corruption.

Obi promised to provide a more detailed policy roadmap on what he described as fair, transparent and affordable petroleum pricing.

He stated that Nigeria needed leadership focused on reducing the cost of living through sustainable policies and accountable administration.

Obi described the 30-day petrol discount intervention as a political gimmick, questioning why the administration introduced a temporary discount after Nigerians had endured years of economic hardship following the removal of fuel subsidy.

He said the policy failed to address the wider consequences of rising petrol prices, including poverty, unemployment, insecurity, and the increasing cost of goods and services.

The former governor also faulted the limited reach of the initiative, saying the discount would be available to about 900 Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited retail stations out of an estimated 24,000 filling stations across the country.

Obi said that meant fewer than four per cent of filling stations would offer the discount, raising questions about how millions of Nigerians would access the relief.

He estimated that, based on a population of about 243 million, each NNPC retail station would serve approximately 243,000 Nigerians if the stations were evenly distributed nationwide.

He said the situation could lead to intense competition among motorists seeking a discount of about N66 per litre, particularly in areas with limited access to NNPC outlets.

“Imagine 243,000 Nigerians struggling for a N66 per litre discount in each of the NNPC petrol stations. This is certainly not how to govern a richly blessed and endowed nation!” he said.

Obi, who questioned the timing of the discount, also queried whether the initiative was designed to test the possibility of restoring fuel subsidy or to influence public opinion ahead of the 2027 general election.

He stated, “What really does the President Bola Tinubu-led government want to achieve with a one-month discount of less than five per cent on fuel cost? Will it reduce poverty, unemployment, insecurity, and inequality? Will it increase productivity and exports?

“Is it a test to ascertain if subsidy should be restored? Is it another political gambit in the face of threats of electoral loss in the 2027 election? Too many questions, no answer!”

The NDC presidential candidate said the government should have conducted a detailed regulatory impact assessment and consulted stakeholders before implementing major economic policies.

He insisted that the initiative was too insufficient to address the economic challenges facing Nigerians, describing it as a policy driven by political considerations rather than a lasting solution.

World.title: Dangote Refinery Extends $1.6 Billion Public Offer By Two Weeks to October 27
World.content:
• Aliko says IPO already four times oversubscribed

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja and Peter Uzoho in Lagos





Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has extended the deadline for its initial public offering (IPO) by two weeks to October 27 to give more investors across Africa the opportunity to participate in what is expected to be the continent’s largest share sale.

The extension, approved by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), moves the closing date from October 13, following efforts to expand access to the offer through stock exchanges and investment platforms in other African countries.

The company said yesterday that the additional time would enable it to broaden distribution channels, facilitate cross-border investments and allow prospective investors to complete account-opening procedures, identity verification and other regulatory requirements.

The IPO, which opened on September 14, is part of the plan by Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, to broaden ownership of the 700,000 barrels per day refinery by attracting as many as 10 million retail investors in Nigeria and other African countries.

The offering comprises 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 each, with a minimum subscription of 10 shares. It is expected to raise approximately $1.6 billion, although the amount could increase to about $2.1 billion if an over-allotment option is fully exercised.

Confirming the extension, the President of the Dangote Group, Aliko Dangote, said the move followed ‘exceptionally strong interest’ from a broad spectrum of eligible investors across Africa and other international markets.

Since the launch of the offer, he stated that investor participation has underscored the growing confidence in Dangote Refinery’s long-term growth prospects and its strategic role in transforming Africa’s energy landscape.

“The IPO is going very well. We will extend the closing date because we want more of our African brothers and sisters to participate. Following our discussions with the Nairobi Stock Exchange, we have identified what we believe is the best way to facilitate participation. We are now trying to replicate that arrangement with other African exchanges to ensure wider participation…

“But when it comes to the amount of money we originally intended to raise, we have already received subscriptions amounting to more than three or four times that figure…So, it is not about the amount of money.

“It is about the number of people who will have the opportunity to participate in this offer. That means quite a lot to us,” the statement quoted Dangote as having said in a chat with media men at the facility.

The company said the additional two-week period will support ongoing market-access initiatives across African jurisdictions, including the expansion of distribution channels and the rollout of unsponsored depository receipt programmes designed to facilitate seamless cross-border investment.

It explained that it will also provide more time for prospective investors to complete account-opening procedures, identity verification processes, and other regulatory requirements necessary for participation in the offer.

Also speaking on the extension, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE, David Bird, stated that the additional time will help extend more opportunities to additional investors.

He said: “We welcome the SEC’s approval of the extension, which will give more investors across Africa the opportunity to participate in the offer. From the outset, our ambition has been to enable as many people as possible to participate in the IPO and share in DPRP’s future growth. The additional time will help us extend that opportunity to more investors across Africa.”

The company noted that it remains highly encouraged by the level of investor engagement received across its target markets and believes the extension will ensure broader participation by retail, institutional and cross-border investors seeking to be part of the refinery’s next phase of growth.

THISDAY learnt that the proceeds are intended to support the expansion of the refinery complex in Lagos, which began processing crude oil in early 2024 and has become central to Nigeria’s ambition to reduce dependence on imported refined petroleum products.

Exchanges across Africa had been in discussions with the company over arrangements to facilitate participation in the listing, which could value the business at close to $50 billion. Global depositary receipts have already been made available to investors in Kenya and Botswana, according to people familiar with the matter.

However, the offering’s prospectus indicates that the share sale is not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, meaning investors in other countries must rely on applicable local regulations or access the shares through eligible investment platforms.

The arrangement highlights the challenges facing efforts to develop a pan-African investor base, as differences in regulations, trading infrastructure and investment procedures continue to complicate cross-border transactions.

Although the refinery is seeking to attract investors across the continent, the absence of a uniform framework for public offerings means that access to the shares may vary from one country to another.

The IPO is therefore being viewed as a major test of whether African exchanges and regulators can support large-scale equity offerings involving investors from multiple jurisdictions.

The listing is also intended to demonstrate the potential of African capital markets to mobilise domestic savings for large-scale industrial development, reducing reliance on foreign financing while expanding public participation in major businesses.

Meanwhile, President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, has said Africa needs to measure economic progress by the productive capacity it develops, the employment it generates and the resilience it builds, rather than relying on growth figures alone.

Dangote spoke at the inaugural Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt, where participants urged African governments to move beyond economic growth figures to building productive industries, creating jobs and retaining more value from the continent’s natural resources.

The two-day forum, held in New Alamein and officially launched by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, brought together heads of state, investors, financial institutions and private-sector leaders to explore partnerships capable of translating Africa’s economic potential into sustainable prosperity.

The meeting was convened by Egypt in collaboration with the African Union (AU), the African Union Development Agency-New Partnership for Africa’s Development (AUDA-NEPAD) and the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank).

Dangote argued that developing local industries, processing raw materials within the continent and producing higher-value goods would help African countries reduce their dependence on imported fuel, medicines and technology.

“Growth does not tell us enough. We should ask: what are we growing, how many productive jobs does it generate, and how much economic resilience does it leave behind?” Dangote said.

Dangote also identified fragmented regulations, inconsistent standards and cumbersome border procedures as major obstacles to businesses seeking to expand across African markets.

He stressed that stronger regional integration was necessary to enable African companies to achieve economies of scale, develop competitive industries and participate more effectively in global trade.

Other African leaders, financiers and business executives at the event called for increased mobilisation of domestic capital, stronger regional integration and greater investment in local industries to accelerate economic growth and reduce the continent’s dependence on imports.

President and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Afreximbank, George Elombi, similarly called for greater African ownership of the continent’s economic future, highlighting the role of homegrown financial institutions in financing development priorities.

“Elombi highlighted Afreximbank’s support for African economies during periods of disruption and called for assessments of African financial institutions to reflect their performance, ownership models and development role,” the forum’s statement said.

He also commended Egypt’s longstanding support for the bank, describing New Alamein as a place where Africans could come together to determine their economic future.

Chief Executive Officer of AUDA-NEPAD, Nardos Bekele-Thomas, called for greater participation by African investors and businesses in financing the continent’s transformation, including through cross-border investments and regional value chains.

“We need more Africans investing in Africa. We need more African businesses able to go beyond national markets, build regional value chains and compete globally,” she said.

President of the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), Abdullah Almusaibeeh, said stronger coordination among development finance institutions could unlock additional funding for infrastructure and other strategic projects.

“When we coordinate with other institutions, we can bring substantially more financing to a project than any one institution could provide alone,” he said, citing opportunities for cooperation with institutions including the Africa Finance Corporation and the Trade and Development Bank.

Chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, emphasised the importance of domestic production and value addition in creating jobs and building wealth across the continent. “Domestic transformation creates jobs, value addition and wealth,” he said.

Youssouf also called for measures to ensure that small and medium-sized enterprises benefited from regional integration, including improved access to finance, payment systems using local currencies and financing guarantees.

The President of Burundi and Chairperson of the African Union, Évariste Ndayishimiye, urged international partners to view Africa as a centre of production, innovation and investment rather than primarily as a market for imported goods.

Secretary General of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat, Wamkele Mene, said the forum’s success should ultimately be assessed by the commercial transactions and partnerships generated by its discussions.

The programme featured sessions on agriculture and food systems, energy, infrastructure and logistics, trade, digital innovation and healthcare markets, bringing together policymakers, investors and businesses to examine potential areas of collaboration.

World.title: International Day of the Girl Child: Makinde Pledges Free Education, Healthcare
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

A Seyi Makinde-led administration would prioritise free education, vocational training, adolescent healthcare and stronger enforcement of child-protection laws to reduce child marriage and keep more Nigerian girls in school, the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation has said.

The campaign organisation said the proposed measures would also include legal aid for vulnerable girls, protection for survivors of abuse and community sensitisation programmes to address harmful social norms associated with early marriage.

Its Director of National Women Coordination, Hon. Toyin Balogun, disclosed this in a statement on Monday to mark the 2026 International Day of the Girl Child, observed annually on October 11.

The 2026 observance is themed, “End Child Marriage, Invest in Girls Rights.”

Balogun, a former Oyo State Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Inclusion, said the proposed administration would replicate the free education policy implemented in Oyo State as part of efforts to reduce Nigeria’s high out-of-school population.

She said vocational and artisanal training would complement conventional education, particularly for girls whose schooling had been disrupted by early marriage, enabling them to acquire skills to support themselves and their families.

According to her, the administration would also strengthen the implementation of existing child-protection laws and address gaps that leave girls vulnerable to exploitation, abuse and forced or early marriage.

She said child-friendly justice mechanisms would be strengthened to enable girls to report violations safely and receive timely support, while legal aid and protection services would be expanded, particularly in poor, rural, remote and underserved communities.

Balogun added that survivors would be protected from retaliation, stigma and further harm when seeking justice, with progress assessed by the number of girls protected and supported, as well as those able to remain in or return to school.

On healthcare, she said the proposed government would introduce inclusive policies to address gaps in services for child brides and prioritise adolescent-responsive sexual and reproductive healthcare.

She also called for community sensitisation programmes to educate families and communities about the consequences of child marriage, including vesicovaginal fistula, maternal deaths and neonatal mortality.

Balogun said protecting girls from early marriage required coordinated action by policymakers, families, communities and government institutions, noting that poverty, harmful social norms, discrimination and weak protection systems continued to limit girls’ opportunities.

Citing available data, she said 33.4 percent of young women in Nigeria were married before the age of 18, while UNICEF had reported that 7.6 million Nigerian girls were out of school, with significant numbers in both the northern and southern parts of the country.

She noted that child marriage went beyond the age at which a girl married, as it could interrupt her education, compromise her health, limit her economic independence and increase her vulnerability to violence and coercion.

Balogun urged stakeholders to work together to ensure that every Nigerian girl had access to education, healthcare and protection, enabling her to realise her potential.

“Together, all hands must be on deck to support the Nigerian Girl Child to enable her to attain her maximum potentials,” she said.

World.title: NHRC Raises the Alarm Over Mental Health Abuses, Says Less than 3% Covered by Insurance
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has raised alarm over the treatment of Nigerians living with mental health conditions, warning that inadequate health insurance, widespread stigma and persistent human rights abuses are denying vulnerable citizens access to care and exposing some to degrading and inhuman treatment.

The commission disclosed that fewer than three per cent of people with mental health conditions in Nigeria were covered by health insurance, leaving many individuals and their families struggling to pay for treatment in a country where mental healthcare services and trained professionals remain inadequate.

It also revealed cases involving children and adults with psychosocial disabilities who were subjected to solitary confinement in Kano State, as well as a child rescued in the Federal Capital Territory from a woman living in what the commission described as an extremely distressing and inhuman condition linked to her mental state.

The Executive Secretary of the NHRC, Chief Tony Ojukwu, raised these concerns in Abuja on Monday while commemorating the 2026 World Mental Health Day, calling on the Federal Government to urgently increase funding for mental healthcare, expand access to treatment and strengthen enforcement of laws protecting the rights of affected persons.

Ojukwu warned that Nigeria could not claim to uphold human dignity while people experiencing mental health conditions were abandoned, discriminated against, denied appropriate treatment or subjected to abuse because of their conditions.

He said mental health must be recognised not merely as a medical concern but as a fundamental human rights issue requiring urgent and coordinated action by government institutions, healthcare providers, civil society organisations and other stakeholders.

“A mental-health condition does not reduce a person’s worth, dignity or human rights,” he said.

The NHRC chief stressed that people living with mental health conditions were entitled to equality, respect, appropriate medical care and the opportunity to participate fully in society, adding that their conditions must never become grounds for exclusion, neglect or the denial of personal autonomy.

The commission’s warning comes amid continuing concerns about the accessibility and affordability of mental healthcare in Nigeria, where poverty, insecurity, displacement and shortages of specialised services place additional pressure on individuals and families seeking treatment.

Citing World Health Organisation estimates, Ojukwu said nearly one in seven people globally lived with a mental disorder, while many requiring care remained unable to access effective treatment.

He noted the situation was particularly concerning in communities affected by terrorism, abductions, armed violence and displacement, where survivors often experienced psychological trauma capable of affecting their daily activities, relationships and ability to contribute meaningfully to society.

According to him, survivors of gender-based violence, torture, trafficking and other serious human rights violations also require mental health and psychosocial support as part of efforts to restore their dignity and help them recover.

He said the government must therefore move beyond general awareness campaigns and make concrete investments in accessible services, trained personnel, health insurance and community-based care.

Of particular concern to the commission is the gap between Nigeria’s legal commitments and the actual experiences of people living with mental health conditions.

Nigeria enacted the National Mental Health Act in 2021, which received presidential assent in December 2022, establishing a legal framework for mental healthcare and the protection of the rights of affected persons.

The country also has a National Mental Health Policy and a National Suicide Prevention Strategic Framework.

However, Ojukwu maintained that the existence of laws and policy documents would have limited impact unless they translated into affordable treatment, accessible services and effective mechanisms for holding perpetrators of abuse accountable.

He called for the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act and Policy, warning that people experiencing mental health conditions continued to face discrimination in education, employment, housing and community life.

Some, he said, were denied the opportunity to make decisions about their own lives or subjected to treatment that undermined their dignity and fundamental rights.

The NHRC executive secretary urged the federal government to expand affordable mental health services through primary healthcare centres, strengthen health insurance coverage and recruit, train and deploy more psychiatrists, psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric nurses and social workers.

He also called for effective oversight of mental healthcare facilities to prevent neglect, unlawful confinement and other forms of abuse.

Highlighting the commission’s interventions, Ojukwu disclosed that the NHRC had handled cases involving children and adults with psychosocial and psychological disabilities in Kano State who had been subjected to solitary confinement before being moved to a welfare facility following the commission’s intervention.

He also recounted a recent case in the Federal Capital Territory in which the commission rescued a child from a woman living in what he described as an extremely distressing and inhuman condition linked to her mental state.

The cases, he said, demonstrated that mental health challenges could affect entire families and communities, requiring responses based on professional care, protection and support rather than punishment, abandonment or abuse.

Ojukwu said the commission had established a Counselling Unit at its headquarters to provide emotional support to victims of human rights violations and traumatic experiences.

The unit also supports NHRC personnel who may experience emotional distress from handling cases involving violence, abuse, bereavement and human suffering.

He added that the commission’s Human Rights Institute had organised training programmes for investigation officers to help them identify mental health and psychosocial concerns, respond appropriately to vulnerable complainants and recognise cases requiring professional intervention.

The establishment of the NHRC’s Vulnerable Group Department had further strengthened its capacity to address the needs of vulnerable populations, including persons experiencing mental health challenges, he said.

The commission had also partnered with the Taipei Trade Office and civil society organisations to provide grants and free mental health sessions to some indigent women who were victims of human rights violations.

Ojukwu said the NHRC was collaborating with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and other stakeholders to incorporate human rights considerations into the proposed National Mental Health Strategic Plan for 2027–2032.

He described the proposed plan as an important step towards establishing a consolidated national direction for mental healthcare, but stressed that its effectiveness would depend on implementation, funding and measurable improvements in access to services.

The commission also participated in training organised by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime on drug prevention, treatment and care, with particular attention to the relationship between substance use, mental health and human rights.

Ojukwu advocated a rights-based approach to drug-related challenges, including access to treatment, rehabilitation and psychosocial support.

The intervention is significant in a country where mental health conditions may intersect with substance use, poverty, violence and social exclusion, making coordinated healthcare and social support essential to recovery.

In a goodwill message, the Founder of the Mandate Health Empowerment Initiative, Ameh Zion, also called for stronger implementation of the National Mental Health Act and greater collaboration among government agencies, civil society organisations and development partners.

Zion said people experiencing depression, psychosis, trauma and psychosocial disabilities must not lose their dignity or fundamental rights because of their conditions.

He expressed concern that stigma, inadequate services and shortages of trained professionals continued to prevent many Nigerians from obtaining the help they needed.

According to him, survivors of terrorism, violence, displacement and abuse often carried psychological wounds that affected their functioning and ability to contribute to national development, while their families and caregivers struggled with emotional and financial burdens.

He urged stakeholders to ensure that mental health legislation translated into accessible services and enforceable protections across the country, rather than remaining largely a policy commitment.

Zion also expressed his organisation’s readiness to work with the NHRC and other African mental health reform stakeholders on public awareness, institutional capacity building, referral systems, psychosocial support for survivors and policy advocacy.

Both Ojukwu and Zion called for a broader national response involving schools, workplaces, families, communities, religious institutions and traditional leaders.

Ojukwu urged religious and traditional leaders to complement professional mental healthcare rather than substitute spiritual or traditional interventions for clinical treatment when such care was necessary.

He also called on the media to report mental health issues accurately and sensitively, warning that sensational or stereotypical portrayals could deepen stigma and discourage affected persons from seeking help.

The NHRC executive secretary said the commission would continue to investigate human rights violations, protect vulnerable persons and advocate policies that upheld the rights and dignity of all Nigerians.

He called for stronger mental health and psychosocial support for survivors of conflict, terrorism, gender-based violence, displacement, torture and trafficking, stressing that their recovery must be treated as an essential component of protecting human rights.

The commission’s position underscores a broader challenge facing Nigeria: ensuring that mental healthcare is treated as an essential public service rather than a privilege available only to those who can afford it.

Without sustained funding, trained professionals, insurance protection and effective enforcement of existing laws, millions of Nigerians requiring mental healthcare risk remaining without adequate support, while stigma and discrimination continue to compound their difficulties.

For the NHRC, the priority is clear: Nigeria must move from policy commitments to practical protection, ensuring that no citizen is denied dignity, safety or access to care because of a mental health condition.

World.title: New restaurants coming to some of Kruger National Park’s biggest camps
World.content:
Several popular Kruger National Park restaurants are getting new operators. Image: wikimedia commons

Visitors to some of Kruger National Park’s most popular camps will soon find some familiar restaurants with very different names and looks.

SANParks has appointed new restaurant operators at Lower Sabie, Pretoriuskop and Berg-en-Dal, while the restaurant at Skukuza is also set for a refurbishment.

The changes follow a competitive tender process and the expiry of previous concession agreements.



Kruger restaurants are getting a major refresh

At Lower Sabie, the former Mugg & Bean will return as Sabie River Café.

Pretoriuskop’s Wimpy will become Le Lapeng Burgers and Grill, while Berg-en-Dal’s Tindlovu Restaurant will be transformed into Eziko Eatery.

At Skukuza, the existing Cattle Baron will undergo refurbishment, with the restaurant receiving a refreshed look and feel.



Kruger National Park camp Current/former restaurant What’s changing Lower Sabie Mugg & Bean Reopening as Sabie River Café Pretoriuskop Wimpy Becoming Le Lapeng Burgers and Grill Berg-en-Dal Tindlovu Restaurant Becoming Eziko Eatery Skukuza Cattle Baron Refurbishment and refreshed look

Temporary dining options

But visitors won’t be left without somewhere to eat while the work takes place.

SANParks says temporary dining facilities with limited menus will be available during the refurbishment periods to maintain some continuity of service.

According to SANParks, the new operators will bring new concepts, investment and energy to some of the park’s busiest camps.



The changes are also expected to boost economic growth and create jobs, while improving the overall tourism offering inside Kruger National Park.

SANParks said it looks forward to unveiling the upgraded facilities in the coming months.

World.title: Matric exams officially begin: What happens if a learner is sick?
World.content:
The 2026 National Senior Certificate exams officially begin on Tuesday 13 October, and run until 26 November. What happens in the case of a learner being sick?

WHAT HAPPENS IF A LEARNER IS SICK DURING THE MATRIC EXAMS?

There are more than a million candidates and the pressure is on. A sudden fever, stomach bug or migraine at just as the exams being is relatively common and a concern. So, what happens?

The first rule is to tell the school and the exam centre as early as possible. You are advised to not just stay home and hope for the best. A learner who is unwell before a paper should contact the school principal or exam centre manager. The principal needs to notify the provincial education department.



A medical certificate is necessary. Learners who miss a paper because due to being sick are generally required to see a registered doctor or clinic and obtain a certificate that confirms the illness and the date it affected them. Officials will need this proof, so parents should keep every document and note the dates.

Learners who are mildly unwell, with a headache, a cold or period pain, are usually still expected to write. Centres may arrange for a learner to sit near a window, take prescribed medication, or have a short supervised break, within the rules. Invigilators cannot add extra time for ordinary illness.

IN THE CASE OF A MORE SERIOUS ILLNESS

For more serious illness, provincial departments have in past years arranged for candidates to write under supervision in a hospital or at home. An invigilator present will be present. This requires the department’s approval beforehand. So, families need to raise it immediately rather than after the paper has been written.

If a learner cannot write at all, the usual route is to sit the missed paper in the supplementary exams. Those are normally held in the following year, around the May/June period. In the meantime the learner’s results may be withheld or marked incomplete until the outstanding paper is written.

Illness on the day is different from poor preparation. A bad day without medical evidence generally cannot be reversed, which is why a doctor’s visit matters even if the learner then decides to push through and write.

Parents and learners should also look after the basics: sleep, regular meals, water and avoiding last-minute all-nighters. Contact numbers for the school and district office are worth having on hand.



Rules and arrangements can differ slightly between provinces. So, learners should confirm the exact process with their school or provincial education department. Take a look at what you can and cannot bring into the exam room here.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs coach to replace his best player
World.content:
Lebohang Maboe collects a Man of the Match award against Siwelele FC in the Betway Premiership. Image: Official PSL

Fernando Da Cruz’s Kaizer Chiefs host Stellenbosch FC at 19:30. Not only is the Frenchman facing with a midfield crisis, but Lebohang Maboe, his team’s best player, is also out injured.

The Heidelberg-born star is the club’s only player with two Man of the Match awards this season in seven games. He picked up the gongs against Siwelele FC and Polokwane City on 6 and 13 September, respectively.

KAIZER CHIEFS TO REPLACE LEBOHANG MABOE

While two other midfielders are also injured, Siphesihle Ndlovu and Adolf Mtasingwa, Maboe’s absence will be felt most. The 32-year-old scooped five Man of the Match awards in last season’s Betway Premiership.



While Kaizer Chiefs have Sibongiseni Mthethwa available to cover for Maboe in the number six role, the 32-year-old lacks Maboe’s ability to drive the team forward through passing or ball-carrying.

With Ndlovu and Mtasingwa also unavailable for selection, coach Da Cruz is expected to improvise. Several squad players have previously played in the number eight role.

They include Nkosingiphile Ngcobo, Ethan Chislett, Reeve Frosler and, very briefly, Mduduzi Shabalala. It remains to be seen who Kaizer Chiefs coach Da Cruz will transfer his trust to.

CAF CONFEDERATION CUP AT THE WEEKEND

Whoever steps up on Tuesday, another opportunity is expected in less than four days. Amakhosi must travel to Zambia to take on Red Arrows in the second preliminary round of the CAF Confederation Cup. The return leg will be held at Moses Mabhida Stadium next weekend.

Victory for Kaizer Chiefs over the two legs will book them a spot in the CAF Confederation Cup group stages, which effectively comprise the last 16 of the competition. From four groups of four teams each, finishing first or second will propel the Glamour Boys to the quarter-finals.

Some of the top teams in this edition include Egyptian giants Al Ahly and Moroccan heavyweights Wydad Casablanca.

World.title: Seven million down, 993 million to go: Inside South Africa’s One Billion Trees drive
World.content:
More than seven million trees have been planted under the Presidential One Billion Trees Programme since April 2026. Image: X @ActionSA

South Africa’s One Billion Trees programme has passed a major milestone.

More than seven million trees have been planted across the country in just six months.

And one province is leading the way by a long shot.



But the journey to one billion is only just beginning.

According to the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), 7,134,711 trees have been planted since the start of the 2026/27 financial year on 1 April 2026.

WHERE THE TREES WERE PLANTED

The Western Cape leads the way, followed by KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng:

Free State: 326,294

326,294 Western Cape: 2,053,786

2,053,786 KwaZulu-Natal: 1,052,494

1,052,494 Gauteng: 1,012,051

1,012,051 Eastern Cape: 736,692

736,692 Mpumalanga: 519,512

519,512 Limpopo: 518,023

518,023 Northern Cape: 515,264, despite being South Africa’s driest province

515,264, despite being South Africa’s driest province North West: 400,619

WHAT IS THE ONE BILLION TREES PROGRAMME?

The Presidential One Billion Trees Programme aims to plant one billion trees over the next five years.

It’s part of the government’s existing National Greening Programme, and it works with communities, traditional leaders and the private sector.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has framed it as a challenge to the legacy of apartheid-era urban planning, saying trees and green spaces provide recreation and shade.



A big boost came from the nationwide Heritage Day tree-planting campaign on 24 September 2026.

Ramaphosa launched it by planting a tree at Bongolethu Stadium in Oudtshoorn, in the Western Cape.

FRUIT TREES, FOOD AND JOBS

It’s not only about greening.

In his weekly newsletter, Ramaphosa said the programme includes fruit trees such as citrus, avocados and grapes.

He said any surplus could help generate income for communities.

The DFFE has also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Department of Human Settlements, so that a fruit tree is planted with every new subsidised house.

The environmental sector also provides work through the Expanded Public Works Programme (EPWP), giving unemployed South Africans skills in conservation, water, waste and fire management.

WHY INDIGENOUS TREES MATTER

The programme deliberately focuses on planting indigenous trees.

That’s because many popular trees are invasive species. Ramaphosa pointed out that this includes Pretoria’s famous jacarandas.

NOT EVERYONE IS CONVINCED

The campaign has had its critics.

Ramaphosa faced a backlash on social media after highlighting the milestone.

Some South Africans questioned whether tree planting should be a priority, given the country’s socioeconomic challenges.

HOW FAR THERE IS TO GO

Seven million trees is a big number. But it’s less than 1% of the one billion target.

To reach one billion in five years, South Africa would need to plant an average of 200 million trees a year.

Deputy Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment Bernice Swarts thanked South Africans for taking part, and encouraged those who haven’t to join in.

HOW YOU CAN GET INVOLVED

Anyone can plant a tree and add it to the national count.

The DFFE encourages South Africans to register their trees online by uploading a photo and the tree’s GPS coordinates.

This helps the department track how many trees survive and grow.

I love that the Western Cape is leading the way on this one.

Seven million trees won’t change the country overnight.

But every indigenous tree planted in the right place is a small win for nature, and for the people who live around it.

My advice? Plant one, register it, and watch it grow.
