World.title: Government to stop drivers’ licences used as ID: What’s changed?
World.content:
The Department of Transport plans to amend the National Road Traffic Regulations to prevent driving licences and other documents from being used as general forms of identification.

GOVERNMENT TO STOP DRIVERS’ LICENSES BEING USED AS AN ID

Have you ever forgotten your ID and used your drivers’ license as an alternate proof of identity? Well, that habit may soon be on it’s way out. The Department of Transport plans to amend the National Road Traffic Regulatiins so that traffic register number (TRN) certificates, learner’s licenses and driving licenses can no longer be treated as general identification.

The proposal follows a 2023 investigation, in which Transport helped the Department of Home Affairs look into the misuse of road traffic documents. The department says the TRN was created only so that people without a South African ID number could transact on the National Traffic Information System while their legal status was being finalised with Home Affairs. It was never meant to serve as a general ID.



However, some institutions have been accepting TRNs and licences as proof of identity, which the department says goes against the Identification Act of 1997. That law makes Home Affairs the sole authority for the National Population Register and for issuing identification documents.

Two regulations will change. Regulation 1 will drop TRNs and all other road-traffic documents from the definition of acceptable identification. For people whp are not permanent residents of South Africa, acceptable ID will mean an unexpired passport together with the relevant Home Affairs permit. Companies will use their registration or incorporation certificates.

Regulation 335 will tighten control of TRNs. Provisions recognising a TRN as acceptable identification will be deleted. A TRN holder who obtains another form of acceptable identification must notify the registering authority within 21 days and surrender the TRN certificate.



A TRN will also be valid only for as long as the passport and permit used to obtain it. Anyone holding a TRN certificate without a validity period must apply for a new one within three months of the regulations taking effect.

FOR ORDINARY SOUTH AFRICANS

For ordinary South Africans, a green ID book, smart ID or passport is the document to carry when proof of identity is needed. A driver’s licence will still prove that you are licensed to drive. However, it should not be the document that proves who you are.

It is important to note that this is not final as yet. The amendments will be published in the Government Gazette, and the public will have 30 days to submit written comments. All submissions will be considered before the final regulations are published.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs news and rumours: Maboe, Ndlovu, Baartman
World.content:
Today’s Kaizer Chiefs news looks at an injury update on several key first-team stars. There’s also a look at their worrying form.

A bad few weeks for Maboe

Chiefs midfield maestro Lebo Maboe pulled up with an injury in Chiefs’ 0-0 draw with Golden Arrows, a match in which he also missed a penalty. The injury ruled him out of Bafana’s AFCON qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea. Now, there’s no certainty as to how long that thigh issue will keep him out of action. After such a strong start to the campaign, these past few weeks have brought the 32-year-old back down to earth.

Kaizer Chiefs will be without Maboe, Siphesihle Ndlovu, Langelihle Phili and Brandon Petersen against Stellenbosch on Wednesday. It’s a blow, given that Stellies have won the last three H2Hs. Meanwhile, Luke Baartman is on the mend but remains a doubt for the clash with Stellies.



“Chiefs still have four major injury concerns, with Brandon Petersen returning to individual training to recover a knee injury, Lebohang Maboe – who has played in all eight of Chiefs’ games this season – nursing an ankle injury, while Phili and Siphesihle Ndlovu remain long-term absentees,” the club confirmed on their website.

World.title: Terrible couple of weeks for Kaizer Chiefs midfielder
World.content:
Things were looking good for Kaizer Chiefs midfield maestro Lebohang Maboe before the break. However, 24 hours is a long time in football.

Maboe has been Chiefs’ main man

Chiefs midfield schemer Lebo Maboe pulled up with an injury in Chiefs’ 0-0 draw with Golden Arrows, a match in which he also missed a penalty. The injury meant he had to pull out of the Bafana squad that beat Guinea and Eritrea in AFCON qualifiers. Now, there’s no certainty as to how long that thigh issue will keep him out of action. He’s almost certain to miss their match with Stellenbosch on Tuesday, 13 October.

Chiefs have drawn four of their last five matches in the league, and can ill-afford to resume their Betway Premiership campaign with more dropped points.



Good and bad injury news for Kaizer Chiefs

Striker Flavio Silva is back in training alongside Khanyisa Mayo, who has recovered after a hernia operation. 21-year-old Langelihle Phili is also nearing a return after a serious ankle injury he sustained in late August during training. Phili could return towards the end of October, but the technical staff won’t rush the exciting winger back.

World.title: Southern African elephants bounce back as continent’s wildlife plunges
World.content:
Some southern African elephant populations are increasing, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2026. Image: Pexels.

Southern African elephants have given conservationists something they rarely get: good news.

A major new global report has named them as one of the world’s wildlife recovery stories.

But the same report carries a stark warning for the rest of Africa’s wildlife.



And the numbers are hard to ignore.

The findings come from the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF)‘s Living Planet Report 2026, released on 7 October.

It’s WWF’s flagship assessment of the state of the world’s nature, subtitled The Science of Hope.

WHY SOUTHERN AFRICAN ELEPHANTS ARE A BRIGHT SPOT

The report highlights recoveries in four groups of animals: green sea turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and southern African elephants.

According to WWF, African savannah elephants are still declining across much of their range and remain Endangered overall.

But in parts of southern Africa, some populations are increasing.



WWF credits this partly to communities.

Southern African countries have built legal frameworks that give local communities a direct stake in looking after elephants, through community-based natural resource management.

THE BAD NEWS FOR AFRICA’S WILDLIFE

The wider picture is far less encouraging.

According to WWF Africa, the average size of monitored wildlife populations in Africa dropped by 80% between 1970 and 2022.

Only Latin America and the Caribbean recorded a steeper regional decline.

Vultures are among the hardest hit. Eight African vulture species have declined by 62%.

Globally, monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73% over the same period.

The report tracked 35,803 wildlife populations across 5,790 species of mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and fish.

WHAT’S DRIVING THE DECLINE?

WWF says the main causes are habitat loss, overexploitation and climate change.

Freshwater species have been hit hardest, with an average decline of 85%. Land-based populations fell by 69%, and marine populations by 59%.

WHY THERE’S STILL HOPE

Despite the losses, WWF says nature can recover.

Around half of the wildlife populations it monitors globally are stable or increasing.

WWF-US chief scientist Rebecca Shaw said the data shows that “nature can rebound when we take action.”

But WWF also warns that conservation wins won’t last unless the world tackles the root causes, including the way we produce food and energy.

An 80% drop in Africa’s wildlife is hard to read.

But the elephant story shows what’s possible when communities are part of the solution, not left out of it.

That’s the kind of news we need more of.

World.title: Man City, PSG clash at contrasting time for state-backed projects
World.content:
MANCHESTER - Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain have reshaped football with the financial backing of Gulf state owners, but there is a stark contrast in the health of those projects ahead of their latest Champions League meeting on Wednesday.

City return to Champions League action for the first time since they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules in a bombshell verdict which could threaten their place in the English top-flight.

PSG strived to follow City's era of sustained success and are now firmly established as Europe's top dogs after successive Champions League titles to go along with their domination of French football.

Abu Dhabi-backed City won the race against Qatar-owned PSG to become European champions first in 2023.

The triumph over Inter Milan in Istanbul that completed a treble of Champions League, Premier League and FA Cup was the pinnacle of City's rise since a 2008 takeover fronted by Sheikh Mansour, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

But a cloud now hangs over City's haul of silverware from the past 15 years unless they can overturn the findings of an independent commission on appeal.

City were found to have used "sham" commercial deals with Emirati companies to inflate revenue and reduce costs to the tune of over £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.

No sanction has yet been meted out, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League are among the potential punishments.

The Premier League season has been thrust into turmoil while clubs await the appeal verdict, with City sitting top of the table after six successive wins, including a 3-0 rout of Liverpool on Sunday.

World.title: Jacob Zuma discharged from Pietermaritzburg hospital
World.content:
PIETERMARITZBURG - Former president and uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party leader Jacob Zuma has been discharged from hospital.

Zuma was admitted to Netcare St Anne’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg last week.

eNCA has learnt that he was discharged on Monday night but was advised by his medical team to remain in the Pietermaritzburg area overnight in case of a medical emergency.

His doctors are expected to assess his condition on Tuesday and, if satisfied, clear him to travel to his Nkandla homestead.

The Presidency previously said the 84-year-old had been admitted for a routine check-up, which he undergoes twice a year, and was under the care of the surgeon-general.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | Sibiya back in court as bail bid continues
World.content:
Editor's note: Please note that some details in the court proceedings may contain graphic details.

JOHANNESBURG - Suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya is expected back in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court as his bail application continues.

Sibiya faces charges including rape, human trafficking and sexual grooming of a child. He has remained in custody since his arrest on 21 September and has denied the allegations.

Meanwhile, Sibiya has resigned from the South African Police Service (SAPS) with immediate effect after his disciplinary proceedings began on Monday.

Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe confirmed that his departure was classified as a dishonourable discharge because he resigned while facing disciplinary proceedings.

His employment was terminated with immediate effect on 12 October.

Sibiya’s criminal case and bail application remain ongoing.

World.title: Baby murder case raises questions over accountability of religious leaders
World.content:
ATTERIDGEVILLE - The case against a self-proclaimed pastor and his two wives has reignited concerns about the safety of vulnerable women and children, as well as the accountability of religious leaders.

The trio appeared in the Atteridgeville Magistrate’s Court facing charges including murder, rape, kidnapping, human trafficking and fraud, following the death of a four-month-old baby and the alleged rape of the child’s mother.

The case has also prompted calls for justice and renewed scrutiny of people who assume positions of religious authority without recognised oversight.

Caiphus Mkhawane and his two wives, Amanda Mnguni and Ntsako Mathebela, face charges including conspiracy to commit murder, murder, rape, kidnapping, human trafficking and fraud.

The allegations have sent shockwaves through the community, with the case drawing attention to the vulnerability of the mother and her infant.

The courtroom was packed, with community members and activists calling for accountability and justice.

The case has also raised questions about how religious leaders are held accountable, particularly where individuals establish themselves as pastors without recognised ordination or oversight.

The accused remain in custody. The matter is expected back in court on 16 October for legal representation and further bail-related proceedings.

World.title: Expert: Sibiya not off the hook after police resignation
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Shadrack Sibiya’s resignation from the South African Police Service (SAPS) does not mean he is off the hook, according to the Institute for Security Studies’ Willem Els.

Els says Sibiya’s departure means he will no longer face the internal disciplinary proceedings instituted against him by the police.

However, this does not prevent criminal investigations or prosecution if evidence shows he broke the law while serving as deputy national police commissioner.

“That’s different from the procedural charges that he has in the police itself,” Els says.

Sibiya faces criminal charges, including rape, human trafficking and sexual grooming of a child.

He has appeared in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court, where he has denied the allegations.

He maintains that the alleged sexual intercourse with his 18-year-old accuser was consensual.

World.title: March and March plans return to Gqeberha Home Affairs
World.content:
GQEBERHA - March and March has vowed to return to the Home Affairs offices in Gqeberha on Tuesday, as tensions over immigration continue.

The protest movement wants Home Affairs to stop serving foreign nationals and says undocumented immigrants should leave the country. However, foreign nationals say they are being harassed and intimidated.

One Somali national who visited the offices on Monday says the group’s actions have left foreign nationals feeling threatened.

Security has been heightened following last week’s clashes, with police and other law enforcement officials monitoring the situation.

March and March says it is frustrated that the offices remain open to foreign nationals. The group claims a national decision was taken to pause asylum applications and says its concerns are being ignored.

But activists warn that frustration over immigration must not translate into intimidation or violence against people because of their nationality.

World.title: US actress Selma Blair arrested after flight altercation
World.content:
NEW YORK - US actress Selma Blair was arrested after an alleged altercation on a flight from Los Angeles to New York City that injured at least two cabin crew members, authorities said Monday.

The "Legally Blonde" and "Cruel Intentions" star was detained at John F Kennedy Airport after her Delta Air Lines flight landed late Sunday following reports of a physically abusive passenger.

US media said that Blair punched one flight attendant and bit another. The 54-year-old then reportedly assaulted a police officer and nurse as she was transported to hospital.

"Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct," a representative for Blair said.

"Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition."

The FBI issued a summons accusing Blair of assaults on the plane, according to a federal judicial source.

Blair was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault Monday night and was released on bail. A new hearing in the case is scheduled for January 19, 2027.

A spokesperson for Delta said the airline "has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behaviour, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first."

In 2016, Blair was removed from a plane on a stretcher after another outburst on a flight.

"I mixed alcohol with medication, and that caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret," she told Vanity Fair after that incident.

She also described in her 2022 memoir having bitten several celebrities, including Kate Moss, often in situations where she had been drinking alcohol.

World.title: 'Devastating' waves leave California beach homes on brink of collapse
World.content:
LONG BEACH - Emergency repairs and cleanup were underway in California's wave-battered city of Long Beach, where several homes appeared on the brink of collapse and remained too dangerous to enter.

Tropical Storm Rachel brought less rain than forecasters had predicted but the heavy surf -- driven by a confluence of factors including the abnormal storm system, high tide, the impact of El Niño and human-caused climate change -- was enough to severely damage some coastal properties.

Dramatic photos and video footage showed homes along the city's peninsula teetering precariously, while its historic boardwalk was partially swept away.

"These kind of impacts are not normal. They're unprecedented for our community," said Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson during a weekend press conference.

"This is a sobering reminder of the power of nature," he added.

Some residents who lived on particularly threatened blocks were issued mandatory evacuation orders through Tuesday.

Richardson urged people to take seriously warnings to prepare, including picking up city-provided sandbags, saying "our infrastructure was not built for this."

"This accelerates all of our urgency to address climate resiliency on our coastline," he added.

The local leader pointed to warnings that El Niño's effects will worsen into the winter and are expected to wreak more havoc along California's coast.

World.title: The Irony: Government splashes billions for politics, zero for university education
World.content:
UASU leaders, led by Secretary-General Constantine Wasonga, address journalists at their Nairobi offices on October 12, 2026. [Nicholas Biwott, Standard]

Students in Public universities are once again paying the price for a government that has failed to secure a lasting deal with lecturers and other university workers, despite having promised to resolve the dispute after a devastating 49-day strike last year.

The strike, which began on October 2, entered its second week yesterday after negotiations between the Government and university unions collapsed, with the unions rejecting the latest offer as inadequate. The absence of the National Treasury from the talks raised further questions about the Government’s commitment to resolving a dispute whose financial implications should be central to the negotiations.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.
