World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: Revealed: 84 Kenyans killed, 52 missing in Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi. [File,Standard]

The government has records of 354 Kenyans linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, including 84 classified as killed or missing in action and five being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine.

Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi gave the updated figures in a response to Parliament on the recruitment of Kenyans into the Russian military and the detention of Kenyans in Ukraine on Thursday, October 8.

The records show that 77 Kenyans remain on the front lines, 38 are in camps, 52 have an unknown or unclassified location and 34 are hospitalised.

Another 62 Kenyans have been repatriated, while one is in detention and another has completed a military contract.

The government said Russia has stopped the enlistment of additional Kenyans after Kenya secured the country’s placement on Russia’s ‘Stop List’ during Mudavadi’s visit to Moscow in March.

“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the Special Military Operation following the implementation of the Stop List,” Mudavadi said.

Russian authorities have told Kenya that requests to terminate military contracts will be considered on a case-by-case basis by individual military unit commanders.

Mudavadi said Kenya continues to engage Russian authorities and affected families over the burial, cremation or repatriation of remains after Russia said its Defence Ministry could not meet the cost of repatriating the remains of deceased Kenyans.

Five Kenyans held in Ukraine

Five Kenyan nationals are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, according to information sent to Kenya by the Ukrainian Embassy in Vienna on September 3.

The government identified them as Evans Kibet, detained since May 2025; Willi Muniu Macharia, detained since November 2025; Haron Kibet Pachenge, detained since March 2026; Joseph, detained since April 2026; and Francis Ndarua Ndungu.

Kenya’s Honorary Consul in Ukraine visited the Zakhid 1 prisoner-of-war camp and reported that the detainees were being held in humane conditions, had access to medical services and were being treated under rules governing prisoners of war.

The government also said Ukraine was holding the remains of four other Kenyans.

They are Simon Gitau, Clinton Nyapara Mogesa, Dennis Bagaka Obwori and Eric Mwangi Nyambura.

Kenya is seeking the release and repatriation of the affected Kenyans through diplomatic channels, including engagement with Ukraine and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The government wants Kenyans held as prisoners of war to be considered as possible victims of international human trafficking.

Mudavadi said many of the affected Kenyans reported that recruiters lured them with promises of employment before they ended up in military service.

The government says the circumstances surrounding their recruitment could fit the definition of trafficking under Article 3(a) of the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, also known as the Palermo Protocol.

It wants the issue considered during negotiations over their repatriation so the Kenyans can access assistance available to trafficking victims.

President William Ruto has also raised the matter directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a telephone conversation, according to the government.

Kenya has further received approval from Kyiv for its ambassador to Ukraine, with the government saying this will improve its ability to respond to cases involving Kenyans in the country.

The State Department for Diaspora Affairs said families should report cases to the government as soon as communication with relatives in Russia is disrupted.

Once a family reports a case, the department collects identification details, travel information and next-of-kin contacts before referring the case to the Kenyan Embassy in Moscow for verification.

The government has also facilitated the return of 62 Kenyans who had been involved in Russia’s military operations.

It has provided affected families with updates from diplomatic missions, information on compensation processes, psychosocial support and guidance on the repatriation or burial of remains.

The government said it is also expanding measures to prevent deceptive recruitment by providing pre-departure information, urging Kenyans to verify recruitment agencies and employment offers and strengthening emergency assistance through Kenyan diplomatic missions.

The scale of the recruitment first emerged publicly in February when Parliament was told that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been recruited to fight for Russia.

The National Intelligence Service report presented to lawmakers said recruiters targeted former security personnel and civilians with promises of lucrative employment, salaries and bonuses.

The figures at the time included 89 Kenyans on the frontline, 39 hospitalised, 28 missing in action, 35 in camps or bases, 30 repatriated, one detained and one who had completed a contract.

The government then stepped up diplomatic efforts. In March, Kenya announced an agreement with Russia to stop further enlistment of Kenyans into its military operations and to facilitate consular support and voluntary disengagement for Kenyans already serving.

The issue remains unresolved for many families. More than 30 families affected by the recruitment were reported this week to be seeking a meeting with President Ruto before Kenya's delegation travels to Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit, demanding answers on missing relatives, repatriation of survivors and the return of remains.

World.title: Wajir patient isolated over suspected viral haemorrhagic fever
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home. [File, Standard]

A 20-year-old man in Habaswein, Wajir County, has been isolated after presenting with symptoms consistent with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever, following recent travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home, where he is being treated after developing fever, headache and cough. He was also found to have severe anaemia, with a haemoglobin level of 4g/dL.

According to a disease surveillance report filed at Habaswein Police Station, the patient told health officials that he had recently travelled to the DRC, where he worked as a “tan boy” on a cargo truck or trailer.

He reportedly developed fever and headache while still in the DRC on September 2, 2026, before traveling by trailer to Uganda, where he stayed for about five days and sought medical attention.

The report states that he was treated with antibiotics in Uganda before travelling by trailer to Malaba. From Malaba, he travelled by motorcycle to a relative's residence, where he stayed for approximately five days.

He later travelled by trailer to Nairobi and proceeded by bus to Isiolo, where he stayed for about 10 days before travelling to Habaswein by Probox vehicle. He arrived in the town around September 20.

Upon arrival, the patient sought treatment at Hilac Medical Clinic, where he was managed for pneumonia and septicaemia for about three days.

However, his condition did not improve and he was subsequently transferred to Albadar Nursing Home, where he remains admitted.

The report adds that the patient is receiving intravenous Augmentin and paracetamol and has been transfused with two units of whole blood.

“Despite the above interventions, the patient remains clinically unwell and sick-looking,” the report states.

Authorities have since placed the patient in isolation as investigations continue to establish the cause of his illness.

“Sample collection has been completed, and the specimen will be shipped to National Public Health Laboratories tonight,” the report states.

World.title: Egypt, UNESCO discuss expanding cooperation in inclusive sport, youth empowerment
World.content:
Minister of Youth and Sports Gohar Nabil met on Monday, October 12, 2026, with Paul Koster, UNESCO Regional Director for Cairo and director of the UN agency’s liaison office to the Arab League, as they discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in several priority areas, particularly sport for development, social inclusion, youth empowerment and digital skills development.

The meeting comes as the Ministry of Youth and Sports seeks to strengthen its international partnerships and leverage available expertise and resources to support Egyptian youth, develop sport practice and reinforce the role of sport in human development and sustainable development.

The talks explored opportunities to build on the existing cooperation between the ministry and UNESCO and develop joint programs and initiatives that use sport as a tool for sustainable development, promote community participation and expand access to sports and youth activities, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals and Egypt’s priorities for investing in people and building young people’s capacities.

Nabil stressed that his ministry attaches great importance to cooperation with international organizations and benefiting from their expertise in developing youth and sportive programs and initiatives.

Such cooperation will help broaden participation in sport, strengthen sport’s contribution to community development and promote the values of participation, tolerance and equal opportunities, he said.

He highlighted the importance of building on existing cooperation with UNESCO and developing joint projects with tangible impact, particularly in inclusive sport, empowering persons with disabilities, developing youth skills and supporting digital innovation.

He also stressed the need to align proposed initiatives with young people’s actual needs and establish clear mechanisms for implementation and follow-up.

For his part, Koster underscored the importance of strengthening cooperation with the Ministry of Youth and Sports in areas that expand opportunities for young people to participate in development and use sport to promote social inclusion and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals.

World.title: One teen killed, others wounded, after explosion on Israeli school trip near Lebanon border
World.content:
One teenager was killed and others were wounded, according to Israeli emergency response services, after an explosion on an Israeli school trip near the Lebanon border.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said an initial review by soldiers at the scene indicated that explosion was caused by an unexploded Hezbollah munition that had fallen in the area. It’s unclear when the projectile was fired. Pictures released by the IDF showed a military helicopter evacuating patients for medical treatment.

“Apparently, the suspicion is that an unexploded munition of some kind exploded in the hands of one of the students,” said Deputy Police Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, a commander in Israel’s northern district, according to Reuters.

According to United Hatzalah, an Israeli emergency response service, three people sustained serious injuries in the explosion, while at least 10 others suffered light-to-moderate injuries. The wounded were evacuated to three hospitals in the area, police said.

In a statement, the Ma’alot-Tarshiha municipality in northern Israel said students and staff were on the local school’s annual trip when the explosion happened. The country’s Ministry of Education said it was an “extremely difficult incident, and our thoughts are with the victims and their families.” Commissioner Daniel Levy told Reuters it was a “very serious incident, in which children who went on a field trip were hurt, to our sorrow.”

On Monday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with Israel’s education minister, visited the wounded and their families at Rambam Hospital in Haifa. Netanyahu instructed the IDF to reinforce the prohibitions against touching unexploded ordinance.

Image provided by the Israel Defense Forces of soldiers operating at the scene. Portions of this image have been blurred by the source. From Israel Defense Forces

Shortly after the explosion occurred on Monday afternoon, Israel Police said the initial suspicion was that the explosion was a result of an unexploded munition along the border near the villages of Yiftah and Manara. Bomb disposal experts were dispatched to examine the cause of the explosion, police said.

MDA said it was a “complex incident” as they sent numerous teams to the site. “We quickly dispatched substantial forces to the scene, including ambulances, mobile intensive care units (MICUs), and an MDA helicopter, which was also scrambled to the incident,” said regional director Itzik Shushan.

A US-brokered ceasefire in late-June was supposed to end months of conflict in southern Lebanon as it paved the way for the deployment of the Lebanese military and the gradual withdrawal of the IDF. Israel pulled back from two small areas along the so-called yellow line that demarcates the zone occupied by the Israeli military, but further progress on the agreement has largely stalled.

Israel has razed entire villages in southern Lebanon and has continued to carry out regular strikes there as it tries to remove Hezbollah from the territory.

World.title: Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 2 as it continues to lash Mexico’s Pacific coast
World.content:
Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 2 storm on Monday with sustained winds of 105 mph as it moves off Mexico’s west coast, according to the US National Hurricane Center.

The storm will likely pack near 100 mph winds as it makes landfall sometime Thursday, though the exact location and timing could change because of the complexity of its track forecast.

The hurricane has been causing heavy rainfall and strong winds. In Mexico’s southwestern Guerrero state, an elderly person died, according to Mexico’s national Civil Protection coordinator during a news conference with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum said the hurricane, which has threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast since Sunday, caused “minor” damage in affected areas.

“The place where there may have been greater damage, although it was not as expected, is Guerrero. There was some damage in Colima, and [the effects of Tropical Storm] Rachel in Baja California, where there were greater impacts.”

The hurricane is bringing heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Jalisco’s coast early Monday, including Puerto Vallarta, a popular resort city destination for US tourists. The conditions are expected to improve that morning as Simon continues to weaken slowly and inch northwest just offshore.

The international airport in Puerto Vallarta suspended operations and will remain closed until 8 a.m. local time on Tuesday, according to Pacific Airport Group (GAP).

The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters on Sunday that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”

Velázquez said Simon’s effects — including “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday. But rainfall is expected to ease during the day, according to the head of Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, Fabián Vázquez Romaña

According to NHC forecasts, Simon’s winds and rain will also spread to coastal areas of Nayarit state Monday and parts of Sinaloa state Tuesday. By Tuesday afternoon, Simon is expected to turn toward the northeast and begin moving toward southern Sinaloa.

The Nayarit coast could see an inch or two of rain but the state’s islands could receive more than 12 inches as Simon passes very close by Monday night into early Tuesday. Rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches are expected along parts of Sinaloa’s coast, with the hardest-hit areas potentially seeing more than 12 inches as Simon approaches on Thursday.

Dangerous flash flooding is possible in any of these areas, while life-threatening landslides could occur at higher elevations.

Coastal areas will experience the hurricane’s strongest winds, which can topple trees and power lines.

Over the weekend, Sheinbaum urged residents from the states of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.

Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.

Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.

Laura Sharman and Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump holds raucous Ohio rally as he tries to shore up base voters for GOP
World.content:
Youngstown, Ohio —

President Donald Trump on Monday kicked off a week of red-state campaigning with a raucous rally in Ohio, where Republicans are fighting to hold onto a Senate seat that could be key to the majority.

He spent portions of his nearly 90-minute remarks railing against Somali and Haitian communities, delivering red meat political attacks and catering to his base. He at times conjured two out-of-state Democrats — Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar and Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — as bigger threats than former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who’s giving GOP Sen. Jon Husted a run for his money in a state that Trump had turned into a reliably red bastion.

After Ohio, Trump’s scheduled to hit Alaska and Montana — states he won by 13 and 20 points in 2024 — as his team banks on him juicing base turnout in conservative areas. But on Monday night — as Trump returned to the same arena where he held a packed 2017 ‘thank you’ tour — large sections of seating on the left and right of the press riser, which came with prime views of the president, were empty.

Still, it was a much livelier affair than some recent rallies, with two significant interruptions. At one point, a brawl appeared to break out between a protester wearing a “Release The Epstein Files” t-shirt and a rally-goer in the stands. Another interruption came from a young woman holding a Mexican flag.

A big part of Trump’s pitch was about immigration, returning to a theme he hit hard in 2024, when he repeated his false claim that Haitian migrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating their neighbors’ pets.

“Just look at what’s happening in the once great state of Minnesota,” he said, teeing up his attacks on Omar — a frequent target of his ire.

Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of the congresswoman, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter.

And while Trump insisted he was not involved in that search, he went on to call Omar — who’s a US citizen — a “disaster” and attack the country where she was born.

“[Rep. Omar] comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, without — all they do is shoot each other — and she comes into our country, and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s got a constitutional right? She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

Supporters cheer for President Donald Trump during a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on October 12, 2026. Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

As he launched into into a tirade against Somalis in the US, supporters in the audience began chanting “Deport!”

“They think they’re in Somalia, where they don’t have pants to wear,” Trump said at one point, going on to repeat his insult about “low IQ people.”

He made blue-state Minnesota the foil. “If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked, and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed, we’re going to stop it. Just like we did with Springfield, we’re going to stop it,” Trump said.

When the president turned to Brown — who holds a 6-point lead over Husted in CNN polling released last week — he tried to link the former three-term incumbent to national Democrats in more generic terms.

“Sherrod Brown is the candidate of the Marxists, the communists, the anti-American radicals, who want to tear down America’s heritage,” Trump said, arguing that he also wants the Midwest “turned into Mogadishu.”

Brown, a progressive populist first elected to the Senate in 2006, held onto his seat in 2018, during Trump’s first term, but lost reelection while on the ballot with Trump in 2024.

“So, what happens is every time I run, we do great,” Trump said, repeating his call for voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this year.

The first days of early voting in Ohio showed signs Democrats are more enthusiastic to vote, with affiliated Democrats making up larger shares of pre-election voters than they did two years ago, even in the most Republican parts of the state, according to data from the secretary of state’s office last week. (But Republicans in recent years have much been much more likely to vote early in person or on Election Day.)

Trump seemed to tacitly acknowledge Ohioans’ previous tendency to back Brown, arguing that a vote for the former senator could have much wider ramifications.

“It’s one vote, but that one vote can steer Congress into a direction that you’re not going to be happy with. And it’s not Ohio values.”

World.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts three missiles as capital’s international airport remains closed after deadly Houthi attacks
World.content:
Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed three Houthi ballistic missiles on Monday, as the main international airport in the kingdom’s capital remained closed following a series of attacks that have killed at least 20 people and wounded hundreds over the past week.

The Saudi military said one missile was intercepted over Riyadh and two others were destroyed over Khamis Mushait in the southwest of the country. The Houthi-controlled armed forces claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying it had targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and a military base. The group also renewed its warnings to international airlines against operating flights to Saudi airports.

The attacks came soon after Saudi authorities announced that King Khalid International Airport would remain closed until further notice. A notice to air missions (NOTAM) indicates it will remain shut until at least October 17.

The latest missile attack came two days after a Houthi strike on the airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Footage of Saturday’s strike shows dozens of passengers waiting to board their flight when a blast suddenly causes part of the ceiling to collapse.

Some clasped their hands over their heads as they ran for safety, while dust filled the area and debris crashed to the floor, the footage obtained by Al Arabiya television news channel shows.

Hours before Monday’s ballistic missile attacks, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation authority said the airport would remain closed, with several hundred flights cancelled, “to complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities.”

The decision follows another missile attack on the airport on Sunday, which killed a Pakistani resident and wounded 11 other people. Saturday’s strike on the airport killed four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian and a Sudanese, and wounded 309 others, Saudi authorities said. The Indian Embassy in Riyadh said Sunday that an Indian citizen wounded in the strike later died.

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Sunday. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation authority confirmed the airport had come under attack Sunday evening and said authorities were assessing damage.

The Houthis said the strikes were in response to an intensified Saudi air campaign in Yemen. The group said on Monday that Saudi warplanes and missile units had carried out 119 attacks over the past 24 hours, claiming these had killed at least 14 civilians, including women and children. CNN cannot independently verify the claim. The group also threatened to continue targeting airports and other sites inside the kingdom.

Following Saturday’s attack, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen, having previously resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention.

Houthi strikes on the King Khalid International Airport began last week. Six people were killed and dozens more wounded in attacks on the airport between Tuesday and Thursday, according to Saudi authorities.

One traveler at the airport during Saturday’s attack told Reuters news agency they saw something fly across the sky outside before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

Another recalled hearing an explosion before seeing several people lying wounded on the ground.

An eyewitness video released by Reuters showed large boards and debris strewn across the terminal floor, with people moving through a dust-filled hall.

Travel warning

King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest, serves the capital, Riyadh, a city of about eight million people.

The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries warning their citizens against using the airport.

The UK government warned Sunday against all but essential travel to Jeddah and Dammam, as well as to all Saudi airports except for Medina. It suggested British citizens consider departing Saudi Arabia via land to neighboring countries.

The US Embassy in Riyadh also tightened its travel guidance on Monday, saying US government employees now require special authorization to use any airport in Saudi Arabia. It urged US citizens to exercise “extreme caution” if using Saudi airports and noted that Americans had been detained for photographing the aftermath of recent attacks.

‌The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Sunday told US ​airlines to exercise caution when flying to or ⁠over Saudi Arabia, citing safety threats and navigation system interference.

Saudi Arabia’s Gulf neighbors have condemned the attacks and some have called for unified action against the Houthis.

“Our security is indivisible,” said United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash on Monday. Targeting Saudi Arabia “undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” and there was a “pressing need to revive joint Gulf action” in security and defense, Gargash said on X.

The attacks have exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.

With Iranian assistance, the Houthis have built up a large arsenal of missiles, including ballistic weapons, as well as a range of drones, capable of reaching all of the Kingdom.

The Houthis on Sunday reiterated a warning to all airlines and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, “as they are vulnerable to targeting … with the exception of Mecca and Medina airports.”

‘We’ll make a decision’

Trump said Saturday he plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman following the attack.

“They’re able to defend. The Saudis are good fighters. But I think the attack was a terrible thing,” Trump said when asked whether Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis.

People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on October 10, 2026. AP People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on October 10, 2026. AP

Asked outside the White House whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, Trump said: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”

On Monday, Trump said he had since spoken with the crown prince. He did not elaborate on the content of their conversation, but described the Houthis as “misbehaving very badly.”

Last month, Trump rejected two appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US strikes against the Houthis.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a US citizen was among those killed and said the attacks showed “a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life,” in a post on X.

Saudi miscalculations

The civil war in Yemen flared up this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm.

In retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, the Houthis announced in July they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, and began a campaign of missile attacks against Saudi infrastructure, including oil refineries.

Last month, they conducted a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mocha and closing in on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

That led the Saudi-backed Yemeni government based in Aden to launch a major offensive, but it has struggled to retake much ground. On Monday, it claimed its forces had carried out 1,879 strikes on Houthi targets and killed about 950 fighters within the past 24 hours. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said Monday that 107 people had been killed and 278 wounded, most of them women and children, by Saudi attacks across 13 provinces since September 3. CNN cannot independently verify either side’s figures.

Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through both force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Houthis, then pursuing talks including with their backer, Tehran.

Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say.

Saudi Arabia ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize armed factions fighting the Houthis.

The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia’s broader ambitions to become an international destination for business and tourism.

On Sunday, the Saudi energy ministry said the World Petroleum Congress began as scheduled in Riyadh. Several major oil companies – including Shell and BP – were not represented.

CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman, Michael Williams and Mostafa Salem contributed reporting.

World.title: Egyptian army issues statement following accusations of attacks on Sudanese border
World.content:
RT reported on Monday that the Egyptian Armed Forces issued a statement following accusations it was responsible for an airstrike targeting an artisanal gold mining site near the Egypt-Sudan border—specifically in the Jebel al-Aqaidat area on Saturday.

The statement neither explicitly denied nor confirmed the execution of airstrikes within Sudanese territory, nor did it specify the locations of the operations it alluded to; instead, it merely affirmed that the campaign targets illegal gold mining activities within Egyptian borders.

It announced that law enforcement personnel—comprising both military and civil police forces—are continuing the campaign.

This follows the dropping of warning leaflets addressed to individuals it called “criminal elements,” with the aim of asserting sovereignty within Egyptian territory and protecting the nation’s assets and natural resources.

The statement stressed the deep political and popular ties uniting Egypt and Sudan, highlighting the coexistence enjoyed by millions of Sudanese people living in Egypt.

The army urged the people of the Nile Valley to obtain information from official sources and to avoid being swayed by rumors or what it described as foreign agendas aimed at undermining the fraternal relations between both nations.

While Sudanese human rights and political groups accused Egyptian aircraft of carrying out the raids, the identity of the party responsible has not been independently verified.

There are conflicting reports regarding the casualty toll.

Media outlets cited the Sudan Doctors Network as reporting 13 miners killed and 28 injured—warning that the death toll could rise due to the severity of injuries and the difficulty of reaching the wounded—whereas the Sudanese Emergency Lawyers group said that the death toll had reached 72.

Egypt’s sweeping campaign

Egyptian authorities had warned miners against remaining in the area prior to the attack—described by the Associated Press as a border zone—whereas Sudanese groups said that the raids took place within Sudanese territory.

The Egyptian army’s campaign against illicit gold mining stems from security operations announced earlier this year – on June 22, the Armed Forces began a sweeping campaign within the Southern Military Zone, conducted in coordination with Interior Ministry, targeting what they described as criminal hotspots involved in illegal gold mining, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and irregular migration.

At the time, the army stated that the campaign resulted in the arrest of 223 individuals—including 87 Egyptians and 136 foreign nationals—and the seizure of vehicles, equipment, weapons, and ammunition.

It emphasized that the targeted activities posed a threat to national security and economic stability, in addition to undermining efforts to protect mineral resources.

On August 2, the Egyptian military spokesperson announced the launch of the campaign’s second phase, involving intensified sweeping and raid operations in areas identified as sites of illicit mining activity, carried out in coordination with relevant state agencies.

World.title: Body of flight attendant Azza Ramzy arrives in Alexandria from Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Egyptian Minister of Civil Aviation Sameh al-Hefny on Monday oversaw the arrival of the body of flight attendant Azza Ramzy at Alexandria International Airport.

Ramzy, 28, worked as a flight attendant for the Saudi airline “Flynas” and passed away due to injuries sustained at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh attack.

The body was transported from al-Qassim Airport in Saudi Arabia following her death in the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

Her family was present to receive the remains—a scene defined by grief and loss.

Hefny expressed his deep sorrow over the tragedy, offering his sincere condolences and sympathy to Hefny’s family.

The minister directed that all necessary measures be taken to facilitate the reception of the body and expedite arrival procedures, while ensuring that the family receives full care and support during this difficult time.

The flight attendant’s body arrived aboard a private “Flynas” aircraft at approximately 11:30 PM on Monday. Afterward, the family transported the body to the al-Atf area in the city of al-Mahmoudiya, Beheira Governorate, for the funeral procession.

Widespread mourning

The Governor of Beheira, Jacqueline Azer, expressed her deepest sorrow and grief over the death of the flight attendant—a native of Atf village in the Mahmoudiya district.

Azer extended her sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to the deceased’s family, relatives, and the community of al-Atf, ​​praying that Allah grant her mercy.

Grief fell over the city of Mahmoudiya in Beheira Governorate following the announcement of Ramzy’s death.

Neighbors gathered outside the deceased’s home on Sunday and Monday to offer their condolences to the mourning family, gripped by shock.

Social media posts paid moving tributes to the late flight attendant, offering prayers for mercy and forgiveness for her, and for patience and solace for her family.

AlQahera News reported that the Egyptian diplomatic mission is monitoring the health status of Egyptians injured in the attack, while simultaneously finalized procedures to repatriate the flight attendant’s body.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation had announced that a Houthi attack on Saturday targeting the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh resulted in 12 deaths and 309 injuries, involving citizens and residents of various nationalities.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Sudan arrests perpetrator of shooting incident which killed 2 Egyptians
World.content:
Sudanese authorities have arrested the perpetrator of a shooting incident targeting two Egyptian nationals in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum.

The Egyptian Foreign Ministry issued a statement reporting that a gunman opened fire on several Egyptian truck drivers, resulting in the deaths of two drivers and the injury of another.

Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty ordered the Egyptian ambassador to urgently contact Sudanese authorities to ascertain the circumstances of the incident, check on the condition of the injured citizen, and take all necessary measures to repatriate the deceased as quickly as possible.

The official spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry, Ambassador Nader Zaki, said that the Egyptian Ambassador to Sudan, Yasser Sorour, immediately contacted Sudanese authorities, who reported that they had succeeded in arresting the perpetrator.

The Egyptian Ambassador met with the Governor of Khartoum, who had come to the embassy specifically to offer condolences and check on the condition of the injured citizen; the medical team overseeing his treatment confirmed that he required urgent surgery.

World.title: Liberia: Gbeisay’s Call to Abolish Jury Trials Sparks Constitutional Showdown, Raises Fears of Concentrating Justice in Judges’ Hands
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberia’s top judge has declared that the country’s trial jury system has been so badly compromised that it may no longer be worth keeping. That position has set the Judiciary against the legal profession and a sitting senator, and has raised the question of what protects a verdict once the jury is gone.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. made the call on Monday at the opening of the Supreme Court’s October Term. He told the courtroom that jury manipulation was eroding the administration of justice in both civil and criminal matters. “A corrupt jury is worse than no jury at all,” he said.



Within hours, the proposal had drawn a response from the Liberia National Bar Association (LNBA), a challenge from Senator Darius Dillon, and warnings from lawyers who say the plan would trade one weakness for another.

The Chief Justice’s Evidence

Gbeisay did not present the call as theory. He pointed to reported cases of jury tampering in Nimba, Grand Gedeh, Bomi and Margibi counties, involving charges ranging from rape to drug trafficking. He also referred to suspected interference in proceedings at Criminal Court “C” in Monrovia.

The earliest example dates to 2022 in the Eighth Judicial Circuit in Nimba County. The Chief Justice alleged that a deputy marshal assigned to the circuit had been used as a conduit to compromise a jury.

In Republic of Liberia v. David Nagbe, a rape trial in Grand Gedeh County during the May Term of 2025, tampering was reportedly identified four days after an acquittal. In Republic of Liberia v. George Bongar, another rape case, this time in Bomi County during the May Term of 2026, alleged tampering surfaced 19 days after an acquittal.

In Margibi County, he cited the drug case Republic of Liberia v. Quita Dolo et al., in which interference was reportedly suspected while proceedings were still pending.

He also discussed a US$100,000 drug-related case before Criminal Court “C” and a separate matter in which allegations of jury tampering and misconduct emerged seven days after an acquittal. According to the address, Judge Ousman F. Fieka investigated the latter and established gross jury tampering.

The Chief Justice also noted that jurors are members of the public, not Judiciary employees, but that their conduct nonetheless reflects on the courts.

The Bar Says Fix It First

The LNBA responded the same day. Its President, Cllr. Juah Lawson, condemned jury tampering and said anyone who corrupts a juror, attempts to, or serves as an intermediary strike at the integrity of the justice system. “Such conduct must have consequences,” he said.

The Bar stopped short of backing abolition. Lawson accepted the Chief Justice’s invitation for the Legislature, the International Bar, the Law Reform Commission and other stakeholders to examine the proposal and pursue constitutional reform, but drew a line around what that acceptance means. “The LNBA accepts the invitation to participate in this intervention,” he said. “However, our participation should not be understood as an endorsement of abolition.”

Lawson said trial by jury holds an important place in Liberia’s constitutional framework and argued for diagnosis before surgery. “Before we contemplate abandoning the institution itself, we should carefully examine why there is failure in particular instances and whether those failures may be corrected,” he said.

The Association listed areas it wants examined first:

– how jurors are selected and vetted;

– jurors’ security and sequestration;

– their compensation and conditions of service;

– access to jurors and their intermediaries;

– the protection of juror information;

– the role of court personnel; and

– the investigation and prosecution of those behind tampering.

“Liberia must have this conversation,” Lawson said, “but it must be a conversation grounded in evidence, constitutional fidelity and broad stakeholder consultation.”

Analysts who spoke to FrontPage Africa said the response shows the legal profession is willing to consider structural change but wants proof that stronger safeguards and enforcement cannot solve the problem.

Senator Dillon: A Referendum, not a Bill

Senator Dillon took the sharpest position. In a Facebook statement, he rejected the proposal and argued that trial by jury is a constitutionally protected right that cannot be removed through ordinary legislation. Citing Article 20(a) of the 1986 Constitution, he said abolition would require a national referendum.

He also argued that the reported cases point to weak enforcement, not a flawed institution. “We cannot simply seek to undo laws because of our failure to summon the courage to implement and enforce the laws,” Dillon wrote.

His reading of the amendment process is a statement of his own legal position, and the correct procedure would ultimately have to be settled by authoritative legal interpretation. But the constitutional text gives his argument weight. Article 20(a) guarantees due process and a fair hearing, while Article 21(h) provides for the right to a speedy, public and impartial trial by jury of the vicinity in the criminal cases it covers. Any move to abolish or substantially alter that right would call for close analysis of the applicable amendment procedures.

Who Watches the Judge?

The sharpest objection to the proposal is not about juries at all. It concerns what replaces them. A lawyer who spoke to FrontPage Africa on condition of anonymity, citing fear of retribution, strongly opposed abolition. The lawyer argued that handing greater decision-making power to judges, without addressing alleged corruption on the bench, could damage public confidence further.

The lawyer alleged that some judicial officers accept bribes to influence judgments, and that some legal practitioners will not take a case unless clients provide money meant to influence jurors. These claims are serious and have not been independently established. But they point to a possible chain of corruption in which several actors exploit the same weak points.

Critics say this is the accountability gap in the Chief Justice’s plan. Removing jurors eliminates one point of manipulation, but it does not eliminate bribery or intimidation. Someone determined to obtain an unlawful outcome could simply redirect the pressure. Instead of approaching several jurors, that person could focus on the single officer deciding the case.

That does not mean judges are generally corrupt, and nothing in the debate establishes that they are. It means that concentrating a verdict in one set of hands raises the stakes on every safeguard around those hands.

Legal systems worldwide operate judge-only trials fairly, but those systems typically rest on independent courts, transparent processes and credible discipline of misconduct. Liberia’s critics ask whether those foundations are in place. If jurors can be bought, they say, the country must also be able to say what happens when a judge is accused of being bought.

Allegations Are Not Findings

Observers also say the details of the cited cases matter. An allegation raised after an acquittal is not proof that a verdict was improperly obtained, and misconduct in one trial does not necessarily mean the whole system cannot function fairly.

What the public still lacks, they say, is a clear account of which allegations were formally investigated, what evidence was found, whether anyone was charged or disciplined, and whether those findings held up in court. Only Judge Fieka’s inquiry was described in the address as having established tampering.

That information would help separate substantiated corruption from suspicion. It would also show whether the failure lay in the jury system or in the enforcement that should have protected it. Without it, critics say, citizens are being asked to give up a constitutional safeguard before getting a full explanation of why existing laws failed.

Enforcement and Its Gaps

Many of those opposing abolition return to the same point: the law already requires protection of jury proceedings. When a juror is bribed, a court official facilitates tampering or a lawyer tries to influence a verdict, the response should be investigation and prosecution where evidence supports charges, along with professional discipline where it applies.

A credible deterrent depends on misconduct being detected, fairly investigated and punished. When it goes unpunished, scrapping the institution can look like a faster fix than confronting the people responsible. But critics argue that redesigning an institution cannot substitute for enforcement.

The same standard, they say, must apply to judges and lawyers. Allegations should be examined through independent and credible procedures consistent with due process. Judicial officers should not be presumed guilty because rumors circulate, but the authority of the bench should not shield anyone from legitimate scrutiny either.

The Judiciary’s credibility, they add, depends not only on the judgments it delivers but on how it responds when its own processes are questioned.

Questions Any Reform Must Answer

If Liberia moves toward a judge-only model, the questions critics want answered are concrete:

– How are complaints of judicial misconduct investigated, and by whom?

– What disciplinary tools exist, and how transparent are their outcomes?

– Are court proceedings documented well enough to permit meaningful scrutiny?

– What protection exists for those who report corruption inside the legal profession?

These questions, they say, go to the legitimacy of whichever system the country chooses.

Neither model is inherently better. Professional judges may be better placed to explain the legal reasoning behind a verdict, while citizen participation can guard against concentrated state power. The question, observers say, is which arrangement can protect constitutional rights and deliver impartial justice under Liberia’s actual institutional conditions.

The Chief Justice’s invitation to the Legislature, the Bar and the Law Reform Commission offers a chance to move beyond competing declarations. Those following the debate say a credible review should:

– examine the cases cited in the address and establish the status of each investigation and prosecution;

– determine how the alleged interference occurred and whether existing laws were enforced;

– assess the vulnerability of judges and court officials to improper influence, and the effectiveness of discipline;

– consider remedies such as stronger juror screening and protection, tighter security around deliberations, stricter controls on contact with jurors, better reporting channels and more effective bribery investigations; and

– weigh every proposal against constitutional requirements, defendants’ and victims’ rights, the need for timely trials and the courts’ practical capacity.

If a judge-only system is ultimately considered, they say, its backers must explain how judicial independence would be protected, how allegations against judges would be investigated, and how pending and future cases would be handled under the constitutional process required for change.

A reform of this size, they argue, should not be driven by frustration with a series of troubling cases. It should rest on evidence of which arrangements are failing, why, and how the alternative would fix them.

The Question That Remains

No one in the debate disputes that jury tampering, if proven, is a grave offense. A verdict obtained through bribery or intimidation harms defendants, victims and public trust in the rule of law.

But the Chief Justice’s critics maintain that removing juries would not resolve the underlying problem. If the jury system is compromised, they say, it must be repaired. If judges face allegations, those must be investigated fairly and independently. If lawyers are implicated, professional accountability must follow where the evidence supports it.

“No institution should be beyond scrutiny,” as critics put it, and no constitutional right should be set aside without a legally sound and publicly examined justification.

For now, the proposal has opened a debate that reaches well beyond courtroom procedure. Remove the jury, critics say, and the judge becomes even more central to the verdict. Until Liberia can say who holds the judge accountable, the question of whether the country is confronting corruption or only moving the power to decide justice from one place to another will stay unanswered.

World.title: Liberian Senator Warns Washington: Mining Giants and Drug Cartels Are Pushing Liberia Toward ‘State Capture’
World.content:
WASHINGTON, DC — A Liberian senator has told American democracy advocates that his country faces two threats at once: multinational mining companies working through legal deals, and drug cartels working through bribes. He said either one could hollow out Liberia’s democracy from within if it is left unchecked.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Senator Amara M. Konneh is an independent lawmaker from Gbarpolu County in northwestern Liberia and chairs the Senate’s Public Accounts and Audit Committee. He spoke at a private roundtable hosted this month by the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), a U.S.-funded



organization that supports democratic institutions abroad. His remarks are drawn from talking points prepared for the session and reviewed by FrontPageAfrica.

“Liberia is not yet a captured state,” Konneh said, “but we are at the most dangerous point since the war and Ebola.”

The West African nation of about 5.5 million people was founded in 1847 with the backing of freed American slaves. It is still recovering from a civil war that ended in 2003 and from the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic that killed nearly 5,000 Liberians.

‘Legal, so it’s harder’

Konneh said mining makes up 12 percent of Liberia’s gross domestic product and 65 percent of its export earnings. Yet less than 3 percent of that wealth reaches communities directly.

The problem, he argued, starts with the way concessions are negotiated. Liberian law gives the executive branch wide discretion over Mineral Development Agreements. These 25-year contracts are ratified by the legislature and are very hard to amend later. “Companies negotiate with three or four people in Monrovia, not with the country,” he said.

He pointed out that several major operators are renegotiating rail, port and royalty terms at the same time: steelmaker ArcelorMittal, gold miner Bea Mountain, Hummingbird and Bao Chico. On paper Liberia keeps 48 percent of mining value, he said, but stabilization clauses, tax holidays and transfer pricing push the real share far lower.

He also described a system of off-budget signature bonuses and “social contributions,” often paid around elections. He said legislators from mining districts are offered jobs, scholarships and “facilitation fees” of $5,000 to $20,000 to vote for ratification. “This is legalized state capture,” he said. He did not tie any particular company to these payments.

He also warned that private security forces at some concessions are larger and better equipped than the county police. And he said community activists who protested environmental damage have been charged with “economic sabotage.” His examples included Kinjor in Grand Cape Mount County, the community most affected by Bea Mountain’s gold concession, as well as communities in Grand Bassa and Nimba.

‘Illegal, so it’s faster’

The drug trade follows “the same playbook, different commodity,” Konneh said. Traffickers don’t need to buy the whole state, only key people: “an airport baggage handler, an evidence clerk, a police crime services officer, and a port scanner operator.”

He cited two seizures this year. In June, 237 kilograms of cocaine worth an estimated $19.2 million were seized at Roberts International Airport, the country’s main airport. In July, 3.9 metric tons worth about $317 million were seized in Duazon, outside the capital, Monrovia. He said the July haul had links to Spain, Colombia, Serbia, Croatia and Ukraine, and that its value was four times Liberia’s national health budget.

He also pointed to cases inside the country’s own anti-drug agency. On September 29, a court in Margibi County convicted Joe Logan and Lovette Flowers, two agents of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA), of colluding with traffickers, and sentenced each to the maximum 20 years. They had resold cocaine seized at the airport. Konneh said a police Commissioner for Crime Services was also dismissed after admitting to taking a $10,000 bribe in the same network.

Konneh also raised the most politically sensitive case. Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested at the airport and charged on August 19 with conspiracy, facilitation and money laundering. She denies the charges. Konneh criticized the government for destroying the 3.9 tons of cocaine before trial. He predicted the case could collapse over constitutional warrant defects or chain-of-custody problems. If it does, he said, “the public will conclude it’s politics, not justice.”

He placed Liberia within a wider regional crisis. According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), 126.4 metric tons of cocaine were seized in or through West Africa between 2019 and 2024, including 30.8 tons in the Gulf of Guinea corridor along Liberia’s coast. The region has become “a destination market, not just a transit zone,” he said. He also described kush, a cheap synthetic drug blend that first spread in Sierra Leone and now reaches Liberia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, The Gambia and Senegal, mostly among unemployed young people.

Why Washington should care

Konneh framed the issue as a test of American credibility. He said Liberia voted with the United States 89 percent of the time at the United Nations last year and hosts the largest U.S. diplomatic presence in West Africa.

“If Liberians conclude that America only cares when there’s a big drug bust but stays silent when a $2 billion mining deal is signed behind closed doors, we lose credibility for democracy,” he said. “China and Russia don’t ask about beneficial ownership. Cartels don’t ask about human rights.”

He noted that Sweden closed its embassy in Monrovia last month. He also urged the European Union to keep its delegation in Liberia fully staffed rather than move its functions to Abidjan in neighboring Côte d’Ivoire.

The asks

At home, Konneh said, the Senate is working on several measures. On mining, it wants to require that all mining agreements, amendments, beneficial owners and payments be published before ratification. It also proposes independent valuation of iron ore transfer pricing, modeled on Botswana’s approach to diamonds, and sending 20 percent of royalties directly to district development funds.

On drugs, the proposals would require that seized evidence be kept until final judgment. Officers at the airport, the Freeport of Monrovia and the security agencies would face polygraphs, lifestyle audits and drug tests. An unexplained-wealth law would allow assets to be seized without a criminal conviction.

From Washington, he asked for help that is “practical, not preachy”:

• Funding to monitor Liberia’s drug court and commercial court

• Forensic audits of the ArcelorMittal rail and port concession and of Bea Mountain’s royalties

• Resumed mentoring of vetted Liberian drug units by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, with oversight

• Equipment for scanners and sniffer dogs, including maintenance

• Help from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) in tracing money in three or four specific cases

• A $10 million pilot program to track large cash donations ahead of the 2029 elections

He also urged that Global Magnitsky sanctions, the U.S. tool for penalizing corrupt officials and human rights abusers, be used “surgically.” Their targets should include enablers in mining licensing who move money into U.S. real estate, he said, and Washington should state publicly why it acts.

“Help us establish transparent regulations before finalizing agreements,” Konneh said, “and support impartial enforcement of laws after confiscation — whether the suspect is an airport baggage handler, a police crimes services director, a former Vice President, or a multinational corporation.”

World.title: Liberia: Saudi Rice Trial: Gbassay Rejects Guilty Verdict, Declares Innocence, Alleges Pressure to Become State Witness
World.content:
The ordained Baptist minister says she refused to testify for the prosecution, and warns that the pursuit of accountability must not become “score-settling masquerading as justice”

MONROVIA — Days after a jury at Criminal Court “C” adjudged her guilty in the Saudi Rice corruption case, former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) official Rosetta L. Gbassay Bowah has rejected the verdict, declaring her innocence in a Facebook post.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

In the lengthy statement, she thanked family, friends, colleagues and fellow clergy for an outpouring of prayers, encouragement, solidarity and love since Friday. She said the support had “renewed my confidence in the face of circumstances that were clearly intended to break me.” As the legal process continues, she said, she wishes to reassure her supporters of her “absolute innocence” and her confidence that “the truth will ultimately prevail.”



Central to her statement is an allegation that she was pressured to cooperate with the prosecution. Gbassay Bowah said that if she has committed any “crime,” it is that she faithfully performed her lawful duties in accordance with her Terms of Reference and the obligations of her office.

She added that her other “crime” may be that she refused what she described as persistent efforts by her accuser and the prosecutors to persuade her to “cooperate” by serving as a State witness.

The post offers no evidence for the claim, and it has not been independently verified. Her position, however, was unequivocal. “As a servant of the living God, an ordained Baptist Reverend,” she said, she could never conspire to testify falsely against any person or speak of matters about which she has no knowledge. “My conscience is not for sale,” she wrote.

She described the personal cost she believes such a compromise would carry. No temporary advantage, she said, is worth “inviting the curse that follows bearing false witness against the innocent.”

That burden, she said, is one she will not bring upon herself, her children or future generations. Regardless of “pressure, intimidation, or schemes,” she said, she remains steadfast in her conviction that God, “in His own time and according to His perfect will,” will vindicate her.

Her statement reads as much like a sermon as a legal defense. Gbassay Bowah, who is an ordained Baptist Reverend, wrote that her faith is “built on nothing less than Jesus Christ, His blood, and His righteousness,” and that it gives her the courage to persevere “through this difficult chapter.” She framed the ordeal as a season of trial and tribulation.

Her appeal then widened from her own situation to the state of the nation. Addressing her “co-workers in the vineyard of the Lord,” she urged fellow clergy to keep praying for Liberia, noting that “it is one thing to preach about injustice, and quite another to experience it personally.”

She warned that the country stands at a “critical crossroads” and risks a “vicious cycle of bitterness, vengeance, political persecution, and score-settling masquerading as justice.” Liberia, she said, needs healing, redemption and a renewed commitment to the rule of law, fairness and national unity. She called on citizens to resist the temptation to weaponize political differences, and to work toward a future in which justice is impartial, truth is honored and every citizen is treated with dignity and respect.

Her words arrive against a very different reading of Friday’s outcome. In a statement dated Oct. 10, the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce (AREPT) welcomed the verdicts as a “significant milestone” in the Government of Liberia’s efforts to combat corruption and protect public resources.

According to AREPT, the jury adjudged eight of the 13 defendants guilty, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf. Three defendants were acquitted, and the jury returned inconclusive verdicts on two others.

The case arose from AREPT’s investigation into the alleged misappropriation of 29,412 bags of rice, valued at about US$500,000, donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 2023 for disaster victims and vulnerable Liberians. The indictment alleged that 25,054 of those bags were unlawfully diverted or misapplied.

According to the jury tally, Gbassay Bowah was adjudged guilty of Theft of Property, Misapplication of Entrusted Property and Criminal Conspiracy. Jurors were hung on the counts of Abuse of Office and Economic Sabotage.

AREPT Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin said the Taskforce is ready for any appeal. “We are prepared,” he said, adding that if the defendants go to the Supreme Court, AREPT will “equally go there and defeat them there.” The Taskforce also said it respects the judicial process and the rights of all parties, including the right to appeal.

World.title: Liberia: Bishop Kortu Brown Backs Growing Calls for a New Political Force ahead of 2029 Presidential Elections
World.content:
Bishop Kortu Brown Backs Growing Calls for a New Political Force ahead of 2029 Presidential Elections

BREWERVILLE, Montserrado County, Liberia, Oct. 12, 2026 — A prominent Liberian clergyman has backed growing calls for a “third lane” in the country’s politics ahead of the 2029 elections. He cautioned, however, that any new movement must offer genuine change rather than recycle familiar faces.

He said such moves were part of the reason ordinary citizens “still yearn for something else politically,” and he urged Liberians to be honest with themselves. “They must mean it when they say they want real change,” he said.

The bishop also said the credibility of any third force would depend on who leads it. “Liberians will not buy an empty third lane,” he said. “It can’t be a contest of political rivals who are dissatisfied with one another, or people who want revenge against one another or to fool one another.”



Instead, he called for “a new line-up of sincere and professional Liberians who are genuinely interested in promoting the political, economic, social and religious causes of the ordinary people.”

“UP and CDC are now brand names with big followings,” Brown said. “However, people are still politically thirsty.”
