World.title: Liberia: House Opens for Third Quarter’s Official Business Today Amid Lawmakers’ Revolt in Demand of Personal Benefits
World.content:
Today marks the first day for official business as members of the Legislature return from their second constituency break, but with uncertainty hanging over one of the chambers – the House of Representatives.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

It all began Friday, October 9, 2026 when the Legislature officially resumed official duty following nearly three months of rest when majority member of the House of Representatives; over 40 numbers, reportedly boycotted and held a separate meeting to discuss grievances against the chamber’s leadership.



What Do They Want?

From inside sources, the aggrieved lawmakers under the banner of “Reformists,” are demanding benefits, legislative support funds and other resources they allege have been withheld under the current leadership.

Representative Frank Saah Foko of Montserrado County District #9 said Friday’s meeting was intended to give lawmakers a collective platform to express their concerns. He indicated that another meeting had been scheduled for Sunday, October 11, when the group was expected to determine its next steps.

Joe described the concerns as recurring and said lawmakers intended to engage the relevant authorities to press their demands. Asked whether the gathering was intended to organize the removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, he said he was unaware of such a plan.

Representative Samuel Enders of Montserrado County District #6 similarly said the discussions concerned benefits and district support, adding that he knew of no effort to remove the House leadership.

Representative Abu Kamara of Montserrado County District #15 described the meeting positively but offered little detail about its outcome.

From afar, this is a precondition set by the Reformists – a group that comprises several of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon’s own allies.

Worst Case

With the overgrown numbers of nearly 50 or more members – both from the ruling class, opposition and independent, reports also have it that the “Reformists” are also thinking otherwise; they are seeking signatures on a proposed 12-count resolution targeting the House leadership.

Though the precise contents of the proposed resolution have not been publicly established, and the lawmakers who addressed the meeting did not openly confirm that removing Koon and Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah was their objective.

These explanations by lawmakers who openly spoke to the matter leave an important gap between the public grievances and the reported effort to circulate a 12-count resolution.

Deputy Speaker Acknowledges Concerns Are Genuine

Since Friday’s showdown, Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah issued his first public response with acknowledgement that the demands are genuine concerns with regard to the payment of lawmakers’ legitimate benefits, which are overdue.

Fallah Gives Hope

On the heel of the rigmarole, Deputy Speaker Fallah has made a promise that his colleagues can hope on.

In a nutshell, the House of Representatives’ second most powerful man informed his colleagues that the deal for the payment of these benefits is almost done, and such, they should return to conduct the Liberian people’s business.

“Let me assure you that under the leadership of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, every legitimate effort is being exerted to engage all relevant government institutions so that these benefits are processed and paid without further delay. The signals we are receiving are positive, and I am confident that this matter will be resolved in the soonest possible time,” wrote T-Five as he is popularly referred to in Liberian politics.

“However, as we have entered the third quarter of our third session, I humbly plead with all colleagues to return to work. The Liberian people entrusted us with a sacred mandate—to legislate, to provide oversight, and to represent their voices. Our absence from the chambers delays the progress of the nation and undermines the very purpose for which we were elected,” he stated.

Lawmakers Called To Order

In a clarion call to order, Deputy Speaker Fallah, who represents Lofa County Electoral District #1 in the 55th Legislature called on members of the House to demonstrate leadership, patience, and unity in times of challenge.

By returning to work, he reckoned, this will send a powerful message to the Liberian people: that while they fight for their rights, they will never abandon their duty to them.

“Let us therefore rise above frustration, stand together in solidarity, and continue the work of nation-building. The benefits will come, but the work of Liberia cannot wait,” Fallah added.

A Test To The Gavel

In the face of the latest drama at the Lower House of Liberia’s bicameral Legislature, and on the heel of the zealous plead by Deputy Speaker Fallah, the First Day Sitting of The Third Quarter of the Third Session of the 55th Legislature poses a stern test to the gable of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon.

It still remains unclear whether the “Reformists” will turn in their huge numbers to sit under the authority of their boss.

A Rebellion From Within

The lawmakers gathered in Schefflin, Margibi County, on Friday, while Koon and a small group of legislators attended the formal reopening ceremony at the Capitol following the legislative break.

The reported boycott was striking: only 13 of the House’s 73 members reportedly attended the ceremony, including the Speaker.

The gathering outside Monrovia also brought together lawmakers who hold influential committee positions, including chairs and co-chairs responsible for scrutinizing public procurement, government contracts, natural resources, the judiciary and public expenditure.

Among those reportedly associated with the Reformist Movement are Jeremiah Garwo Sokan Sr. of Grand Gedeh County District #1, chairman of the House Committee on Mines, Natural Resources and Environment; Prince K. Koinah of Bong County District #1, chairman of the Committee on Contracts, Monopolies, Public Procurement and Concessions and co-chair of the Public Accounts and Expenditure Committee; and Sam P. Jallah of Bomi County District #3, co-chair of the Hydrocarbon Committee.

Other lawmakers reportedly linked to the movement include Bernard Blue Benson Jr. of Montserrado County District #17, chairman of the Committee on Information, Broadcasting, Culture and Tourism; Anthony Williams of Maryland County District #2, co-chair of the Peace, Religion and National Reconciliation Committee; Augustine B. Chiewolo of Lofa County District #5, chairman of the Committee on Resettlement, Repatriation, Relief and Readjustment; and Johnson S. N. Williams Sr. of River Gee County District #3, chairman of the House Committee on Judiciary.

Their reported involvement gives the agitation institutional significance. These are not merely lawmakers expressing dissatisfaction from the margins of the chamber; several occupy positions that place them at the center of legislative oversight and administration.

Why Koon’s Own Allies Matter

The political significance of the agitation lies partly in the reported involvement of lawmakers who have worked alongside Koon and occupy senior committee positions.

Leadership in the House depends not only on formal authority but also on the ability to maintain working relationships with members, coordinate legislative business and secure cooperation across committees.

When discontent emerges among lawmakers associated with the leadership, it can complicate that process even if no formal removal motion is ultimately pursued.

The reported involvement of lawmakers overseeing procurement, public accounts and other major portfolios also places questions about financial administration at the center of the dispute. Their allegations, however, should not be treated as proof of misconduct without supporting documentation or findings by an appropriate authority.

The movement’s leverage will depend on more than the number of lawmakers attending a meeting. Its members would need to demonstrate sustained coordination, agreement on their demands and a willingness to pursue a common course of action.

The next meeting could therefore be an important test of whether Friday’s gathering was a temporary show of discontent or the beginning of a more organized challenge.

The Koffa-Koon Crisis Offers a Warning

The confrontation inevitably recalls the prolonged leadership dispute that preceded Koon’s emergence as Speaker.

During that earlier crisis, lawmakers aligned with what became known as the Majority Bloc boycotted sessions and held parallel meetings. They subsequently declared Koon Speaker and Fallah Deputy Speaker while Cllr. Fonati Koffa remained the sitting Speaker.

The dispute eventually reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that actions taken outside the House chamber while the Speaker remained in office and present were ultra vires.

Koffa later resigned, clearing the way for Koon’s election as Speaker, while Fallah retained the deputy speakership.

That episode exposed deep divisions within the House and demonstrated how disagreements over legislative leadership can disrupt institutional operations and raise questions about the validity of decisions taken during a political confrontation.

The current agitation does not automatically mean the House is headed for a repeat of that crisis. The circumstances may differ, and the Reformist Movement has not publicly confirmed that removing Koon and Fallah is its objective.

Nevertheless, the earlier dispute provides an important institutional backdrop. Any attempt to change the leadership would have to be assessed against the House’s rules and applicable constitutional requirements, rather than simply the strength of a faction’s public declarations.

The previous crisis also illustrates the risks of parallel meetings and competing claims to authority when lawmakers fail to resolve disputes through established legislative procedures.

The Speaker’s Office Keeps Its Distance

When contacted about the reported effort to remove the Speaker, Vehzelee Sumo, head of communications for the Speaker’s Office, declined to comment, saying the office would respond at the appropriate time.

The office had previously said it was unaware of any plan to remove Koon and would not comment on rumors.

The limited response leaves unanswered questions about the allegations involving benefits, legislative support funds and administrative irregularities.

A substantive response from the leadership could clarify which resources have been requested, what has been disbursed and whether disagreements exist over the procedures governing legislative support. Such information would help distinguish a political dispute from a documented administrative failure.

World.title: Liberia: Climate Change and Liberia: What It Means and What We Must Do
World.content:
When floodwater enters a home, a farmer loses a harvest, or the sea washes away land, families suffer. Children miss school, businesses lose income, and communities struggle to recover. Climate change increases these risks. Understanding it helps us protect ourselves and our country.

By Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo

Executive Director, Environmental Protection Agency of Liberia

Climate change means lasting changes in the Earth’s temperatures and usual weather patterns. Weather is what happens today: sunshine, rain, or wind. Climate is the pattern we expect over many years, including our rainy and dry seasons.



The Earth is warming mainly because human activities release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere. Burning coal, petrol, diesel, and gas produces these gases. Cutting and burning forests adds to the problem because trees absorb carbon dioxide, one of the main gases warming the planet. These gases act like an extra blanket around the Earth, holding in more heat.

Liberia contributes very little to global emissions, yet we are highly vulnerable. Many Liberians depend on farming, live near the coast, or lack strong roads, proper drainage, and reliable basic services. These conditions make climate pressures harder to withstand.

Along our coast, rising sea levels increase the danger of flooding and erosion, threatening homes, roads, businesses, and livelihoods. For farmers, changing rainfall makes planting decisions harder. Heavy rain, dry spells, and higher temperatures can damage crops and reduce harvests. When farmers produce less, their incomes suffer and food supplies come under pressure.

Health and daily work are also affected. Extreme heat makes outdoor work more difficult. Floods can contaminate drinking water and damage roads, disrupting access to clinics, schools, and markets. Families with fewer resources often have the greatest difficulty recovering.

Not every flood or damaged shoreline is caused by climate change alone. Blocked drains, poorly planned construction, and destruction of wetlands can worsen the damage. We must address both climate change and the local practices that make communities more vulnerable.

We cannot end climate change overnight, but we can slow it down and reduce its harm. This means cutting the gases that cause warming while preparing for changes already happening. Cleaner energy, forest protection, stronger infrastructure, and better weather warnings all have a role.

The Government of Liberia, through the EPA and its partners, is already acting. Coastal protection projects in Sinoe County and metropolitan Monrovia are being implemented to reduce risks from coastal flooding and erosion and protect livelihoods. The Climate Information Systems project is strengthening weather monitoring and early warnings so that farmers, fishermen, and communities can better prepare for dangerous weather.

Government is also turning waste into a resource. Working with the Monrovia City Corporation, the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, and international partners, the EPA has helped establish a composting facility in Fiamah. It is designed to turn food scraps and other organic waste into compost that improves soil for farming. This shows how better waste management can support cleaner communities and agriculture.

The EPA is also enforcing environmental laws. Nationwide inspections have covered mining operations, industrial sites, coastal areas, and waste facilities across all 15 counties. Actions include stopping illegal operations, ordering corrections, and imposing fines. Protecting rivers, forests, wetlands, and farmland also helps communities withstand climate pressures. Development must provide jobs without sacrificing people’s health and livelihoods.

However, the needs exceed available resources. Coastal protection, drainage, weather services, and nationwide monitoring require sustained funding, equipment, trained personnel, and maintenance. Families also need affordable alternatives to activities that damage the environment.

Large emitters carry a greater responsibility. Countries and industries that have released the most warming gases, especially over many decades, should make deep and rapid emissions cuts. Financing tree planting elsewhere should accompany real reductions from their own factories, power plants, and transport systems.

Wealthy developed countries also have responsibilities to help poorer countries respond. The Paris Agreement requires developed countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing emissions and preparing for climate impacts. Liberia needs accessible funding, useful technology, and training that reach communities most at risk.

Major emitters should also support people facing losses that cannot be prevented, including destroyed homes and lost livelihoods. Liberia should not carry an unfair financial burden for a crisis it contributed little to creating. This is a matter of fairness.

Our small contribution to global emissions does not remove our own responsibilities. Citizens should join government’s efforts by reporting pollution, protecting public facilities, keeping rubbish out of drains and streams, avoiding waste burning, saving electricity, and following official weather warnings. Keeping drains clear will not stop global warming, but it can reduce local flood damage.

Businesses must respect environmental permits, reduce waste, and correct damage from their operations. Schools, religious institutions, traditional leaders, and the media can explain climate issues in everyday language and local languages. Communities should help shape projects affecting their homes and livelihoods, while holding government accountable for results.

Every Liberian deserves a safe home, clean water, dependable food, and a secure future. Government is taking action, but lasting progress requires citizens, businesses, and international partners to contribute. Large emitters must fulfil their responsibilities, and we must fulfil ours. Protecting Liberia is a shared responsibility.

World.title: Liberia: Chief Justice Gbeisay Calls for Unity Among Liberians, Particularly People in Gompa City, Nimba County
World.content:
Liberia’s Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr.

MONROVIA – Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. has called on all Liberians, particularly the People of Nimba County to remain united and respect the rule of Law.

Speaking during the opening of the Supreme Court October Term on Monday, October 12, he said, “I want to use this occasion to call on all Liberians, especially my fellow Citizens in Gompa City, Nimba County, to unite irrespective of tribe or ethnic background. Tribalism destroys national unity and peace, and further triggers violence and war. Liberia has traveled down that road before and we know where it led us. We must not go there again. The Gbeisay’s Bench will enforce all legitimate judgments without fear or favor and irrespective of its consequences.’’

Chief Justice Gbeisay pointed out that the law is blind and the only tribe recognized before a court of competent jurisdiction is Justice. He expanded on the court’s enforcement of judgments, particularly in Montserrado and Nimba Counties.



He said that as the court works to expand access to justice across the country, enforcing court judgments remains a daunting challenge. The Chief Justice pointed to an incident of the court’s final judgment at the 8th Judicial Circuit Court in 2018, wherein some members of the Mandingo Ethnic Group in Gompa mobilized and violently obstructed the enforcement of judgment against a member of their tribe.

Speaking further, he said the spokesperson of the group, Mark Jabateh, took to the media and openly declared that he could kill the former Chief Justice, Francis Korkpor, if he had laid eyes on him. “The past government took no action; instead, the present government rewarded him with a ministerial position in government.’’

On the recent incident in Gompa City, he said that, in an effort to enforce the final judgment, the former Gompa City Mayor used tribal sentiment, claiming that Mandingo people have no land rights in that city.

Accordingly, the former Mayor of Gompa City mobilized some members of the Mano and Gio Communities against the court and especially against him as Chief Justice.

“Up to and including today, my family remains under threat and subject to constant attacks. Some individuals have vowed to kill me for allegedly giving their land to Mandingo people.’’

Among other things, he added, ‘‘the Judgments of our courts are based on evidence and the applicable laws. This is the oath I took and continue to hold.”

World.title: Peter Bon Jallah Trial Nears Showdown as Defense Rests; Verdict Expected October 22
World.content:
Prosecution Set to Present Rebuttal Witnesses Next Week as Court Moves Toward Closing Arguments in High-Profile Sexual Assault Case

By:Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-The trial of Peter Bon Jallah, alleged rape defendant, at Criminal Court “E” at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia is approaching a decisive stage, with the defense having rested its case and the court expected to hear prosecution rebuttal witnesses next week before closing arguments and a possible verdict on Thursday, October 22.



The case, being heard by Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. without a jury, is expected to conclude, if the remaining proceedings proceed according to the current schedule.

Following the defense’s presentation of eight witnesses, including Jallah himself, the court convened for the appearance of representatives from three institutions subpoenaed by the defense.

These institutions include, Orange GSM, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, and the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital, JFK.

The defense sought the institutions’ participation in connection with documents relevant to issues raised during the proceedings.

Their appearance forms part of the final evidentiary steps before the case moves into its rebuttal and closing-argument phases.

The court is scheduled to resume on Monday, October 19, and Tuesday, October 20, when the prosecution is expected to present rebuttal witnesses in response to evidence introduced by the defense.

Sources familiar with the trial indicate that the prosecution could call as many as eight rebuttal witnesses, although the final number will depend on how the proceedings unfold.

If the prosecution completes its rebuttal evidence within the anticipated period, the parties are expected to present their closing arguments on Thursday, October 22.

Judge Wesseh Aphansus Wesseh could then deliver a verdict the same day, determining whether Jallah is guilty or not guilty of the charges against him.

The projected timeline, however, remains dependent on the completion of the outstanding proceedings and the court’s directions.

A Trial Marked by Contested Testimony and Forensic Evidence

Jallah’s trial has drawn attention because of the seriousness of the allegations, the testimony of the 16-year-old alleged victim, and the competing arguments over forensic evidence, medical findings and the circumstances surrounding the alleged incidents.

The defendant is facing allegations involving rape, gang rape or statutory rape, and kidnapping in connection with the case. He has pleaded not guilty and denied the allegations.

During the prosecution’s presentation, the alleged victim testified about alleged sexual encounters involving Jallah between November 2025 and January 2026.

The prosecution also presented police investigators, medical personnel and forensic evidence in an effort to establish its case.

The prosecution’s witnesses included Rwandan forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije, whose testimony concerning DNA analysis became one of the central evidentiary issues in the trial.

Bavugirije testified that DNA profiles recovered from clothing submitted for examination were consistent with a match to Jallah’s profile.

His testimony also addressed the limitations of the forensic findings, including the fact that DNA evidence alone cannot establish when or how a sexual act occurred or independently determine whether force, consent, penetration or criminal intent was involved.

The handling of the samples also became a point of dispute, with questions raised about collection, packaging, transportation and the chain of custody.

Those issues featured in the defense’s challenge to the prosecution’s forensic evidence.

Defense Challenges Prosecution’s Account

Throughout the trial, Jallah and his lawyers have disputed the prosecution’s account and questioned whether the evidence presented established his criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.

Jallah denied the alleged encounters and challenged aspects of the alleged victim’s account, including the circumstances surrounding the reported incidents.

He also raised an alibi involving the Du-Port Road and Mikey Gray areas.

The defense questioned the significance of the medical evidence, arguing that the findings presented should not automatically be treated as proof that the alleged crimes occurred as described.

Jallah also disputed the circumstances under which biological samples were collected, alleging that the police planted saliva DNA evidence.

That allegation remains a defense claim and has not been established as a finding of the court.

Questions concerning mobile-phone records were another feature of the defense case.

Defendant Jallah had sought records covering January 1 to 3 and the Christmas period, arguing that the information could help address disputed issues about his movements and the allegations against him.

The defense’s presentation of eight witnesses, including Jallah, marked the conclusion of its main evidentiary case, although the scheduled appearance of institutional representatives and the prosecution’s anticipated rebuttal evidence remain important steps before the matter can be submitted for a final decision.

Judge Previously Rejected Acquittal Motion

The approaching conclusion follows an earlier critical ruling by Judge Wesseh, who on September 30, rejected a defense motion seeking Jallah’s acquittal after the prosecution had presented 12 witnesses.

At the time, the court determined that the prosecution’s evidence was not “wholly insufficient” to warrant allowing the case to proceed.

That ruling required Jallah to present his defense but did not constitute a determination of guilt.

The defense had challenged several aspects of the prosecution’s case, including the identification of the alleged crime scene, the interpretation of medical findings and the reliability and handling of the DNA evidence.

The rejection of the acquittal motion allowed the trial to proceed into the defense phase, culminating in Jallah’s testimony and the presentation of additional defense witnesses.

With the defense now having rested, the prosecution will have an opportunity to respond to relevant defense evidence through rebuttal witnesses before both sides make their final submissions.

October 22, A Potential Turning Point

The next two scheduled court days could prove decisive in determining whether the case reaches closing arguments and a verdict within the anticipated timeframe.

The prosecution is expected to use Monday, October 19, and Tuesday, October 20, to present rebuttal witnesses.

If the proceedings are completed as planned, the lawyers will argue their respective cases on Thursday, October 22, after which the judge could make a decision.

Unlike a jury trial, the final determination in this case rests with the presiding judge, who must assess the evidence admitted during the proceedings and apply the relevant law to determine whether the prosecution has proved the charges.

For the prosecution, the remaining task is to respond to the defense’s challenges and establish that the evidence satisfies the applicable criminal standard of proof.

For the defense, the closing arguments will provide an opportunity to consolidate its challenges to the credibility of the testimony, the interpretation of the forensic and medical evidence, and the prosecution’s overall case.

Until the judge delivers a verdict, Jallah remained entitled to the presumption of innocence, and the allegations against him remain allegations to be determined through the judicial process.

The scheduled conclusion on October 22 would bring the trial to a major turning point in a case that has tested the court’s consideration of witness testimony, forensic evidence and competing accounts of the alleged events.

World.title: There is no minor sport in Zambia – HH
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says sports development has emerged as an important driver of social and economic development in the country.

Delivering his address to the 14th National Assembly, President Hichilema said there is no minor sport in Zambia.

He said government is expanding and modernising sports infrastructure across all provinces, strengthening talent identification and development, and supporting greater participation in international competitions.

“Sports development has emerged as an important driver of social and economic development. There is no minor sport in Zambia,” President Hichilema said.

The Head of State said government is promoting professionalism and will work closely with the private sector to commercialise sport.

He said the move is aimed at creating employment, generating income and expanding opportunities for young people.

“We are expanding and modernising sports infrastructure across all provinces, strengthening talent identification and development, and supporting greater participation in international competitions,” he said.

President Hichilema concluded: “We are promoting professionalism and we will work closely with the private sector to commercialise sport, to create employment, to generate income and to expand opportunities for our young people.”

World.title: OPINION: Rule of Law should prevail on political chants at Stadia
World.content:
By Mwewa Senkwe

So, over the weekend, we saw political chants at two stadia on the Copperbelt. I personally don’t find such behaviour appropriate at a football stadium. Football should remain football. But whatever rules apply must apply equally to everyone.

But is this the first time we are seeing political gestures at stadia in Zambia? Certainly not.

What I find interesting is that football players have been doing the “salt sana” gesture for some time now. Nobody was yapping. Nobody seemed particularly bothered. Now that some soccer fans are chanting opposition slogans, as always, the powers that be are up in arms. The impression being created is that when people chant slogans in support of the ruling party, everything is fine, but when they chant something supporting the opposition, it suddenly becomes intolerable.

While I find the behaviour by some football fans inappropriate, I find the reaction from some sections of the ruling party even more worrying.

If political slogans and gestures are prohibited at football matches, then let the rule apply to everyone – ruling party, opposition, players and supporters alike. We cannot have one standard when the political message favours us and suddenly discover the law when the message is against us.

Dear Red Team, it is a fact that you can never be loved by the whole country.

In a functioning democracy, disagreement should not automatically be treated as hostility. People must be free to express their political opinions within the confines of the law. And when they break the law, let the law deal with them – not political intimidation, threats or selective outrage.

If the fans broke the law, let the law deal with them. If they breached football regulations, let the competent football authorities’ deal with them. What should concern us is when political power attempts to substitute itself for either process.

Somehow, I think it is the duty of patriotic Zambians to continuously school our political parties and politicians on the fundamental principles of democracy. I say this because no political party in Zambia can honestly claim to be fundamentally democratic. They are all, to a large extent, owner-led, and too often tolerance for opposing views disappears once political power is at stake.

So, colleagues, allow people to express themselves freely, of course within the confines of the law. Where the law has been broken, let the law take its course. Where no law has been broken, let people speak, even when what they are saying makes those in power uncomfortable.

Allow the rule of law to prevail, not political convenience.

World.title: Zambia Takes Debt, Power And Lobito Corridor Agenda To IMF-World Bank Meetings In Bangkok
World.content:
Zambia has taken a financing and investment agenda to the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. Its aims are to secure approval of a new IMF programme, raise money for power and transport projects, and pitch the country to global investors.

Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane is leading the delegation to the meetings, which run until October 18. With him are Secretary to the Treasury Mr Felix Nkulukusa, Bank of Zambia Governor Dr Denny Kalyalya, Ministry of Energy permanent secretary Mr Arnold Simwaba and Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development permanent secretary Mr Hapenga Kabeta, among others.

The delegation arrives on the back of two recent developments. On October 9, Zambia reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF on a proposed 36-month, US$1.47 billion Extended Credit Facility. Days earlier, on October 5 and 6, Lusaka hosted a World Bank-supported coordination meeting on the Lobito Corridor.

A statement from the Office of the Secretary to the Treasury said these milestones give Zambia a foundation for talks on macroeconomic stability, fiscal and debt sustainability, infrastructure financing and investment. It said the engagements are aligned with the Grow Zambia Agenda championed by President Hakainde Hichilema.

The Government expects the Bangkok talks to strengthen the country’s productive capacity, support technology transfer, expand market access and secure sustainable development financing. The statement said that should ultimately mean higher household incomes and better living standards.

Most immediately, the delegation is focused on the new IMF programme. The statement said the talks with the Fund will advance the successor facility, including the agreed reforms, prior actions and other requirements for consideration by IMF management and approval by its executive board.

“The delegation’s programme includes the International Monetary and Financial Committee Plenary, consultations with the IMF’s African and Fiscal Affairs Departments, and the African Caucus and Governors’ meeting with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva,” the statement said.

Beyond the programme itself, the discussions will cover sovereign debt vulnerabilities, borrowing costs, domestic revenue mobilisation and reform of the international financial architecture. The Treasury said all of these bear directly on Zambia’s fiscal space and development financing.

With the World Bank, the priorities are infrastructure, energy security, private capital mobilisation, enterprise development and job creation. The delegation is scheduled to attend the Development Committee meeting, hold consultations with World Bank Group president Mr Ajay Banga and regional leadership, and take part in the International Development Association Forum.

Zambia will also hold talks with the United States Treasury, the Borrowers Platform Governing Council and development partners on sovereign financing, debt management and international financial cooperation.

The most concrete project discussions are scheduled with Africa50. Those consultations will explore financing for the Angola-Zambia electricity transmission interconnector, domestic power transmission projects, road and border infrastructure and the Kazungula Bridge Corridor.

The Lobito Corridor, which links Zambia, Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo, is a central item for the delegation. The Treasury said the corridor offers opportunities to strengthen regional transport and energy connectivity, expand trade and attract investment into mining, agriculture, manufacturing and related value chains.

The Minister and his team will also meet commercial lenders and investors, including Standard Bank, Standard Chartered, Citi and J.P. Morgan. Those meetings will focus on Zambia’s economic outlook, fiscal framework and investment opportunities.

Global conditions will shape the meetings. Finance officials are gathering as the war in the Middle East widens, energy supplies face severe disruption and interest rates are rising. The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, is expected to dominate the agenda.

It is the first time in three years that the annual meetings have been held outside Washington. Ms Georgieva said 18,000 people had registered to attend, 4,000 more than at the last off-site meetings in Morocco in October 2023.

Some senior figures are staying away. US Treasury Secretary Mr Scott Bessent is absent and has sent two senior officials in his place. Federal Reserve chairman Mr Kevin Warsh will attend and is due to appear at a public event with Ms Georgieva on October 16.

For Zambia, the outcome to watch is whether the Bangkok talks bring the US$1.47 billion programme closer to executive board approval and turn the corridor and power pitches into financing commitments before the meetings close on October 18.

World.title: Moody’s Projects Steep Debt Fall For Zambia As Hichilema Warns Against Complacency
World.content:
Global credit ratings agency Moody’s Ratings projects that Zambia will record one of the largest reductions in government debt in sub-Saharan Africa. President Hakainde Hichilema welcomed the forecast and pledged to turn the recovery into jobs and higher incomes for ordinary citizens.

Moody’s expects Zambia and Ethiopia to post the region’s biggest declines in government debt, and Botswana and Gabon the sharpest increases. The agency also placed Zambia among eight sub-Saharan African countries with a positive outlook.

The forecast is a sharp reversal from 2020, when Zambia became the first African country to default on its sovereign debt during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Head of State dedicated the achievement to Zambians in a statement issued by State House Chief Communications Specialist Mr Clayson Hamasaka.

“In 2020, Zambia was in default. Today, one of the world’s leading ratings agencies says our debt is set to fall further than almost anywhere else in the region,” Mr Hichilema said. “That is the result of hard choices, taken together, and of the patience and sacrifice of the Zambian people. This achievement belongs to them.”

The recovery was not a smooth one. The New Dawn administration inherited the debt crisis when it took office in 2021, and the President’s first term also included a devastating El Niño-induced drought that hit both agricultural production and electricity generation.

The Government responded with a series of fiscal and economic measures. The main one was an external debt restructuring aimed at reducing repayment obligations and easing pressure on public finances. It cut annual debt repayments from US$2.3 billion to US$900 million, generating savings of about US$1.4 billion and creating fiscal space for recovery.

The President linked the falling debt directly to his economic programme. “Every Kwacha freed from debt is a Kwacha we can put to work for Zambians,” he said. “That is the purpose of the Grow Zambia Agenda: to turn stability into jobs, investment and rising incomes in every province.”

He did not declare victory, however. “We are not complacent. The cost of servicing our debt remains too high, and that is why we will hold firmly to fiscal discipline under the new programme. We have restored stability. Now we are delivering growth,” Mr Hichilema said.

The new programme he referred to is a 36-month, US$1.472 billion Extended Credit Facility. Zambia reached a staff-level agreement on it with the International Monetary Fund on October 9, after the Moody’s outlook was published. It succeeds the US$1.7 billion programme that ended in January and is expected to support the country’s transition from stabilisation to growth.

Under the agreement, funds will be released in seven instalments, with the first amounting to about 15 per cent of the total. The proposed programme also seeks to raise the primary fiscal surplus gradually to three per cent of gross domestic product by 2029, starting in 2027. The measures include improved tax administration, stronger compliance and a review of tax exemptions.

Economists welcomed the deal. Economics Association of Zambia national secretary Dr John Musantu said the facility would support macroeconomic stability and help Zambia manage external shocks, including geopolitical conflicts affecting the global oil market and unfavourable weather patterns.

Dr Musantu said domestic financing alone could not fund the country’s development agenda, so concessional loans with favourable terms should be prioritised. He welcomed the IMF facility because it came at zero interest. Once finalised, he said, it would also reduce the Government’s borrowing on the domestic credit market as it meets its spending obligations.

Manufacturers have pointed to the wider economic picture. Zambia Association of Manufacturers president Mr Mohammed Umar said inflation had fallen from more than 24 per cent in 2021 to 6.1 per cent in September 2026. He added that the Kwacha had remained stable, foreign exchange reserves had reached record highs and growth had rebounded to 5.2 per cent in the second quarter.

Economist Mr Andrew Chibuye said the improvement still has limits. Stronger economic activity does not automatically produce stronger public finances, he said, citing weaker-than-expected revenue collections and higher-than-budgeted spending by the Food Reserve Agency.

Households, Mr Chibuye added, are still waiting to feel the benefits. Lower inflation does not necessarily mean prices have fallen, he said, and many families continue to face high costs for food, transport and education.

The President said the Government would continue working with the IMF, cooperating partners and investors to ensure the gains of recent years reach the daily lives of Zambians.

Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane is now leading Zambia’s delegation at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, which run until October 18. Talks with the IMF there will focus on advancing the successor programme, including the agreed reforms and prior actions required for consideration by IMF management and approval by its executive board.

World.title: Government Tells Clerics Facing Charges To Step Aside As MPs Press Archbishop Banda
World.content:
The Government has called on clergy facing serious legal or ethical allegations to consider stepping aside while the courts establish the facts. Catholic Church-aligned lawmakers have separately urged Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda to withdraw temporarily from pastoral duties while he answers criminal charges.

Archbishop Banda was arrested on September 28 and charged by the Drug Enforcement Commission with possession of property reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained. He is defending himself before the courts.

Ministry of Information and Media permanent secretary Mr Thabo Kawana set out the Government’s position in a statement that named no cleric. He said the Government remained firmly committed to the rule of law and to the constitutional principle that no person is above the law, regardless of position, status, profession or religious office.

Applying that principle, he said, depends on being clear about who actually stands accused when a priest appears in court. “It is important, however, that we make a clear distinction between a church as an institution and individual members of the clergy,” Mr Kawana said.

He described the Church as “a respected faith community with a long history of spiritual guidance, social service and national contribution.” Clerics, by contrast, are citizens who are personally accountable for their conduct under the law.

On that basis, court action against a priest should not be read as action against the faith he serves. “A case concerning an individual cleric is exactly that: a matter concerning an individual, not an attack on a denomination, a faith community or the Church as an institution,” the permanent secretary said.

He then turned to what accused clergy should do. As a matter of good governance and institutional integrity, he said, clerics facing serious allegations should consider stepping aside, taking leave or, where appropriate, relinquishing their responsibilities while competent authorities establish the facts. “This is not a new or unusual principle,” he added.

Mr Kawana pointed to clerics from different Christian traditions and other faith communities around the world who had voluntarily stepped aside during investigations. Religious institutions had also placed affected clerics on administrative leave, suspended their ministerial duties or accepted temporary resignations pending judicial or disciplinary outcomes.

None of these measures amounts to a declaration of guilt, he said. Their purpose is to protect the integrity of the offices concerned, safeguard public confidence and let due process proceed without the perception that an entire institution is on trial.

“The matter before the courts should remain a matter concerning the individual concerned, while the institution continues its mission and responsibilities unhindered,” Mr Kawana said. He cited examples from the Catholic, Anglican and evangelical traditions as evidence that the approach is widely recognised as a responsible way to protect both individual rights and institutional reputation.

Lawmakers who share the Archbishop’s faith have taken a similar view. Kazungula North MP Dr Clement Andeleki, nominated MP Mr Noel Nkoma and Rufunsa MP Ms Sheal Mulyata said the senior cleric should take leave from his position while he answers charges they described as grievous in nature.

Dr Andeleki was the most direct. “It is taboo for someone facing such serious charges to continue presiding over Mass,” he said, citing the resignation of the Chaldean Catholic Bishop of San Diego, California, which the Pope accepted after the bishop faced criminal charges.

In his view, a church leader facing serious criminal charges should temporarily vacate the altar until the matter is concluded. He said Archbishop Banda should not preside over Mass while the case remains active, because those entrusted with the word of God must be morally upright and beyond reproach.

Like the Government, the Kazungula North lawmaker kept the man and the institution apart. He said the Archbishop was arrested as an individual and not as the Catholic Church, and that personal legal matters should not be conflated with a Church that belongs to all believers and whose integrity must be safeguarded at all times.

Mr Nkoma was harsher, accusing the Archbishop of embarrassing the Church and of portraying himself as a politician. “I don’t know why the Pope has allowed him to soil the entire Mission,” he said.

Ms Mulyata described the matter as important but declined to comment further. She said she was unwell and would give a detailed view once she had recovered.

The Government, for its part, said it would continue to respect the rights of all citizens, including the presumption of innocence, while applying the law fairly, impartially and without exception. The case against Archbishop Banda remains before the courts.

World.title: Man arrested for suspected copper theft
World.content:
Police have arrested a 34-year-old man in connection with a suspected attempt to steal 29 copper blisters from a truck parked along the Luanshya–Masangano Road.

Copperbelt Police Commissioner, Rae Hamoonga, says officers on motorised patrol found the truck parked off the road near Avic International at about 22:00 hours on Saturday, October 10 2026.

In a statement, Mr Hamoonga said the truck’s tarpaulin and ratchets had been cut and removed, and were found lying beside the vehicle.

Mr Hamoonga said investigations revealed that the Tanzanian driver had allegedly parked the truck there with the intention of stealing its consignment.

He said the driver fled the scene and remains at large.

Mr Hamoonga identified the arrested man as Edward Kulaisha of Mukolwe Village, under Chief Mushili in Ndola District.

He said Mr Kulaisha was reportedly employed to keep watch over the truck.

Police are searching for the driver as investigations continue.

Mr Hamoonga said further details would be released as police were still investigating the matter.

World.title: Lusaka residents happy with CBD hygiene
World.content:
Lusaka residents and traders have praised the return of order and hygiene at the Central Business District (CBD) especially at Simon Mwewa Lane Market.

The traders have expressed gratitude to Lusaka Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, and the Lusaka City Council for implementing the Operation Clear Path Campaign which has allowed them to operate in a clean environment.

In an interview with the media during a spot check at the market one of the traders, Rhoyday Phiri, said the government should be hailed for cleaning up the city.

Ms Phiri said that hygiene and order has been brought to the market, adding that Lusaka mayor should be commended for the great job done.

“I am grateful to the government for the Operation Clear Path Campaign, it is a great initiative because sanity has returned to the city,” Ms Phiri said.

She added that the traders are happy because now they can operate in a clean environment.

Ms Phiri has however appealed to the government to quickly complete the construction of the nearby market so that more traders can be accommodated there.

Another trader at Simon Mwewa Lane Market, Fatima Banda, has thanked the government for ensuring the cleanliness of the city.

Ms Banda has since appealed to the Lusaka City Council to create more trading space so that more traders can be accommodated.

Meanwhile, a Lusaka resident, Paul Chitalu, has hailed the government for the Clear Path Operation.

Mr Chitalu said that with the clean trading environment customers are able to buy fruits and vegetables without being worried about diseases.

“You see, I can even buy banana’s from this market, because it is clean and there are no flies,” Mr Chitalu said.

World.title: Nalumango calls for regional unity to curb illegal mineral exploitation
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has called for stronger regional cooperation among Great Lakes countries to combat the illegal exploitation of minerals.

Mrs Nalumango has also urged Member States to curb the illegal cross-border trade in minerals while ensuring that natural resources contribute to peace, economic growth and sustainable development.

She said individual countries could not effectively address illegal mineral exploitation in isolation, stressing the need for coordinated regional action, information sharing and stronger implementation of agreed regional instruments.

Mrs Nalumango, who was represented by Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development Siazongo Siakalenge, was speaking during the official opening of the 10th Meeting of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) Council of Ministers Responsible for Mines in Lusaka today.

She said progress in implementing the six tools of the Regional Initiative on Natural Resources had remained uneven, with only five Member States having fully implemented the regional certification mechanism more than a decade after the adoption of the Lusaka Declaration in December 2010.

Mrs Nalumango said the situation highlighted the need for Member States to address persistent implementation challenges and strengthen accountability in the management of natural resources.

She said the meeting provided an opportunity for countries in the Great Lakes Region to renew their commitment to responsible mineral governance, regional economic cooperation, peace and stability.

The Vice President said the proposed inclusion of mineral value addition and cross-border trade in the revised Regional Initiative on Natural Resources would broaden the regional approach beyond mineral traceability and certification.

She said the move could help Member States derive greater economic benefits from their mineral wealth through investment, industrial development, employment creation and increased participation in mineral value chains.

Meanwhile, ICGLR Committee Chairperson Louis Kabamba has urged Member States to strengthen mineral traceability, information sharing and regional cooperation to curb conflicts linked to natural resources.

Mr Kabamba said Member States needed to translate their commitments into concrete action to ensure that minerals traded across borders were legally sourced.

And European Union Ambassador to Zambia Karolina Stasiak has called for stronger regional cooperation to combat the illegal exploitation and trafficking of mineral resources in the Great Lakes Region.

Ms Stasiak said illegal mineral activities deprived governments of public revenue and contributed to corruption, organised crime, human exploitation, environmental degradation and conflict.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 13, 2026
World.content:
WHO Launches Five-Year Strategy to Detect Health Threats Faster

The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new five-year strategy to help every country detect and understand emerging health threats within 24 hours of their appearance by 2030. The strategy builds on the work of the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, established in 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps. Since its creation, the Hub has worked with 160 WHO member states, 190 partner organisations and thousands of scientists and policymakers to strengthen global disease surveillance. The plan focuses on five key initiatives, including using artificial intelligence to identify potential health threats, strengthening genomic sequencing to track emerging pathogens and connecting experts in data science and disease modelling. It will also support countries in sharing health data securely and improving cooperation between human, animal and environmental health systems. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the strategy provides a clear path towards a world where countries can respond to health threats before they develop into major crises. The organisation says sustained investment and international partnerships will be essential to achieving this goal.

South Africa's Deputy Police Chief Resigns Amid Criminal Charges



South Africa's Deputy National Police Commissioner, Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya, has resigned from the police service three weeks after being charged with sexual offences. His lawyer submitted the resignation letter during a disciplinary hearing. Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said his departure would be treated as a dishonourable discharge because he was still facing disciplinary proceedings at the time of his resignation. Sibiya has been in custody since his arrest in September. Sibiya faces several serious allegations, including the sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl, rape, human trafficking and links to organised crime figures. He denies the allegations of criminal links and sexual grooming. He admits having sex with an 18-year-old woman but maintains that it was consensual. Allegations against him also emerged during the Madlanga Commission, a public inquiry investigating claims of police corruption and collusion with criminal networks. He has been accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal and receiving cash and 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. Sibiya has denied the allegations.

Renewed Fighting in Tigray Raises Fears of Wider Regional War

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is raising fears of a wider conflict involving Eritrea and other neighbouring countries. Tensions escalated after reports that Eritrean forces crossed into Ethiopia, prompting Ethiopian forces to launch drone strikes against troops and equipment. Eritrea has denied reports of the incursion, while accusing Ethiopia of using the allegations as a pretext to pursue its ambitions for access to the Red Sea port of Assab. Local sources, however, reported clashes involving Eritrean forces at several locations in Tigray. The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile peace agreement that ended the 2020–2022 war. The conflict is unfolding amid shifting alliances between rival armed groups and growing tensions between Ethiopia and its neighbours. Tigray's ruling Tigray People's Liberation Front has vowed to continue fighting after federal forces and a pro-government militia captured the regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. The TPLF has also aligned with other opposition groups seeking to challenge Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Analysts warn that the conflict could develop into three possible scenarios: the proliferation of armed groups, a prolonged military stalemate, or a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The humanitarian consequences could be severe, particularly in Tigray, where about one million people remain displaced, and nearly four million need urgent assistance. Drought, food shortages, and difficulties delivering aid are adding to the crisis.

Drought and Conflict Push Sudan Closer to Famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan as severe drought worsens the humanitarian crisis caused by ongoing conflict, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global food security monitoring partnership supported by United Nations agencies. A new alert warns that malnutrition is worsening in several areas, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Aid organisations are struggling to reach affected communities because of insecurity, restricted access and a severe shortage of funding. In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, surveys in two displacement camps found acute malnutrition among children at 38% and 30.8%, both above the threshold associated with famine. More than half of Sudan has been affected by the drought, destroying crops and leaving families without enough food or income. In North Darfur, 64% of cropland is showing poor plant growth and late rains have not managed to save most cereal crops. Food prices are expected to continue to rise. There has also been mass displacement in Greater Kordofan, where since October 2025 more than 300,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. Attacks and insecurity are putting aid workers at risk, while many children are going without life-saving treatment for severe malnutrition. By 8 October, less than half of Sudan's humanitarian appeal had been funded. The IPC has called for an end to the fighting, safe access for aid agencies and a major increase in funding to prevent further loss of life.

Lagos Court Clears Way for Inquest into Chimamanda Adichie's Son's Death

The Lagos State High Court has cleared the way for a coroner's inquest into the death of Nkanu Esege, the son of renowned Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. Justice Aishat Opesanwo dismissed an application by Eurapharma Care Services Nigeria Limited, which operates Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital, seeking to stop the inquiry. The hospital argued that the cremation of Nkanu's body made a post-mortem examination impossible and deprived the coroner of the authority to proceed. Nkanu died on 7 January 2026 following medical procedures, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death. In her ruling, Justice Opesanwo said the law requires an inquest when the circumstances of a death meet the conditions set out in the Coroners System Law of Lagos State 2007. She said that the absence of the body did not automatically prevent the inquiry from taking place or make it speculative. The judge also rejected the hospital's arguments concerning the handling of statements and evidence from medical personnel, saying the coroner has discretion over how the proceedings are conducted. She stressed that a coroner's inquest is a fact-finding exercise intended to establish who died, and how, when and where the death occurred. It is not a criminal trial to determine guilt or assign blame. The ruling allows the inquest to proceed.

World.title: Liberia: Sen. Konneh Asks U.S. to Sanction Mining Enablers, Warns Liberia At 'Most Dangerous Point'
World.content:
Monrovia - Gbarpolu County Sen. Amara M. Konneh has asked the United States to impose Global Magnitsky sanctions on people who enable mining licensing deals in Liberia and move the proceeds into US real estate, telling a Washington policy audience that the country faces its gravest threat since the civil war and the Ebola epidemic.

By Lennart Dodoo

Sen. Konneh made the request Oct. 7 at a private roundtable convened by the National Endowment for Democracy in Washington, according to a statement his office released Oct. 12. He also asked Washington to support court monitoring in Liberia, resume mentoring of law enforcement officers vetted by the US Drug Enforcement Administration "with appropriate oversight," and engage the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network on active financial intelligence cases.

"Liberia is not yet a captured state. But we are at the most dangerous point since the civil war and the Ebola epidemic," Konneh said. "My request is straightforward: help us establish transparent regulations before agreements are finalized, and support impartial enforcement of the law after confiscation, whether the suspect is an airport baggage handler, a police crimes director, a former Vice President, or a multinational corporation."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Sen. Konneh, an independent who chairs the Senate Public Accounts and Audit Committee and previously served as minister of finance and development planning, described two threats he said are unfolding at the same time: corporate capture of the mining sector and the infiltration of state institutions by drug traffickers.

On mining, he said broad executive discretion in negotiating 25-year Mineral Development Agreements has created conditions for companies to capture the country's regulatory and fiscal institutions. Mining accounts for 12% of gross domestic product and 65% of export earnings, he said, yet affected communities receive less than 3% of direct revenue. The statement does not give a source for those figures.

On narcotics, Konneh said transnational trafficking networks have shown they can penetrate Liberia's law enforcement, judicial and financial systems. He pointed to two seizures this year: 237 kilograms intercepted at Roberts International Airport in June, valued at $19.2 million, and 3.9 metric tons seized in Duazon in July, valued at $317 million. He said the seizures had links to trafficking networks in Spain, Colombia, Serbia, Croatia and Ukraine.

He also described the spread of kush, a cheap synthetic drug now present in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Gambia, Guinea and Senegal, as both a public health and a governance emergency. Citing the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's World Drug Report 2025, he said opioid use in West and Central Africa stands at 2.35%, above the global average, and that Africa accounted for 57% of pharmaceutical opioids seized worldwide between 2019 and 2023.

Close 

Sen. Konneh said he is advancing a set of reforms in the Senate. They would require publishing all Mineral Development Agreements before ratification, create independent oversight of transfer pricing in iron ore concessions, mandate preserving evidence in drug cases, make financial investigations compulsory in all first-degree drug felonies, and introduce unexplained wealth legislation that allows assets to be forfeited without a criminal conviction.

World.title: Nigeria: Court Clears Way for Inquest Into Chimamanda's Son's Death Despite Cremation
World.content:
The Lagos State High Court sitting in Ikoyi on Monday cleared the way for a coroner's inquest into the death of Nkanu Esege, son of renowned Nigerian author, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, ruling that the cremation of his body did not, in itself, prevent the inquiry from proceeding.

Justice Aishat Opesanwo gave the ruling while striking out an application by Eurapharma Care Services Nigeria Limited, operators of Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital, seeking to stop the inquest.

The hospital had argued that the cremation made a post-mortem examination impossible and deprived the coroner of jurisdiction.

It also challenged the procedure for receiving statements and evidence from medical personnel and other parties connected with the facilities where Nkanu was treated before his death.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nkanu died on January 7, 2026, following medical procedures, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death.

In her ruling, Justice Opesanwo held that conducting an inquest was a statutory obligation where the circumstances of a death met the conditions prescribed by law.

She said the hospital had failed to disprove the conditions empowering the coroner to proceed under Section 15 of the Coroners System Law of Lagos State 2007.

The judge explained that the law did not require the deceased's body to remain within the coroner's district when the inquest was held.

She also rejected the argument that the absence of the body would necessarily render the inquiry speculative.

Describing the hospital's concerns about the eventual outcome as premature, she noted that the inquest had yet to commence formally.

Justice Opesanwo said a coroner's inquest was a fact-finding exercise intended to establish who died, how, when and where the death occurred, rather than a trial to determine guilt or apportion blame.

"It is not a trial, no one is on trial in a coroner's court," she said.

The judge also dismissed the hospital's fair hearing argument, holding that the coroner had the discretion to determine the sequence in which statements and evidence would be received.

She said disagreement with the exercise of that discretion did not, in itself, establish a breach of fair hearing. She added that the rules governing ordinary civil proceedings did not apply in the same manner to a coroner's inquest.

The court upheld the respondents' preliminary objections and struck out the hospital's application, clearing the way for the inquest to proceed.

World.title: South Africa: Police Call Sibiya's Exit 'Dishonourable' As He Quits Amid Disciplinary Proceedings

Sibiya's lawyer tendered his resignation straight after his disciplinary hearing began, and his employment ended immediately, police said.

Police say he had an ongoing disciplinary case when he resigned, so his exit counts as a dishonourable discharge.

Shadrack Sibiya is no longer a member of the South African Police Service (SAPS). He resigned as his disciplinary hearing began on Monday.

SAPS said in a statement that his legal representative tendered his resignation immediately after the proceedings had started. Police said his employment has been terminated with immediate effect.

Because he had an ongoing disciplinary case against him when he resigned, SAPS said his departure is regarded as a dishonourable discharge.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The hearing related to allegations that came out of the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry. Sibiya was placed on special leave in July 2025 and suspended in September 2025.

He was served with notice of the hearing on 29 September, and it was set down for 5 October. It was postponed to 12 October after he asked for time to consult his lawyers. He also approached the Labour Court in an attempt to halt it.

SAPS spokesperson Brigadier Athlenda Mathe said the hearing and the court case were separate matters.

Sibiya also faces a separate criminal case. He was arrested on 21 September, and the charges include rape, human trafficking, sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl and a firearms charge. He denies the allegations.

He remains in custody while his bail application continues, and the matter returns to the Randburg Magistrate's Court on Tuesday, 13 October.

Sibiya has not been convicted of any offence. His resignation means the disciplinary hearing will not go ahead, so the allegations against him in that matter were not decided.

World.title: Africa: WHO Pandemic Hub Sets Ambitious Goal to Detect New Outbreaks Within 24 Hours
World.content:
blog

The World Health Organization (WHO) launched a new five-year strategy for its Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, charting a path towards a world where every country can detect and understand emerging health threats within 24 hours of their appearance by 2030. Strengthening rapid detection is a cornerstone of global health security, helping countries contain outbreaks before they escalate into larger epidemics or spread internationally.

The Hub's strategy aims to equip every country with the capabilities needed to rapidly identify and understand emerging health threats, thus supporting them in developing the systems, capacities and partnerships necessary to prevent outbreaks from escalating into epidemics or pandemics.

Speaking at the opening of the World Health Summit in Berlin, in the presence of Germany's Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Health, Georg Kippels, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus reflected on the Hub's achievements in the five years since its creation.

"Five years after its establishment, the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence has become an integral part of the global health security system," he said. "Its new strategy charts a clear path towards 2030, uniting governments and partners around a shared goal: a world in which every country can rapidly respond to health threats before they turn into major crises."



The WHO Hub was created in 2021 with foundational support from the German Government in response to the critical gaps exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. Since then, it has worked with 160 WHO Member States, 190 partner organizations, and thousands of scientists and policymakers to detect new epidemic threats, sequence and identify pathogens, and support rapid action to protect communities around the world.

Under the next five-year strategy, the Hub will build on the achievements and deliver its work through five priority initiatives:

Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) uses artificial intelligence to scan thousands of publicly available sources in real time each day to identify signals of potential health threats. It brings together a global community of over 4000 experts and is being used by over 125 Member States and 30 regional and international organizations.

It brings together a global community of over 4000 experts and is being used by over 125 Member States and 30 regional and international organizations. The International Pathogen Surveillance Network (IPSN) strengthens capacities in genomic sequencing and bioinformatics to identify and understand emerging pathogens. This helps accelerate the development of tests, treatments and vaccines.

The Hub is a critical pillar of the WHO Health Emergencies Programme and of our collective ability to respond to emergencies. It acts as a convener of partners, a catalyst for innovation, and a mobilizer of expertise and resources. Achieving the ambition of the strategy will require sustained investment, trusted partnerships, and strong cooperation across sectors, disciplines, and borders.

About WHO

Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations' agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations - leading the world's response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. "Together for health. Stand with science", the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.

World.title: South Africa: Court Bars Anti-Immigrant Protesters From Going Near Home Affairs

24 people appeared in the Durban Magistrates Court on Monday

Two men facing charges related to last week's anti-immigrant violence have been released on R1,000 bail, on the condition that they not participate in any violent protests or go within 500 metres of a Home Affairs office.

Malizo Dzanibe, Sphelele Shinga (known as Magolide) and Wandile Nsibande appeared in the Durban Magistrates Court today after being arrested on Saturday. They were among 24 people who appeared in court.

Shiga's charges were related to statements he made about his intention to shut down the MTN8 final at Moses Mabhida. Dzanibe and Nsibande's charges related to last week's protest action, during which immigrants were targeted, businesses were vandalised, and vehicles were burnt.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Dzanibe and Shinga were granted bail, while Nsibande remains in custody. During the proceedings it emerged that Nsibande was on parole for a kidnapping conviction and has a pending assault case in Eshowe.

They were represented by a team of lawyers led by Xolani Zuma, husband of March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma. Ngobese-Zuma was also in the public gallery on Monday.

Another 21 accused also appeared in the same court on related charges on Monday. Only one was granted bail. Hundreds of March and March members gathered outside the court entrance to show support for the accused. All 24 accused will return to court on 16 October for a second round of bail hearings.

Throughout last week, protesters harassed asylum seekers queuing at the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre in Durban. On Thursday, hundreds of people marched from the reception centre. A scrapyard reportedly owned by an immigrant was set alight, dozens of shops were vandalised, and some were looted. Acting National Police Commissioner Puleng Dimpane said 14 vehicles were torched.

By Sunday, the army was deployed to parts of KwaZulu-Natal.

The unrest followed false claims about the Constitutional Court's Scalabrini judgment of 7 July. Online posts said it gave asylum seekers citizenship. In fact, the court only struck down procedural barriers in the Refugees Act that let officials to turn asylum seekers away before their claims were heard.

Home Affairs called the claims about citizenship or "blanket legalisation," "categorically false" and said there appeared to be a coordinated disinformation campaign. An analysis of about 98,000 posts on X traced the earliest high-engagement posts to March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma.

World.title: Africa: General Assembly Adopts Pandemic Declaration, but Not By Consensus
World.content:
Laboratory technicians testing samples from suspected Bundibugyo virus disease cases in Bunia, Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The General Assembly on Monday adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, by 153 in favour to three against (Argentina, Israel and United States) with two abstentions (New Zealand and Paraguay).

The text was due to be approved by consensus at a high-level meeting on 25 September.

Objections from the United States and a few other States blocked that, pushing the issue back to the assembly.

Read the full political declaration here.



Chile's representative summed up one prevailing view, saying that "no country, no matter how big it might be or how prepared it might be, can alone address a threat that knows no borders."

The declaration is political and non-binding. It calls for stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year's landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement.

Unfinished annex

The agreement cannot be opened for signature until Member States complete an annex on pathogen access and benefit-sharing - the system by which countries would share samples and genetic data.

Those that do so would receive a share of any resulting vaccines, treatments and diagnostics.

Talks have stalled amid a standoff between developing countries and some high-income European nations together with the US.

The World Health Assembly - comprising the WHO's 194 members - is due to return to the annex next May.

The US representative had previously cited "divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus" as well as the declaration's references to the continuing annex negotiations.

More action in the General Assembly

In addition to adopting the pandemic declaration, the 193-member world body had a number of items on its agenda on Monday, including the consideration of draft resolutions on the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise and a political declaration of the high-level meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the anti-racism Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.

Read a summary of the meeting here.

WHO aims to spot new outbreaks within 24 hours

The World Health Organization (WHO) on Monday launched a five-year strategy for its Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, with the goal of detecting emerging health threats within 24 hours.

Set up in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the hub wants every country to be able to identify and understand new threats quickly, so outbreaks can be contained before they become epidemics or spread internationally.
