World.title: US military archbishop urges Catholic soldiers to refuse involvement in Army firing squad execution
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Catholics serving in the Army should request to be excused from participating in the planned firing squad execution of a convicted Fort Hood mass shooter, which the Pentagon has proposed livestreaming, a prominent U.S. archbishop who oversees Catholic pastoral services for the military said on Monday.

Archbishop Timothy Broglio raised several objections to the Pentagon's unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base. Hasan, now 56, uses a wheelchair, after being shot by responding officers during the attack.

Hasan is set to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, at 1 p.m. CST, according to the U.S. Army, which would make him the first person to be executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945. It would also mark the first U.S. military execution by any method since 1961. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said he wanted soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of the shooting and has argued that making the execution public would help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio recalled presiding over the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack, and expressed sorrow over the deadly shooting. But the archbishop questioned whether the U.S. government wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries."

POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION

Hasan's crime "was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?" Broglio asked in a statement.

"I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," he continued.

Army regulations permit soldiers to seek religious exemptions or accommodations.

It is unclear how the military intends to select members for the firing squad.

"The U.S. military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world," Broglio said. "Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?"

A U.S. government execution has never been broadcast to the public, making it an unprecedented plan that has drawn backlash from political and religious leaders.

Broglio joins other Catholic leaders in criticizing the Pentagon's plans to livestream the execution.

The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" about the public execution plan and urged the U.S. to reconsider.

"In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement on Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, called the proposed broadcast "truly incomprehensible" and warned that it was "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."

"The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent," Parolin told reporters on Friday.

According to the English translation published by Vatican News, Parolin said, "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age. I do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways."

Parolin added that the death penalty "is incompatible with human dignity and does not serve as a deterrent."

Pope Leo XIV reiterated the Catholic Church's opposition to the death penalty as "inadmissible" in a social media post on Saturday marking World Day Against the Death Penalty.

Citing Catholic doctrine revised under his predecessor, Pope Francis, Leo emphasized that the death penalty violates human dignity.

"The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo, the first American pope, wrote on X without specifically mentioning the Pentagon's execution plan for Hasan.

FORT HOOD SHOOTER SHOULD BE EXECUTED '13 TIMES OVER' — BUT NOT ON LIVE STREAM, SURVIVOR SAYS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Donald Trump said Saturday he had not yet decided whether to allow the livestream plan to move forward, although he has reportedly expressed doubts in private about broadcasting the execution.

Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic, expressed skepticism about whether the Pentagon would proceed with a public execution. He said he would not watch the livestream if it were carried out.

Several lawmakers, including Republicans, have spoken out against plans to broadcast the execution.

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said on Thursday. "It should not be happening in America."

A back-and-forth battle that saw 35 total fourth-quarter points, an overtime period filled with clutch plays, and more led the Bills to beat the Rams, 37-34, to improve to 4-1. The Rams fell to 2-3, a record nobody predicted through their first five games, but they are still a top NFC contender.

In a game filled with offensive fireworks from both Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford, it was Rams defensive captain Nate Landman who came through with the most important play of the game in overtime.

Allen and the Bills got right into Rams territory on the opening drive thanks to Khalil Shakir’s 57-yard catch-and-run on second-and-long. On the very next play, James Cook, who had two touchdowns but a fumble earlier in the game, wasn’t cautious with the football when he got the handoff from Allen. Stafford did just that, using his star receiver Puka Nacua, who exploded for 17 catches on 25 targets for 138 yards and a touchdown, to get into field goal range for kicker Harrison Mevis to try a 48-yard field goal for the win.

But just when it seemed one team would finally come away with the win and get the final word, the other team stepped up.

The Rams have dealt with special teams woes in recent seasons, and Mevis, who had missed a 50-yarder earlier in the game, had his game-winning field goal blocked. The game remained tied, and the Bills’ offense breathed a sigh of relief knowing they could rectify Cook’s mistake.

Allen took matters into his own hands, rushing for 32 yards on the drive and getting well within field goal range for Tyler Bass to get his shot at glory. In the box score, Allen threw for 210 yards with one touchdown and one interception, while rushing for a game-high 121 yards on just 10 carries with his score. Cook finished with 111 yards on the ground with his two touchdowns, while both Kyren Williams and Blake Corum scored for the Rams.

World.title: Former Eagles CB Asante Samuel calls out coach Nick Sirianni after brutal London loss: 'You lost the game'
World.content:
The Philadelphia Eagles flew all the way across the Atlantic Ocean just to hand a victory to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Unsurprisingly, former All-Pro cornerback Asante Samuel has seen enough.

Eight seconds left, a one-point lead, and a squib kick sealed it. Instead, Nick Sirianni gifted Jacksonville a live return, setting up an improbable walk-off win.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Speaking on the "Say What Needs To Be Said" show, Samuel put Sunday's 19-17 collapse squarely on Philadelphia's head coach.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"You lost the game for your team," Samuel said. "Of course, the team was going to have his back and say, 'No, coach, it's not on you. It's on us.' But all the coach had to do was call a squib kick. A squib kick at the end of the game is normal and done all the freaking time."

Samuel torched Sirianni for his lack of awareness in crunch time.

"Nick Sirianni must have had a lapse in his brain or something and wasn't paying attention for him to miss out on that situation," Samuel said. "There's no way your team fights that hard for that long, and you let your team down by not making sure the right call is being made."

The blunder erased what should have been a gritty road win. Down Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith to hamstring injuries, Philadelphia took a 17-16 lead with eight seconds left on Jake Elliott's 48-yard field goal.

NFL WEEK 5 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: RODGERS DEFIES FATHER TIME, COEN GETS BAILED OUT, 49ERS SURVIVE UGLY PERFORMANCE

Jacksonville's Ameer Abdullah responded by fielding a clean kickoff, ripping off a 53-yard return, and setting up Cam Little's walk-off 57-yarder as time expired.

The loss dropped Philadelphia to 2-3 while pushing the Jags to their third-straight victory.

Sirianni fell on his sword Sunday right after the final whistle.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I didn't make the right decision and I lost us that game," Sirianni told reporters. "And that's what I said to our guys. What hurts there is that the guys fought so hard, and then I don't make the decision that I should make at the end of the game and I cost us that game and I put that fully on me."

When asked why Philadelphia left eight seconds on the board before Elliott's kick, Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts made it clear game management was outside his control.

"It’s not my place, and we’re prepared, I’m prepared as a quarterback to not worry about those things," Hurts told reporters Monday. "So I’m honoring a play call, honoring the things that are coming in the game. When I’m up at night, yeah, I think about, 'Man, should I have said something, or should I have took a step back and said, "Wait"?' But ultimately, there’s a commitment to that and going out there and executing. And so this was one where it did not work in our favor."

JALEN HURTS SAVES EAGLES FROM UGLY UPSET AS PHILADELPHIA ESCAPES TITANS TO REMAIN UNBEATEN

Sirianni doubled down Monday, shutting down any idea that Hurts should have overruled the sideline.

"Jalen’s playing," Sirianni told reporters. "We’re coaching and calling the plays, and Jalen’s got to go execute what we call in that moment, 100 percent. We’re not asking him to make play calls in that scenario. He’s already got enough to worry about to go out and execute. That’s where we were there in that situation."

CASE KEENUM'S PERFORMANCE IN WIN OVER EAGLES SHOULD TELL BEARS THIS: DON'T RUSH BACK CALEB WILLIAMS

Sirianni can preach staying in your lane all day, but Hurts is losing sleep over brain-dead strategy, and Samuel wants the head coach held to the fire.

Good luck fixing that mess.

World.title: Man admits to dismembering ex-girlfriend, keeping severed head in suitcase after she played him 'like a fool'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A New York man pleaded guilty to murdering and dismembering his ex-girlfriend and putting her severed head in a suitcase with a flower after she ended their relationship, later telling investigators she had "played me like a sucker," according to authorities.

Damon Foy, 50, of Kerhonkson, pleaded guilty last week to second-degree murder in the 2024 death of Alberta Dale, 44, of Pennsylvania, according to the Ulster County District Attorney's Office.

Between March 31 and April 1, 2024, Foy killed and dismembered Dale and was in the process of disposing of her body when law enforcement intervened, according to the district attorney's office.

The Ulster County Sheriff's Office began investigating on April 1, 2024, after Dale's family members in Pennsylvania contacted law enforcement because they were concerned about her well-being, the district attorney's office said. Deputies first conducted a welfare check before launching a missing person investigation.

SISTER OF MISSING DC MOM SPEAKS OUT AFTER EX’S ARREST EXPOSES 'HORRIFYING' ABUSIVE RELATIONSHIP

Deputies first went to Foy’s apartment on April 1, 2024, and found Dale’s car, according to the New York Post. The next day, deputies returned to question Foy after a member of the public found Dale’s phone on the side of the road and turned it in to authorities, leading investigators to suspect potential foul play.

"She’s in there," Foy whispered to investigators, when they arrived at his home during the missing person investigation. "I killed her," he added, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.

Investigators obtained a search warrant for Foy's home and found a suitcase in a closet that contained the victim's remains. Foy was then arrested and charged in connection with Dale's death.

After shining a flashlight on the suitcase, investigators "immediately noticed what appeared to be dried blood," according to the documents.

"Officers opened the defendant’s suitcase and found Alberta Dale’s partial dismembered remains, including her severed head," the court documents read, according to the New York Post.

"The remaining portions of her dismembered body were not located during the execution of the search warrant," the documents add.

When he was later interviewed, Foy told investigators he "loved her," according to the documents.

"The only thing she kept doing after the time throughout the whole relationship was just play me, play me like a fool, play me like a sucker, and just took advantage of the whole f–king system," he said.

"That’s it. I was told to leave my own home. I was told to leave my own f–king home, not a bill in her name, and I was told to leave my own f–king home. Get out. Then it all started coming clearer to me," he added.

When asked about the flower in the suitcase, Foy only said he was thinking about "what still happened last night to take s— over the top."

Foy had a history of domestic violence against Dale, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.

A previous domestic incident involved a gun, and investigators had also observed an axe at Foy’s property when they were searching for Dale.

Dale had previously warned authorities that "if she went missing it was because [Foy] killed her," according to the court documents.

Under a plea agreement, Foy is expected to receive 23 years to life behind bars, with a minimum term two years shorter than the maximum of 25 years to life, according to the Daily Freeman.

MAN UNLEASHES DEADLY ‘REVENGE’ RAMPAGE ON EX’S FAMILY, KILLS 4 PEOPLE, 3 DOGS BEFORE TORCHING HOME: DA

Chief Assistant District Attorney Liz Culmone-Mills told the outlet that the agreement was backed by Dale’s family.

"The District Attorney’s Office would not be making this recommendation were it not for Alberta Dale’s family," Culmone-Mills told the outlet.

Foy is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 16.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The total selfish disregard for the life and dignity of another person is at the heart of domestic violence; Damon Foy has shown that to us," District Attorney Emmanuel C. Nneji said in a statement. "We must recognize in our laws the rights of victims of domestic violence to be physically, psychologically, and emotionally safe from their tormentors and the dangers specifically targeted for them, and demand procedures that actually protect victims for real, not just on paper."

The Green Bay Packers-Chicago Bears rivalry is one of the best in football, and one viral moment added to it during the Packers’ 31-7 beatdown at Lambeau Field over their NFC North foe in Week 5.

Packers receiver Matthew Golden fielded a punt by the Bears toward the end of the first half, and after returning it 17 yards, he ran out of bounds on the Chicago sideline.

Still running at full speed, Golden crashed into an unsuspecting Bears coach, who went tumbling to the ground after the blindside hit.

Bears kicker Cairo Santos seemed to witness the act by Golden, and his reaction was one some fans on social media called dirty.

As Golden ran back onto the field, Santos clearly tried to trip the second-year receiver before he got between the white lines. Santos was unsuccessful, but as the broadcast caught the entire act from Golden hitting the Bears coach to the attempted trip, it quickly went viral on social media.

And while Golden took the high road, his teammates weren’t as humble. Linebacker Zaire Franklin took aim at Bears receiver Luther Burden III, suggesting that he "ain’t wanna play anymore" and that he "quit today."

World.title: ABC accuses FCC of trying to 'inflict maximal coercive pressure' with probe against network
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Disney and ABC accused the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Monday of using the license renewal process to circumvent "judicial review" and inflict "maximal coercive pressure" against the network and company.

Disney originally sued the FCC in August over what it claimed was a "retaliatory campaign against ABC" regarding the agency's early broadcast license renewal proceedings for eight ABC-owned stations earlier this year. The stations, according to the FCC, must demonstrate they are operating in the public interest as the agency investigates diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices.

However, in Disney's latest filing, the company asserted that the FCC could have used "a number of different tools" to investigate Disney and ABC's DEI practices that did not involve forcing stations to renew their licenses years ahead of schedule, suggesting it was done to avoid legal scrutiny.

ABC MORE CAUTIOUS OF BOOKING CANDIDATES ON 'THE VIEW' AMID FCC PRESSURE, DISNEY'S FIRST AMENDMENT LAWSUIT SAYS

"These are not merely 'theoretical' tools ... they have been used by the agency for decades," the filing read. "Yet the agency tried none of those less intrusive tools here, instead taking the unprecedented step of calling for early license renewal of all eight ABC-owned stations at once. Defendants’ own admissions leave no doubt as to why — Defendants sought to inflict maximal coercive pressure on the media company whose speech the Administration sought to curb, while deliberately evading judicial review."

Disney cited a court hearing last week in which the FCC was instructed to provide a supplemental filing on alternative methods the agency could have used. During the hearing, the FCC suggested that additional procedures would have required federal court enforcement.

"That Defendants openly describe judicial review as an obstacle demonstrates what Plaintiffs have been saying all along: shielding their unconstitutional campaign against ABC from judicial review is part of Defendants’ retaliatory strategy," the filing read.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, FCC spokesperson Adam Jackman dismissed the latest filing as an effort to block the FCC in court procedures.

CONSERVATIVE GROUPS URGE FCC TO BACK OFF ABC LICENSE REVIEW, WARNING IT COULD HURT RIGHT-LEANING MEDIA

"Disney’s latest filing only confirms that they’ve filed a meritless case in the wrong court at the wrong time," Jackman said. "They want a district court to prevent the FCC from even considering whether Disney has complied with its longstanding obligations as a broadcaster. The law does not allow that. The FCC will continue to hold broadcasters accountable to their regulatory obligations."

Fox News Digital also reached out to ABC and Disney for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Disney and ABC have repeatedly attacked the FCC's probes and investigations into the company as a form of retaliation over programs and hosts that are critical of President Donald Trump, such as late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

DISNEY ACCUSES TRUMP'S FCC OF ATTEMPTING TO 'SUPPRESS SPEECH' WITH LICENSE RENEWAL INVESTIGATION

In addition to the license renewal proceedings, the FCC has launched a probe into the ABC daytime talk show "The View" based on the agency's demand that broadcast stations adhere to the equal opportunity requirement stating opposing political candidates receive equal time. Disney has maintained that "The View" is a "bona fide news" program exempted from the rule.

World.title: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
World.content:
Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.

Brent crude oil jumped 2% to almost $108 per barrel and U.S. crude oil rose more than 2% to about $94. Meanwhile, diesel futures fully erased a small drop they saw last week.

Just weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the price pressures are mounting. Republicans face a steep climb to maintain their majorities in Congress, and voters across the country cite high gas prices as a key issue affecting their votes.

The average nationwide price of diesel fuel Monday was $6.26 per gallon, nearly 80% higher than it had been at the start of the year, according to AAA data.

The rising prices Monday came less than 24 hours after Trump declared that a ceasefire had been agreed to.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Shortly after the president’s post, Russia renewed strikes against Ukrainian energy assets.

Pressed by reporters Monday as to why neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had firmly committed to his ceasefire, Trump indicated that he knew when he made the announcement on Sunday that he did not yet have a commitment from either side.

“They agreed, you know why? Because I said ‘You agree,” Trump told reporters at the White House. As for getting Russian President Vladimir Putin to commit, Trump said, “We’re going to see what happens.”

Asked if he was aware that Russia had already violated the ceasefire Trump had announced, the president replied, “I’m not sure about that,” before claiming there had been “violations on both sides.”

Ceasefire déjà vu

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine learned about Trump’s ceasefire from media reports and was given no advance warning. He reiterated his position that Ukraine was open to an agreement not to target enemy energy infrastructure as long as Moscow agrees to it, too.

In the meantime, Russia continued with “glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that a power plant in Kharkiv had recently been attacked.

“Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet,’” Zelenskyy said, using the Russian word for “no.”

The Kremlin on Monday neither confirmed nor denied having agreed to a deal.

Trump’s Sunday announcement closely mirrored a similar post he made in September, when he announced that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”

There, too, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s participation hinged on Russia’s agreement to comply, which never came. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian strikes on the other’s energy assets slowed down in September.

Trump’s deal with Putin

The dubious ceasefire Trump declared over the weekend followed a stunning announcement Friday in which the president said Russia would supply millions of barrels of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.”

The announcement came after a phone call Friday between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin that reportedly lasted over an hour.

Trump said the deal with Putin would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” That would translate into about 2.25 million barrels of diesel, or less diesel than the United States uses in just one day.

Further details and logistics of Russia’s plan had yet to be announced Monday.

In addition to the Russia deal, Trump has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel fuel supplies in recent days and lifted domestic restrictions on an off-road variety of diesel.

In order to clear a legal path for the diesel deal, the Treasury Department announced a six-month suspension of the fuel sanctions imposed on the Kremlin in 2022 for its illegal invasion of Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials, European allies and some U.S. lawmakers were aghast at the deal and the U.S. decision to unilaterally ease Russia sanctions.

Trump defended the deal Monday, calling it “the right choice for the American People.”

Trump also said more diesel fuel would be made available “within a short period of time,” if Russia’s refineries could produce it.

Questions about Russia’s capacity

Yet experts are highly skeptical that there will be any significant resumption of Russian diesel exports in the near term.

Due to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, refiners that produce oil, gas and diesel have suffered heavy damage.

“Reported gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to protect domestic supplies,” analysts at the International Energy Agency wrote in a September report.

For weeks, Trump has focused on the price of diesel fuel, which began rising as a result of the Iran war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.

In July, escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war began adding to the pressure on diesel prices.

As Ukrainian drones systematically targeted Russian energy assets, the Kremlin responded by restricting diesel exports in order to preserve its supply for domestic use.

Until then, Russia had been one of the world’s top exporters of refined oil products, which include diesel fuel.

Russia said Friday that it would lift some of its export restrictions in order to accommodate the deal with Trump. But it was unclear how fast that would happen.

World.title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. on ‘Breaking Bad,’ dies at 34
World.content:
Actor RJ Mitte, known for playing the son of Walter White in the hit AMC series “Breaking Bad” and as an advocate for the rights of those with disabilities, has died at age 34, his representatives said Monday.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his representatives said.

They did not provide details about the cause of death.

Mitte died Monday in Brownsville, Texas, where he had moved, Brownsville Justice of the Peace Cyndi Hinojosa said.

Hinojosa said that she declared him dead at 1:32 p.m. but that she could not disclose the cause of death.

00:30 'Breaking Bad' actor RJ Mitte dies at 34 00:00 00:00

In the award-winning “Breaking Bad,” Mitte played Walter White Jr., the teenage son of a high school teacher who becomes a methamphetamine producer.

The series, which debuted in January 2008, when he was 15, provided his breakout role.

Mitte had cerebral palsy, which was reflected on “Breaking Bad,” and he was an advocate for the rights of people living with disabilities.

“Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” his representatives said in the statement.

“Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s,” they said in the statement.

“He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities,” they said.

The representatives asked for privacy for Mitte’s family and loved ones.

Mitte also starred in the 2020 horror film “The Oak Room” and the 2017 sci-fi film “The Recall.”

In “Triumph,” which was released in 2021, Mitte stars as a high schooler who fights to become a wrestler despite having cerebral palsy. The film won a Ruderman Family Foundation Seal of Authentic Representation, an award for the portrayal of people with disabilities.

Hinojosa, the justice of the peace, said Mitte “will be very, very much missed” in Brownsville.

“He was so gracious to our town,” Hinojosa said in a phone interview.

Mitte was born in Jackson, Mississippi, and doctors diagnosed cerebral palsy when he was 3 years old, he told Vice in a 2016 interview. He was 12 or 13 years old when he moved to Los Angeles, he said.

“I started acting to meet kids my own age,” he said in the Vice interview.

In a 2021 interview, Mitte told Big Issue that favorable media and critical reception of “Breaking Bad” helped keep the show on the air in its first few years.

“It wasn’t the viewers, because we didn’t have the numbers to stay as a network show,” Mitte said.

It wasn’t until later seasons that “we really got the viewership,” he said.

The show ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013.

In that interview, Mitte credited his family for supporting him when the public perception of people with cerebral palsy was negative.

When he was younger, he said, some believed he would never walk or talk properly or have a typical life or career.

“That was the perception when I was a kid,” Mitte said in the interview. “And my family was like, ‘No. He’s going to go do things.’”

Mitte told Vice in 2016 that he considered himself fortunate to be able to make a difference.

“I’m lucky that I can be an advocate. I’m lucky that I can do what I do and talk to the people I get to talk to,” he said.

“I think we all have an obligation to have an impact for the positive,” he said.

World.title: Trump says ‘we’re looking at’ firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece
World.content:
President Donald Trump indicated Monday that he’s considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former top Trump campaign surrogate who has served as the U.S. ambassador to Greece since 2025.

“We’re looking at it,” Trump said when asked if he’s weighing firing Guilfoyle, as first reported by The Associated Press, amid allegations of misconduct related to her role as ambassador.

“We’re not happy,” Trump added.

His comments come days after he struck a softer tone when asked Friday about the alleged conduct of Guilfoyle — a former Fox News personality who used to be engaged to Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

“I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice,” he said at the time.

Guilfoyle and the U.S. Embassy in Greece are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News last week.

The probe came after reports in The Wall Street Journal of misconduct in her role as ambassador, including allegedly bragging about her connections to Greek tycoons who she said funded luxury trips for her. The story cited people who heard the conversation and an audio recording. The reports have not been independently confirmed by NBC News.

Last week, a Trump donor named Eric Deters came forward accusing Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 confirmation hearing in the Senate in exchange for access to senior administration officials.

“She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview last week.

“She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he said, adding he did not pay her the money.

Attorneys for Guilfoyle said in a statement that Deters had owed her the money for speaking engagements, which he denies.

The attorneys, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also denied allegations of any impropriety involving her travel, saying she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”

The attorneys added that Guilfoyle “has made American energy leadership and the advancement of U.S. energy security interests across Europe defining priorities of her tenure under President Trump.” She “has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction .We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action,” they said.

World.title: Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ monologue slammed as sexist for comments about women
World.content:
Comedian Shane Gillis drew controversy again for his “Saturday Night Live” monologue Saturday after commenting that he “didn’t know women just dress like whores now” at the gym.

Gillis appeared to draw few laughs from the studio audience after making the remark during the monologue, which marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch comedy show. (“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.)

After lamenting that he needs to lose weight, he went on to describe the “neon, artificial-vape colored” shorts that women are wearing to work out, and the fact that men are not allowed to look at women in those shorts.

The bit drew an outpouring of backlash toward Gillis online, with hundreds of people sharing their negative reactions on TikTok, Instagram, X and Threads.

Representatives for “SNL” and Gillis did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Gillis, who is known for his raunchy style of comedy, has a history of placing women — and other marginalized groups — at the butt of jokes. Many people called it tone-deaf of Gillis to make such comments following the reports around a former Cornell University student who alleged she was gang-raped at an on-campus fraternity house in 2024.

Among the chorus of vocal critics was actor Dan Levy, who on Sunday posted an Instagram video in which he said, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists. There’s a difference there.”

Levy, who created and starred in “Schitt’s Creek,” said he is “speechless that something like that can exist on live national television.”

“And to be perfectly honest,” Levy continued, “more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment with which women are sexually assaulted, and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a crime.”

Levy called on men to defend women more often and said it is not a women’s issue — “this is an everybody issue,” he added.

“The more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects,” he said. “They are not objects. They are superior human beings to men.”

Some used Gillis’ monologue to show solidarity for Cornell’s Jane Doe, who accused seven Chi Phi fraternity members of plying her with drugs before sexually assaulting her overnight following a fraternity party.

As the investigation made headlines, women began sharing their own experiences with sexual assault on campus and what they say were inadequate responses from their universities and their police departments, with some coalescing around the hashtag #iamjanedoe.

Writer Jessica Valenti said that she thinks Gillis was probably aware about the “major national conversation happening right now about sexual assault” in relation to the Cornell case.

“This is his contribution to that conversation,” she said. “This is him telling us what he thinks of the discourse on sexual assault. ... That is rape culture.”

Others, like writer and comedian Sophia Benoit, said Gillis’ joke about how women dress at the gym was not funny.

It “has been a very common joke for AT LEAST fifteen years, and it has never once that I can recall been performed with a punchline,” she wrote on X.

Gillis’ career has been fraught with controversy, mainly, his time with “SNL.” He was hired as a cast member in 2019, before he was quickly canned for previously making racist jokes on his podcast. The criticisms of Gillis piled on when other clips of him using offensive language went viral at the time.

At the time, he apologized but said he would continue to make shocking and taboo jokes.

“We want SNL to have a variety of voices and points of view within the show, and we hired Shane on the strength of his talent as a comedian and his impressive audition for SNL,” a spokesperson for “SNL” executive producer Lorne Michaels told NBC News in 2019. “We were not aware of his prior remarks that have surfaced over the past few days. The language he used is offensive, hurtful and unacceptable.”

The show, which was home to Bowen Yang (the show’s first Asian American cast member) at the time, chose to fire Gillis, but invited him back to host in 2024 and 2025 before Saturday’s appearance.

Later during Saturday’s episode, Gillis accidentally slipped an f-bomb during a sketch and later apologized. The Federal Communications Commission “prohibits obscene, indecent and profane content from being broadcast on the radio or TV.” The agency defines “profane content” as “grossly offensive” language that is “considered a public nuisance,” according to its website.

Some online pointed out that Gillis apologized for cursing during a sketch but not for offending people during his monologue.

“That’s a pretty ridiculous contrast,” one social media user wrote. “An accidental swear gets an apology, while insulting women is supposed to pass as edgy comedy.”

World.title: Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh Airport Hit With 2 Strikes in 2 Days
World.content:
Copied

Videos show the moments Riyadh Airport, the main airport in Saudi Arabia, was hit in a deadly attack on Saturday and then again on Sunday, killing more than a dozen including one American. Now questions swirl about whether the United States will join airstrikes against the Iranian-backed Houthi militants responsible for the attacks, which would widen the U.S.-Iran conflict just weeks before the midterm elections. NBC’s Keir Simmons reports for TODAY.Oct. 12, 2026

World.title: The Bills and Rams just played the thriller of the NFL season — and perhaps a Super Bowl preview
World.content:
The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams needed nearly 70 minutes to decide a winner on Monday.

If we’re lucky, they’ll play at least 60 more in February.

The Bills beat the Rams 37-34 in an overtime thriller on “Monday Night Football.” The game, a matchup of championship contenders and the last two NFL MVPs, lived up to its billing as a seismic showdown — and perhaps provided a preview of Super Bowl 61.

Buffalo outlasted Los Angeles in a back-and-forth affair featuring numerous twists, turns, touchdowns, turnovers and game-changing plays. After the teams combined for 33 points through the first three quarters, they combined for a whopping 38 in the fourth quarter and overtime.

Josh Allen, the 2024 NFL MVP, completed 12 of 19 passes for 210 yards, one touchdown and one interception. He was also an absolute bruiser on the ground, running 10 times for 121 yards and a score.

Matthew Stafford, the reigning MVP, was also sensational. He completed 40 of 54 passes for 383 yards and three touchdowns — the third straight game in which he’s attempted at least 50 passes.

Both quarterbacks conducted nearly perfect offenses in the second half.

After scoring a touchdown on their final possession of the third quarter, the Bills entered the fourth leading 19-14. The teams then traded touchdowns on their next five drives. In the second half, the offenses combined for seven touchdowns and only two punts.

After an eight-play, 71-yard jaunt by the Rams tied the game at 27 with seven minutes and 14 seconds to go, the teams traded especially textbook scoring drives.

First, Buffalo went on an 11-play, 71-yard journey that included a 21-yard run by Josh Allen on second-and-17.

Two plays later, the Bills got in the end zone with only 99 seconds left in the game. That’s when Stafford got to work, marching Los Angeles 63 yards in only eight plays for the game-tying score with only five seconds left on the clock.

In overtime, the Rams won the toss and elected to defend first, a decision that soon proved to be genius by coach Sean McVay.

On the third play of overtime, Allen found Khalil Shakir for a 57-yard pass that was incredibly close to being a touchdown. Shakir was streaking down the left sideline when Kam Kinchens dove and just barely was able to swipe at Shakir’s feet, causing the receiver to go down.

The touchdown-saving tackle proved to be massive, because on the very next play, running back James Cook fumbled.

Los Angeles took over needing only a field goal to win, and promptly drove 50 yards down to Buffalo’s 30-yard line, setting up a huge moment in the game. On third-and-5, McVay opted to stay on the ground instead of a more aggressive approach to attempt a closer field goal.

The decision backfired, as Rams kicker Harrison Mevis’s 48-yard game-winning field goal attempt was blocked by defensive end Greg Rousseau — much to the relief of Cook.

“I wish I would have had a better play call and gone for it and got it a lot tighter,” McVay said postgame about his third-down call. “I’m sick right now with myself...I’ll be regretting kicking that and not having a better call...it’s on me.”

He added: “Been a while since I have been this pissed after a game, too.”

After four runs following the missed kick, Bills kicker Tyler Bass drilled home a 45-yard field goal, securing the win for Buffalo.

“It’s football. You can be down and out one play and another play on top of the world,” Allen said of the overtime rollercoaster. “That’s just how it rolled for us today.”

The Bills improved to 4-1 with the victory, remaining in first place in the AFC East.

The Rams, on the other hand, fell to 2-3, including 1-2 at home. Los Angeles has yet to win two straight games this season, alternating losses and wins in each of the first five weeks, putting it in third place in the NFC West.

Monday’s game was an instant classic, and a similar rematch would make for a fantastic Super Bowl. With the loss, though, the Rams will be facing a particularly uphill climb for these two teams to play each other again this season.

World.title: Hurricane Simon lashes Mexico's Pacific coast, pounds resorts and towns
World.content:
Hurricane Simon weakened Monday to a Category 2 storm, but it continued to pound the coast of west-central Mexico as its eye remained just offshore.

Dangerous winds lashed the region, threatening coastal areas with flooding rain, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. With its center still swirling near the coast, Simon's most damaging winds and rain were forecast to persist near the Puerto Vallarta area, a coastal town known for its beach resorts.

The storm's maximum sustained winds have decreased below the 111 mph needed to make it a major Category 3 storm, as it was previously categorized, according to the hurricane center. Simon had been weakening gradually since the early hours of Monday morning, but forecasters warned it could strengthen again, and, regardless, it remained a dangerous hurricane.

Map shows hurricane's path

On Monday night, Simon's eye was about 85 miles west of Cabo Corrientes and inching west-northwestward at about 3 mph, the hurricane center said.

Hurricane Simon's projected path early on Oct. 12, 2026. CBS News

The storm was expected to change directions midweek and eventually approach the coast of west-central Mexico on Wednesday into Thursday. The hurricane center warned that Simon "could re-intensify some" and "is expected to remain a hurricane through midweek" before it weakens and moves inland.

Simon is expected to bring heavy rain to the U.S. Southern Plains from Tuesday afternoon through Friday morning, CBS News and Stations meteorologist Nikki Nolan said. That region could see 3 to 5 inches of rain and more in some places.

Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 10 miles, and tropical storm-force winds were reaching up to 45 miles from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

Hurricane warnings and watches for Simon

A hurricane warning is in effect for Las Islas Marias, which means hurricane conditions are expected in the area. A hurricane watch is in effect along the coast of Mexico from North of Esuinapa to Bahia Tempehuaya, where hurricane conditions are possible within the next two days.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Philippe Papin, a senior hurricane center specialist, said over the weekend. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

The hurricane center said early Monday that Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches, in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.

"Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco," the center said in its latest advisory. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any ongoing flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain."

People standing near an emergency vehicle watch as the authorities assess whether the area needs to be evacuated in Costalegre, Jalisco state, Mexico, on Oct. 11, 2026. Daniel Becerril / REUTERS

Tourists arrive as Puerto Vallarta residents brace for Simon

Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

Hurricane Simon as seen from a satellite churning off Mexico's west-central coast early on Oct. 12, 2026. NOAA / National Hurricane Center

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to social media to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.

"Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote.

Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he couldn't go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.

Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting.

"It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again."

People watch waves crash against the waterfront promenade in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, on Oct. 11, 2026. Christian Ruano / REUTERS

Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.

Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.

"The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone.

Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital.

"We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on."

Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo, which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

World.title: Selma Blair arrested after allegedly biting flight attendant
World.content:
Actress Selma Blair was arrested after allegedly biting a flight attendant on board a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on Sunday night. Following her arrest, she allegedly kicked a police officer and a nurse and is facing two assault charges.

Two flight attendants reported injuries during the flight, and one was taken to the hospital after the incident, according to the Port Authority Police Department. One of the flight attendants was bitten and the other sustained a laceration, according to a law enforcement source.

Her attorney said Blair experienced a "medical emergency" on the plane, but did not get into specifics. Blair has been outspoken about her struggle with multiple sclerosis.

The incident happened at 11 p.m. on Delta Air Lines Flight 938. The flight crew needed to restrain Blair, a law enforcement source said.

On air traffic control audio, the pilot could be heard calling for medical personnel to come to the plane.

"Ah, a bloody nose as well as some bite marks as well, so I don't think we need an ambulance or anything like that but if we could get some medical personnel at the gate, to look at their injuries," the pilot said in audio captured on ATC.com. "It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that, so we'll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as well as law enforcement."

Port Authority Police were called to the plane, along with the FBI. Blair was transported to Jamaica Hospital for evaluation after the incident. While in the ambulance, she allegedly kicked a PAPD officer, and once at the hospital, she allegedly assaulted a nurse, prosecutors said.

Blair was later released from the hospital and taken to Queens Central Booking. She was then arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault at a court in Queens, where she pleaded not guilty. A judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for Jan. 19.

The assault charges are state charges related to the alleged incidents in the ambulance and hospital.

This isn't the first time Blair has been removed from a flight. Back in 2016, she was removed by stretcher after an episode on another Delta flight. As for what allegedly happened on Sunday night, the FBI gave her a summons for assaults within special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States, a federal law enforcement source said.

No date has been set for the federal case against her.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," the airline said in a statement.

Blair was traveling with her service dog, which is now in the custody of her attorney.

Blair has been outspoken about her struggle with multiple sclerosis. In 2025, she gave an interview to People magazine and Travel & Leisure talking about the difficulties she had traveling. In her 2022 memoir, she also has a chapter called "Bite Me," where she wrote about past instances where she bit other celebrities while drinking.

Blair has appeared in such films as "Cruel Intentions," "Legally Blonde," and "Hellboy," among others. In 2022, she was a contestant on "Dancing with the Stars."

World.title: Talarico was at home in Texas during campaign trail absence, photos indicate
World.content:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign shared security camera footage with CBS News that appears to show Talarico at his home in Texas for the first eight days of this month — pushing back on claims that Talarico was hiding the reasons for his disappearance.

Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for almost two weeks, saying he caught a bad case of the flu. The disappearance drew criticism and speculation from his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

But on Monday, Talarico's campaign shared a set of security camera images that they say show the state lawmaker and Democratic candidate at his home in Texas every day from Oct. 1 to Oct. 8, one day before Talarico made a public appearance.

The eight timestamped images — which include watermarks from home security camera company SimpliSafe — appeared to have been taken from a camera in the backyard of Talarico's house in the state capital of Austin. CBS News matched features in the backyard to recent satellite imagery of Talarico's address. Though low resolution, the photos show a male figure with brown hair at various times of day and wearing different outfits.

The images were first reported by The New York Times.

The mental health facility at the center of the conspiracy theories, Lindner Center of Hope in Mason, Ohio, also wrote on social media that Talarico "has never received treatment" there.

Talarico campaign spokesman J.T. Ennis said in a statement that claims Talarico was elsewhere were "a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory."

"Last week James Talarico was home in Austin, Texas recovering from the flu," Ennis said.

Timeline: What we know about James Talarico's whereabouts

Talarico was not seen in public for just under two weeks, from late September to late Friday.

His last known in-person event in Texas took place on Saturday, Sept. 26, in the Dallas suburb of Carrollton. Two days later, he was in New York City for a series of fundraisers, including a joint fundraiser with Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown hosted by Robert De Niro.

On Sept. 30, Talarico pulled out of an in-person conversation with Javier Palomarez, president of the United States Hispanic Business Council. He instead appeared for a virtual Q&A.

"I was starting to feel under the weather a few days ago," Talarico told the audience, apologizing for not appearing in person. "And last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas and I was diagnosed with the flu. So I'm running a fever and I'm at my most contagious right now." (He later told a reporter he went to his primary care physician.)

A day later, on Oct. 1, Talarico's campaign called to cancel an appearance at the Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium scheduled for the upcoming week, according to Essien Ita, the group's leader. Ita told CBS News that Talarico's staff declined to reschedule the appearance, and said they had canceled other events through Oct. 5.

The following week, President Trump traveled to San Antonio to campaign with Paxton. The president and Paxton, the state attorney general, both referenced Talarico's absence.

"I hear the guy has disappeared – nobody knows. You know where he is? He's sick because he's forced to eat meat for political reasons and he's throwing up all over the place," Mr. Trump said, referencing Talarico's past comments on trying to reduce meat consumption. (Talarico has denied that he is a vegan.)

Earlier in the rally, Paxton said: "When I came in here today, we were on day 11 of James Talarico not showing up in public and canceling all public appearances. Where do you think they hid that little socialist?" He then had the audience yell "Where Is James Talarico?" in unison.

Talarico was seen in public for the first time this month on Friday, Oct. 9, when a campaign spokesperson posted a video of him greeting festivalgoers at the Austin City Limits Music Festival.

On the same day, Talarico told CBS News in a text: "Feeling much better. Back on the trail!"

Talarico had several other public appearances over the weekend, attending a Kasey Musgraves concert in San Antonio on Saturday and giving interviews on Sunday to NBC's Dallas-Fort Worth station and The Dallas Morning News' editorial board.

"It wasn't anything worse than a nasty case of the flu. And so I was in bed and, you know, drinking lots of liquids. Unfortunately, the campaign made me work from home, so I didn't even get full days off," he told a local NBC reporter, saying he didn't want to get anyone else sick.

Paxton suggested something was amiss, saying Talarico "owes Texans answers."

"James Talarico claims he was missing for 13 days because he had the flu," Paxton wrote in a post on X over the weekend. "Who actually believes that?"

At around the same time, social media users began speculating — without evidence — that Talarico had flown to Ohio for mental health treatment.

Then, on Sunday, conservative social media personalities shared an unverified recording in which somebody appeared to call Ohio's Lindner Center of Hope to ask whether Talarico was checked in. A staff member at the mental health center ostensibly said he had been discharged.

CBS News could neither authenticate nor debunk the veracity of the call. The Lindner Center of Hope said publicly that Talarico did not receive treatment at the mental health facility.

The local NBC station asked Talarico about the rumors. He denied them and said: "It's a good reminder that you can't believe everything you read on the internet."

World.title: RJ Mitte, "Breaking Bad" actor, dies at 34
World.content:
RJ Mitte, who rose to fame playing Walter "Flynn" White Jr. on the hit series "Breaking Bad," has died, his representative confirmed to CBS News. He was 34.

A cause of death was not provided. Cameron County Justice of the Peace Cyndi Hinojosa told The Associated Press that Mitte was pronounced dead around 1:30 p.m. on Monday in Brownsville, Texas.

Mitte played the son of Bryan Cranston's high school-teacher-turned-drug-kingpin Walter White and Anna Gunn's Skyler White on the AMC series, often cited as one of the greatest TV shows ever made.

Mitte, and by extension Walter Jr., had cerebral palsy.

"Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative, Sean Riley, said in a statement.

As a member of the "Breaking Bad" cast, Mitte won a Screen Actors Guild Award for best drama ensemble in 2014 for the show's final season.

Cranston wrote on Instagram on Monday night that he was in "deep despair."

"That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor," he wrote. "He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community. All that promise and potential now is such a loss."

RJ Mitte on Sept. 30, 2026, in Beverly Hills, California. Unique Nicole / Getty Images

Cranston said he and Mitte had been texting a few weeks before his death to try to plan a lunch.

"I don't know if that lunch would have changed his future," Cranston wrote. "But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I'll miss you, son."

Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr.'s uncle, Hank Schrader, on "Breaking Bad," said, "Though RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can't believe it. Thinking of him and his family."

In addition to his acting, Mitte was an advocate for those with disabilities and sought to raise awareness for a variety of conditions while pushing for expanded roles for people with disabilities in Hollywood. In 2014, he received the SAG-AFTRA Howard Russell Award, named in honor of the first actor with a disability to win an Oscar.

"Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities," Riley said.

Last year, Mitte partnered with Can Do Canines, which helps provide service dogs in Wisconsin and Minnesota.

"I'm very lucky with my disability that I have worked very hard to have the mobility I have today, but I see in many people's lives, they don't get the same opportunities," Mitte said at the time.
