World.title: DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs
World.content:
DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs

toggle caption i Philippe Magoni/AP

NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday.

Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.

One painting, "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," suffered a tear. The other, "Young Woman at the Well," had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million).

The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that "apparently caused the perpetrators to panic," Bessone said.

Sponsor Message

"As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve," he said.

Vehicle tracking led to the suspects

The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.

Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.

Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection.

The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.

Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent."

The paintings were hidden behind a wall

The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of "theft committed by an organized gang" and "criminal association," among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said.

toggle caption i Philippe Magoni/AP

The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.

Sponsor Message

The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of "concealment" of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.

Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.

The theft renews concerns about museum security

The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.

The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.

Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country "is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage" in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.

French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

World.title: New White House press secretary a 'devoted fan' of Trump and MAGA
World.content:
New White House press secretary a 'devoted fan' of Trump and MAGA

toggle caption i Terry Wyatt/Getty Images North America

President Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is expected to take the podium on Tuesday for her first press briefing. Zacharia steps in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.

The Trump administration is also engaged in a legal battle with the press corps that work to cover Trump. Last month, the White House restricted access by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, news organizations that Trump views as unfriendly. The Justice Department has since launched an investigation into the five television networks that share pool video coverage of Trump.

Sponsor Message

In a post on social media, Zacharia, an attorney and a mother of four , offered no hint of the challenges ahead. She described her new job as the "honor of a lifetime" and praised Trump's policies. "His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country," Zacharia wrote on Friday .

In naming Zacharia, Trump praised her longstanding personal loyalty . "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," Trump said. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"

Zacharia, 41, a graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has worked for a number of conservative organizations, according to her online resume . She served on the advisory board for an anti-abortion group called The White Rose Resistance that took its name from Christian students who challenged the Nazis. White Rose says it's working to counter "the same evils, the same apathy " faced by opponents of the Nazi regime.

More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.

Sponsor Message

During an appearance in August on the network Real America's Voice , Zacharia weighed in on the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, arguing that "toxic feminism" had skewed the public's view of the case. Clancy was charged with killing her three children. The 5-week trial ended in a mistrial after sparking a national conversation over postpartum depression.

"This started with the advocation of abortion," Zacharia said. "When women are championing the death and murder and the ability to murder their children from conception all the way through, when does humanity begin and end?"

Zacharia has also used her social media posts to amplify right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that Democratic leaders took part in pedophile rings. In one post from 2022, she described former Democratic White House chief of staff John Podesta as "Pedo Podesta." That same year she shared a post from a far-right commentator who claimed Democrats "want to mask and rape your children."

NPR asked the White House for comment on the posts, which were first uncovered by the online progressive media site , Popular Information. Administration officials responded in an email by praising Zacharia without addressing her social media comments.

After being named to serve as White House press secretary, Zacharia drew praise from other administration officials. FBI director Kash Patel described her as "sharp, fearless" and someone who "knows what it means to stand for the American people."

Karoline Leavitt, who held the press secretary post until August before stepping down, also praised Zacharia. "I have no doubt Katie will do great work for President Trump and our country," she said on X .

In an appearance on Fox News on Saturday , Zacharia boosted Trump's controversial plan to import Russian diesel fuel, which has drawn bipartisan criticism . She also praised Trump's efforts to rally GOP support ahead of the November vote, while suggesting congressional Republicans may be to blame for any losses.

Sponsor Message

"President Trump has made the case and delivered historic results. I would have loved to see more from our congressional Republicans and Senate," she said.

World.title: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
World.content:
Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.

An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social.

Sponsor Message

"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."

The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.

The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.

The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.

Sponsor Message

The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged s, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."

Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.

"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."

The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.

It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.

World.title: Actor Selma Blair removed from plane by police after altercation
World.content:
Actor Selma Blair removed from plane by police after altercation

toggle caption i Chris Pizzello/AP Photo

Actor Selma Blair was taken into custody after a flight from Los Angeles to New York for being physically abusive and injuring two flight attendants, authorities said Monday.

Police took Blair, 54, into custody late Sunday night when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. There was no immediate response to a request for comment from the airline.

Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said.

Sponsor Message

The FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, declined to release details.

"Yesterday, we were informed by our partners at Port Authority Police Department of a potential assault aboard a flight that arrived into JFK. As per long-standing DOJ policy, we do not comment on ongoing investigations," said Sydney Kleinmann, a spokesman for the FBI NY.

Messages seeking comment were not immediately returned by the state and federal prosecutors' offices in New York.

A message left with Blair's publicist seeking comment was not immediately answered.

In a statement to several media outlets, a Blair representative said she had a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct.

Blair had major roles in films including 1999's "Cruel Intentions," 2001's "Legally Blonde" and 2004's "Hellboy."

In recent years she has been an advocate for disability rights. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018. In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.

Associated Press journalist Michael R. Sisak contributed reporting.

World.title: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's DC home, DOJ says it approved the warrant
World.content:
Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's DC home, DOJ says it approved the warrant

toggle caption i Luke Garrett / NPR News

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Monday morning.

The Department of Justice said in a statement to NPR that agents with Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant."

The warrant was approved by the DOJ and is part of an "ongoing federal investigation." Federal authorities did not give further details on the reason for the probe.

Details about the investigation were confirmed by current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly.

One current official said this search is part of a multi-year probe that includes whistleblower complaints. A former official, who had previously been briefed on the matter, said the investigation deals with immigration fraud allegations.

Sponsor Message

Omar criticized the search on social media.

"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar posted on social media. "I will not be silenced."

toggle caption i Luke Garrrett / NPR News

Several HSI agents could be seen walking near and around Omar's home on Monday.

Jackie Rogers, a spokesperson for the congresswoman, called the search an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

Sharon Jackson, 79, lives across the street from the congresswoman and said federal agents woke her up around 4:30 a.m. Monday morning.

"I got awakened by boom, boom, boom," Jackson said. "They were out here with a great big truck."

The search took place ahead of next month's midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking reelection.

Vice President Vance has previously alleged Omar committed immigration fraud — something she denies.

World.title: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
World.content:
India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate

toggle caption i Manish Swarup/AP

NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.

Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.

Sponsor Message

Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.

"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.

Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.

The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

World.title: DOJ launches antitrust probe of TV networks. And, Trump says Ukraine needs new leader
World.content:
DOJ launches antitrust probe of TV networks. And, Trump says Ukraine needs new leader

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

President Trump is urging Ukrainians to hold wartime elections and replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as he blames him for not ending the war. He accuses Zelenskyy of causing rising global fuel prices due to Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel on Friday temporarily, and stated both sides agreed to an "energy ceasefire."

toggle caption i Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images

🎧 Trump has urged Ukrainians to elect a new leader before, but each time he does that, Zelenskyy's popularity rises, NPR's Joanna Kakissis tells Up First. She adds that, through conversations with Ukrainians in Kyiv, a common sentiment emerges: while they see Zelenskyy as imperfect, they believe outsiders shouldn't dictate their electoral process or leadership changes. Most Ukrainians acknowledge that holding elections now would be risky, given the ongoing conflict, with Russia bombing their cities daily. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said yesterday that he was unaware of any plans for a ceasefire, which would require both sides to stop attacking energy facilities.

The Justice Department has opened a formal antitrust investigation into five major U.S. television networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — for their actions during a legal battle over access to the White House. Press rights groups have denounced the move, which comes after Trump barred CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, citing unfair negative coverage. The administration revoked White House press passes for more than 70 journalists. The affected news organizations have sued to restore their access. The Justice Department is citing national security grounds for its actions, while a federal judge has temporarily ordered the restoration of their passes, with a final decision expected by Tuesday evening.

Sponsor Message

NPR confirms that at least four people died from storm-related incidents after Hurricane Isaias struck the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm on Friday night. Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are assessing the damage and power outages caused by the storm. Isaias brought 105-mph winds, snapping trees and knocking out power, while officials warn of ongoing flash-flood threats farther inland.

Houthi forces in Yemen are attacking Saudi airports, including a deadly strike on a passenger terminal in the capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia says at least 20 people have died from these recent attacks in the last week.



🎧 Global condemnations have followed these attacks, but the spotlight is on Trump, NPR's Aya Batrawy says. The Saudis have requested U.S. refueling support for their fighter jet strikes on Yemen's Houthis, but Trump has yet to agree. While the U.S. provides intel on the Houthis, Trump remains hesitant to get involved in another Gulf war, especially with ongoing Iranian attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis, backed by Iran, in an unsuccessful attempt to reinstate the Yemeni government. These latest attacks challenge Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's efforts to secure the country and implement reforms to attract foreign investors and tourists, Batrawy says.

Sponsor Message

Today's listen

NPR

Suicide is a growing public health crisis in the U.S., especially within the Black community, where rates have increased more than 50% in the last decade, according to CDC data. Black youth suicides by firearms surpassed those of white youth in 2022. As public health initiatives increasingly pull away from issues that affect different communities, Morning Edition's Michel Martin wanted to address this issue with care and honesty. Martin led a live event titled Going There: A Matter of Life and Death, uniting clinicians, lawmakers, and individuals affected by this epidemic to try and find out why this crisis is happening, how it affects us and how we can take action. The speakers included influential voices like CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor. Watch and listen to the event here.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

Picture show

toggle caption i Ethan Miller/Getty Images

BTS frontman RM is showcasing art from his personal collection for the first time in a collaboration with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The K-pop idol's real name, Kim Nam-joon, has prompted the group's fanbase, known as ARMY, to coin the term "Namjooning" to describe the star's interests. RM collaborated with two of the museum's curators for the exhibit RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me. The works on display feature mostly RM's own art collection alongside works from SFMOMA, like a Mark Rothko painting, shown side by side with one by Yun. The museum's director of retail Shane Salvata says, "This is hands down the most inventory that we've ever front-loaded for an exhibition." If you can't visit the exhibit in person, check out some photos of what's on display.

Sponsor Message

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Gregorio Borgia/AP

Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung, which doctors found at a "very early stage." The Kennedy Center has appointed Rick Canny, a talent manager known for working with acts like ZZ Top and Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. In today's economy, many job seekers are facing longer periods of unemployment, with nearly 40% exhausting their benefits before finding new work.

This newsletter was edited by Christina Romano. Suzanne Nuyen contributed.

World.title: U.S. restrictions on Chinese drones are hurting cash-strapped police departments
World.content:
U.S. restrictions on Chinese drones are hurting cash-strapped police departments

Loading...

For hours, bullets tore through the home, hitting neighboring houses and cars.

Inside, a man wanted by police for allegedly killing his ex-girlfriend was holed up with his new girlfriend.

As the SWAT team prepared to enter, Kevin Fennessy with the Ocean County Sheriff's Office tried something new first. He sent in a tiny assistant: a small drone equipped with a camera.

From a safe position outside, Fennessy slowly piloted the device through a blasted-in window, while he and other officers watched on a monitor. The video, viewed by NPR, showed hallway walls and furniture riddled with bullet holes.

As it entered a back bedroom where the couple had holed up, footage showed the man's body on the floor. He had killed himself. With the drone still hovering above the macabre scene, police deployed two flash bangs into the room. The woman rushed out and surrendered.

The incident, which happened about three years ago, sticks in Fennessy's mind when he considers the value of his department's drone program, which he heads.

"No one's hurt. Everyone's safe," Fennessy says. "Forty-one times they shot out the house at us. But at the end of the day, we were able to clear the house."

toggle caption i Albert Yee for NPR

New Jersey's Ocean County Sheriff's Office is one of an estimated 6,000 law enforcement agencies across the country that now have drones, used for search and rescue, fire and traffic crash investigations, and tactical response, according to the Law Enforcement Drone Association. It's an organization that advises, trains and certifies police across the country on their drone programs.

Sponsor Message

Ocean County's entire fleet is from DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones. LEDA estimates that about 80% to 90% of law enforcement agencies flying drones use DJI devices. China controls a vast majority of the global drone market, and it's the dominant source for the minerals and raw materials needed to build them, researchers say.

The Trump administration wants that to end. It's made several moves to bolster U.S. drone makers, including by banning many new foreign-made drones from entering the American market. Most recently, his administration announced tariffs of 15% to 100% on some foreign-made drones, making it much more expensive for agencies to buy these devices.

Critics of these moves say the American drone industry is not yet able to keep up with demand, nor can it match the high-quality and low-cost drones made in China. Law enforcement agencies that rely on these drones are getting caught up in the fight as the federal government pushes back on the dominance of Chinese technology.

"We're seeing lives being saved with the use of this technology," says Jon Beal, head of LEDA. He says the organization supports efforts to boost the American drone industry, but that reducing access to Chinese drones is not a good solution.

Sponsor Message

"What that's going to do is cancel out perfectly viable drone programs that are doing great work out there," he says. "We don't want to cut off our nose to spite our face."

How much does this cost?

Agencies pay for drone programs in various ways, including with grants and fundraising. The Ocean County Sheriff's Office uses profits from asset forfeiture and through their municipal operating budget to cover their fleet of 25 drones.

"We have to be cost-effective. And to do that, get the best product that's available to us," Ocean County Sheriff Michael Mastronardy says.

Loading...

toggle caption i Albert Yee for NPR

For them, that meant turning to DJI drones.

In the parking lot of the Ocean County Sheriff's Office in early August, Fennessy breaks down the costs of the equipment one of his deputies carries in his vehicle.

A DJI Matrice 300 RTK: $13,699

A set of two batteries: $1,400

A camera with infrared thermal imaging: $11,499

A (very fancy) remote controller: $1,600

A RESTUBE Automatic, a flotation device that can be dropped into water for rescues by the drone: $130.99

A payload release system: $1,099

That comes to a total of $29,427.99

Fennessy acknowledges this is a huge investment, but says the devices are well-used and well worth it — especially in the summertime, when Ocean County's population nearly doubles. Major events constantly pose a policing challenge for the department, and they've found that drones have helped keep an eye on big crowds.

In July, the department used a drone to drop flotation devices to two swimmers in distress, and rescuers were able to bring them to shore.

Fennessy has become passionate about drones professionally and as a hobbyist. He's done a lot of research, including into the American drone market. "All their stuff is good," he says. "I've flown almost all of them. And I like them. I do. They make good products, but probably about three times the cost" of the DJI tools.

Sponsor Message

Beal, who says his organization is "agnostic" when it comes to what drones departments use, says he thinks Chinese-made drones are "light years ahead of what our American drones are able to do."

For instance, Beal says DJI offers a drone with an impressive, high-resolution thermal camera that costs less than $10,000 right now. He says American-made drones have worse flight-time capabilities, thermal imaging and zoom. And still they usually cost between $20,000 and $50,000, depending on the type and the model.

NPR compared the cost of two drones with similar features. The DJI Matrice 400 drone retails for about $10,500. The American-made Inspired Flight IF800 TOMCAT is going for $21,000.

U.S. actions against DJI cite national security concerns

Ocean County is closely monitoring recent actions by the Trump administration that could limit options for updating its fleet in the future.

Agencies in other states like Florida, Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee have had to terminate their drone programs or plans for one after state lawmakers passed bans on agencies using foreign drones. Beal says some were left scrambling to find ways to pay for more expensive American alternatives when tight department budgets couldn't cover the additional costs.

And there are more federal actions in the works.

The Federal Communications Commission is considering a new rule that would reclassify drones that use tech like thermal imaging as "military grade" — effectively banning many Chinese-made drones that have this integrated technology. Ocean County and other law enforcement use thermal imaging to assist in finding lost people or pets.

toggle caption i Albert Yee for NPR

The FCC already bans the sale of some new models of foreign-made drones without the agency's approval. Federal agencies and contractors cannot use certain foreign-made drones.

The FCC said in response to NPR's questions, "Thanks to President Trump's leadership, America's drone industry is booming with new investment, manufacturing, and jobs. At the FCC, we're doing our part — working hand-in-glove across government and the private sector to make sure that U.S. drone and counter-drone supply chains are safe, secure, and reliable for all."

Sponsor Message

The administration says that Chinese-made drones, and DJI drones specifically, pose a threat to national security — with, for instance, their potential for major attacks during large public gatherings, like the recent World Cup games, among other concerns.

DJI has pushed back against claims that its tech is shared with the Chinese government or that it accesses cameras and other footage collected by users, even hiring a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm to test the company's products for vulnerabilities.

Adam Welsh, head of global policy at DJI said in a statement published in May, "These findings confirm what DJI has consistently maintained: our products are secure, our data practices are transparent" and the concerns that led to the company being banned "are not supported by technical evidence."

There's also the allegation that DJI uses forced labor from Uyghurs, a primarily Muslim ethnic group facing human rights abuses under the Chinese government, to build its products. In 2024, the Customs and Border Protection blocked certain DJI drone imports under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. DJI has strongly denied these allegations, too.

Fennessy says he understands these concerns. "But to be honest, right now," he says, "I want something that's capable to go out there and do the job. And I have it."

Beal says he's seen no hard evidence that China is using these drones or its technology to spy on communities that are using them. He says he can understand the argument to bring more of the drone supply chain stateside.

But that's a problem too, right now.

"We don't have a lot of the minerals. We can't produce the battery now. Even the American companies are using Chinese batteries," he says. "We're kind of limited to the resources that we have in-country or in an allied country, and sometimes that's just not there."

Sponsor Message

Who's likely to absorb the costs? Taxpayers

The National Sheriffs' Association, which represents more than 3,000 sheriffs, has called for the FCC to reconsider the proposed reclassification of certain drones as military grade. In a recent letter, the association wrote that it "recommends that the FCC confirm the adequacy of the domestic market for [Unmanned Aircraft Systems] and [Unmanned Aircraft Systems]-critical components for sheriffs and their colleagues in public safety to acquire drones to fulfill their various mission types, including drones that meet the definition of military grade." In addition to thermal imaging, that classification includes capabilities such as the ability to spray aerosols and lidar, or laser-based sensors.

The NSA recommends that otherwise the FCC add an exemption for state, local, tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to continue to purchase and operate this equipment until the domestic market is built up.

toggle caption i Albert Yee for NPR

Keith Miao, the CEO and founder of Birdstop, a Detroit-based manufacturer of autonomous drone technology, says China "hands down" dominated what he calls "the first era" of drone technology. He says American manufacturers have the potential to "define the next era of enterprise and government use of drone technology."

To Miao, the federal government's latest moves are an acknowledgment that this is a critical technology that, if not manufactured at home, could be a serious problem down the road.

"I think this is going to give American manufacturers an opportunity to rethink … and build out drone manufacturing," Miao says. "We are going all in on manufacturing drones in America and building up the supply chains to do that long term. And so we obviously believe it can be done."

There are several federal and state grants that law enforcement can use to buy American-made drones. But they are competitive.

Fennessy hopes more federal funding comes through, especially if the government eventually wants them to park their DJI drones for good.

Sponsor Message

"If the federal government wants to say, hey, listen, you can't fly your DJI drone anymore, well, that's cool. Um, how am I going to afford to buy the drones that you want me to fly? The taxpayers of Ocean County are going to absorb that," he says. "The funding's got to be there."

World.title: Canadians are still boycotting Las Vegas. The Sin City slump is now a major election issue
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian travel to Las Vegas continues to crater amid U.S. President Donald Trump's attacks on Canada, and the tourism slump in Sin City has become a major midterm election issue.

Nevada Democrats are trying to capitalize on the decline, blaming Trump's trade war and threats toward Canada — the state's largest source of international tourists.

"The Trump Slump is real, and Las Vegas tourism is tanking," the party said in one of its campaign messages ahead of the November vote in this crucial swing state.

"Nevadans are struggling under Trump's tourism crisis," is another line the party has deployed as it puts the fractured relationship with Canada front and centre in this election.

Pedestrians cross an overpass along the Las Vegas Strip, with the Trump International Hotel visible in the background. Nevada Democrats are trying to capitalize on the economic fallout from Trump's trade war with Canada, which they blame for hurting tourism. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

The party and its ally, the powerful Culinary Workers Union Local 226, which represents about 60,000 casino and hospitality workers in the state, are trying to tie the decline in Canadian tourism to local Trump allies such as incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who is in a suddenly close race despite his earlier popularity.

"Donald Trump is directly responsible for this — it's all his fault and it's totally unnecessary," Diana Valles, the president of the union, said in an interview with CBC News.

"God knows why he's doing it, Canadians are our biggest customer. But, at the end the day, Trump's not paying any price. It's the workers and the families that are here," she said, while vowing to ramp up attacks on the GOP as the midterms loom to at least inflict an electoral price.

Visitor numbers, airport arrivals and hotel occupancy rates all fell again in August. Barely half of all rooms in downtown Las Vegas were occupied that month, and casino executives are pointing to the Canadian boycott as one reason for weak demand.

Canadian visits to Las Vegas dropped by 17.4 per cent last year — easily one of the sharpest declines on record. In fact, Canadians staying away contributed to the largest in drop in visitors outside the COVID-19 pandemic since the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority began keeping records in 1970.

Data from Harry Reid International Airport compiled by CBC News shows Canadian airlines are bringing even fewer passengers to Las Vegas than in 2025, suggesting this year could be even worse.

"If you look at a place like Canada, we are off considerably," MGM Resorts CEO Bill Hornbuckle said on the gambling giant's recent earnings call. "Las Vegas is still down on international travel."

In an Oval Office meeting with Trump in September, Hornbuckle said a travel industry plan to draw 100 million international visitors to the U.S. each year depends on the president's actions.

"Travel is difficult," he said. "We need your help, we need your direct involvement, and we know we can make this better."

Trump's one-word response: "Right."

People walk along Fremont Street Experience past an animatronic Donald Trump fortune-telling machine modelled after the classic Zoltar arcade figure in June 2026, in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Caesars Resorts CEO Tom Reeg characterized it this way when discussing the company's recent quarterly loss: "There's a unique flavour to what's gone on with Canada."

What's unique is travel from Canada has fallen far more than from any other country tracked by local authorities. Visits from Mexico, which is also caught up in a tariff dispute with the U.S., are actually up slightly year over year.

Martyn Daly of Winnipeg made annual trips to Vegas for years but has avoided the city since Trump began lashing out at Canada, threatening its sovereignty and imposing tariffs.

"We're just so upset with Trump's total lack of respect, the way he's been treating Canada — he's just totally lost it," Daly said in an interview.

"We don't agree with the 51st state stuff," he said. "Not going to Vegas is just our small way of saying, 'We're not going to take it.'"

Daly is happy to see that Trump's treatment of Canada has become an election issue in Nevada.

"I just think the more pressure he's under, the better," he said of the president.

Daly is facing some pressure of his own: he's been bombarded with casino offers for complimentary nights at various hotels, deals he says are noticeably better than before the Canada-U.S. dispute began. Some casinos have even been accepting the Canadian dollar at par.

As Canadians such as Daly stay away, some casino workers say the official numbers don't fully capture the impact on a city that has long relied on visitors from its northern neighbour.

Spencer Ridenour, a bartender at Chandelier inside the Cosmopolitan casino on the Strip, said his workplace is "losing customers left and right."

A Vegas Golden Knights hockey game did not sell out Thursday, the first time that's ever happened in the franchise's nine-year history. The team's opponent? The Toronto Maple Leafs.

"We used to have Canadians coming for hockey games, they used to come out before and after a game. I have not ID'ed a Canadian in months — this is serious stuff, it's not good for our economy," he said.

Patrons exit the Cosmopolitan hotel on Las Vegas Boulevard in Las Vegas in August 2026. Visitor numbers to the city have fallen 7.5 per cent — the largest decline outside the COVID-19 pandemic since the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority began keeping records in 1970. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP/Getty Images)

Nevada's unemployment rate is among the highest in the U.S., and workers in its tourism-dominated economy are reporting more frequent shift cuts and fewer hours.

"Our members are paying the price of this craziness that is going on in the White House," Valles said.

Republicans in the state have highlighted Trump's "no tax on tips" policy, enacted last year, which has benefitted hospitality workers in Las Vegas in particular.

But if the tips dry up, the policy means less.

"We are in a silent recession here in Las Vegas, and it is because of Donald Trump’s trade war," Ridenour said.

A spokesperson for the state's Republican governor did not respond to a request for comment.

People walk along Las Vegas Boulevard in Las Vegas in August 2026. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP/Getty Images)

Canada has also become an election issue in closely fought congressional races.

Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who faces a tight race in her suburban Las Vegas district, is leaning into an anti-trade war message. In her 30-second campaign ad, Lee twice mentions the trade war and says her Republican opponent, Marty O'Donnell, supports Trump's "expensive" tariffs on Canadian and other goods.

O'Donnell has defended Trump's trade policy as "a form of diplomacy to level the playing field on trade or to protect our national security."

David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, said it's unusual for Canada to factor into any U.S. election, let alone become a significant talking point in a key battleground state.

"The Democrats are certainly playing this up quite a bit. And these races probably wouldn't be as close if it weren't for the tariffs and the lack of Canadians coming across the border," Damore said.

People walk through the casino floor at Resorts World Las Vegas. Political observers say locals are well aware of the drop in Canadian visitors — and that it could influence the midterm election results. (Bridget Bennett/AFP/Getty Images)

He said locals are well aware of the absence of Canadian visitors, making the issue easy for Democrats to campaign on.

"So, between the tariffs, the high gas prices, the decline in visitation, it's really combustible for the Republicans out here right now," he said.

But even if the Democrats take control in Nevada or D.C., he's not expecting much to change.

"There's nothing they can do about a president who goes out of his way to insult our neighbour and one of our biggest allies."

World.title: Billions more for defence, but Canada's military still faces an old budget squeeze
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian military is on the verge of another round of internal belt-tightening, despite an enormous influx of cash from the federal government, CBC News has learned.

It appears to be a combination of past and current budget initiatives colliding with the expectations and demands associated with the gush of defence spending.

The Department of National Defence has been told to focus its billions of extra dollars on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed new combat equipment.

At the same time, it is still subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.

Those cuts — described at the time as internal reallocation by former defence minister Bill Blair — saw an $810-million reduction in the year they were introduced and planned for $908-million cuts each following year. A federal official, who spoke on background, said that schedule is unchanged and the previous government's budget directive has not been rescinded.

To that end, the federal Treasury Board Secretariat, which directs day-to-day government spending, is examining defence operational spending with an eye to reducing expenses by 10 per cent, said two confidential sources who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Defence is getting more money overall, just not as much as may have been expected. Experts warn care needs to be taken with how and where the internal cuts are made and expenses reined in.

Military readiness has suffered over the years because of an absence of operations and maintenance funding. According to the latest federal budget, the current operational readiness of the military overall hovers around 61.3 per cent.

WATCH | Carney on increases to defence spending: Canadians 'expect us to be sensible' around ramped up defence spending, Carney says | Duration closed caption 2:55 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canadians 'expect us to be sensible' around increased defence spending. Carney said what matters is what Canada is spending the money on, pointing to a pay increase for military members.

A little over three weeks ago, the vice-chief of the defence staff, who manages day-to-day activities within the military, delivered the news that internal savings needed to be found and that the military's aggressive growth plans will also have to be tempered, said a third source, with knowledge of the presentation.

In 2025, when Prime Minister Mark Carney's government came in, it imposed its own sweeping expenditure review process across the whole of the federal government, but largely exempted the Department of National Defence (DND).

DND has been told to take serious steps to reduce outside consultants, like the rest of the federal government.

As part of meeting Canada's NATO defence spending commitment, tens of billions of fresh dollars have been poured into the military over the last year along with plans to spend more in the coming decade. But a lot of that cash is being chewed up by a bevy of promises made by the Liberal government and the wage increase given to members of the Forces.

A spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the new government's intention is to protect the Defence Department as much as possible.

"We have however asked DND, as with every other department, to reorient its spending such that it prioritizes capital expenditures — mechanisms that grow and modernize the [Canadian Armed Forces], improve its readiness in an increasingly dangerous world and render it more competitive — and spends less on operating expenditures," said John Fragos, Champagne's press secretary, in a written statement.

"We want results and our plan to spend less on operations and more on capital expenditure is central to that work and in keeping with our plan to rearm the CAF, grow the economy all while balancing operating expenses by 2027-28.”

New dollars already earmarked

Dave Perry, president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute and one of the country's leading experts on defence finances, said in the past when there's been internal belt-tightening it has meant a straight cut, rather than internal reallocation of funds to higher priority areas.

There's been a lot of fanfare around the enormous increase in defence spending and Perry said that has led to a lot of high expectations within the military about what's possible.

"I think it's created this impression that there's gazillions of dollars that could be allocated to any number of new initiatives in the near-term window," Perry said. "And I think that's not really the case."

He said he believes there's not nearly as much "available, investable and disposable cash" as people have been led to believe.

Defence spending is set to rise from the current $75 billion annually to $95.6 billion by 2030, the Parliamentary Budget Office recently reported. Perry said the Defence Department and the military are discovering that much of that cash is already spoken for.

Sources say there's also legacy equipment that Defence continues to pay for and plans that have been made which — if stopped — could generate internal savings. One area mentioned was several IT projects that were planned with the thought that the money will come but are now deemed as unaffordable.

HMCS Corner Brook sits in drydock at CFB Esquimalt in B.C. in 2023. Only one of the military's four submarines are currently operational. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

There are also expensive, outdated pieces of equipment with hefty maintenance bills that, if retired, could produce savings. The Victoria-class submarines are an often cited internal example at the Defence Department.

Only one of the four boats are operational. There are both deep maintenance and modernization plans extending to 2038.

It is conceivable, now that the government has initiated the process of replacing the submarines, that some of those projects could be scaled back.

In 2011, retired lieutenant-general Andrew Leslie was asked to conduct a landmark study of DND that recommended cutting over $1 billion annually by slashing headquarters staff and shifting resources to front-line combat units. It recommended moving or eliminating thousands of civilian and military personnel, primarily concentrated at National Defence Headquarters in Ottawa.

The report also advocated for streamlining structures, including reducing the number of reservists, cutting back on outside contractors and consultants and reorganizing command levels to maximize efficiency.

Leslie's blunt recommendations faced significant political and bureaucratic resistance. Only a portion of the sweeping cuts he recommended were implemented.

In a recent interview, Leslie said he had one clear, simple message for the Carney government: "If you have to make budget reductions, reduce the Department of National Defence. Don't touch the Canadian Armed Forces."

With the threat of war in Europe and elsewhere, he said there's some funding that needs to be protected at all costs.

"Whatever you do, do not cut operations, training and maintenance because that is the lifeblood of the military," Leslie said. "In the final analysis, the people who get the money first are the troops. Air, land, sea, special forces and coast guard, who actually can go out there and do the work."

Leslie said the military has less margin for error than when he wrote his report 15 years ago.

"Our side won't be deciding when the next war or conflict occurs," Leslie said. "It'll be Russia, probably. They have to be well equipped, they have to have the right equipment. And the whole purpose of the prime minister's rearmament for Canada was to make sure that we married together well-trained troops with the right equipment, the right leadership, the right support."

World.title: Ottawa wants to expand the oilsands, but the industry's wastewater problem will grow with it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The recent decision by Prime Minister Mark Carney to fast-track a new oil export pipeline to the West Coast is adding urgency for Ottawa to finally decide what to do with a long-standing environmental issue plaguing the oilsands in Northern Alberta — what to do with tailings ponds.

Oil output in the region is set to grow and the Alberta government wants to double the amount of crude production.

Yet, ever since the first oilsands mine was built about 60 years ago, the industry has been banned from releasing any water. As a result, large tailings ponds throughout the region are filled with decades worth of industrial mining wastewater. The fluid is toxic and harmful to wildlife. For those who live in the region, they fear the harmful health effects, in addition to the impact on the environment.

All day, every day, every few seconds, air cannons blast on the edge of the tailings ponds to help deter birds, ducks and other wildlife from the water, in addition to dozens of makeshift scarecrows dressed in overalls and hard hats.

The problem is as big as 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools or the area of the Island of Montreal under three metres of water.

An aerial view of a tailings pond, which holds mining wastewater and contains various contaminants. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

The amount of tailings fluid continues to increase after growing by 50 per cent over a 10-year period from 2014 to 2024, according to the Alberta Energy Regulator.

As tailings ponds fill up, the industry is urgently pushing for government regulations allowing for the fluid to be treated and then released. At the same time, some Indigenous leaders are calling for oilsands production to slow down until this issue is properly resolved.

Tailings ponds are at capacity and no one wants more of the storage lakes built, said Alberta's Environment Minister Grant Hunter, in an interview with CBC News in Fort McMurray.

"The solution isn't just to keep doing nothing and put our head in the sand. The solution is to actually prove out the science," he said. "We cannot say to industry, 'we want you to double production,' and then not give them the tools to be able to do proper treat-and-release."

Prime Minister Mark Carney announces the proposed Pacific Link pipeline will be fast-tracked during an event in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Oct. 1. (Todd Korol/Reuters)

Alberta's proposal

By the end of the year, the Alberta government plans to lay out exactly what quality standards have to be met for water to be released. Still, the waterways fall under federal jurisdiction, so it will be up to Ottawa to adopt those proposed regulations, suggest changes or keep the ban in place.

Companies insist they have the technology and expertise to treat tailings water. They just need the regulations to know what water quality standards have to be reached. Companies say they will never be able to properly clean up large amounts of land until the tailings ponds are addressed.

"Treating and release is really critical to enabling the large-scale reclamation of these facilities," said Claire Greenwood, a vice-president with Suncor Energy, while speaking at a recent energy conference in Fort McMurray.

"These tailings facilities are not meant to be permanent parts of the landscape in the region. We have full intention of actually turning those tailings ponds into reclaimed sites. And so that's why we're looking for that treatment release."

The company rejected interview requests from CBC News and would not provide access to a water treatment demonstration facility near Fort McMurray.

From left: Suncor's Claire Greenwood, Imperial's Jessica Dillabough and Alberta Environment Minister Grant Hunter speak in favour of developing a treat-and-release policy for the industry, while speaking on a panel during the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray on Sept. 16. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

If treat-and-release is allowed, the water would be pumped into the Athabasca River, which flows directly north from Fort McMurray and the oilsands region to several Indigenous communities before the water eventually drains into the Northwest Territories and the Arctic Ocean.

For Lenny Hansen, the Athabasca River has always been a part of his life, since he was a kid growing up in Fort McMurray. He's caught walleye, northern pike and other fish, with frequent sightings of other wildlife near the banks such as bears, moose and geese.

For 33 years, he worked in the oilsands. In retirement, he's a tour guide taking visitors up the river in his boat.

For him, treat-and-release is not a concern.

"I think it's a great idea and I've seen what they do. I think it's a really good process," said Hansen, a member of the Fort McMurray Métis District 17.

WATCH | A birds-eye view of the tailings and a look inside the treat-and-release debate: Alberta oilsands push for a decision on toxic tailings ponds | Duration closed caption 6:11 A new proposed pipeline has oil boom anticipation high in Alberta, but as CBC’s Kyle Bakx explains, it’s also adding urgency for a federal government decision on what to do about the decades-old problem of toxic tailings ponds.

Frustrations growing

Treating and releasing tailings pond water into the Athabasca River has alarmed some Indigenous leaders and their communities.

When representatives from Suncor Energy visited Fort Chipewyan last month, they hoped to demonstrate to the community how their treatment technology worked. Instead, they quickly left when they were greeted by protesters.

Chief Melody Lepine leads the Mikisew Cree First Nation (MCFN), which is based in the Fort Chipewyan region, north of Fort McMurray. She feels the provincial government is forcing her community to accept treat-and-release, especially after the federal and provincial governments signed their MOU this past summer.

Lepine said the protest against Suncor came from a feeling among residents that their concerns are being ignored. She said her First Nation would consider legal action if her community felt treat-and-release threatened Fort Chipewyan.

"This is not the first time where things have been forced, in terms of decisions made that impact us, that we have to deal with the consequences later," she said.

"Exploring all of the options of how to reverse those decisions and activities would be definitely something we would seriously consider."

At least one Indigenous-led company in the region hopes to find an alternative. Tũ Nipi Water Solutions was recently given conditional approval of a $4.6 million provincial grant to begin researching other proposals for treating tailings.

The company's CEO, Ron Quintal, hopes to find technology that can treat and reuse — not release — tailings water. He says the fear behind treat-and-release among Indigenous people is because of "generational trauma" associated with water.

There are fears that contamination from the oilsands has made its way into waterbodies and contributed to cancers in Fort Chipewyan, for instance. Lepine points to the 5.2 million litres of oilsands wastewater that overflowed from Imperial Oil's Kearl Lake facility in 2023.

"We don't drink the water in the community and that's going back to that generational trauma," said Quintal, who is also the former president of Fort McKay Métis Nation.

"Treat-and-release is not something that my ownership, my leadership and my community could ever support," he said, describing debate about the issue as "white hot."

Lepine also wants to see industry groups and different levels of government pursue alternatives to treat-and-release. She says the only way MCFN would accept treat-and-release is if leadership are confident the technology will not harm human health or the environment.

"But we're nowhere near that today," she said.

"It is a situation of environmental racism. We often say if the rivers flew in the opposite direction to non-Indigenous communities, would things be like this?"

Oilsands facilities are shown near the Athabasca River at Suncor's Base Plant near Fort McMurray. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Pressure on Ottawa to act

Industry players say they have spent several years developing and testing various technologies to treat the wastewater, in addition to supporting ongoing water monitoring programs in the region.

"If we take these elements together, we think that gives confidence that a treatment technology is effective, environmentally protective and capable of building, delivering long term results," said Jessica Dillabough, a sustainability manager with Imperial Oil.

The industry is testing various chemical and biological methods of treating tailings water and filtering out contaminants. Major oil companies have partnered with university scientists on dozens of research projects focused on water and tailings in the oilsands.

For now, Ottawa is tight-lipped about its next move. The federal environment minister declined interview requests from CBC News and a spokesperson wouldn't provide any timeline on a decision.

Last month, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson answered a question from Radio-Canada during a press conference in Alberta about tailings ponds, remarking "We will do the work to make sure we have the right regulations with respect to tailings ponds."

Hodgson said the regulations would be developed by the end of 2027.

However, later that day, his spokesperson said to CBC News that the minister had misspoken and there is no timeline.

World.title: This Canadian-Punjabi rapper was murdered in 2022. His new tour is testing the market for holographic concerts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ravinder Sidhu and his sister Nav travelled to Toronto from India to see Sidhu Moose Wala’s Signed to God world tour kick off at Scotiabank Arena last Friday, dropping $550 each on tickets. They knew it would be no ordinary performance.

That's because the Canadian-Punjabi rapper died in 2022 after gunmen fired a hail of bullets into a vehicle he was in near his hometown in Northern India. A hologram replaced Moose Wala on stage Friday, testing the technology’s ability to deliver a memorable fan experience at a premium price.

"Maybe it will be futuristic," Ravinder told CBC News outside the venue before the show. "We can't express it. We're over-excited."

Another fan, Harry Singh, says he spent $270 for his ticket, plus airfare from California.

"If you waited until last minute, that same ticket I got is now like $1,500," Singh told CBC News hours before the show. "I got pretty lucky. I bought them early."

WATCH | Sidhu Moose Wala fans share what they paid to see the hologram concert: How much would you spend on a hologram concert? | Duration 1:52 The Signed to God Hologram World Tour opened in Toronto on Oct. 9 in honour of the late Punjabi singer and songwriter Sidhu Moose Wala, who died in 2022. The show featured several musical guests and was headlined by a 3D hologram of the late artist. CBC News caught up with several fans ahead of the show to ask how much they paid for their tickets.

Some tickets for the Toronto show advertised online cost nearly $2,000 before taxes and fees. Prices for the next stop in Vancouver on Thursday are similar.

"They're saying it's going to look like it's completely real, but we'll find out," Singh said.

In a text message after the show, he says the concert featured an unreleased song called Rebirth, and an on-stage appearance by the late rapper's younger brother. In one video he recorded during the show, Singh is seen surrounded by a sea of smartphones held in the air as people sing along with the crowd and the hologram of Moose Wala on stage.

Sidhu Moose Wala, a Canadian-Punjabi rapper who was shot and killed in northern India in 2022, appeared on stage as a hologram during a concert on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 at Toronto's Scotiabank Arena. (Submitted by Harry Singh)

From ABBA to Ozzy

Music journalist and historian Alan Cross says the rise of digital-first performances is real. He points to the commercial success of ABBA Voyage in London , which features de-aged digital avatars of the Swedish pop group performing with a live 10-piece band.

A cohort of aging rock stars, the transfer of musical catalogues into the hands of savvy investors, and modern audiences accustomed to the digital world are all things he says will contribute to the growing holographic concert trend.

"Not only do artists become stubbornly dead, but they also get tired. They want vacations. They want to spend time with their families," Cross told CBC News in an interview.

"In the next five years we're going to see a mass extinction event with all these rock and roll heroes and music heroes that we've known our entire lives," he said.

He noted that though their deaths are inevitable, technology can give them a second life on stage because "we're raising a new generation of people who live digitally."

David Nussbaum, founder of Los Angeles-based hologram company Proto says using the technology to bring back stars who have died "makes a lot of sense."

"We're working with Jack and Sharon Osborne right now to bring back Ozzy, who passed just about a year ago."

Nussbaum calls his company's recreation of the Black Sabbath frontman an "agentic AI avatar." Not only does it possess encyclopedic knowledge of Osbourne’s work and public life, he says it can speak to fans in languages the real rock star never knew.

"If you're Chinese and you ask that question in Chinese, he's gonna answer you in Chinese. If you're Italian, and you asked him that question in Italian, he's going to answer you in Italian," he said.

He says that with hundreds of dialects available, fans can communicate with their favourite artists, living or dead, in the language of their choice. "This is the ultimate form of connecting."

Once the stuff of fiction, people have been developing this technology for entertainment purposes for years.

Flash back to 14 years ago, when another famous rap star murdered in his prime was digitally resurrected for thousands of fans at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.

Rapper Snoop Dogg, left, and a hologram of the late rapper Tupac Shakur perform onstage during the third day of the 2012 Coachella Valley Music & Arts Festival at the Empire Polo Field in Indio, Calif. (Christopher Polk/Getty Images)

"I don't think I'm the only one who watched that video of Tupac Shakur at Coachella in 2012," said tech expert Carmi Levy.

"It almost felt like lightning had struck the entertainment and tech industries at the same time," said Levy, noting that the experience of viewing video hadn't changed much for generations until that Coachella set, which "used some very cutting-edge techniques for the time."

He also noted that the quality of the technology has improved a lot since 2012, and continues to evolve with advancements in artificial intelligence.

What's next?

Proto's Nussbaum agrees and says his company aims to "seamlessly integrate" realistic, AI-powered holograms into the real world.

Proto's products include a life-sized holographic display units that project photorealistic, 4K volumetric people or objects inside a light box, allowing subjects to beam in live, or interact with AI avatars.

"The olden days of hologram performances were mostly magic tricks and theater and fun experiences. But now, this technology, although it's being used quite a bit in music and entertainment, most of the time it's been used in enterprise," he told CBC News.

"It's being used by doctors to beam into rural remote clinics, where patients are having trouble finding expert doctors and health care providers. It's being used by educators to beam onto lecture stages from all over the world, without having to get onto an airplane and fly to a college or university. It's been used in museums. It's being used in lots of different settings."

Nussbaum's company is also expanding the celebrity hologram experience off the stage.

He says Proto recently worked with Bon Jovi during the band’s residency at New York’s Madison Square Garden to create what it called an interactive hologram of rock star Jon Bon Jovi so fans could pose for realistic-looking photos.

Levy says it’s only a matter of time before consumers can enjoy holographic experiences at home.

"If you look at the typical smartphone today, which has photo and video capabilities that would have made an advanced photographer and videographer blush just a few years ago, it's easy to appreciate that at some point, advanced 3D AI capabilities — holographic capabilities even — will ultimately be built into the multimedia capabilities of a smartphone, or whatever it is that replaces it," he said.

"The industry is certainly heading toward that point."

World.title: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive who negotiates with ransomware hackers has been arrested in Pennsylvania as authorities investigate a hacking group that claims to have stolen FBI employee information.

Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear that a prominent ransomware negotiator had been arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.

FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday confirmed the arrest of a "suspected co-conspirator" in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov which exposed a trove of sensitive data about FBI staff.

"We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," Patel said on social media.

Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers.

Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during a Senate Judiciary hearing on Oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in September 2026 in Washington. Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters investigation. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

'A sense of shock'

"For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday.

Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened."

"This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well."

The ​court records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of the suspect's last ⁠name — "Dobrovsky" or "Dobrosky" — and do not identify his age, profession or employer.

Prison records show a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is being held at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

Reuters reported that electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a 54-year-old resident of Richmond Hill, a suburb of Toronto.

Long history in cybersecurity

Dubrovsky's LinkedIn profile describes him as a specialist in ‌negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments, as well as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert, business leader, speaker, author and educator."

According to his profile, Dubrovsky has held senior positions in cybersecurity for decades.

He wrote on LinkedIn last month that he would be attending the NetDilligence conference in Philadelphia in October with cybersecurity firm CyberSteward. The company posted photos of Dubrovsky at the conference a week ago and said he was signing copies of a book he recently published about handling cyber extortion.

WATCH | Experts say AI will drive future cybercrime: AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter | Duration closed caption 1:29 A new EY report suggests AI will become a major force behind cybercrime in 2026 as programs help attackers hone their scamming skills.

In the book's introduction, Dubrovsky writes: "I have negotiated with criminals who viewed themselves as martyrs, criminal masterminds, and patriots of their own countries even after deploying malware against critical infrastructure and causing billions of dollars in damage. Such people could still look in the mirror and see goodness."

CBC News reached out to CyberSteward by phone, email and in person at its Toronto address, but did not get a response Monday.

The FBI's national press office declined to comment directly on Dubrovsky's arrest and referred CBC News to Patel's statement.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon told The Canadian Press on Friday that "the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack," but directed all further questions to the FBI.

ShinyHunters 'poked the bear': expert

ShinyHunters is known as one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups, typically demanding ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it has obtained.

The hacking group caused chaos at universities around the world in May, including in Canada, with a cyberattack on Canvas, an online learning-management system that connects millions of students with their instructors.

ShinyHunters has also been associated with high-profile cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, Ticketmaster , Pornhub and Rockstar Games.

Last month, the group claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — in what it said was retaliation for the law enforcement agency making false claims about the group.

ShinyHunters later told CBC News they would not release the data.

David Shipley, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of Fredericton-based Beauceron Security, said the stunt "poked the bear" and has "literally unleashed the most powerful law enforcement agency in the world on them."

WATCH | Canvas strikes deal with hackers: Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 6:25 The parent company behind Canvas, a widely used learning management platform connecting students with their schools or universities, has struck a deal with the hacking group claiming responsibility for last week's massive cybersecurity breach.

Shipley said surprise was the first thing that came to mind when he heard of the latest arrest.

"I knew the ShinyHunters investigation was going to go in interesting places because it's already the stuff of Hollywood movies," he told CBC News.

"I don't think anyone saw this twist coming."

Shipley said Dubrovsky was well regarded and worked for "top-tier" cybersecurity firms.

"I feel terrible for his former colleagues, both at his current firm and his past firms, who have been dragged through these awful headlines," he said.
