World.title: By-election breach
World.content:
In this file photo, Jamaicans wait in line to cast their ballots at a polling station in rural Jamaica.

CITIZENS Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) has joined calls for municipal corporations to hold four overdue by-elections, warning that the prolonged vacancies are leaving constituents without representation and undermining democratic accountability.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at CAFFE’s New Kingston offices last Thursday, former Chairman Dr Lloyd Barnett described the municipalities’ failure to fill the vacancies as a disregard of the law.

“They have completely ignored the law… There are four vacancies now. That’s a great concern to CAFFE,” Barnett argued.

CAFFE is an internationally acclaimed independent organisation that monitors voting locally and, in recent years, across the region. Its observers assess whether democratic principles are upheld, including ballot secrecy and freedom from intimidation.

The organisation has observed multiple elections since its establishment in 1997.

Barnett’s call for action follows a warning issued by the Electoral Commission of Jamaica (ECJ) in March 2026 — when it wrote to Morant Bay Mayor Louis Chin, Savanna-la-Mar Mayor Danree Delancy, and Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby — highlighting their responsibility to fill vacancies for councillors within the stipulated time period.

The commission reminded mayors that, in accordance with the Representation of the People Act, a by-election is to be held within approximately three months of the vacancy in an electoral division being recorded in the minutes of a municipal corporation.

The vacancies arose after three sitting councillors — Yvonne Rosemarie Shaw, Dennis Gordon, and Delroy Williams — were elected Members of Parliament in the September 3, 2025 General Election, while Councillor Patrick Forrester (People’s National Party, Petersfield Division) in Westmoreland died in a motor vehicle crash on September 17 last year.

Shaw was the People’s National Party (PNP) councillor for the Morant Bay Division in St Thomas; while Gordon, the PNP represetnative for Maxfield Park Division, and the Jamaica Labour Party’s Williams, a former Kingston mayor, represented the Seivwright Gardens Division, both in the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC).

At the time, Mayor Swaby acknowledged the commission’s notice and had indicated that conversations would begin in short order to stage by-elections in the Maxfield Park and Seivwright Gardens divisions, which were represented by the People’s National Party’s Gordon and the Jamaica Labour Party’s Williams, respectively.

As Swaby delivered his statements and announcements during a monthly KSAMC meeting, he explained that the election process was delayed due to the impact of last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

According to him, conducting polls in the immediate aftermath of the Category 5 storm, which devastated Jamaica’s south- and north-western parishes, would have been distasteful.

“Councillors will recall that the by-elections to fill these vacancies were due by mid-December 2025.

However, in the aftermath of the significant destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa on October 28, 2025, I wrote the Honourable Desmond McKenzie, [minister of local government], seeking an extension of the time within which the KSAMC could complete these by-elections.

“While the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew were spared the most severe direct impact, the entire country was actively involved in helping persons affected to put their lives back in order.

I strongly believe it would have been highly insensitive to engage the residents in an election at that time,” said the mayor.

Nearly a year since Hurricane Melissa, and six months since the ECJ’s written notice, all four vacancies remain unoccupied, leaving residents unrepresented. “That, in fact, illustrates the importance of continuous vigilance.

Because here is an important part of your democracy and you have people not being represented over here because the Government and the authorities failed to act,” Barnett said, urging the municipalities to fill the vacancies as soon as possible.

World.title: Observer, NEPA launching Fi Wi Land environmental series October 19
World.content:
This video grab shows National Environment and Planning Agency Environmental Officer Damany Calder being interviewed by Jamaica Observer online reporter Carlysia Ramdeen for the first in an environmental series being launched October 19 by the State agency and the newspaper.

BATS have long been the subject of fear, folklore, and ‘duppy’ stories but these creatures we’ve spent generations running from are some of nature’s hardest-working environmental protectors.

A single insect-eating bat can consume up to 1,000 mosquitoes in an hour, providing natural pest control, while others help pollinate plants and disperse seeds, contributing to the regeneration of our forests.

Jamaica is home to an impressive 21 species of bats, including five found nowhere else in the world and eight others native to the wider Caribbean.

Yet, despite their importance, bats remain among the island’s most misunderstood creatures.

We’re putting bats in the spotlight in the premiere episode of Fi Wi Land, a brand-new environmental series from the Jamaica Observer and the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) as part of the agency’s activities in recognition of its 25th anniversary of serving the island.

Over the next 12 weeks we’ll explore the wildlife, ecosystems and natural resources that make Jamaica unique while highlighting NEPA’s work to safeguard our environment for future generations, including air and water quality management, tree reforestation, coral reef restoration, beach conservation, protection of Jamaica’s iguana population, and mangrove restoration.

The first episode of Fi Wi Land premieres October 19, 2026, on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and social media platforms.

World.title: $96 billion in missed opportunities
World.content:
NEARLY $100 billion allocated to Jamaica’s capital budget over the past decade went unspent, leaving major road, water, and health infrastructure projects severely underfunded and depriving Jamaicans across the island of critical improvements, Opposition Senator Ramon Small-Ferguson has charged.

He made the claim during his contribution to the State of the Nation Debate in the Senate on October 9, arguing that the Government’s failure to utilise the allocated funds has hampered investment in essential public infrastructure.

According to Small- Ferguson, the economic reforms that started under the Portia Simpson Miller Administration, when Dr Peter Phillips was finance minister, created the fiscal space from which the current Andrew Holness-led Government has benefited.

But, he lamented what he called “missed opportunities”.

Citing that the country’s capital budget finances roads, water systems, hospitals, and other infrastructure that improve public services and expand our capacity to grow, Small-Ferguson said, “Budgeting for that investment is a commitment.

Delivering it is the responsibility [of Government].” The Opposition senator told Parliament that over the 10 financial years from 2016/17 to 2025/26, approximately $635.7 billion was originally budgeted for capital expenditure by central government.

Of that amount, approximately $539.4 billion was actually spent.

“That is a cumulative shortfall of $96.3 billion,” he noted.

Small-Ferguson highlighted that actual expenditure fell below the original allocation in nine of the 10 years.

He said approximately $61.8 billion of the cumulative gap arose through budget reductions while another $34.5 billion remained unspent against revised allocations.

The lawmaker, who is also chief executive officer at Barita Investments Limited, outlined that in 2023/24 the Government originally budgeted $75.4 billion and spent $55.9 billion, leaving a $19.5-billion gap.

In 2024/25, delivery fell $22.5 billion short of the original allocation, while in 2025/26 it was $14.8 billion short.

Reiterating that this was a “massive missed opportunity”, Small-Ferguson stated that a $96.3-billion shortfall could fund a “massive programme of works”.

“It could fit four Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopments; it could fit two SPARK programmes; we could build 10 Spanish Town Hospital redevelopment projects; we could do seven Rio Cobre Water Treatment projects; we could build 100 health centres with this money,” he said.

“Together, these amount to approximately $92.5 billion — still $3.8 billion below the shortfall.

This comparison illustrates the scale of roads, water systems, hospitals, and community health care that could have been advanced through more consistent investment and delivery,” he added.

Small-Ferguson argued that delay carries a cost, as transport operators pay for repairs, farmers lose time and produce reaching markets, businesses lose productive hours without reliable water, and patients wait for improved facilities.

“We pay through higher eventual costs and years of benefits foregone,” he insisted.

He also acknowledged that the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent hurricanes imposed extraordinary demands on the budget but argued that they cannot explain a delivery problem that persisted across the decade, “including in the better years when we had the opportunity to strengthen Jamaica before the next crisis”.

“Again, I say that we did not take sufficient advantage of those years.

Roads, water systems, and health facilities that could have strengthened communities and supported production remained undelivered.

We entered harder times still carrying weaknesses we should have addressed,” he argued.

“This is one reason we struggle to grow.

Businesses need reliable infrastructure to expand.

After 10 years, procurement difficulties and capacity constraints cannot remain recurring explanations without a programme to correct them.

Jamaicans should not face the next crisis still waiting for projects promised before the last one,” Small-Ferguson said.

He made several recommendations to the Government that he said could reverse the current trend.

Among them was that within six months the Government should lay before Parliament a programme identifying the principal sources of delay, the reforms required, the institution responsible for each reform, and its implementation deadline.

World.title: Can the chancellor really win back business?
World.content:
Reform is under pressure again – but could the coming weeks prove make-or-break for Nigel Farage’s party?

With fresh undercover filming threatening to cause trouble and a crucial report into the £5m gift looming, how serious could the fallout be?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy also unpack the latest polling: is Kemi Badenoch enjoying a post-conference bounce, or are internal divisions across the political landscape reshaping the race?

Elsewhere, the battle for the budget narrative is heating up, and Sam has some intel on why business leaders could be getting extra attention from No 10.

Plus, with a date set for an EU-UK summit, Anne gauges the opinion across the continent.

World.title: The Ceuta fears shaping Spain’s election
World.content:
As the United States looks towards Russia for diesel, European leaders are doubling down on their support for Ukraine.

On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart unpack all the ways the EU plans to put its money where its mouth is and help Kyiv. Expect it to be the talk of the town at this week’s meeting of leaders at the European Council summit.

Next, exclusive polling coming out of Spain shows that 58% of Spaniards fear tensions with Morocco over Ceuta and Melilla could spiral into an armed conflict in the next 10 years. We discuss what this means for a country that’s heading into a snap election at the end of next month.

Speaking of Spain, we’re launching Madrid Playbook today! For our Spanish-speaking listeners, subscribe why don’t you?

Finally, Ursula von der Leyen may have been smiling in influencer videos filmed after her State of the Union speech, but behind closed doors, her comms teams was furious.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s Trump dilemma: Fight back or fold?
World.content:
The question for Zelenskyy is just how angry he can actually afford to be.

“His showing his frustration is understandable, but there are downsides,” said Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat and fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.

The Ukrainian president immediately dubbed Trump’s deal a “weak decision” and “a gift to Putin” that will fund Russia’s war. Even more defiantly, he approved further drone strikes on Russian refineries, prompting Trump to call for Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader.

Zelenskyy shows no signs of heeding Trump’s command to “better damn well stop” striking at Russia’s energy industry. That’s very much a continuation of his loss of patience this year, which has seen him sharpening his rhetoric toward both critics and allies, rebuking European leaders for moving too slowly with support, trading barbs with Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, and openly questioning Trump’s approach to the war.

The tougher tone reflects mounting exasperation in Kyiv — especially with the U.S. president. Ukraine’s defense resilience and innovations with drones and missiles have augmented Zelenskyy’s confidence and readiness to push back. And yet, venting his frustration is not without risks.

Willasey-Wilsey suspects Zelenskyy may be calculating that Trump could emerge weakened from next month’s midterms, especially as some Republicans are already breaking ranks over the diesel deal. But the Ukrainian leader risks provoking Trump into cutting off vital U.S. intelligence support or pressuring Elon Musk to disable SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, on which Ukraine’s military heavily relies.

World.title: Poll: Spaniards say Ceuta crisis could spark armed conflict with Morocco
World.content:
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s Party currently polling ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists, claimed the crisis has been “spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco” and that the government had covered it up. Sumar, a junior partner in Sánchez’s government, also questioned Rabat’s role, and a police report alleged Moroccan agents had helped orchestrate the mass movement.

The people, power moves and policies shaping Spanish politics. Email Address This site is protected by Turnstile and the Cloudflare Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Subscribe now

Sánchez described the surge as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity but repeatedly dismissed claims that Rabat was behind it, instead accusing smugglers.

Still, in the POLITICO survey, three-quarters of Spaniards said Morocco poses a real threat to their country’s territorial integrity.

People who said they’d cast their votes for Feijóo or the far-right Vox party in the next election were both more likely to consider Morocco a threat to Spain, and more likely to think that tensions over the exclaves could lead to an armed conflict this decade. More than three-quarters of Vox supporters and 68% of People’s Party supporters thought a conflict in the next decade was likely.

Even among supporters of Sánchez’s own Socialist Party, nearly two-thirds considered Morocco a genuine threat. The party’s support base was split about the likelihood of a conflict, with 47% saying an armed conflict is likely but 43% saying it is not.

The poll shows that Morocco was widely seen as a threat to Spain. Over 80% of Spaniards said it posed a moderate to significant risk to Spain, putting the country well ahead of other foreign powers such as China, the U.S. and Russia.

World.title: France’s Glucksmann notched a crushing primary victory. But he needs more allies to win the presidency.
World.content:
“We’re still a long way from the final list of candidates, and the political landscape is far from set in stone,” said Socialist MEP Christophe Clergeau, who had backed Glucksmann’s rival Olivier Faure in the center-left primary. “It’s up to [Glucksmann] to build momentum, unite the Socialist family … [and] reach out to all left-wing voters to demonstrate his ability to be our camp’s voice.”

But Glucksmann and his allies are confident that his strong showing in the primary — he won more than 66% of the vote in the first round, more than four times as many votes as his nearest competitor — is a sign of good things to come.

“All the citizens of the left who came, voted, took part have given me tremendous hope,” Glucksmann said in his victory speech. “The result is indisputable: I am tonight the candidate of the democratic left.”

Aurore Lalucq, a fellow S&D MEP and co-president of Place Publique, said the result “isn’t far from a landslide.”

“There is no doubt that his platform is widely supported, and that gives us the strength to rally others behind us,” she said. “The ability to unite comes from strength.”

The next battle

Glucksmann faces stiff competition from Mélenchon and his party, France Unbowed, for voters who lean left.

World.title: Encuesta: Los españoles afirman que la crisis de Ceuta podría desencadenar un conflicto armado con Marruecos
World.content:
Un 58% de los españoles teme que las tensiones bilaterales por Ceuta y Melilla probablemente acabarán con un conflicto armado con Marruecos en los próximos diez años, según una encuesta de POLITICO Poll, realizada por la firma independiente PF Global en septiembre y publicada en exclusiva por el nuevo Madrid Playbook.

Los jóvenes de 18-24 son los que están más alarmados. En torno a un 75% ve probable que lleguemos a las manos, la cifra cae en los mayores de 65 a un 47%, según el estudio realizado antes de que Sánchez anunciara el adelanto electoral.

El briefing imprescindible para quienes deciden, negocian y marcan la agenda política. Dirección de correo This site is protected by Turnstile and the Cloudflare Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Regístrate ahora

El temor a un conflicto armado con el país norteafricano en la próxima década está más consolidado entre los votantes conservadores de Feijóo (un 68%) y los de extrema derecha de Vox (75,7%). Los socialistas están divididos en este punto, con un 47% que cree que es probable y un 43% que desestima el escenario bélico.

El líder del Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quien encabeza actualmente las encuestas para el 29 de noviembre, ha acusado a Rabat de “coordinar” una crisis y que el Gobierno lo ha ocultado. Sumar, el socio minoritario de la coalición, también ha cuestionado abiertamente la actitud marroquí. Un informe policial apuntó a que agentes marroquíes habrían ayudado a orquestar el movimiento masivo de personas hasta la frontera española.

Aunque en un primer momento Sánchez describió la entrada como una agresión contra la integridad territorial española, después suavizó el tono y ha negado en todo momento que Rabat esté detrás, o supiera con antelación, del desplazamiento masivo de migrantes. En su lugar, el Gobierno ha señalado a las “mafias migratorias”.

Pese a ello, tres de cada cuatro españoles creen que Marruecos supone una amenaza real para la integridad territorial de su país. Una afirmación que se repite mayoritariamente en todas las demografías (71% en la franja 18-24 años y 76% en la de más de 65; 76% de hombres y 73% de mujeres; 77% de universitarios y 74% de no universitarios) y por votantes de todos los partidos (90% en VOX, 85% en PP, 64% en PSOE y 61% en Sumar).

World.title: Northern Ireland secretary denies he ‘bent the knee’ to Sinn Féin
World.content:
Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson accused Bryant of bowing to a threat of violence from Irish Republican Army militants who featured prominently within the Garvaghy Road crowd. Most IRA members have observed a cease-fire since 1997 and officially disarmed in 2005, but several small factions still plot occasional bomb and gun attacks.

Robinson said Northern Ireland’s unionists “know that this British government has bent the knee to them.”

But Bryant said his decision to bar the Orangemen — despite a decision last month by the region’s independent Parades Commission to permit a heavily restricted march by 35 Orangemen — had so far kept violence at bay.

“I utterly reject the charge that I have in any way succumbed to mob rule. The truth is, things have actually passed remarkably peacefully,” he said, adding: “I don’t think anybody seriously proposed that the police should drag people off the street.”

He spoke hours after two courts in Northern Ireland tangled with the conflict of rights stirred up by the revival of the Orange marching demands in Portadown, a sectarian dispute that triggered bloodshed and rioting across Northern Ireland in the mid-1990s.

The Court of Appeal, overseen by Northern Ireland’s highest judge, rejected a lawsuit by the Garvaghy Road protesters seeking to challenge the original Parades Commission ruling. Orange supporters said this judgment kept the door open for an eventual parade down Garvaghy Road for the first time since 1997, when police backed by British soldiers forced the parade through with the use of armored vehicles and volleys of plastic bullets.

World.title: Europe pushes tougher line on Russia in growing split with Trump
World.content:
"Russia is not interested in deescalation, ceasing fire or peace," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a security conference in Warsaw on Monday. "That is why I will go to Brussels to ask my partners to consider seriously increasing sanctions against Russia."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also called for further restrictions, pointing to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure despite Trump's announcement of a ceasefire.

"Russia will only negotiate in good faith under pressure," Merz said Monday. "Following Moscow's reckless attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy supply, we must even tighten [sanctions] further."

German Chancellor and leader of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Friedrich Merz at the two-day retreat of the CDU leadership on Oct. 12, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

The push comes after EU foreign ministers on Monday approved the bloc's largest-ever addition to its Russia sanctions list, targeting more than 1,600 individuals and entities. The European Commission is also preparing a 23rd package of sectoral sanctions, which Kyiv expects to be circulated to EU governments by the end of the year, according to a senior Ukrainian official who was, like others in this article, granted anonymity to speak frankly on the sensitive negotiations.

Other European countries are taking a similar position. Britain and Norway have also pledged to increase pressure on Moscow.

"It's important to sanction Russia not to finance the war," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO, calling for loopholes in existing restrictions to be closed.

World.title: LVMH sales miss growth forecasts as China luxury demand slows
World.content:
The fashion giant, once Europe’s most valuable listed company, reported revenue of €18.5 billion in the three months to the end of September.

 

The firm, whose brands include Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and drinks maker Hennessy, saw a revenue increase of 1.2% year on year in the third quarter, after a 0.1% rise in the second quarter and a 5.9% fall in the first.

However, organic sales growth, which excludes currency movements and changes to the group's business portfolio, fell short of expectations. Growth slowed to 1% in the third quarter from 3% in the second.

Overall, in the first nine months, sales were €57.1 billion, with organic sales up 2%.

The company praised its diverse business portfolio in a statement, saying it provided resilience in an uncertain geopolitical and economic environment.

LVMH said sales growth was good in the United States, Europe and Japan, but it faced a less favourable environment in China.

As a result, the fashion and leather goods segment saw sales drop 5% on an organic basis as weaker demand in the world's second-largest economy weighed on the business. The decline was steeper than the roughly 2% fall expected by analysts, according to Deutsche Bank.

Louis Vuitton also saw its public image take a hit in China after suing local tea company Molly Tea for copying its logo. While it won the case, the dispute provoked a wave of indignation on social media and calls to boycott the brand.

Overall, the quarter proved to be a setback for the fashion and leather goods segment, as the drop in sales followed the division posting its first organic sales gain in two years in the previous quarter.

But LVMH's selective retailing division, which includes the Sephora perfume and cosmetics retail chain, posted an 8% organic sales increase, while the watches and jewellery and wines and spirits segments both managed 6% organic gains.

Deutsche Bank analysts said the results could prompt further cuts to earnings forecasts for the second half of 2026 and 2027.

“It is hard to see what could change investor sentiment in the short term,” they wrote, although they viewed the weakness as cyclical rather than structural.

"Overall, recovery is taking longer due to the weaker Chinese demand, but the company do not see it as a structural issue. Brand initiatives are producing results and they expect these bottom-up measures to be more gradual," they wrote.

LVMH's share price has dropped nearly 40% since the start of the year. In September, L'Oréal overtook the group as France's most valuable listed company. LVMH’s share price was down more than 1.6% at around 10am CEST in Paris.

World.title: Benjamin Netanyahu orders prosecution of 'NAZA' documentary interviewees
World.content:
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of officers interviewed in the award-winning film NAZA.

 

Netanyahu is ordering for the filmmakers, Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be prosecuted for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

He has asked for attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara, IDF chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and Shin Bet head David Zini, to “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

NAZA, which premiered in Venice and won the Special Jury Prize, is currently being screened in cinemas in more than 50 countries, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.

Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, it features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.

The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.

It received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at Venice – the longest in the festival's history.

The Israeli government has previously attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship.

As reported by the Guardian, Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest.”

Regarding Netanyahu’s threats, he added: “I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

NAZA has been released in select cinemas more than 50 territories. It is being made free-to-watch on The Guardian’s website in November.

World.title: Child marriage in southern Germany: Over 350 cases recorded, some brides as young as 11
World.content:
In the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg, a total of 358 so-called child marriages have been officially recorded since 2012. Only eight of these forced marriages have so far been legally annulled. According to authorities, the other 350 cases were brought to an end in other ways.

 

This alarming finding comes from a response by the Baden-Württemberg state government to a minor inquiry submitted by AfD state parliament members Nikolaos Boutakoglou and Emely Knorr.

The Tübingen regional authority is responsible for recording the data, the answer came from the Ministry of the Interior.

11-year-old Iraqi girl married off

The eight final annulments took place between 2018 and 2024. Among the documented cases was the marriage of an 11-year-old girl from Iraq to a 17-year-old Iraqi, which was annulled in 2020.

As early as 2018, the marriage of a 14-year-old Afghan girl to a 30-year-old man had been ended. In 2024 two further annulments were added: they concerned a 16-year-old German girl and a 25-year-old Pakistani man and a 16-year-old Syrian girl and a 27-year-old man from the same country.

State parliament member Nikolaos Boutakoglou wrote on Facebook that the issue was "really awful" but was being treated as a taboo.

According to its own account, the ministry deals exclusively with such marriages entered into abroad.

Since summer 2017, the Act to Combat Child Marriages has been in force in Germany. In 2024, the Bundestag adopted new rules to protect minors in marriages concluded abroad.

Hundreds of cases without state intervention

The significantly higher number of cases concluded in other ways raises questions about how these marriages continued. For the period from 2015 to 2026, the regional authority lists a total of 350 proceedings under the heading "other disposals."

But what became of the other child marriages? The state government cites, among other things, the death of a spouse, reaching adulthood, a decision not to seek annulment or a new marriage concluded abroad. In these cases, there was therefore no legally binding annulment.

For 2023, the records include the case of a 12-year-old Afghan girl who was married to a 21-year-old Afghan man. Girls aged 13 and 14 also appear several times in the statistics.

The most recent entries in the overview relate to 2026. They include, among other things, marriages of 16- and 17-year-old girls to adult men. The statistics record the age of the spouses at the time of marriage and their respective nationalities.

According to the Interior Ministry, at the time the inquiry was answered there were no court proceedings pending to annul child marriages.

State parliament member Emely Knorr, who co-initiated the inquiry, demanded on the social media platform Instagram: "Child marriages are incompatible with our values. Children have a right to safety, education and a self-determined future. That is why we need effective protection, early intervention and resolute action against forced marriages."

How many pupils are affected?

The two MPs wanted to know what impact forced marriages have on their schooling.

The Ministry of Education explained that no such data are collected. According to the state government, it also has no information on the countries in which the recorded marriages were contracted.

The age and nationality at the time of marriage are recorded, as these are relevant for possible annulment proceedings.

Another question from the MPs concerned how often the YASEMIN counselling centre, which is funded by the state, had been called in for cases of forced marriage involving pupils at schools in Baden-Württemberg.

In its reply of 9 September 2026, the Interior Ministry wrote that the counselling centre does not break down its cases by the school status of the people it advises or by school year.

Instead, cases are recorded by the age of those affected and by calendar year. The precise number of counselling sessions remains unclear.

Threat of forced marriage: 80 cases recorded

In the 2025 calendar year, YASEMIN recorded a total of 271 counselling cases. In 80 cases, the people concerned were at risk of being forced into marriage. Of these 80 people, 33 were minors.

Four of the minors were under 12 years old, five were 12 and another two were 13. The counselling centre distinguishes between people at risk of forced marriage and other counselling issues; it does not carry out any school-related analysis.

According to the MPs, the trigger for the parliamentary inquiry was an emergency checklist by the women's rights organisation Terre des Femmes, published at the end of July 2026 and aimed primarily at teaching staff.

In legal terms, people up to the age of 14 are considered children in Germany; from then until the age of 18 they are deemed adolescents.

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, everyone up to the age of 18 is regarded as a child. Only once they reach adulthood are people allowed to marry in Germany. Forced marriage is defined as a separate criminal offence in the Penal Code.

With a population of around 11.24 million people, Baden-Württemberg accounts for just under 13.5% of the total German population of about 83.5 million inhabitants.

World.title: Ceuta awaits King Felipe after summer migration crisis
World.content:
Spain's royal couple are expected in Ceuta on Tuesday, 13 October, as the North African enclave continues to recover from an unprecedented migration crisis. On 30 and 31 July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco, a figure approaching the city's entire population of 80,000.

 

Most returned within hours, but thousands remained in makeshift camps and emergency shelters for weeks. On Sunday, more than 350 police officers and soldiers took part in an operation to clear the last major informal settlement at El Guano, transferring its residents to reception centres.

The crisis has exposed deep divisions in Ceuta, where Muslims make up around 40% of the population. While some residents have called for tighter border controls, others have criticised hostility towards migrants. In the predominantly Muslim neighbourhood of El Príncipe, locals sheltered women and children, while community representative Ahmed Enfed-Dal condemned attacks on shelters and attempts to obstruct Red Cross food deliveries.

The royal couple are expected to meet local officials and civil society representatives before travelling to Melilla on Wednesday. Their first visit to the two enclaves since 2007 comes ahead of Spain's 29 November general election, with migration a major political issue. Morocco's territorial claims add a further diplomatic dimension to the trip.

World.title: Fuel prices: Sébastien Lecornu promises €10 cut per fill-up
World.content:
This is news that may go some way towards easing French anger. Thanks to the strategic reserves released by the government, diesel prices will fall by up to 18 cents per litre from Sunday 1 November. That means a cut "of around 10 euros for a full tank", the prime minister promises.

 

"Facing a crisis we did not choose, [...] the state is shouldering its responsibilities," Sébastien Lecornu said on X on Monday 12 October, after a meeting with fuel distributors. "This reduction will also feed through to the price of domestic heating oil, to diesel sold to transport professionals as well as to off-road diesel, used by farmers, fishers and construction workers," the resident of Matignon also stressed.

This measure, scheduled to run until the end of January, is made possible by "selling at cost price 10 million barrels of diesel from our strategic reserves" bought before the start of the war in Iran, at 0.28 euro per litre.

53 litres of diesel for one day’s wages

Government support seemed inevitable. France is currently one of the EU countries where pump prices are highest, with an average of 2.355 euros per litre of diesel as of 5 October, according to the comparison site fuel-price (source in French). That is well above the EU-27 average of 2.149 euros per litre. Only Finland (2.553 euros), the Netherlands (2.506 euros) and Denmark (2.488 euros) are more expensive.

However, the surge in prices at the pump is not limited to France. Among its European neighbours, prices are also reaching record levels. In Belgium, a litre sells for an average of 2.349 euros, compared with 2.254 euros in Germany and 2.273 euros in Italy.

Spain, meanwhile, is one of the countries with the lowest average price, with a litre selling for 1.918 euros.

But the price displayed at the pump is not enough to gauge how hard the bill hits motorists. Wage levels also play a decisive role. While Spain appears to be doing better, a worker on the country’s average wage can buy 54.2 litres of diesel with one day’s pay. In France, one working day buys 52.8 litres, compared with 47 litres in Italy and 62.3 litres in Germany.

And when it comes to filling up the tank, France sits around the European average, with a full tank equivalent to 4.4% of the average net monthly wage.

The price of a full tank in France corresponds to 4.4% of the average net monthly salary. fuel-price

The situation is broadly similar for petrol. France is among the countries where a litre is most expensive, at an average of 2.212 euros on 5 October. Here too, the country’s average prices are much higher than those in the EU (2.006 euros), but below the average litre price in Denmark (2.605 euros, a figure that takes into account potential discounts), the Netherlands (2.432 euros) and Finland (2.370 euros).

However, France is also close to the European average when the petrol price per litre is set against the cost of living. One day’s work buys 56.2 litres, compared with an EU average of 57.4 litres.

Heating oil far pricier than the European average

Motorists are not the only ones bearing the brunt of soaring energy prices. As winter approaches, heating costs are also a source of concern for households that use heating oil. On 5 October, 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil were selling for 1,907.08 euros in France, 165.14 euros more than the EU average and 179.09 euros more than in the euro area, according to the European Commission’s figures.

In recent months, prices in France have followed the same trajectory as in Portugal and Italy, where 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil now sell for 2,204 euros and 2,063.10 euros respectively.

Other countries have nonetheless managed to keep prices more affordable. This is notably the case in Germany, where heating oil sells for 1,726.40 euros per 1,000 litres. In Belgium and Spain, heating oil is cheaper still, at 1,533.40 and 1,495.34 euros respectively, 19.6% and 21.6% less than in France.

World.title: 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'
World.content:
This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of middle-class ideals.

Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?

Life as a literary model

Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.

'Buddenbrooks' by Thomas Mann To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.

Appearance over substance

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.

That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

People were initially shocked over 'Buddenbrooks' in Lübeck, but now, Thomas Mann's statue stands tall in the city Image: picture alliance/AP

This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."

Failing grandly

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.

Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.

Language as a mirror

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

Heinrich Breloer turned the novel into a film in 2008 Image: picture-alliance/dpa/Bavaria Film/S. Falke

The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.

Stuffy husbands and anxious sons

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.

Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.

This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.

World.title: Pope Leo in Rome hospital for lung surgery
World.content:
Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung, the Vatican has confirmed, and determine if it is cancerous.

He is being seen at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades.

Shift in transparency

Leo, 71, disclosed the issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.

In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.

Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The pontiff will be put under general anesthesia and require a weeklong hospital stay. All of his engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.

According to oncologists, this type of surgery is usually necessary to determine if a lump is malignant. However, if it is, Leo has an excellent prognosis since it was caught so early.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has called for greater pressure on Russia ahead of talks with his Polish, Norwegian and British counterparts in Warsaw, warning that Moscow's attacks on Ukraine threaten Europe as a whole.

World.title: What is holding back Cyprus's Schengen ambitions?
World.content:
The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's border-free travel zone.

Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.

Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.

After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countries Image: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.

Austria, the Netherlands express reservations

However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.

Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.

Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.

Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.

What is the Green Line?

Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.

The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.

Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.

Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.

Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.

Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.

Political negotiations with EU countries

In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the island Image: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.

In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.

Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: India opposition to huddle over tea after thousands march in their Delhi protest
World.content:
Skip next section Tea and game plan: Rahul Gandhi expected to host INDIA bloc MPs after Supreme Court rally

10/13/2026 October 13, 2026 Tea and game plan: Rahul Gandhi expected to host INDIA bloc MPs after Supreme Court rally

Monday's opposition protest snaked through a heavily barricaded part of central Delhi Image: Priyanshu Singh/REUTERS

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has invited fellow lawmakers of the INDIA bloc of opposition parties over high tea on Tuesday, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

The meeting comes after thousands of opposition demonstrators, including activists and civil society members, marched to the Supreme Court on Monday evening in a protest heralded by Gandhi and the INDIA bloc.

Monday's large demonstration was the latest in a series of protests the world's largest democracy has been witnessing over an alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has come under public and opposition ire, with calls for him to resign amplifying, after a report last month found that Kumar took alleged unilateral decisions that resulted in a mass deletion of voters, allegedly violating the law.

Around 130 million names have been struck off so far from electoral rolls under the process called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which began last year.

Critics say the exercise favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata (BJP).

The Election Commission of India and the BJP deny the allegations.

Kumar and Modi have not yet given a statement on the issue.

On Saturday, another protest called by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement was thwarted by a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary, leading to mass detentions,

BJP has slammed the CJP and INDIA bloc as 'anarchists'.

"There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together. Every single person is going to stand against these killers of our Constitution, these killers of our democracy. And we're not going to back down," Gandhi wrote on X after the rally.

Monday's opposition protest, that snaked through a heavily barricaded part of central Delhi, culminated with the opposition filing a joint petition in the Supreme Court against the SIR and the alleged irregularities.

On Tuesday, the opposition MPs are expected to discuss further plans in their joint protest, PTI reported.

World.title: US: Man killed in Six Flags roller coaster incident
World.content:
Local media showed passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster, which reaches a maximum height of 61 meters and speeds of up to 113 km/h.

One person has died and several others were injured in an incident on Monday involving a roller coaster at a Six Flags theme park in the United States.

The incident occurred at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.

Witnesses told local media outlets that they saw a man fall from the ride.

"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," said Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners.

Six Flags temporary closes 9 roller coasters

Following the incident in Georgia, Six Flags temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks.

According to a park spokesperson, similar attractions were closed across their parks "out of an abundance of caution" following the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.

This comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California announced it would retire its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging the ride caused serious brain injuries.

What do we know about the roller coaster?

Althought the park did not identify the ride involved in Monday's incident, local media showed passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.

Built in 2006, Goliath can reach speeds of 113 km/h (70 mph) and a maximum height of 61 meters (200 feet).

According to the theme park's website, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills."

Monday's death would be at least the seventh to occur at the Georgia theme park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.

That includes one 2006 incident when a man had a likely heart attack while riding the same roller coaster, Goliath.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte dies
World.content:
RJ Mitte said his lived experience with cerebral palsy was an asset for his role as Walter White's son Flynn on "Breaking Bad."

American actor RJ Mitte, whose lived experience with cerebral palsy was channeled into a key role in "Breaking Bad," died on Monday at the age of 34.

"It is with profound ​sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights ​advocate RJ Mitte," his management agency said in a statement.

No other details about the circumstances of his death were given.

In addition to his breakout role in in "Breaking Bad" and later credits including "Switched at Birth" and "Guardians of Justice," Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Hospitals for Children.

An 'authentic' breakout role

In "Breaking Bad," Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston's character, chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White. Mitte's character used crutches and spoke with a slur, and gained greater prominence as the series progressed.

"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built ​a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said.

"Breaking Bad" ran from 2008 until 2013. With 16 Emmy awards, it's often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time.

Shortly after the series wrapped up, Mitte told the Associated Press that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all of which featured in the show — made him better in his role.

"You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," he said in 2024.

"You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder," Mitte added.

World.title: UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident
World.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament there were "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. The government summoned Iran's ambassador. The scare at RAF Fairford led to the withdrawal of USAF B-1 heavy bombers.

The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month, summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals.

Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions, and another arrest followed days later.

Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran.

Some of the more advanced US bombers at RAF Fairford were ordered home after the incident [FILE: September 29, 2026] Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response.

He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."

The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited.

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.

Burnham told the Commons that Iran could potentially face further sanctions Image: House of Commons/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."

Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."

Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification.

He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."

How viable or dangerous the attack plot really was remains something of an open question, what's certain is that the young men were able to cause a major disturbance and an international incident [FILE: September 27, 2026] Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks'

Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks."

It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.

In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase. The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there.

RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon.

As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn
