World.title: US wants Poland to join G20 “as soon as possible”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The United States wants Poland to join the G20 “as soon as possible” and intends to raise the issue with other members of the international forum at its forthcoming summit in December in Miami, the US State Department has told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Having previously endorsed Polish membership of the G20 in May, the US now says it intends to “continue discussions with G20 members this year on making Poland a full member as soon as possible”. “Poland’s long-term and steady economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant,” the State Department told PAP. Stany Zjednoczone oficjalnie zadeklarowały, że będą zabiegać o stałe członkostwo Polski w G20 https://t.co/lnZ583HIus — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) October 11, 2026 The G20, a major intergovernmental forum that brings together 19 major countries together with the European Union and the African Union, is set to meet at a golf resort owned by President Donald Trump in Miami on 14-15 December. Poland is also participating this year as a guest of the United States. PAP reports that the US has proposed that one of the points in the final declaration adopted by leaders at the conclusion of the summit refer to Poland’s permanent membership. However, this would require the assent of all current members, including Russia. The issue is likely to be discussed in a pre-summit online meeting of so-called “sherpas” negotiating the text of the declaration, reports PAP. After visiting Washington earlier this month, Marcin Przydacz, the head of President Karol Nawrocki’s international policy office, said that joining the G20 permanently is “Plan A”, but acknowledged that receiving a consensus from existing member states made this variant difficult. He added that Nawrocki would travel to London before the summit to discuss the possibility of continuing Poland’s guest status next year, when the UK will host the G20. At a meeting of G20 trade ministers last week, finance minister Andrzej Domański said that Poland has a good chance of being invited next year. Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed. A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain. The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026 Poland has long lobbied for membership in the group. In 2010, then-President Lech Kaczyński said “the place of my country is among the members of the G20”. In 2022, following the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Polish government argued that their country should replace Russia. Last December, the US invited Poland to join this year’s summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Poland was “assuming its rightful place” at the forum. Poland has argued that its membership is justified by its economy being on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world. Though G20 membership is not decided solely on that basis, the G20 does include most of the world’s 20 largest economies (only Switzerland and the Netherlands have larger economies than Poland but no G20 membership). Polish President @NawrockiKn “does not like” the fact that Donald Trump has invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, says his chief foreign policy aide. However, Nawrocki still plans to attend the event, which Poland is invited to as a guest https://t.co/JojsFB4NX6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2026 In September, the United States provoked criticism from European leaders, including Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, when it announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be invited to the Miami summit. Subsequently, Przydacz confirmed that, although Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Trump, “does not like” the fact that Putin has been invited, the Polish president was still planning to attend the summit. Sikorski likewise said he would attend a G20 meeting of foreign ministers in Atlanta in October even if a Russian representative was there and agreed that Poland should not boycott the summit in December. World.title: Independent beats PM Tusk’s candidate in Kraków mayoral election
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. Turnout was 44.3%. “Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.” The victory marks a blow for Tusk – whose Civic Coalition (KO) party has its strongest support in large cities – just a year before he seeks to win another term at parliamentary elections. The prime minister had visited Kraków to campaign alongside Piątkowska. Dziś 11 października 2026 roku, po 24 latach, mieszkańcy odzyskali swoje miasto. Chciałbym podziękować wszystkim Krakowianom, którzy mi zaufali i zdecydowali się oddać ma mnie głos. To nasze wspólne zwycięstwo. Dziękuję mojej partnerce Adzie, sztabowi i współpracownikom ze… pic.twitter.com/0FsNYwjPkj — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) October 11, 2026 For Gibała, a wealthy businessman who has largely funded his own political career, this was victory at the fourth attempt, having stood in every mayoral contest since 2014, obtaining a growing share of the vote each time. He stood as an independent, promising to sort out the city’s finances, end cronyism in the appointment of municipal officials, improve public transport and reverse ticket-price increases, and hold a referendum on Kraków’s controversial clean transport zone for vehicles. He also pledged to favour residents over developers in planning decisions and to counteract the negative effects of tourism in what is Poland’s most-visited city, including by restricting short-term-rental properties. Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off. Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government. She has, since last year, been a member of the Senate in Warsaw. Previously, she worked in Kraków city hall during the mayoralty of Jacek Majchrowski, who held office from 2002 to 2024. Piątkowska received the personal backing of Tusk, who announced her candidacy in June alongside PSL leader and deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (though critics noted that they held the event in Warsaw rather than Kraków). Tusk also visited Kraków before the first round to support his candidate. Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Kraków’s election was held in unusual circumstances after the previous mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, also from KO, was removed from his position in May, just two years into his term. He had faced accusations of cronyism and poor financial management, as well as criticism over the introduction of the clean transport zone. A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. In the subsequent referendum, 97.3% supported removing the mayor (Miszalski had appealed to his supporters not to vote in an unsuccessful effort to keep turnout below the 27% needed for the result to be binding). Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”. The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party). World.title: Polish security services report alleged assassination plot against PM Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, or what the source of the information was. W związku z informacją, która wpłynęła do @PolskaPolicja i dotyczy możliwego zamachu na premiera @donaldtusk oraz wicepremiera, ministra obrony narodowej @KosiniakKamysz, minister koordynator służb specjalnych @TomaszSiemoniak oraz minister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 11, 2026 On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister. Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat. Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police. “We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt. “We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.” Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack or where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation. "Sprawę traktujemy śmiertelnie poważnie. Mówimy o dużym prawdopodobieństwie spełnienia tych gróźb" Rzecznik prasowy ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych o możliwym zamachu na premiera i szefa MON. pic.twitter.com/2xoWrZJT2w — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 11, 2026 Government spokesman Adam Szłapka, speaking to broadcaster TVN, acknowledged that the authorities constantly receive a “cascade of indications” regarding potential threats. However, “this signal was more disturbing than previous” ones, he added. Szłapka also indicated that one element of the warning had come via email, but added that “it was not just an email” that had raised concern. Like Dobrzyński, he said that further information would be released in due course. Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reports that an unnamed “official close to the prime minister” had said that the threat came from “right-wing extremists” and that the perpetrators were Poles. Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz. Poland has charged a 17-year-old with planning neo-Nazi terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. Two other Polish teenagers who were part of the same online community promoting neo-Nazism and violence have also been detained https://t.co/86AnIHWFe8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 Last month, police detained a 56-year-old man in the city of Przemyśl after he posted a video on social media threatening Tusk. Earlier in September, a 52-year-old man in the town of Oława was likewise arrested for making criminal threats against the prime minister online. Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. This week has also seen Poland facing an unprecedented security challenge after three knife attacks took place on schools, leaving one person dead and many injured. In response, the police have since Friday carried out checks at over 64,000 locations, including many schools, and detained over 100 people, most of them teenagers found to have made threats or been in possession of weapons. World.title: Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. World.title: Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Sinatra Tribute Pairs Frank Sinatra Classics With 1930s Dining at Prague’s Mánes
World.content:
Prague’s Art Restaurant Mánes combines live performances of Frank Sinatra’s best-known songs with a three-course dinner inspired by traditional Czech cuisine of the 1930s.

The functionalist building offers views of the Vltava River and nearby Žofín Island, providing the setting for an evening dedicated to the music and style of Sinatra’s era.



The Sinatra’s Tribute musical programme features acclaimed soloists, including baritone Daniel Klánský and jazz singer Sophie Lamoš. They perform some of Sinatra’s best-known songs, including *My Way* and *Fly Me to the Moon*, accompanied by a group of musicians.

Rather than simply imitating the legendary American singer, the Sinatra Tribute offers its own interpretation of his musical legacy.

One of the programme’s highlights is a restored 1897 Steinway & Sons grand piano, an instrument once played by Czech composer and pianist Jaroslav Ježek.

The music is complemented by a three-course dinner served before the concert.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sinatra Tribute Koncert & Večeře / Sinatra Tribute Show & Dinner (@sinatratributeprague)

Created exclusively for the programme by Mánes Restaurant head chef Jaroslav Zahálka, the menu draws inspiration from Prague’s culinary traditions of the 1930s, reflecting the period associated with the evening’s musical theme.

Visitors can contact the venue for current dates, ticket prices and reservations.

World.title: From Lisbon to Hanoi, New Flight Options From Prague This Autumn
World.content:
The autumn school break is approaching, and travelers departing from Prague still have options for trips abroad.

However, those hoping to find cheap flights may struggle to secure a good deal, as fares tend to rise closer to departure and fewer seats remain available at lower prices.

Families face an additional challenge. When booking four tickets together, they may discover that the cheapest fare is available for only one or two passengers, forcing them to pay more for the remaining seats.



Airlines are also dealing with high fuel costs and strong competition, making it important to fill as many seats as possible.

A search conducted on Wednesday, October 7, found that Kraków and Gdańsk were among the cheapest destinations available for the autumn break week.

New flights from Prague and postponed routes

Prague Airport has announced several new connections for the autumn and winter seasons, although some airlines have postponed their planned launches until spring.

Smartwings, for example, has delayed the introduction of flights to Venice, Italy, and Bergen, Norway. Both routes were originally scheduled to begin before the autumn break but are now expected to launch in March.

Despite the changes, Prague Airport continues to list the destinations among its new routes, with their original launch dates still displayed. According to the current schedule, Smartwings’ next new connection is to Lisbon, with flights due to begin on October 23.

Travelers heading farther afield have another option. Vietjet Air launched its Prague–Hanoi service on Saturday, October 10. The route includes a stopover in Kazakhstan, rather than offering a nonstop connection to Vietnam.

Closer to home, easyJet’s new route from Prague to Hamburg provides another option for the break. Return fares were available for around CZK 4,000.

Marrakech joins the network as winter routes target skiers

EasyJet is also scheduled to launch flights from Prague to Marrakech, Morocco, on October 25. The new connection will increase competition on the route, although fares during the autumn break are relatively high.

A return ticket can cost as much as CZK 16,000, excluding baggage. Prices can be considerably lower outside the peak travel period.

Wizz Air is adding flights to Poprad, Slovakia, while Sky Alps is expected to begin services to Bolzano, Italy, in early December. Both destinations provide access to mountain regions popular with winter sports enthusiasts.

Another seasonal option is Eurowings’ planned route to Rovaniemi, Finland, which is scheduled to launch on December 20. Located on the Arctic Circle, the city is closely associated with Santa Claus and attracts visitors during the Christmas season.

World.title: RestaurantWeek Prague Returns With 75 Restaurants and Autumn Menus
World.content:
RestaurantWeek® returns to Prague from October 13 to November 18, offering diners the chance to try menus at around 75 restaurants across the capital at reduced prices.

The three-course menus available for CZK 490 or CZK 790, plus a reservation fee.



The autumn edition features a mix of established Prague restaurants and newcomers to the festival. Among the first-time participants are U Malířů 1543 in Malá Strana and Buddha-Bar Prague, both well-known names on the city’s dining scene.

Participating restaurants are incorporating seasonal ingredients into their menus, including pumpkin, game, poultry, forest fruits, plums and quince. Truffles and shrimp are also expected to feature prominently.

Pumpkin will appear in dishes ranging from soups to mousses, while restaurants focusing on seafood and creative interpretations of Czech ingredients will offer alternatives for diners looking to explore different flavours.

The festival aims to make restaurants more accessible while encouraging people to dine out and meet in person. This year’s edition includes a partnership with Singles Club, an initiative promoting face-to-face social connections as an alternative to app-based dating.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Singles Club (@singlesclubcz)

Connecting Prague restaurants with local producers

RestaurantWeek® is also collaborating with the Regional Food (Regionální potravina) project, which supports small Czech food producers. The partnership aims to connect restaurants with local suppliers and help regional products reach more customers.

For the first time, the festival will also recognise restaurants that work with regional ingredients, adding a new category to its traditional awards for popular and highly rated establishments.

Three-course menus cost CZK 490 or CZK 790, depending on the restaurant, with reservation fees of CZK 49 or CZK 79, respectively. Some venues offer a fourth course, an amuse-bouche, and are marked as premium on the festival website.

World.title: Prague’s SaSaZu Club to Host Central Europe’s Largest Halloween Party

Bloody Sexy Halloween festival, described as Central Europe’s largest Halloween event, will return to Prague’s SaSaZu Club for its 2026 edition.

The two-night celebration will take place on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, promising an extensive lineup of shows, performances, and music acts.



Founded in 2009, the event has grown into one of the most attended Halloween parties in the region, regularly attracting more than 4,000 visitors each year. Organizers say this year’s edition will feature immersive decorations, live performances, and sets from both Czech and international DJs.

A traditional highlight of the weekend will be the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest, open to all attendees.

Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight, with costumes judged on creativity, originality, and presentation. The winner, selected by audience applause at midnight, will receive a cash prize of CZK 40,000.

The event will run across both nights with multiple performances and themed productions throughout the venue.

Tickets for Bloody Sexy Halloween 2025 are priced between CZK 510 and CZK 1,450, depending on the category (Regular, Badass Babes, or VIP).

World.title: The Story Society Is Bringing an English-Language Book Community to Prague
World.content:
Meet Julia and Ioana, the founders behind The Story Society, a new English-language bookstore and community project in Prague.

Their idea combines a selection of books with a space for reading, book clubs, events and meeting other people.

The project is still in development, with the founders currently looking for a location and working towards opening the bookstore in early 2027.

Why a bookstore?

For Julia, the idea started from a personal need. “I wanted to create a place where introverted people like myself could spend time comfortably, discover books at their own pace and potentially meet others with similar interests,” she says.

But there was also a practical reason behind the idea. According to the founders, finding a wider selection of English-language books in Prague can be difficult, particularly when it comes to special editions. Ordering books from abroad can also mean higher shipping costs, taxes and waiting several weeks for delivery.

“I wanted to solve two problems. One is community, and the other one is buying books in English here,” Julia says.

The Story Society plans to source books from the UK and offer a selection that the founders feel is currently difficult to find locally.

What they hope The Story Society to be

The Story Society is intended to be more than a place to buy books, although the physical bookstore remains an important part of the idea. Julia and Ioana imagine a colorful, cozy space with areas for reading, book clubs and other events.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Story Society (@thestorysociety.prague)

They are also considering collaborations with authors and artists, pop-ups and other activities connected to books and the community around them. “We want to make a third place in Prague,” Ioana says.

The idea is that people could come not only to buy a book, but also to stay for a while, read, meet friends or take part in an event.

The expat/local divide

The Story Society was initially imagined largely with Prague’s expat community in mind. But “when the project took shape, we got a huge response from locals, and we learned that they are also interested in it,” Julia says. The attraction is the chance to have an English-language space where they can read books, meet people and be part of a bookish community.

That response has broadened the founders’ idea of who The Story Society is for. Rather than separating Prague’s expat and local communities, they hope the project can help mend the gap between them.

“If you like English, if you can speak English, and if you like books, we don’t care where you’re from,” Julia says. “Just be there and enjoy it with us.”

Where the project stands now

The Story Society doesn’t have a physical location yet. Julia and Ioana are currently exploring the market and looking for a suitable space in Prague’s city centre, while also working on the book supply and other practical foundations of the project.

In the meantime, they plan to take The Story Society to pop-ups and other events. These will give them an opportunity to introduce the project to more people, build a community around it and raise visibility for their crowdfunding campaign.

Everyone can help

For now, support can take different forms. Sharing the crowdfunding campaign, introducing the project to someone who might be interested or simply helping spread the word can help The Story Society reach more people as Julia and Ioana work towards opening their first space.

They also want people to feel that contributing does not necessarily mean making a financial donation. Ideas, feedback and suggestions can help shape the project as it develops. As the founders put it, “any thought counts.”

World.title: Which Stores Will Be Open in the Czech Republic on October 28
World.content:
Most large supermarkets and retail chains in the Czech Republic will close on Wednesday, October 28, as the country marks the Day of the Establishment of an Independent Czechoslovak State.

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area exceeding 200 square meters must close on the public holiday. The restriction covers most major supermarkets as well as large retailers selling clothing, electronics, furniture and other goods.



Major chains including Lidl, Kaufland, Albert, Billa, Penny Market and Tesco are expected to close their large stores for the day.

The restrictions apply nationwide and are based on Act No. 223/2016 Coll., which regulates retail opening hours on selected public holidays.

October 28 commemorates the establishment of an independent Czechoslovak state in 1918, following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the end of World War I.

Which shops can remain open

Not all retailers are subject to the closure requirement. The law provides several exceptions, allowing certain businesses to operate as usual.

These include:

Small grocery stores and convenience shops with a sales area of up to 200 square meters

Pharmacies

Shops at petrol stations

Retail outlets at airports

Shops located at railway and bus stations

Shops within medical facilities

Smaller shops are not required to open, however. Their owners can decide whether to operate on the holiday and may introduce shorter opening hours.

Customers are therefore advised to check the opening times of individual stores before setting out to shop.

What about shopping centres in Prague

Shopping centres may continue operating on October 28, even though their largest retail outlets must remain closed.

Smaller shops that fall below the 200-square-meter threshold may open, while restaurants, cafés, cinemas and other leisure businesses can continue serving customers.

Opening arrangements may differ between individual shopping centres, so visitors should check the holiday schedules published on their official websites before travelling.

World.title: Mayors and Independents Come First in Prague Elections as Pirates Fall Back
World.content:
The opposition Mayors and Independents (STAN) party came first in municipal elections in Prague, with 23 percent of the vote.

Led by Prague Deputy Mayor Petr Hlaváček, secured more than 23 percent of the vote, up sharply from 7.8 percent four years ago. The party recorded the largest increase among the main political groups contesting the capital’s city council.



The Spolu coalition, comprising the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and TOP 09, finished second with approximately 22 percent. Its result was around three percentage points lower than in the previous election.

Praha Sobě, another group led by a serving deputy mayor, also improved its position. Under Adam Scheinherr’s leadership, it won nearly 18 percent of the vote.

The ANO movement, the strongest party in the Czech national parliament, finished fourth in Prague after losing support.

In 2022, ANO won 19.3 percent of the vote in the capital. This time, it failed to reach 15 percent.

The Pirate Party suffered an even steeper decline. After finishing third with 17.7 percent of the vote in 2022, it received just over 9 percent this time, narrowly securing representation on the Prague City Council.

The election results set the stage for negotiations over Prague’s next city government.

World.title: Police Car Ends Up in Vltava River, Three People Treated for Hypothermia
World.content:
A police car plunged into the Vltava River in Prague on Saturday morning after crashing through the guardrails of Hlávkův Bridge.

The vehicle’s two occupants and a man who jumped into the water to help them were treated by emergency crews for hypothermia.

The accident was reported to police at around 8 a.m. on October 10. A man and a woman, both approximately 30 years old, were inside the car when it went into the river.



A witness jumped into the water after the vehicle fell from the bridge and helped the occupants. Emergency services subsequently treated all three people at the scene.

Prague Emergency Medical Service dispatched three ambulances, a medical inspector and a rapid response vehicle to the incident.

All three were suffering from hypothermia but were not in life-threatening condition, according to emergency responders.

“We are very grateful to the rescuer for their help,” Prague Emergency Medical Service said in a statement, confirming that all three people were in its care.

Police are investigating the circumstances of the crash, including what caused the vehicle to break through the bridge’s guardrails and fall into the Vltava.

World.title: Orbán missing from Fidesz’s big 23 October event? Former president Áder to take the stage instead
World.content:
Fidesz has announced that former president János Áder will speak at its 23 October commemoration of the 1956 Revolution in Budapest, alongside historian Mária Schmidt and parliamentary group leader János Bóka. Viktor Orbán is conspicuously absent from the announced line-up, raising questions about whether the former prime minister will address supporters at all.

Fidesz will hold its commemorative event at Bem Square in Budapest on 23 October, marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. However, the list of speakers announced by the party does not include Viktor Orbán, leaving uncertainty over whether he will appear at one of the most significant dates on the political calendar.

According to a statement from Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s press chief, the speakers will include former Hungarian president János Áder, historian Mária Schmidt and János Bóka, the party’s parliamentary group leader.

Hungarian news outlet Telex reported that it had contacted Havasi to ask whether Orbán would speak at the event or attend as a member of the audience. No answer was included in the report.

Former president János Áder giving a speech during Fidesz and KDNP’s protest against the removal of President Tamás Sulyok. Photo: MTI/Illyés Tibor

Áder steps into the spotlight as Orbán’s role remains unclear

Áder’s prominent role is notable given that Fidesz previously turned to the former president for a public appearance at its July demonstration in Buda Castle, titled Stop Arbitrary Rule (“Stop Önkény”). Orbán had encouraged supporters to attend that protest through social media posts but did not appear in person. Afterwards, he thanked those who had taken part and shared a photograph that had also been posted by Gergely Gulyás.

Last year, Orbán delivered a speech in front of Parliament on Kossuth Square following the Peace March. This year, however, the party’s announced programme offers no confirmation that he will take the stage on 23 October. The absence of his name from the speaker list does not necessarily mean Orbán will stay away altogether. Whether he will attend, and in what capacity, remains unclear.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Peace March cancelled, replaced by a giant flag procession

Another major change to this year’s commemorations is the cancellation of the traditional Peace March, which has featured prominently at Fidesz-linked national events in previous years. The Civil Union Forum (CÖF), which previously organised the march, announced in September that it would not go ahead this year.

Instead, the 56 Lángja Public Benefit Foundation is organising a procession called The Nation’s Flag. Its centrepiece will be a Hungarian national flag measuring 1,848 metres in length, a reference to the year of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848.

The procession is planned to follow the Buda riverbank, passing locations associated with the 1956 Revolution. A large Szekler flag is also expected to join the procession during its final section.

The foundation has described the event as an opportunity for a large-scale and uplifting commemoration, while acknowledging that the cancellation of the Peace March may leave some regular participants feeling that something is missing.

If you missed it: Viktor Orbán defends Ukrainian gold convoy operation as lawyer says motion filed to name him as suspect

A (not-so-new) slogan that signals the event’s political message

The procession’s announced motto is: “No war, no gender, no migration – God, homeland, family.”

The organiser, Ákos Szilágyi, has become known in recent years for wearing striking T-shirts featuring Viktor Orbán at pro-Fidesz events.

With the Peace March replaced by a flag procession and Áder announced as a speaker, this year’s 23 October programme will look different from previous years. Whether Orbán himself will appear is one of the key unanswered questions ahead of the commemoration.

World.title: ‘Sopron is Hungary. Period.’ TISZA MP demands answers from Fidesz after German far-right map prompts controversy
World.content:
A controversial map depicting Sopron as part of Germany has triggered a political row in Hungary, with a Tisza Party MP demanding that Fidesz and Mi Hazánk distance themselves from their German far-right allies. The map’s creator has already resigned following the backlash in Germany.

“Sopron is Hungary. Period.” With these words, Anikó Hallerné Nagy, a Tisza Party MP and Deputy Speaker of Hungary’s National Assembly, responded to a controversial map shared by a leading figure in the youth wing of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

The map depicted Sopron, a city in western Hungary, as part of Germany, alongside Austria, much of Switzerland and areas of France. The post has since been deleted, and its creator, Luca Moritz Strauß, has stepped down from his position in the AfD’s youth organisation.

In a Facebook post on Monday evening, Nagy called on Fidesz and Mi Hazánk to distance themselves from the German party, pointing to their political ties with the AfD.

‘When will Fidesz and Mi Hazánk distance themselves?’

Nagy accompanied her post with two photographs: one featuring Mi Hazánk leader László Toroczkai and another showing Viktor Orbán alongside AfD leader Alice Weidel.

She highlighted that Mi Hazánk sits in the same European Parliament political group as the AfD, while Fidesz maintains political ties with the German party.

The MP argued that the map could not simply be dismissed as a bad joke, warning against attempts to redraw borders under the pretext of historical justice.

“The history of the 20th century has shown where this kind of map-drawing and suspicion towards neighbouring countries can lead,” she wrote, drawing parallels with the territorial revisionism that preceded the Second World War.

Nagy also outlined Tisza’s foreign policy position, describing it as pro-Western, pro-European and committed to the transatlantic alliance. She argued that Hungary’s security depends on democratic European cooperation, NATO and good relations with neighbouring countries, rather than political movements that entertain ideas about changing borders.

Her central question was direct: when would Fidesz and Mi Hazánk politicians distance themselves from their German allies?

Why Sopron’s history makes the map particularly sensitive

Sopron’s inclusion is especially significant because of the city’s place in Hungarian history. Following the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, a 1921 plebiscite determined that Sopron and the surrounding area would remain part of Hungary. The city subsequently became known as the City of Loyalty.

Nagy invoked this history in her statement, writing: “Sopron became the City of Loyalty in 1921. It still is today.”

She also pointed to the importance of cross-border cooperation in the region. Thousands of Hungarians travel to Austria every day for work, education, shopping and family visits, she noted, arguing that peaceful relations and open borders should not be taken for granted.

The MP further recalled the 1989 Pan-European Picnic, held near Sopron, which became a landmark in the process leading to the fall of the Iron Curtain and the reunification of Europe.

Nagy, who has lived in Sopron for 34 years, said strengthening relations with Austria had been one of her priorities since entering parliament. She criticised what she described as the previous government’s neglect of relations with Hungary’s western neighbour.

AfD youth leader resigns after controversial map

The controversy began on 3 October, when Strauß, a figure in the AfD’s youth organisation, published the map depicting an expanded Germany that included territory belonging to several neighbouring countries.

The post attracted criticism and was later deleted. Strauß subsequently resigned from his leadership position in the youth organisation, with reports indicating that AfD leaders had also put pressure on him to step down.

The party’s response suggested that the map had gone beyond what its leadership was prepared to defend. AfD politician Torben Braga reportedly described the post as “incredibly stupid”, while the youth organisation distanced itself from the publication.

The available reports do not establish that the map represented official AfD territorial policy.

World.title: Travel agency bankruptcy: Hungarian holidaymakers face huge losses as insurance falls short
World.content:
Hungarians affected by the collapse of Robinson Tours fear they will recover only a fraction of the money they paid for cancelled holidays. The Bulgarian travel agency’s insurance cover is worth just HUF 23.3 million (approx. 64,000), while claims had already exceeded five times that amount by the end of August. Legal action against the Bulgarian state could be the next step.

More than two months after Bulgarian-registered travel agency Robinson Tours became insolvent, Hungarian customers are still waiting for compensation. With the total value of claims far exceeding the company’s available insurance cover, many travellers fear they will lose most of the money they paid for their holidays.

According to a report by Hungarian broadcaster RTL Híradó, the Bulgarian insurer is due to finalise its assessment of passengers’ claims on 25 October. However, the limited funds available mean that affected customers are unlikely to receive their money back in full.

Families face losses worth millions of forints

The financial impact has been devastating for some customers. Flóra Szabó, one of those affected, told RTL Híradó that she had contacted her hotel after the travel agency collapsed, only to discover that Robinson Tours had cancelled the booking itself.

The cancellation left her facing a loss of HUF 4 million (approximately EUR 10,000) for the planned holiday.

Another customer said their family had lost almost HUF 1 million (around EUR 2,500) because of the failed trip. They now hope to recover at least a small percentage of the money.

Some affected travellers have also faced language barriers while trying to navigate the claims process, although customers have reportedly been helping one another.

Insurance cover is worth just a fraction of the claims

The biggest problem is the gap between the compensation available and the money owed to customers. Robinson Tours’ insurance cover amounts to a maximum of HUF 23.3 million. By the end of August, however, the total value of claims was already more than five times that sum, according to previous reports by Index.

The situation may have deteriorated further since then. Tamás Pakuts, editor of the travel industry blog szálloda.blog, told RTL Híradó that the figures initially recorded around 300 claims involving approximately 500 people.

He estimated that the number of affected travellers could now exceed 1,000, meaning the total value of claims could be considerably higher. Unfortunately for customers, compensation is expected to be distributed proportionally, rather than allowing everyone to recover the full amount they paid.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Could customers sue the Bulgarian state?

Travel law specialist András Salamon believes that affected customers could pursue the outstanding sums through the courts. He argues that Bulgaria may be held responsible for failing to implement EU rules on financial protection for travel organisers properly. On that basis, he believes travellers could bring legal proceedings against the Bulgarian state to recover losses not covered by the insurer.

Salamon expressed strong confidence in this legal argument, although the outcome of any potential proceedings would ultimately depend on the courts.

The Budapest Government Office has said that the compensation process falls under Bulgarian jurisdiction. Meanwhile, the Bulgarian insurer has reportedly failed to respond to enquiries.

There has also been a development in the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collapse. In September, the Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office reviewed the information submitted and concluded that the reported facts could potentially indicate a criminal offence. On 18 September, it transferred the full case file to the Sofia District Prosecutor’s Office on jurisdictional grounds.

How the travel agency Robinson Tours collapsed

Robinson Tours, a Bulgarian-registered travel agency specialising mainly in holidays in Bulgaria, ran into serious difficulties at the beginning of August.

On 1 August, the company informed customers by text message that its airline could not operate a scheduled Budapest charter flight. Travellers already staying in Bulgaria were told they would be brought home by bus, while the outbound flight was cancelled.

A few days later, managing director Áron Jakócs reportedly still held out the prospect of holiday flights resuming. However, the company subsequently declared itself insolvent. In a letter sent to customers in early August, Robinson Tours said it no longer had the financial means to meet its obligations and had initiated liquidation proceedings at the Sofia City Court.

The company attributed its financial difficulties to several factors, including uncertainty linked to the Middle East crisis, high kerosene prices, competition from low-cost airlines and changes in the Hungarian travel market. At the time, customers were instructed to submit compensation claims to Bulgaria-based Axiom Insurance Company AD.

World.title: Ukraine signs minority education law: What it means for Hungarians in Transcarpathia
World.content:
The Ukrainian parliament’s adoption of the law on education in minority languages is an important step forward for the educational rights of Hungarians in Transcarpathia, Ukraine, the foreign minister said in a Facebook post on Monday.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed in her post that the Ukrainian parliament’s decision was an important step forward, but the process had not yet been concluded.

“We await the Ukrainian president’s signature, the entry into force of the law and the actual implementation of the commitments,” she wrote.

Update: Since then, President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed the law.

She said she had consulted Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on current issues in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations on the margins of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg. “The adoption of the Ukrainian legislative amendment affecting the educational rights of national minorities gave our meeting particular significance,” she stressed.

“The decision is the result of many months of persistent Hungarian-Ukrainian negotiations. We worked with the involvement of representatives of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia to ensure that adequate legal guarantees protect the education of Hungarian children in their mother tongue and the operation of Hungarian schools,” Orbán added in her post.

The Ukrainian law is aimed at settling the educational rights of national minorities. The amendments concern school education, the issuing of education documents, the conduct of external assessments and the preservation of the special status of educational institutions.

The language of instruction will remain Ukrainian. At the same time, in schools where classes are taught in the language of an indigenous people of Ukraine or of a national minority speaking an official EU language, the use of that language alongside the state language is guaranteed in education, as well as in communication between students and other participants in the educational process inside the building and on the grounds of the institution.

The law makes it possible for schools where more than 50 percent of students study in a national minority language that counts as an official language of the EU to be granted the status of national minority educational institution.

The law’s adoption will facilitate the opening of the second and third clusters of the European Union’s accession negotiations with Ukraine, after Hungary signalled last week that it would not stand in the way of the launch of a new, for now technical stage of the negotiations if the Ukrainian parliament approved the law.

World.title: Fake Hungarian government officials arrested after trying to get HUF billions from a man
World.content:
Two men have been remanded in custody in Hungary after allegedly posing as fake government officials from the newly assembled government asset protection and recovery office and attempting to extort HUF 2 billion (almost EUR 5.5 million) from a man in exchange for making criminal proceedings against him disappear.

The two men tried to make billions by posing as government officials

The suspects are accused of pretending to hold official government positions and claiming they could influence legal proceedings in the victim’s favour. According to the Budapest Regional Investigation Prosecutor’s Office, the scheme began in July 2026, when one of the men approached the victim at a petrol station and claimed to work for the national security services.

He allegedly told the man that he knew about criminal proceedings pending against him and offered to have the cases dropped in exchange for HUF 2 billion. The victim refused, but the fake government official reportedly contacted him repeatedly afterwards, attempting to put pressure on him. Among other claims, he allegedly told the man that he was under constant surveillance.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Alleged fake police operation

After the victim continued to reject the offer, two associates of the first suspect allegedly turned up at his home on 8 October. According to the prosecution, they posed as police officers and pretended to be carrying out an official procedure, claiming they were taking the man to the National Office for Asset Protection and Recovery.

The two fake government officials allegedly searched the victim, took his mobile phone and put him in a vehicle fitted with emergency warning lights before driving away with him. During the journey, they called their alleged accomplice. Acting on his instructions, they returned the victim to his home, handed back his phone and told him to contact the first suspect as soon as possible.

The three men were subsequently arrested in an operation involving the tactical unit of the National Police Headquarters’ Criminal Support Directorate, the National Protective Service and the Riot Police. Investigators suspect them of influence peddling by impersonating public officials, as well as unlawful deprivation of personal liberty committed by feigning an official procedure and causing significant harm.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian woman hides daughter from Italian father for 10 years, gets prison sentence

Court orders two suspects held in custody

The Buda Central District Court ordered two of the suspects to be held in custody until 10 November, citing the risk that they might flee or go into hiding. The ruling is not final. According to the court, one suspect has close ties abroad through his family and employment, while the other allegedly attempted to evade police during his arrest. The court considered the seriousness of the suspected offences and the potential penalties when assessing whether the men would remain available throughout the proceedings.

The court also noted that the suspect who allegedly posed as a national security official had no previous criminal record and had made a full admission, providing a detailed account and co-operating with investigators. It therefore did not consider him to pose a risk of reoffending. Nevertheless, the court ruled that detention remained necessary at this stage because the suspects’ living arrangements, personal circumstances and financial situations had not yet been sufficiently established to justify a less restrictive measure.

The investigation concerns three alleged participants, although the latest custody order applies to the two men who faked being government officials. The suspects have been detained pending further proceedings. The allegations have not been established by a final court judgment.

World.title: Hungarian woman hides daughter from Italian father for 10 years, gets prison sentence
World.content:
A Hungarian woman has received a two-year suspended prison sentence for hiding her daughter from the girl’s Italian father for almost a decade, during which the child grew up without attending nursery or school.

Woman hid daughter from her father for a decade

The Mezőtúr District Court sentenced the 43-year-old woman for endangering a minor and suspended the prison term for four years. She has also been banned from working in any role involving the education, supervision, care or medical treatment of people under the age of 18 for two years. According to a statement from the Szolnok Court, the woman ignored a final court ruling that had terminated her parental custody rights and awarded custody of the child to her father.

From November 2014 until June 2025, she concealed the girl and refused to hand her over to the Italian man. The girl, now 15, was born in Italy to the Hungarian woman and her Italian partner. Their relationship subsequently broke down, and the mother took their three-month-old daughter to Hungary following an argument, cutting off contact with the father.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A whole childhood spent in hiding

According to the court’s findings, the girl grew up without attending either nursery or school. Her mother initially taught her, after which she educated herself using textbooks and the internet. The child lived largely within a small circle consisting of her mother and other family members. She reportedly feared that her father or the authorities would find them and separate her from her mother. The court said she knew her father mainly through what it described as frightening stories told by her mother.

Meanwhile, the Italian father made repeated efforts to locate his daughter. A businessman from Padua appeared on television programmes, searched for her on social media, hired a private investigator and offered a EUR 10,000 reward for information leading to her discovery. He also wrote to the Pope seeking help. In 2018, a joint Hungarian-Italian investigative team was established following an agreement between the countries’ interior ministers at the time, Hungary’s Sándor Pintér and Italy’s Matteo Salvini. The initiative did not lead to the girl being found.

Hungarian police later commissioned an expert illustration showing how the child might look and offered a reward of HUF 500,000 (EUR 1,370) for information. In 2023, the father also appealed to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni for assistance. He reportedly travelled to his former partner’s hometown of Mezőtúr several times in an attempt to see his daughter. The court proceedings eventually resulted in custody being awarded to the father, while an international warrant was issued for the mother.

Mother and daughter found in 2025

The long search ended in the summer of 2025, when Hungarian and Italian police carried out a joint operation in Mezőtúr and arrested the woman, who had been wanted by the authorities. Her daughter was with her at the time. Both were taken to the local police station. The Mezőtúr District Prosecutor’s Office brought charges on 21 July 2026. At a preparatory hearing on 6 October, the woman admitted the offence as charged and waived her right to a trial.

The prosecution, the defendant and her lawyer all accepted the court’s decision, meaning the judgment became final on the day it was delivered. The case highlights the consequences of the prolonged concealment of a child in defiance of a final custody ruling, as well as the years-long efforts made by the father and authorities to locate her.

World.title: Horror in Hungary: Man accused of attacking parents with a knife and setting fire to their home
World.content:
An 80-year-old woman died in a house fire in Szentendre, near Budapest, after her 51-year-old son allegedly attacked his parents. His father escaped, while firefighters later discovered the woman’s body in the badly damaged property.

A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder with particular cruelty after a fatal house fire in Szentendre on Sunday afternoon, 11 October. Police say the 51-year-old allegedly attacked his 82-year-old father with a knife before fleeing from officers. Firefighters subsequently discovered the body of a woman inside the burning family home.

According to Hungarian news outlet Blikk, the suspect, identified as András B., had a history of mental health problems. The authorities have not released further details about the circumstances of the woman’s death, citing the ongoing investigation.

Father escaped knife attack before son fled

Police were alerted on Sunday after an 82-year-old Szentendre resident reported that his 51-year-old son had attacked him with a knife. Officers arriving at the scene attempted to take the suspect into custody, but he fled. He was caught a short time later and taken into police custody.

The Pest County Police Headquarters confirmed that proceedings had been launched on suspicion of murder with particular cruelty. Investigators have declined to disclose further details while the case remains under investigation.

Blikk reported that the father, described as a respected professor, managed to escape the attack. He returned to the family property on Monday but was reportedly too distressed to speak to the newspaper.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fire destroyed much of the family home

The incident also involved a serious fire at the family’s house on Cseresznyés Road in Szentendre. According to Attila Csámpai, spokesperson for the Pest County Disaster Management Directorate, the flames broke out on the ground floor of the approximately 80-square-metre building before spreading rapidly to the upper floor and roof.

By the time firefighters arrived, much of the property was already ablaze. Emergency crews brought the fire under control by early evening and searched the building, where they discovered a woman’s body.

Police said the woman had suffered fatal burns. Her exact cause of death is being examined with the involvement of experts.

Although much of the house was destroyed, firefighters managed to prevent the flames from spreading to neighbouring properties.

Szentendre’s official Facebook page reported the incident on Sunday, describing it as a suspected deliberate arson attack. The local authority confirmed that one person had died and that police had detained the suspected perpetrator.

Have you heard? Romanian man beat and forced Hungarian man to work for food in Hungary

Neighbours describe a night of fear

The tragedy shocked residents of the otherwise quiet street. One neighbour told Blikk that they knew the family well and were deeply saddened by what had happened. They also described fearing that the fire might spread to their own home.

The neighbour said the wind was blowing in the opposite direction and firefighters worked quickly, helping to prevent the blaze from reaching nearby buildings. The family living next door reportedly spent the night without sleep because of the incident.

Blikk also reported that the suspect had previously displayed disturbing behaviour and that neighbours had complained about him. According to the newspaper, he had allegedly threatened another local resident with a knife on an earlier occasion.

Another local resident told Blikk that, after his arrest, the man appeared confused and shouted about Satan while waiting in a police car. These accounts have not been independently confirmed by the authorities.
