Under fifth-freedom traffic rights, passengers can travel along the full Hanoi–Almaty–Prague route or book flights separately between Almaty and Prague, according to Almaty’s tourism department.

The route is expected to improve the city’s accessibility for travelers from Europe and Southeast Asia while creating additional opportunities for inbound tourism.

The number of tourists from Vietnam visiting Almaty increased 20% in 2025 compared with the previous year. The new service is expected to further strengthen tourism ties between Kazakhstan and Vietnam and make Almaty more accessible to Vietnamese travelers.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Business Tourism Market Expands: Which Region Attracts Most Visitors?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s resort areas received 510,800 visitors traveling for business and professional purposes in the first half of 2026, with the Almaty Mountain Cluster accounting for 77.3% of the total, according to an analysis by Ranking.kz. The figures highlight the growing role of business tourism in the country’s tourism industry, as companies increasingly combine professional events with leisure and wellness activities.

Business tourism, also known as MICE tourism, encompasses meetings, incentive trips, conferences and exhibitions. In Kazakhstan, the sector is developing along two main directions: hosting international events in major cities and organizing business gatherings directly at resort destinations.

International events generate revenue

The first direction has significant export potential. According to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, Kazakhstan hosted 13 major MICE events in 2025, generating nearly $18 million in revenue, up 20% from 2024.

Almaty plays a key role in this segment. International events held in the city contributed nearly $3 million to its budget in 2025. The second direction involves organizing business events outside major cities, including off-site conferences, national and international exhibitions, industry forums, seminars and corporate incentive programs at resort destinations.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, business tourism at Kazakhstan’s resort areas has grown in recent years. In 2024 and 2025, the number of visitors staying at accommodation facilities in these areas for business and professional purposes reached record levels, exceeding 1.1 million. Nearly one in four guests staying at hotels and recreation facilities in resort areas traveled for business purposes.

Almaty Mountain Cluster leads resort destinations

In January-June 2026, resort areas welcomed 510,800 business and professional visitors. Kazakhstanis accounted for 64% of the total, while foreign visitors made up 36%. The Almaty Mountain Cluster was the leading destination, attracting nearly 395,000 business travelers, equivalent to 77.3% of all visitors traveling to resort areas for professional purposes.

The cluster has increasingly become a destination not only for holidaymakers but also for visitors combining work and leisure. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of business and professional travelers staying at hotels in the area increased 2.5 times.

In 2025, hotels in the Almaty Mountain Cluster accommodated 925,700 business and professional visitors, up 7.1% from 2024.

Business travelers contribute to tourism revenue

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, accommodation facilities in Kazakhstan’s resort areas provided services worth 91.2 billion tenge (US$202.1 million) in the first half of 2026.

Spending by foreign visitors traveling to Kazakhstan for business purposes also increased. According to the Bureau of National Statistics’ visitor expenditure surveys, their total spending in the first half of 2026 rose 5.4% compared with the same period in 2025.

Expenditure on accommodation increased 9.7%, while spending on food rose 7.7%. The strongest growth was recorded in culture-related spending, up 24.1%, followed by recreational and sporting activities, up 22.2%, and medical and wellness services, up 13%.

According to Ranking.kz analysts, the spending patterns may indicate that business trips to Kazakhstan are increasingly combined with leisure, cultural experiences and wellness activities.

The growth of MICE tourism in major cities and resort destinations offers Kazakhstan an opportunity to broaden its tourism market, generating additional revenue for hospitality and related services.

World.title: Kazakh Foreign Ministry Condemns Attacks in Saudi Arabia, Issues Advisory for Kazakh Citizens
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has urged citizens in Saudi Arabia to exercise heightened caution following attacks on the country’s civilian infrastructure that caused casualties, according to the ministry’s spokesperson Zhanbolat Ussenov.

The ministry advised Kazakh citizens to follow instructions from local authorities, avoid airports unless necessary and check flight statuses with airlines before traveling to terminals. It also recommended avoiding crowded places and high-risk facilities, and postponing non-essential trips where possible.

Ussenov also noted that citizens facing emergencies can contact Kazakhstan’s Embassy in Riyadh or its Consulate General in Jeddah through the following emergency numbers.

The ministry urged citizens to follow official updates from Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and the relevant Saudi authorities.

Earlier, the ministry strongly condemned attacks by Houthi militants on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, which resulted in casualties. It described the attacks as violations of international law and humanitarian principles.

Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry called for an immediate halt to the attacks and urged the parties to resolve the crisis exclusively through political and diplomatic means. Kazakhstan also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its right to protect its sovereignty and security in accordance with the United Nations Charter.

World.title: Can Agricultural Growth Make Kazakhstan Regional Food Security Hub?
World.content:
ASTANA – The global food system is facing several pressures at once. Population growth and rising incomes, particularly in middle-income countries, are changing consumption patterns. Demand for meat, dairy products, and other protein sources is increasing.

At the same time, agriculture faces growing climate risks. Water scarcity, higher input costs and supply chain disruptions linked to geopolitical tensions are adding to the pressure.

Against this backdrop, Kazakhstan is seeking to strengthen its role in regional food security. The country is increasing agricultural production and expanding exports. It is also investing in irrigation, processing, logistics and agricultural technologies.

Agriculture gains momentum

Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector continues to show growth. Gross agricultural output increased 4.4% in the first six months of 2026 to 2.2 trillion tenge (US$4.9 billion), according to the government.

Investment has been a major driver. Investment in agriculture increased 36.4% in the first five months of 2026, while investment in food production grew 2.7 times to 207.3 billion tenge (US$464 million).

The country is also progressing with its harvest campaign. At a Sept. 18 operational headquarters meeting, Vice Minister of Agriculture Nazgul Khatepova reported that Kazakhstan’s total sown area reached 24.2 million hectares, including 15.6 million hectares planted with grain and leguminous crops.

As of the meeting, farmers had harvested 11.3 million hectares, with an average yield of 14.2 centners per hectare. Grain harvesting had covered 72.5% of the total grain area. Farmers had harvested 16.2 million tons of grain. Around 74% of the soft wheat delivered for storage was classified as third-grade wheat.

The livestock sector is also expanding. Cattle numbers increased by 5.8% to 9.3 million head, while horse numbers rose by 7.4% to 5 million and camel numbers increased by 3.6% to 312,000. Meat production in slaughter weight rose by 5.5% to 559,000 tons. Milk production increased by 2.4% to 1.9 million tons, while egg production grew by 7.9% to 2.4 billion eggs.

In addition, Kazakhstan is preparing for the 2027 harvest as the current harvesting campaign continues, Deputy Agriculture Minister Azat Sultanov said at a government meeting Sept. 29.

According to Sultanov, the country has stored 2 million tons of seeds, or 90% of the 2.3 million tons required for next year’s harvest.

Winter plowing is also under way, with 2.1 million tons of fertilizer applied so far, or 66% of the scientifically recommended amount, compared with 58% last year.

Kazakhstan has also completed the digitization of all agricultural land to support soil-quality monitoring and crop-yield forecasting.

Logistics strengthen export potential

Growing agricultural output is driving higher grain transportation and export volumes. Kazakhstan’s strategic location between major consumer markets across Eurasia further strengthens its position as an agricultural exporter. For the agrifood sector, this provides access to markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus, the Middle East and beyond.

According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the country transported 9.3 million tons of grain during the first eight months of the year. This was 13% more than in the same period in 2025. Domestic transportation accounted for 2.1 million tons, an increase of 8%.

August saw a record monthly volume of grain transportation following the start of the new harvest. The figure reached 1.157 million tons, up 35%.

Kazakhstan exported 7.1 million tons of grain from January through August. Of this amount, 4.8 million tons went to Central Asian countries, an increase of 37%. Uzbekistan received 3.6 million tons, up 50%. Exports to Tajikistan reached 998,000 tons, up 17%. Another 562,000 tons were transported to China, an increase of 34%.

According to the Ministry of Agriculture, agricultural exports reached $3 billion in January-April 2026, up 36% from $2.2 billion a year earlier, and are expected to reach $7.2 billion by the end of 2026.

Grain market faces price pressure

Strong production and export capacity, however, do not eliminate market risks.

Kazakhstan’s grain market entered the autumn season under pressure from growing supplies of the new harvest and cheaper Russian wheat, according to Yevgeny Karabanov, head of the Analytics Committee of the Grain Union of Kazakhstan.

“The supply of grain and oilseeds on the domestic market is increasing. Prices for grain and oilseeds from the new harvest are continuing to form on both domestic and foreign markets,” Karabanov said in his Telegram channel.

He noted that prices for some wheat grades on the domestic market fell by 1,000-3,000 tenge (US$2.2-US$7) per ton over one week, while export prices declined by up to $5 per ton.

Karabanov identified two main factors affecting the market. One is the growing supply of Kazakhstan’s new harvest. The other is the availability of Russian wheat at lower prices.

Export shipments are beginning to increase, but logistics costs have also risen. Karabanov said transportation costs increased 10%-15% over the week, or about $3.50-$5.50 per ton.

He emphasized that buyers also remain cautious about purchasing large grain volumes. Importers are expecting further price declines and are looking for cheaper Russian wheat.

“Amid restrictions on wheat exports in Russia, due to the effective blocking of Black Sea and Azov Sea ports, wheat prices in Russia continue to decline. Proposals to supply Russian wheat to Kazakhstan and Central Asian countries were increasing, while the weakening ruble was making Russian wheat more attractive to regional importers,” Karabanov said.

He warned that increasing supplies of cheaper Russian grain could intensify competition in Central Asian markets for grain, flour and vegetable oils.

According to Karabanov, tighter restrictions on Russian wheat imports into Kazakhstan could temporarily support domestic prices, but competition from Russian agricultural products in Central Asia would remain.

From grain exporter to food security hub

Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector faces challenges amid a broader shift in how food security is understood.

In a written response to The Astana Times, the Islamic Organisation for Food Security (IOFS) said food security is no longer measured solely by the volume of food produced. It increasingly depends on the resilience of the entire food system, from genetic resources and agricultural production to storage, transportation, trade and access to food.

“Whoever controls the seeds controls the food,” the organization said, highlighting the importance of conserving genetic resources and developing crop varieties that can withstand changing climate conditions.

Agriculture faces growing pressure from climate change, water scarcity, land degradation, pests and diseases. According to IOFS, countries need to invest in agricultural research, plant breeding, biotechnology, innovation and resilient seed systems.

Production must also be supported by reliable supply chains, adequate storage, food processing, transport and open trade. IOFS noted that effective governance, early-warning systems, and coordination across agriculture, water, trade, transport, energy, and finance are also important.

“Ultimately, food security is not simply about producing more food. It is about building resilient food systems capable of withstanding shocks, adapting to changing conditions, and ensuring that safe, nutritious, and affordable food remains accessible to all, even in times of uncertainty,” the IOFS said.

Kazakhstan’s strategic assets and remaining gaps

IOFS identifies several advantages that could strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in regional food security. These include extensive land resources, a developed grain sector, strong livestock production and an established scientific and research base.

The country also has plant genetic resources and experience in crop breeding, seed production and agricultural research. Some crop varieties have been adapted to harsh continental and water-scarce conditions.

“This makes them increasingly relevant as countries seek to adapt their agricultural systems to climate change,” IOFS said.

The organization identified several areas where Kazakhstan could contribute to regional and international food security, including agricultural science and innovation, climate-resilient seed systems, technology transfer, logistics and trade connectivity, and the exchange of agricultural expertise.

For Kazakhstan to become a regional food security hub, several challenges still need to be addressed, particularly water management, technology, processing and logistics.

Agriculture will increasingly depend on efficient water use as climate pressures intensify. Kazakhstan is modernizing irrigation and introducing digital solutions, while IOFS recommends more precise water management through better measurement, digital allocation, satellite monitoring, telemetry, and data-based decision-making.

Technology also needs to reach farmers faster, including digital agriculture, precision farming, modern breeding and climate-adaptation solutions. At the same time, Kazakhstan could strengthen its position by expanding food processing and exporting higher-value products rather than raw commodities.

“Storage and logistics remain important because Kazakhstan is landlocked,” IOFS said, adding that long-term competitiveness will depend on integrating water management, science, technology, processing and logistics.

World.title: Kazakhstan Can Build on Its Strengths, Advance Digital Entrepreneurs, Says NVIDIA’s VP
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan can turn its strengths in energy, mining, transport and industrial operations into an AI competitive advantage by investing in infrastructure, encouraging local talent and supporting entrepreneurs. In an interview with The AT, NVIDIA Vice President of Physical AI Simulation Rev Lebaredian said access to intelligence will influence where companies are built, where research happens and how productive an economy can become.

During his visit to Kazakhstan this October, Lebaredian held talks with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev about the company’s plans for Kazakhstan’s AI infrastructure development, as the nation has already launched two supercomputer clusters based on NVIDIA technologies.

The country has emerged as the second market for US-based AI infrastructure company Firebird and NVIDIA, which are developing a computing facility in Ekibastuz. The project envisages developing computing infrastructure with a capacity of approximately 300 megawatt, with the potential to expand to 1 gigawatt.

In a Q&A interview below, Lebaredian discussed the infrastructure needed to support the transition, the opportunities AI agents and physical AI offer local businesses and why access to computing, practical education and opportunities for young entrepreneurs to solve real-world problems will be critical to building a sustainable AI ecosystem.

Kazakhstan is developing its AI ecosystem, from public-sector digitalization to private-sector innovation. From NVIDIA’s perspective, what are the country’s key strengths today, and what capabilities could be strengthened further as Kazakhstan develops its AI ecosystem?

Kazakhstan is thinking about AI at the level of national development. President Tokayev’s vision recognizes that this technology will shape the economy and the opportunities available to the next generation.

The country has energy resources, substantial industries and people who understand difficult physical problems. Mining, energy, manufacturing and logistics are all places where AI can create tremendous value.

The next step is to connect those strengths. Computing infrastructure should be accessible to entrepreneurs, researchers and students. Industrial companies should become customers and development partners for local teams. Universities should give people opportunities to build with technology.

I would put particular emphasis on entrepreneurship. A country captures more of the opportunity when its people create the products and companies that others use. Kazakhstan has an opportunity to develop that capability and serve markets far beyond its borders.

AI infrastructure is becoming a critical factor in a country’s ability to develop and deploy AI. What infrastructure does Kazakhstan need to build or strengthen — including computing capacity, data centers and networking — to support the next stage of its AI development?

AI is becoming essential infrastructure. Access to intelligence will influence where companies are built, where research happens and how productive an economy can become.

You have to think about the whole system: energy, chips, infrastructure, models and applications. Power and cooling enable the computers to operate. Networking connects them into an AI factory. Software and models turn that capacity into something people can use.

An AI factory produces intelligence. That intelligence can power agents doing useful work across an economy—helping design products, develop software, serve customers and operate industrial systems. Infrastructure investment creates the foundation for that productive activity.

Kazakhstan also needs people who can design, operate and continually improve these systems. And it needs access models that put the capacity within reach of small teams. The value of the infrastructure grows with what people build on top of it.

Beyond infrastructure, what opportunities do you see for Kazakhstan’s local technology companies, startups and researchers to develop AI solutions of their own? Are there particular sectors where Kazakhstan could build distinctive capabilities?

Start with problems Kazakhstan understands deeply. The country’s experience in energy, mining, transport and industrial operations is a source of valuable knowledge.

A team that understands how a mine works could develop intelligence for autonomous equipment. Researchers working on materials or energy systems could build AI tools that help engineers explore designs much faster. A logistics company could turn its operational knowledge into software used across many markets.

AI agents expand who can participate. People with deep knowledge of an industry will increasingly be able to direct agents to build software, construct simulations and test ideas. Their expertise becomes much more powerful when they can translate it into a working system.

That opens the door to a new generation of entrepreneurs. The ambition should be to solve important problems in Kazakhstan and build companies that serve the world.

Your work at NVIDIA focuses heavily on Omniverse and simulation technologies. How could digital twins, simulation and physical AI be applied in Kazakhstan — for example, across industry, energy, mining, logistics, urban planning or other areas of the economy?

Simulators are time machines. They let us explore possible futures before committing to one in the physical world.

You can test how a factory will operate before building it. You can explore changes to a mine without interrupting production. You can train an autonomous machine through situations it might take years to encounter in reality.

Physical AI depends on that capability. Robots and autonomous systems need a place to learn, practice and be tested. We need to understand how they will behave before putting them around people and valuable equipment.

Until now, building these simulated worlds has required specialized skills and a great deal of manual work. AI agents are beginning to remove that barrier. With simulation libraries and the right tools, agents can help write the software, construct environments and run experiments.

The direction is clear: everyone should be able to build and use a simulation. Someone who understands a physical problem should be able to describe what they want to investigate and work with an agent to test it. The results still need to be validated against reality. But the ability to ask and explore those questions can reach far more people.

That is a profound opportunity for a country with Kazakhstan’s industrial base.

As Kazakhstan looks to strengthen its role in the regional AI ecosystem, what capabilities would help it become a place where developers and companies build AI products and services, rather than simply consume AI technologies?

Build a culture of creation, and give people the means to act on it.

Computing access, strong education, open models, software tools and capital all matter. So do customers willing to work with a young company and institutions willing to let people experiment.

Education should give people the confidence and ability to create. Put powerful tools in students’ hands. Have them build things, test ideas and solve real problems. Connect them with engineers and companies so they can see where their knowledge can take them.

At NVIDIA, we build platforms that others can build on. AI agents are extending that opportunity to far more people. Someone with deep knowledge of an industry will increasingly be able to turn an idea into software or a simulation without having to master every underlying technology.

Kazakhstan can develop a generation of entrepreneurs around that capability. The ambition should be that a young person in Kazakhstan can imagine something important, build it from home and bring it to the world.

World.title: Tokayev, King Philippe Pledge to Deepen Kazakhstan-Belgium Ties in Joint Statement
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations, focusing on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and cooperation on international topics, according to a joint statement adopted by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe of the Belgians on Oct. 12.

The statement followed talks during the Belgian royal couple’s state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 11-14, which both officials described as an important milestone in bilateral relations.

Middle Corridor and digital technologies

The two countries underscored the growing role of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, as a reliable and sustainable transport link between Asia and Europe.

They also reaffirmed the importance of developing transport and logistics cooperation and enhancing connectivity between the two regions.

Digitalization, artificial intelligence and innovation were identified as increasingly important for sustainable economic development and competitiveness. The two leaders expressed interest in developing cooperation in artificial intelligence, big data, cloud technologies, supercomputing infrastructure and data centers.

During the press briefing, Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s interest in expanding cooperation across emerging industries, including digitalization and space technologies.

King Philippe, in turn, underlined Kazakhstan’s technological development, noting that the country was “at the forefront of digitalization” and had developed unique solutions, notably in artificial intelligence.

“We are keen to visit the Alem.AI center and discuss synergies between our countries,” he said.

Critical minerals and economic cooperation

The joint statement reaffirmed the importance of cooperation in critical minerals, petrochemicals, industry and mechanical engineering, and renewable energy.

The leaders welcomed the holding of a roundtable on critical minerals during the state visit, underscoring the strategic importance of cooperation in this field.

They also highlighted the potential to expand agricultural trade, develop the food industry and introduce modern agricultural technologies.

Tokayev noted that Belgium had invested more than $15 billion in Kazakhstan’s economy since 2005, describing economic cooperation as a cornerstone of bilateral relations.

The leaders welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Business Council’s activities and the fourth meeting during the visit as an important mechanism for strengthening ties between the two countries’ business communities.

The statement also reaffirmed their commitment to the Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement between Kazakhstan and the European Union and its member states, signed on Dec. 21, 2015.

Education, healthcare and cultural ties

The two officials welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Rectors’ Forum and expressed support for joint educational programs, academic mobility, scientific research and partnerships between universities and research centers.

They also reaffirmed the importance of strengthening healthcare cooperation, including enhancing the role of primary healthcare within the World Health Organization Global Coalition for Primary Health Care.

The leaders referred to the principles of the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration on Primary Health Care and the 2018 Astana Declaration, as well as initiatives to be discussed following the conference Towards the 50th Anniversary of the Alma-Ata Declaration: Building Strong Primary Health Care for Future Generations, scheduled for Oct. 14 in Almaty.

The discussions also featured cultural cooperation. Tokayev welcomed the presentation of works by Belgian artist James Ensor at Kazakhstan’s National Museum and cooperation between the Almaty Museum of Arts and KANAL-Center Pompidou.

Tokayev and King Philippe further welcomed the entry into force of the protocol amending the agreement between Kazakhstan and the Benelux countries on visa exemption for holders of service passports.

They also expressed their intention to conclude negotiations and sign a bilateral agreement on remunerated employment for family members of diplomatic missions as a deliverable marking 35 years of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Belgium in 2027.

Commitment to international law and dialogue

On international and regional matters, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to multilateralism, international law and the United Nations’ central role in maintaining international peace and security, promoting sustainable development and addressing global challenges.

They agreed to intensify bilateral political dialogue on international affairs and economic development within the United Nations, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), and multilateral platforms in the Kazakhstan-EU and Central Asia-EU formats.

The statement also highlighted the importance of strengthening the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on Their Destruction, adopted on April 10, 1972.

The leaders expressed satisfaction with the outcomes of their talks and reaffirmed their determination to give new impetus to the Kazakhstan-Belgium partnership.

Both officials expressed confidence that King Philippe’s first state visit to Kazakhstan would lay the foundation for the further qualitative development of bilateral relations.

World.title: Kazakh President Terminates Maslikhats’ Powers, Orders Snap Elections
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on Oct. 12 terminating the powers of maslikhats, local representative bodies at all levels, before the end of their term.

The decision followed consultations with Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Kurultai Chair Aibek Dadebay, in accordance with Article 88, Paragraph 5 of Kazakhstan’s Constitution, Akorda reported.

The Central Election Commission has been instructed to take all necessary measures to appoint, prepare and conduct snap elections to maslikhats at all levels.

World.title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
World.content:
Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products.

The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures.

Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year.

Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets.

The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Ukraine and Iraq.

More than 94% of exports went to three countries

According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026:

48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan,

around 34% went to Georgia,

approximately 12% went to Ukraine.

Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July.

State budget compensation for exporters

In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets.

In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches.

Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume:

“The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.”

Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers.

How the compensation was distributed

The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports:

The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots.

Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m).

The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller.

Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents.

Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram.

Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

World.title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
World.content:
Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth.

Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula.

A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience

Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience.

“I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says.

Иветта с мужем и сыновьями

Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”.

She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth:

“Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try.

“My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.”

Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers.

“Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.”

Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia.

Who are doulas?

Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support.

During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome.

Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain.

According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive:

“Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.”

Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward.

Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work.

There are only five or six doulas in Armenia

Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama.

In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants.

A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room.

Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice.

Why do women turn to doulas?

Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence.

“Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm.

“They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says.

A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia.

The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence.

In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions.

Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching.

Why don’t women turn to doulas?

Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support.

Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

“But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says.

Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission.

“Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.”

She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour.

Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her.

“Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says.

Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support

Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

World.title: ‘Take off your hijab and come into class’: what is happening in Azerbaijan’s schools?
World.content:
The hijab ban in Azerbaijan’s schools

In Azerbaijan’s schools, a ban on wearing the hijab has led to female students being barred from classes, demands for female teachers to remove their headscarves and protests.

On 12 October, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of 37 people in connection with incidents over compliance with school uniform rules.

The authorities justify the restrictions by citing the need for a uniform school dress code and secular education. However, the consequences for students barred from classes are tangible: they must give up religious clothing to attend lessons.

At the heart of the dispute is the question of how the state exercises its authority to set school dress code requirements and how these restrictions undermine children’s right to education.

Schoolchildren show solidarity with classmates who wear hijabs

Videos shared today from several settlements in Baku show schoolchildren gathering at school entrances. Some of the girls are wearing hijabs. Students at School No. 322 are protesting the ban on wearing hijabs and demanding that the girls be allowed to attend classes.

A video published on 9 October and filmed outside School No. 69 in Baku shows schoolchildren refusing to go to lessons in solidarity with their classmates who wear hijabs.



Protest outside School No. 69 in Baku’s Balakhany settlement: “The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education.”

Schoolchildren have also staged protests at a school in the village of Mollaoba, in the Masally district.

A video shared from School No. 9 in the Jalilabad district shows girls being barred from entering the building because they wear hijabs. In another video, published in the Baku settlement of Khokhmeli, parents warn that they will stop sending their sons to school as well.

Protesters are expressing their discontent in various ways: gathering outside schools, refusing to attend classes and calling for boycotts. But they all have the same demand: girls who wear hijabs must not be denied access to education.

While families face demands to change their religious practices, children bear the brunt of this confrontation.

From school uniform requirements to a ban

Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309, adopted on 21 September, prohibits additional items of clothing that violate uniform school dress code requirements and contradict the principle of secular education.

Although the document does not explicitly mention the hijab, complaints from schools indicate that, in practice, the provision applies specifically to headscarves.

Barring female students who wear hijabs from classes effectively amounts to a ban on wearing this head covering.

When authorities present such measures solely as a way to enforce school uniform rules, the issue of restricting children’s access to education takes a back seat.

The amendments introduced by the resolution do not, however, explicitly provide for suspension from classes as a separate measure. This raises the question of what legal grounds school administrations rely on when adopting this practice.

On 9 October, the Baku City Education Department announced inspections to check whether students and teachers comply with clothing requirements. This suggests that the problem extends beyond decisions made by individual school administrations.

The question remains open as to who should ultimately ensure that children have access to education, and how.

Criminal proceedings launched against protesters

In a statement issued on 12 October, Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry directly linked the detention of 37 people to events surrounding the introduction of uniform school dress code requirements.

Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 233 of the Criminal Code, which provides for liability for organising actions that disrupt public order or actively participating in them.

The ministry accuses the detainees of provoking confrontations with education workers in Baku, damaging educational institutions and attempting to obstruct school operations and traffic.

However, the statement does not specify which schools sustained damage or what specific actions the detainees allegedly committed. It also does not disclose their names or ages.

The lack of this information raises serious questions, particularly against the backdrop of protests involving schoolchildren.

Are any of the detainees minors? On what grounds do law enforcement agencies distinguish between peaceful protest and the specific actions they accuse the detainees of committing?

The ministry says the measures are necessary to ensure the safety of students and teachers. However, opening a criminal case amid protests over the right to education could deter other families from taking part in similar demonstrations.

Parents demanding that schools allow their children to attend classes must now also consider the risks associated with participating in protests.

Aliyev’s remarks and the Iranian factor

On 2 October, speaking at the 8th congress of the New Azerbaijan Party, Ilham Aliyev placed particular emphasis on the role of education in safeguarding ideological security:

“Therefore, we must protect ourselves from ideological provocations. How? First and foremost, of course, through education.”

The president also criticised Azerbaijani-language media outlets operating in neighbouring countries. Although he did not explicitly mention Iran or the hijab in this part of his speech, some political commentators interpret his remarks as a signal directed against Iran’s religious influence in Azerbaijan.

Asif Narimanli, a political commentator close to the authorities, links the events surrounding the hijab ban to attempts by Iran at “political and ideological interference”. In this context, he refers to a religious gathering in Qom and a protest in Istanbul. Aygun Muradkhanli, a journalist at a pro-government media outlet, has also argued that religious groups opposing the ban have links to centres abroad.

This interpretation risks pushing demands to allow female students who wear hijabs to attend classes into the background, as debate over foreign influence takes centre stage.

Parents’ rights and the state’s obligations

Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights enshrines parents’ right to ensure the religious and moral education of their children in accordance with their own beliefs.

Experts point out that articles 5 and 14 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child also recognise the role of parents in raising their children and guiding their development.

The secular nature of education does not negate a family’s right to provide religious education for its children. Many in society believe that the authorities enforcing these restrictions should explain exactly how wearing a headscarf disrupts the learning process.

Teachers risk losing their jobs

Following the approval on 6 October of separate dress code requirements for teachers, reports emerged of pressure on teachers who wear hijabs. Teachers told Toplum TV that some schools in Sumgayit were demanding that they remove their hijabs or submit letters of resignation.

Journalist Arzu Abdulla reported a similar situation at School No. 90 in the Ramana settlement.

Requiring them to submit letters of resignation can create the impression that they are ending their employment voluntarily.

Some educators point out that teachers’ dress ultimately seems to matter more than their professionalism and experience.

Public opinion on the ban is divided.

Press Council chairman Rashad Majid defends the restrictions as necessary to protect the secular nature of the state and says he sees foreign influence behind the protests.

Jailed journalist Polad Aslanov, by contrast, announced a hunger strike to protest restrictions imposed on female students and teachers who wear hijabs.

Comments on a HamamTimes post about protests at a school in the Buzovna settlement also include claims that the protesters have links to Iran.

Other discussions express a view: some participants oppose children wearing hijabs but nevertheless believe that barring schoolchildren from classes for this reason is unacceptable.

Turkey’s reaction

On 3 October, protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul in a demonstration. They demanded that the restrictions be lifted and called on the Turkish authorities to intervene.

However, on 7 October, Omer Celik, spokesperson for Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), said that groups opposing Azerbaijan had no ties to either the party or the government.

Previous attempts to ban the hijab in schools

The current developments come against the backdrop of earlier protests against attempts to introduce similar restrictions, although those efforts were not backed by specific legislation at the time.

Protests against the hijab ban in Azerbaijan have previously led to arrests and criminal proceedings. On 6 May 2011, police intervened during a demonstration outside the Education Ministry, followed by arrests and the opening of a criminal case.

Abgul Suleymanov, known for taking part in protests against the hijab ban, was arrested that year and later sentenced to 11 years in prison on charges he denied.

In September this year, authorities placed him under administrative arrest for another 30 days. His family links the arrest to his posts about the hijab.

It is currently unknown how many girls across the country are missing school because of the new dress code restrictions, and how many teachers are at risk of losing their jobs.

The hijab ban in Azerbaijan’s schools

World.title: Russian passport in Abkhazia: ticket to better life or risky luxury?
World.content:
A reform of the consular department at the Russian Embassy in Abkhazia has cut the time needed to process citizenship applications by a factor of 3.5. This seemingly dry statistic illustrates one of the most important and contentious aspects of life in Abkhazia.

For some Abkhaz people, a Russian passport offers the only way to see the world. For others, it provides a chance to build a career or enjoy a decent retirement. For still others, it raises doubts and fears.

Most countries around the world do not recognise Abkhazia as an independent state, leaving its passport with virtually no value beyond the republic’s borders. In practice, this means that Abkhaz passport holders cannot travel anywhere except Russia. Many residents of Abkhazia therefore acquire a second citizenship, Russian citizenship. But freedom of movement is not the only issue.

Processing applications 3.5 times faster

Until recently, residents of Abkhazia frequently complained about the slow-moving queue for Russian citizenship. The consulate could accept applications from only 120 people a month, despite a waiting list of 3,000. As a result, applicants faced a wait of more than three years.

To address the problem, Russia’s new ambassador to Abkhazia, Vyacheslav Gladkov, sought assistance from the Russian presidential administration. Experts from the Senezh Management Workshop joined the effort. They specialise in modern workplace organisation based on the methodology of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. Their main task was to eliminate unnecessary steps in the document submission process, simplify logistics and spare applicants a lengthy wait.

Abkhazia State University also supported the project. Student volunteers from its law faculty took on the initial consultations and helped applicants complete their citizenship paperwork correctly.

By the end of September 2026, the consulate had increased its application processing rate 3.5-fold. The embassy expects to reduce the backlog significantly by the end of the year.

But who are the people queuing for Russian citizenship, and why do they need it? Are there also people in no hurry to obtain it, even under the simplified procedure?

To find out, we spoke to residents of Sukhumi and collected their stories.

A passport as a way out of isolation

For 38-year-old Diana Chelidze, obtaining a Russian passport means an end to the isolation she has experienced for almost her entire adult life.

Diana lived in Russia as a child and attended school there, but her parents never managed to obtain Russian citizenship for her. She later tried to resolve the matter herself but ran into insurmountable bureaucratic obstacles. She finally obtained the long-awaited document after Russia resumed issuing passports to Abkhaz residents under a simplified procedure in 2025.

“I waited for this opportunity for many years. I spent my entire youth within the borders of Abkhazia and Russia. The first place I travelled to after getting my passport was Istanbul. It’s an indescribable feeling to simply buy a ticket and fly somewhere. I’m now actively saving for a trip to the Maldives. I’m 38, and only now have I gained the opportunity to see the world. I’m incredibly happy to have this freedom,” Diana says enthusiastically.

Starting a career and securing a pension

While a Russian passport has given Diana the freedom to travel, many of her compatriots see it not as a luxury but as a basic necessity for social and professional stability.

Liana Georgievna Avidzba, 71, worked throughout her life but now receives a meagre Abkhaz pension of 6,000 roubles [around $70].

“It’s practically impossible to live on that amount today. I obtained a Russian passport solely so I could use my Soviet-era employment record to qualify for a Russian pension. Now that I have the document, I’ll start the pension application process straight away,” Liana says.

Young people who see their future in Russia have different reasons for seeking citizenship. Milana Kvitsinia, a student at a Russian university, is currently applying for citizenship.

“Without a Russian passport, it’s extremely difficult to find a decent, formal job in Russia today. Employers are reluctant to hire foreign nationals. I’m studying in Russia and plan to stay there for work, so a passport is a necessity for me,” Milana explains.

A second citizenship? No, thank you!

But not all residents of Abkhazia are eager to become Russian citizens.

Albina, a mother of three boys aged 10, 12 and 17, is deliberately putting off applying for Russian passports for her sons. Her main fear is that the authorities will register them for military service and conscript them into the Russian army.

“People tell me that dual citizenship will allow the boys to choose where they do their military service. But I don’t believe that. I see how the authorities immediately register the sons of my friends who are studying in Russia for military service. Their parents live in constant fear that the boys will be sent to the front.

I’m sure they will never stop issuing [Russian] citizenship here. When my sons grow up, they can apply themselves if they want to. But as their mother, I’m not going to take that risk for now,” Albina says.

Leonid Topchyan, 24, is ethnically Armenian and believes he has no need for a Russian passport at all. He and his parents run a family business in Abkhazia, growing mandarins, persimmons and feijoa. They use the fruit to make homemade compotes, fruit pastilles and dried fruit for sale.

“I work on my own land and make my living from agriculture. I’m happy with how things are. I simply don’t need a Russian passport.

If I ever apply for a second citizenship, it will only be Armenian. I can’t travel to Armenia at the moment, although many of my friends and relatives go there even with Abkhaz passports. The local Armenian community helps them a lot,” Leonid says.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russia bans imports of several drinks from Georgia
Georgia marks 1,700 years of Christianity: Patriarch and officials reflect on faith, identity and the future
World.content:
1,700 years of Christianity in Georgia

An international academic symposium titled “God, Homeland, Human” took place at the Radisson hotel in Tbilisi to mark 1,700 years since Georgia declared Christianity its state religion.

The event was attended by Georgian Patriarch Shio III, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and President Mikheil Kavelashvili.

The main political message of their speeches was that Christianity, national identity and traditional values should form the foundation of the Georgian state and society. They presented the preservation of these values as a response to the challenges of the modern world.

Key points from the speeches

● Cooperation between the state and the Church: Irakli Kobakhidze said that the government would continue to protect Georgia’s Christian heritage and national values in close cooperation with the Church.

“The state pays particular attention to these enduring values. In close cooperation with the Church, we will firmly defend the heritage on which our national unity and development rest.”

● National identity and statehood: According to Shalva Papuashvili said, a state may temporarily lose its independence, but preserving its national identity leaves open the possibility of restoring it.

“The world has once again entered an era of great change. Technology, economic relations and the international order are changing rapidly. However, as history has taught us time and again, societies that preserve their identity stand firmest during periods of change,” Papuashvili said.

● Seven eternal values: Mikheil Kavelashvili identified God, the Homeland, the Individual, the Native Land, Language, Faith and Family as the foundations of thinking rooted in Georgian statehood. In his view, these values help preserve national identity in the age of globalisation and artificial intelligence.

“Today, as the modern world faces a crisis of values and geopolitical upheaval, we have a duty to ask a fundamental question: what should form the foundations of the Georgian state, society and individual?

These seven symbols form the basis of our identity. Even today, as the age of globalisation and artificial intelligence seeks to devalue human identity, these eternal values serve as our main existential shield,” Kavelashvili said.

“God, Homeland, Human” — an international symposium marking 1,700 years since Georgia declared Christianity its state religion. Tbilisi, 11 October 2026.

● Technology and spirituality: Patriarch Shio said that technological progress should serve humanity and that the growth of knowledge should not distance society from faith and spiritual values.

“Technology should serve humanity, not humanity technology. Knowledge should not distance us from faith, and progress should not make us forget spirituality,” Shio III said.

● Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region: The Patriarch addressed the residents of these regions and expressed hope that peace, unity and brotherly relations between Georgia’s historic regions would be restored.

“We must continue to live peacefully alongside our homeland,” the Patriarch said, expressing hope that “brotherly unity and love will be restored between us”.

● Ties with emigrants: Shio III addressed Georgians living abroad, saying that the Church prays for them and awaits their return to their homeland.

1,700 years of Christianity in Georgia

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi highlights systemic problems in prisons. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 682 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office launches investigation into National Bank Council member
World.content:
Georgia national bank member in corruption probe

Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office has launched an investigation into the possible unlawful involvement of Nana Keinishvili, a member of the National Bank of Georgia’s Council, in business activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, its investigative department launched a probe under Article 337 of the Criminal Code, which criminalises the unlawful involvement of a public official or an equivalent person in business activities. The investigation follows complaints by the management of Bitexchange LLC, which were forwarded by the National Bank.

According to an investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, the National Bank fined cryptocurrency company Bitexchange, in which Keinishvili had unsuccessfully sought a stake, in what could be seen as an act of retaliation.

The National Bank said that, in order to protect the institution’s reputation, its Council would consider at its next meeting temporarily suspending Keinishvili’s participation in Council meetings while the investigation is under way, until the circumstances of the case are fully clarified.

Nana Keinishvili was elected to the National Bank’s Council in September 2023. From 2012 to 2016, she served as a member of parliament representing the ruling Georgian Dream party and as deputy chair of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said former president Salome Zourabichvili should be asked how she selected Nana Keinishvili as a candidate for the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

“This once again shows how important it is for parliament to also familiarise itself with these matters and, in this case, examine in detail the issues surrounding the election of Council members. Salome Zourabichvili herself should answer the remaining questions. What matters is that the state is responding to this issue,” Papuashvili said.

He added, however, that he could not go into the details of the investigation.

It has emerged, however, that the parliament speaker, like current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, voted in parliament in favour of appointing Nana Keinishvili to the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

Details of the case

According to the National Bank, it reviewed submissions from the management of Bitexchange LLC and conducted a preliminary internal investigation within the scope of its authority.

The materials were forwarded to the relevant authorities for legal assessment, as the matter falls outside the mandate established for the National Bank by law. The bank expressed hope that the facts of the case would be established objectively as soon as possible.

The bank also explained that Bitexchange, a virtual asset service provider, had been fined following a routine inspection for violating anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing regulations.

Nana Keinishvili

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the management of Bitexchange claims that Keinishvili is involved in business activities and directly controls a network of companies subject to regulation by the National Bank.

They allege that shares in these companies are registered in the names of her family members and affiliated individuals. The company’s management also claims that Keinishvili attempted to acquire a stake in their business.

The Prosecutor’s Office notes that Georgia’s Law on the Fight Against Corruption prohibits public officials from engaging in business activities. Furthermore, under the Organic Law on the National Bank of Georgia, members of the National Bank’s Council and their family members are prohibited from being partners in a Georgian financial sector entity or a legal entity affiliated with one.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the investigation will examine the circumstances surrounding Nana Keinishvili’s possible unlawful involvement in business activities. The public will be informed of the results of the investigation in due course.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation

The National Bank has not disclosed the amount of the fine. However, according to the investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Nana Keinishvili demanded a stake in a cryptocurrency company regulated by the National Bank. The company’s owner refused to give up a share, after which the National Bank fined the company 572 million lari (approximately $211.85 million).

The investigation also found that Keinishvili and her family members own and manage profitable businesses regulated by the National Bank.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty obtained documents indicating that the National Bank and the State Security Service had been aware of information about Keinishvili’s alleged violations for at least several months. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent inquiries to both agencies on 6 October.
