World.title: Turkic states plan digital identity system (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. A digital identity system is planned to be rolled out among Turkic states, Chairman of the Board of the Azerbaijan Fintech Association (AzFina), Edgar Abdullayev, told Trend in an exclusive interview.

He said that the integration of digital identity and payment systems among Turkic states can create new opportunities for expanding cooperation in the fintech sector.

According to him, there is significant potential for the development of the fintech sector in Azerbaijan.

"Realizing this potential requires expanding the capabilities of companies operating in the financial technology field, strengthening cooperation with regulatory bodies, and applying international best practices.

Alongside the development of financial technologies, requirements regarding financial security and the fight against money laundering must also be taken into account. In this regard, sector regulation should be risk-based while simultaneously fostering an environment conducive to the creation of new services and the implementation of innovative solutions," Abdullayev explained.

He noted that cooperation and dialogue between the Central Bank of Azerbaijan and fintech companies play a crucial role in the sector's development. Solutions such as the instant payment system and the AZQR standard are significant for expanding payment services and creating new technological capabilities.

Abdullayev emphasized that the development of the fintech sector in Azerbaijan also opens up new prospects for regional cooperation.

"In this regard, the platform of the Fintech Alliance of Turkic States (TURKFIN), established in 2024, holds special significance. The platform was founded by the Azerbaijan Fintech Association and the Payment and Electronic Money Institutions Association of Türkiye (TÖDEB). Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan also participate in this cooperation framework," he remarked.

The AzFina chairman highlighted that one of the platform's primary objectives is to coordinate fintech ecosystems among Turkic states, develop payment services, and deepen cooperation in the field of financial technologies.

"The integration of digital payment systems and the harmonization of digital identity mechanisms among Turkic states could create broader opportunities for users. This could enable the seamless use of financial services developed in one country across other countries as well," he said.

According to Abdullayev, the cross-border use of services provided by electronic money institutions and the interconnection of instant payment systems could become key areas of cooperation in the future. Such integration could help accelerate money transfers, reduce operational costs, and facilitate user access to financial services.

He added that digital identity solutions could play a significant role in this process.

"Harmonizing user identification mechanisms across different countries could facilitate the cross-border use of financial services. However, the implementation of such mechanisms must also take into account issues regarding data security, the resilience of financial systems, and national economic sovereignty," he mentioned.

The AzFina chairman noted that technological solutions alone are insufficient for fostering regional integration. It is also essential to harmonize legislative and regulatory approaches and to strengthen coordination among the relevant institutions of the respective countries.

He pointed out that reporting requirements for the operations of e-money and payment institutions also serve to ensure the transparency of the financial system and the effectiveness of oversight mechanisms.

According to Abdullayev, expanding cooperation in digital identity, instant payment systems, and electronic money services could facilitate the entry of Azerbaijani fintech companies into regional markets while simultaneously contributing to the development of digital economic ties among Turkic states.

World.title: KEGOC sets about $49M dividend payout for H1 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. KEGOC (Kazakhstan Electricity Grid Operating Company) has announced the upcoming dividend payment on its ordinary shares for the first half of 2026 following the decision made at its extraordinary General Meeting of Shareholders on October 8, 2026.

According to the company’s publication, the total amount of funds allocated for dividend payments to shareholders will reach 22.368 billion tenge ($49.56 million). The dividend per ordinary share has been set at 81.25 tenge ($0.18).

Dividend payouts are scheduled to commence on November 1, 2026.

“Dividends will be paid in cash within ninety (90) calendar days from the date of this decision by non-cash transfer to the bank accounts of shareholders through the payment agent, Central Securities Depository JSC”, KEGOC said.

The currency conversions are based on the official exchange rate of the National Bank of Kazakhstan of 1 USD = KZT 451.31, as of October 13.

KEGOC is the national operator of Kazakhstan's unified power system and main electricity grids. In 2025, the company recorded a 3.8% increase in electricity consumption to 124.6 billion kWh, while electricity generation rose by 4.4% to 123.1 billion kWh. Peak consumption was recorded on December 18, reaching 17,724 MW, further highlighting the growing load on the power system. Peak generation amounted to 17,273 MW, up 7% year-on-year.

World.title: Bir brings its digital banking experience to Istanbul Fintech Week
World.content:
Bir, the Caucasus’ first integrated banking, payments, and e-commerce ecosystem, presented its roadmap for national digital financial services at Istanbul Fintech Week 2026.

Speaking at the Digital Banking Summit on October 7, Javid Mirzayev, Head of Fintech business of the Bir ecosystem and First Deputy Chairman of Kapital Bank, outlined how an established bank successfully scaled a digital ecosystem to over 5 million users. “At Bir, we connected banking, payments, and shopping under a single umbrella to simplify everyday life,” Mirzayev said. “We are showing the international community that legacy banks don't have to be disrupted by fintechs. By adapting to practical customer needs, they can lead the digital shift.”

During “The Digital Bank: Born or Built?” panel, moderated by KOOP Ventures Co-Founder Mustafa Baltacı, Mirzayev joined Bank of Valletta's Head of Innovation, Ludwig Mallia, to explain Bir's structure. He described how the Bir ecosystem integrates Kapital Bank’s digital banking brand, Birbank, alongside the Birmarket online marketplace, the m10 digital wallet, and Milliön payment terminals to create seamless digital experiences for customers.

Mirzayev also detailed how tools like Bir ID, Bir Bonus, and Bir Pay unify these platforms, giving users a single way to move between Bir ecosystem services, earn rewards, and pay online or in-store. For example, a customer can shop on Birmarket and secure Birbank financing directly at checkout. He highlighted the resulting shift in consumer behavior, noting that 90% of customers now use the Birbank app for daily banking. Furthermore, operational efficiency has surged, with 60% of all customer support requests now resolved entirely without human intervention – nearly double last year’s level of 31%.

Mirzayev’s participation in Istanbul Fintech Week comes as Bir continues to communicate Azerbaijan’s digital transformation on the global stage. Since 2019, the event has brought together more than 17,000 participants from 62 countries, establishing itself as one of the leading international platforms in the financial technology sector.

World.title: Azerbaijan parliament ratifies Non-Aligned youth body host deal
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. The Azerbaijani Parliament has ratified the Host Country Agreement regarding the Secretariat of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Organization (NAMYO), which was submitted for consideration at today’s plenary session of the parliament, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

During the session, it was noted that the purpose of the agreement, signed in Baku on September 10, 2026, is to create conditions for the NAMYO Secretariat to effectively perform its functions and duties in Azerbaijan, define its legal status, privileges and immunities, and regulate relations between the Government of Azerbaijan and the organization.

The agreement consists of a preamble and 12 articles. The preamble refers to the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Network, the creation of the Youth Organization based on the Shusha Declaration adopted in 2022, and the provisions of its Statute, which stipulate that its headquarters be located in Baku.

The document establishes the Secretariat’s status as a legal entity, granting it the right to conclude contracts, acquire and dispose of movable and immovable property (excluding land), and initiate legal proceedings. It also defines the inviolability of the Secretariat’s premises, property, archives and documents, as well as the privileges and immunities of its staff members in relation to the performance of their official duties. These privileges and immunities are granted to staff members to enable them to perform their functions and not for their personal benefit.

The agreement provides for the Secretariat’s exemption from taxes, customs duties and related charges on goods imported or exported for official use. It also grants the Secretariat the right to hold currency, maintain foreign currency accounts, transfer funds and convert currencies. Certain privileges do not apply to staff members who are citizens of Azerbaijan or permanent residents of the country.

The Government of Azerbaijan undertakes to provide the Secretariat with suitable premises, extend the necessary financial support for its operations and ensure appropriate living conditions for its staff members. The annual financial contribution allocated from the state budget is capped at 877,114 manat ($515,950). The Secretariat submits its projected annual budget to the Government, and the allocated financial contribution is transferred to its bank account no later than March 1 of each year. Responsibility for maintaining the premises and covering utility expenses rests with the Secretariat.

The document also establishes procedures for issuing visas free of charge to staff members and their family members entering Azerbaijan for official purposes, providing accreditation cards to relevant individuals, and notifying the Government of changes in personnel.

The agreement enters into force on the date the organization receives official notification from the Government confirming the completion of internal procedures required for its implementation. Amendments to the agreement may be made through separate protocols upon mutual consent of the parties. Any disputes arising from its interpretation or application will be resolved through negotiations between the parties.

The draft law on the approval of the "Host Country Agreement between the Government of Azerbaijan and the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Organization regarding the Secretariat of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Organization" was adopted in a single reading following discussions.

World.title: Azerbaijan ratifies alliance pact and $200M fund deal with Kyrgyzstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. The Azerbaijani Parliament has ratified several documents signed between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan, which were submitted for consideration at today’s plenary session of the parliament, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Draft law on the approval of the "Agreement on Alliance Relations between Azerbaijan and the Kyrgyz Republic"

The "Agreement on Alliance Relations between the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Kyrgyz Republic" was signed on July 31, 2026, in Cholpon-Ata by the heads of state of Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan.

The purpose of the agreement is to elevate bilateral cooperation to a new level based on the principles of mutual respect for the independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the parties.

The agreement consists of 21 articles.

Under the agreement, the parties reaffirm their commitments not to participate in any blocs directed against each other and to refrain from activities that could harm their strategic partnership and alliance relations.

The parties will cooperate in the field of foreign policy and hold consultations on international issues of mutual interest.

The agreement stipulates that the parties will deepen cooperation in military and military-technical fields, including the training and development of personnel and specialists, taking into account their international obligations and national legislation, in order to ensure security, peace and stability.

The sides will also promote deeper parliamentary cooperation through friendship groups and within international inter-parliamentary organizations of which they are members.

The agreement also covers cooperation in areas such as energy, renewable energy, transport, logistics, high technologies, digital development, agriculture, tourism, trade, economy, investment, science, education, culture, sports and arts.

Expressing concern over international terrorism, extremism, separatism and other security threats, the parties agreed to further develop cooperation in combating these challenges.

Amendments and additions to the agreement may be introduced by mutual consent of the parties and formalized through separate protocols, which will constitute an integral part of the agreement.

Any disagreements arising during the implementation of the agreement will be resolved through negotiations and consultations.

The agreement will enter into force on the date of receipt of the final written notification from the parties regarding its ratification through diplomatic channels.

Draft law on the approval of the "Agreement between the Government of Azerbaijan and the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic on International Road Transport"

The "Agreement between the Government of Azerbaijan and the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic on International Road Transport" was signed in Cholpon-Ata on July 31, 2026.

The agreement aims to further develop road transport links between the parties, facilitate transit through their territories and simplify transportation procedures. It regulates relations related to the transportation of passengers and cargo.

The document consists of 24 articles. Under the agreement, regular and irregular road transportation of passengers and cargo may be carried out both within the territories of the two states and in transit through them, using vehicles registered in either country and operating on roads open to international traffic.

Regular passenger bus services will be organized based on prior coordination between the competent authorities of the parties. Proposals submitted to the other side must include information on the carrier, route, schedule, tariffs, stops, and the planned duration and frequency of services. Permits issued by the competent authorities are required for irregular passenger bus transportation.

Cargo transportation between the parties, in transit through their territories or to third countries, will be carried out using registered freight vehicles based on permits issued by the competent authorities. Special permits will be required for the transportation of hazardous, heavy and oversized cargo. However, permits will not be required for certain types of shipments, including postal items, human remains and ashes, and theatrical scenery.

Under the agreement, border, customs, veterinary, phytosanitary and sanitary controls will be carried out on a priority basis for the transportation of seriously ill patients, regular passenger bus services, animals and perishable goods.

The provisions of the agreement do not prevent the introduction of restrictions on transit transportation that may pose a threat to the national security of either party.

The parties agreed to establish a Joint Commission to oversee the implementation of the agreement and resolve issues arising in the field of international road transport.

Any disagreements regarding the interpretation or implementation of the agreement will be resolved through negotiations and consultations.

Amendments and additions to the agreement may be introduced by mutual consent of the parties and formalized through separate protocols, which will constitute an integral part of the document.

Draft law on the approval of the "Second Supplementary Agreement to the Agreement dated October 11, 2022, between the Government of Azerbaijan and the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic on the Establishment of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund"

The "Second Supplementary Agreement on Amendments to the Agreement dated October 11, 2022, between the Government of Azerbaijan and the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic on the Establishment of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund" was signed in Cholpon-Ata on July 31, 2026.

The agreement aims to increase the authorized capital of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund in order to expand investment cooperation between the two states and finance joint investment projects.

Under the amendment, the authorized capital of the fund, previously set at $100 million under Article 4 of the agreement and Clause 2 of Article 6 of the fund’s charter, has been increased to $200 million.

The supplementary agreement forms an integral part of the original agreement and will cease to be effective on the date the agreement is terminated.

Following discussions, all three draft laws were put to a vote and adopted in the first reading.

World.title: EDB places debut 630M-yuan dim sum bonds in Hong Kong
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) has made its debut issuance of dim sum bonds in Hong Kong's offshore Chinese yuan market, placing a three-year tranche of senior unsecured bonds worth 630 million yuan (about $94 million), the bank reported.

The bonds are listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange and were issued under the EDB's new $3.5 billion medium-term note (MTN) program. The offering was oversubscribed more than 2.5 times, while the final coupon rate was set at 3.9%.

The issue has an Ag rating from Hong Kong-based China Chengxin (Asia Pacific) Credit Ratings Company Limited (CCXAP).

China Galaxy International, China International Capital Corporation (CICC) and CITIC Securities acted as global underwriters for the debut dim sum bond issuance. Fosun International Securities and Orient Securities (Hong Kong) served as joint arrangers.

According to the bank, the transaction attracted interest from investors in Asia and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), giving the EDB access to a new source of yuan liquidity in addition to its existing credit lines from Chinese banks.

The proceeds will be used to finance the construction of a border crossing and railway line on the Kazakhstan-China border, as well as other projects in Kazakhstan involving Chinese participation, including Chinese contractors, suppliers, investors, sponsors or co-founders.

EDB Chairman of the Management Board Nikolai Podguzov said the debut issuance was an important milestone for the bank.

“The debut dim sum bond transaction is an important event for the EDB. It strengthens the Bank's position in Asian capital markets, broadens its investor base and creates an additional source of yuan funding for projects that promote economic cooperation and connectivity between Eurasia and China, including the Belt and Road Initiative,” he said.

In August 2026, China Chengxin's rating group assigned the EDB investment-grade credit ratings. CCXAP, a Hong Kong-based agency, assigned the bank an Ag long-term rating with a stable outlook for the first time. Meanwhile, Chinese rating agency China Chengxin International (CCXI) upgraded the EDB's global-scale rating to Ag from A-g and affirmed its AAA rating on the domestic scale.

The EDB is a multilateral development bank that invests across Eurasia. Over the past 20 years, it has supported stronger economic ties and comprehensive development among its member countries.

As of the end of June 2026, the bank's cumulative portfolio comprised 348 projects with total investments of $22.1 billion. Its portfolio is primarily focused on projects with an integration effect in transport infrastructure, digital systems, renewable energy, agriculture, industry and mechanical engineering.

The bank's activities are guided by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles. Under its 2022-2026 strategy, the EDB is implementing three megaprojects: the Central Asia Water and Energy Complex, the Eurasian Transport Framework and the Eurasian Commodity Distribution Network.

World.title: Driver who allegedly crashed into Newcastle Knights crowd faces more charges
World.content:
An 18-year-old who is accused of driving a car that hit and injured a crowd of Newcastle Knights fans has been served with eight more charges.

P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe allegedly injured 10 people during the incident on October 3, including a five-year-old girl.

Thousands of fans had lined the streets to wave the Newcastle Knights off to their first NRL grand final in 25 years.

The new charges include dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, and six counts of causing bodily harm by misconduct using a motor vehicle.

This brings the total number of charges to 17.

World.title: The secret to a long-term happy relationship may not be what you expect
World.content:
Amanda's husband Caleb is her best friend.

"I would prefer to hang out with him than anyone else," the 43-year-old from Canberra/Ngunnawal country says.

"If people ask me to go out, it's really hard to say yes, because I'd prefer to stay home with him.

"I know I'm just going to have a really nice time."

Amanda says while their relationship may seem "vanilla and boring", they're a safe space for one another.

"Our relationship is really comfortable. We're not looking for something new and exciting. We're really looking at investing in what we already have."

That's partly how they've been able to stay happy in their long-term relationship, Amanda says.

And experts would agree.

Yumi Stynes, host of ABC podcast Ladies, We Need to Talk, explores what couples who like each other are doing behind closed doors to keep the love alive when life gets busy and unsexy.

Good friendship key to long-term happiness

Gemma Cribb is a clinical psychologist and says happiness in long-term relationships "basically boils down to a really good friendship".

Ms Cribb says research has found that "keeping in touch with each other's internal world" is key to that foundation.

"Actually asking each other ongoing questions, not just 'How was your day?' but 'What's going on for you that I need to know about?'"

Fondness and admiration are also important, she says.

"Making a conscientious effort to appreciate what your partner brings to your life, not just focusing on the negative.

"Looking for how they add value and how they make your life easier and feeding that back to them."

Lastly, Ms Cribb says couples need to respond to one another's needs. For example, noticing when your partner seems stressed and offering support.

Listen to the episode Yumi Stynes speaks to women about how they found love that's stable, healthy and fun. And clinical psychologist Gemma Cribb talks through the foundations that all happy couples build their relationships on.

We're often told shared interests and humour are what keeps couple together, but Ms Cribb says those factors can be overrated.

"People's interests change over time, so if you connect purely over your shared interests of yachting and somebody gets a permanent injury, which means they can no longer yacht, we want to have something else underneath that … keeps that friendship alive."

Not trying to change one another

Ms Cribb says real love is "accepting your partner, warts and all".

She says research on happy couples shows they had "no change agendas" for the repetitive issues in the relationship.

"Most couples argue about money, sex, time, mess, and kids, and most of those arguments will never get resolved because it's just based on who you are as a person. Someone's messy, someone's not as messy. Someone's always late, someone's always on time.

"Healthy couples still talk about those sort of friction points, but they do so with humour and affection, not with a change agenda."

Amanda and husband Caleb make time for one another when their kids have gone to bed. (Supplied)

Amanda says when she was first with Caleb, his introverted nature bothered her.

"I always imagined someone who would kind of match me as … someone who was social and had a lot of friends.

"I would definitely be frustrated with him for not wanting to go to social events."

She eventually decided to "love Caleb no matter what and have his back".

"If he never changes, that is totally fine."

But then to her surprise, he did.

"When I accepted him utterly and completely for every bit of him, including his introvertedness, that was when I think he felt totally supported and he was able to start to change," Amanda says.

Rituals to connect

Sarah, not her real name, has been with her partner since she was 15 — although for a long time they were just friends.

The 35-year-old from Melbourne/Naarm says no matter how chaotic life gets with their little one, they always make time to connect.

"We always kiss each other goodbye. And now our son will say, 'Dad, kiss Mum.' So he'll give us a little reminder, which is really helpful.

"Also just little things like the end of the day when the baby's gone to bed, I will always lie my head on [my partner's] lap and he will just comb my hair, and we'll just sit together and watch crap TV."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Sarah says finding time to be intimate can be hard with a toddler, but they know it's just a phase in their lives.

" We wrote on our whiteboard on the back of the front door, 'We still love each other, we're just tired.' "

Ms Cribb says intentionally creating rituals to connect keeps couples together.

For example, spending a few minutes chatting over a cup of tea in the morning about what is coming up for the day.

We don't see enough happy relationships

Sarah says it's kind of expected that couples "bitch about" their partner, and that her happy relationship doesn't always fit the stereotype of parents of young children.

Women 'quiet quitting' relationships "Quiet quitting" began as a social media trend where workers were encouraged to avoid burnout in their jobs by doing only the bare minimum. Some women are applying that to their romantic relationships.

"Sometimes I do find when people are complaining about their partners, I have to almost not lie, but just highlight things about [my partner] that annoy me so I can join in the conversation."

Ms Cribb says we're not shown what relationships should look like after the Hollywood ending of sparks and passion.

"We don't actually get taught the skills of how to keep that interest and connection alive.

"It requires as much work as anything else in your life that you want to maintain for the long-term."

World.title: Anne Aly accuses Liberal MP of racism after 'stoning' comment
World.content:
Small Business Minister Anne Aly has accused a Liberal MP of making racist and misogynistic comments in parliament, saying they are contrary to Australian values.

During a fiery speech in the lower house, shadow minister Angie Bell called for the prime minister and Ms Aly to be "shamed and stoned in the square" over the tax office's decision to ban credit card payments.

The ban has sparked backlash from the business community, with the government last week intervening to ensure the ATO delays the measure until July next year.

In her speech to parliament, Ms Bell, who holds the arts and sport portfolios on the opposition frontbench, called on the government to overturn the credit card ban.

Angie Bell called for the prime minister and Ms Aly to be "shamed and stoned in the square" over the tax office's decision to ban credit card payments. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"We're talking about millions and millions of Australians who are employed by small business," Ms Bell said.

"And this minister and this prime minister should be absolutely shamed and stoned in the square."

Ms Bell subsequently withdrew the comments after Leader of the House Tony Burke raised concerns with what he described as "some physically violent imagery".

Ms Aly, the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament, later posted a video on social media, describing Ms Bell's comments as racist and misogynistic.

"This past week alone, I have had 19 death threats on my social media, and in the past I have had death threats that are couched in that exact same language," she said in a video posted to Instagram and TikTok.

"It's not just something that a parliamentarian shouldn't say in terms of advocating violence against another parliamentarian.

"It is something that stands against our Australian values. We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women, and against regimes that use brutal methods like stoning against women."

Bomb threat reveals crisis Spitting, assault and online abuse are rising signs of a dangerous political culture in Australia.

A spokesperson for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was appropriate that Ms Bell had withdrawn the remarks.

But they also demanded Prime Minister Anthony Albanese show the same accountability, referring to comments he made earlier this year about melons being gifted to him by the Japanese prime minister.

"Australians are still waiting for him to apologise to Japan's prime minister and [for] his own litany of broken promises," they said.

"The prime minister cannot demand accountability from others while refusing to take responsibility for his own failures."

Speaking on Afternoon Briefing, Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien also said Ms Bell did "the right thing" by withdrawing the remarks.

He also praised her as someone who is doing a "wonderful job" on the frontbench and as a local member in her Gold Coast electorate of Moncrieff.

World.title: Liberal stands alongside water buyback supporters despite party opposition
World.content:
A group of South Australian politicians say they have had enough of other states not pulling their weight under the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, and it is affecting their communities.

Keen fisher Neil Burton said the River Murray was the lifeblood of South Australia's Riverland.

"Without the Murray, we're all buggered," he said.

Its future and ability to provide water to 2.4 million people across four states, including more than 1 million people in Adelaide, is under scrutiny.

A recent report from the Murray-Darling Basin Authority shows the Basin Plan has a shortfall of 265 gigalitres due to a failure to deliver a swathe of state-run water-saving projects.

The projects were introduced to avoid further buybacks.

The Murray-Darling Basin Plan has been under review this year. (ABC News: Jessica Schremmer)

With federal water and agriculture minister Murray Watt considering how to address the 265GL shortfall, MPs and senators from South Australia came together in Canberra to put their state first.

Labor, Liberal, the Greens and an independent joined together at a press conference to demand the plan be delivered in full, including meeting its water recovery targets.

Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan said South Australia had already done its fair share of the work and other states needed to step up.

"It has suffered from the incompetence and greed of New South Wales and Victoria," he said.

" We need that water otherwise our society, our communities will die. "

Andrew McLachlan says he wants to see goodwill from other states to make up the shortfall. (Four Corners: Greg Nelson)

The conference was also attended by the Murray-Darling Conservation Alliance, which said water purchasing would be the most cost-effective and efficient way to claw back the shortfall.

It was in conflict with the Coalition's policy demanding an end to water buybacks.

Labor MP Louise Miller-Frost was expected to attend, but at the last minute did not show to speak to the media.

Communities relying on the Murray

Mr Burton has lived along the River Murray for decades, growing up in the Riverland and returning for his retirement.

He is shocked other states have not met their targets more than a decade after the plan was introduced.

"I can't believe that after all these years of having a Murray Basin Plan they can't rectify it and get water down the river when it's needed," he said.

Neil Burton says without the River Murray, the Riverland's country towns would be cut off. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"In the 70s we did a lot of rehabilitation around here with all the channels going and put into pipelines. A lot of the growers paid for that.

" Surely if one state can do it, the rest can do it. "

He said it might be time for states outside of the basin to mediate the delivery of water to combat parochialism.

But as for the system's survival, he said it was up to everyone.

"The whole nation needs to get behind it," he said.

"They need it to grow food, to cook, to wash. Everyone needs it."

A review of the Basin Plan is due to be completed later this year.

World.title: PM says government trying to stop 'abhorrent' US execution live stream
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government will do everything it can to stop the "abhorrent" live stream of a firing squad execution in the United States from being shown in Australia.

Last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch, but Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt about whether that would occur.

The potential live stream has elicited a strong response in parliament, with federal members across the political divide urging the government to "pull every single lever" to block the broadcast.

On Tuesday Mr Albanese told Afternoon Briefing that the government would do whatever it could, but acknowledged it was not as simple as "turning off a light switch".

eSafety can't prevent execution live stream The office of eSafety says it does not have the power to proactively block the live streaming of a US execution in Australia, but online services have the responsibility to protect users from harmful material.

"Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty and I find the idea of live streaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent," he told ABC.

"We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring."

He said the government was seeking advice on its options.

On Monday the eSafety Commission said it could not prevent Australians from seeing the execution.

"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson told the ABC.

The prime minister said he would make it "very clear" to social media platforms that the content had no place in Australia.

"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he said.

US President Donald Trump has said he will ultimately make the call about the proposed live stream. (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they plan to restrict the content, but has not received responses.

Asked whether he had made representations to Donald Trump on the issue, Mr Albanese said the US president had indicated in the media that he was weighing the matter.

"President Trump has already said he is giving consideration to this and I hope that there is a response in the United States as well," he said.

If the broadcast goes ahead, it will mark the first time an execution in the US has been live streamed.

Politicians express concern

Greens Leader David Shoebridge grilled Foreign Minister Penny Wong over the proposed live stream during Tuesday's Question Time and asked about the "shared values" between Australia and "a government that publicly broadcasts state-sanctioned snuff films".

Senator Wong said it would be "deeply distressing for any such vision to be live streamed".

"We don't believe anyone should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians," she said.

Senator Wong said Australians had a right to expect such content would not appear on their screens.

"We believe that platforms do have a responsibility to meet these expectations," she said.

Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien said the government needed to ensure Australians could not view the execution.

"That concerns me deeply. We cannot have young Australians watching an execution," he told Afternoon Briefing.

"That would be appalling, repugnant, and that is why we need to be looking at every possible lever to ensure that is not live streamed, if indeed it goes ahead."

World.title: Reports of bed bugs on a Qantas flight prompt warning from expert
World.content:
Air travel can be stressful at the best of times, but imagine adding bed bugs into the mix.

Passengers on a recent flight from Australia to Italy were reportedly faced with that nightmare.

A bed bug expert says once the blood-feeding insects are onboard, it is difficult to avoid them.

What happened?

Over the weekend, Australian media reported that bed bugs grounded a Qantas plane, after passengers complained of itchy bites aboard a flight from Perth to Rome on Friday.

The plane was grounded in Rome, with passengers scheduled to return to Perth given accommodation and re-booked on different flights within two days.

Qantas is still investigating the cause.

Bed bugs get on flights via people's clothings and belongings. (ABC News)

"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue identified on a small number of economy seats," a spokesperson said.

How common are bed-bugs on flights?

Bed bug expert Stephen Doggett told ABC News Radio that incidents of bed bugs on flights were well-documented.

"It's not particularly common, but it does occur," he said.

"My gut feeling working on bed bugs for 25 years is that it's probably been in the plane for sometime and just simply not detected."

In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family who said they were bitten by bed bugs while on a flight from Vancouver to London.

Mr Doggett said bed bugs find their way onto flights via clothes and belongings.

"People will stay in some location, some hotel or a hostel that has bed bugs, the bed bugs get into the belongings and they're carried on the flight. It's that simple," he said.

He says the higher risk areas of the plane are where the crew sleep.

"Because they're travelling so often, they're staying in hotels just for one night, and there's a huge turnover and that's a high risk for bed bugs," he said.

"They'll get deep into the seats, into the crevices."

How do airlines mitigate bed bug risks?

Qantas said it disinfected its aircraft every 50 days as part of its standard maintenance program.

But Mr Doggett said bed bugs were a hard bug to get rid of.

He said aircraft were regularly sprayed to keep certain exotic mosquitoes out of Australia, but bed bugs were a harder challenge.

"They're really hard to get rid of because they're highly resistant to insecticides and they're amongst the most resistant insects on the planet," he said.

"There's very few chemicals actually approved for use because many chemicals can damage aircraft, can damage the aluminium."

He said using a combination of a vacuum, steam and certain insecticides can be effective, but that was an expensive task.

How can you avoid them on a plane?

Unfortunately, Mr Doggett says there is virtually nothing passengers can do once they are aboard a bed bug infested flight.

"There's nowhere to go, but certainly if you think you've got bed bugs, then look in the seat, look for signs of bed bugs and most importantly take photos because you could use that even in litigation against the airline," he told ABC Perth Breakfast.

He said they will hide in the crevices and the cracks of the seats.

"Sometimes you may not see bed bugs themselves, the adult bed bugs about the size and colour of an apple seed … but the juvenile stages tend to be much smaller, and they'll be a light colour green," he said.

World.title: Canberra's V8 Supercars rookie Zach Bates 'put everything on the line'
World.content:
Canberran Zach Bates "still can't believe" he finished third at the Bathurst 1000 on Sunday.

It was the rookie's second time competing in the iconic race at Mount Panorama, where he started in pole position after topping Saturday's Top 10 Shootout.

"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I'd be starting on pole for the great race. That was unbelievable," Bates said.

" I knew I had to put everything on the line. "

Zach Bates (far right) took pole position after the Top Ten Shootout at the Bathurst 1000. (Supplied: Matt Stone Racing)

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His father Rick Bates said he "knew Zach had it in him", and added the 22-year-old had a "very good feel for a car".

"He's pretty determined, and he does push it, which you need to," Rick Bates said.

" All those drivers, they're the top 25 drivers in Australia, and you've got to be on your A-game when you turn up. "

Rick Bates says a driver has to bring their A-game to the Bathurst 1000. (ABC News)

The rookie's surprise success comes after his mother and motorsport broadcaster Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished tenth.

The young driver said his mother's death was "incredibly difficult to take".

"[It] definitely gave me a bit of fire in my belly to get up every morning and try and do the best that I can," Bates said.

'Decent talent' in Canberra

Bates became a petrol head when he started recreational go-karting at the age of 10.

Zach Bates says go-kart racing acts as a gateway for young people to get into motorsports. (Getty Images: Daniel Kalisz)

To some in the racing dynasty, that is considered late, as some young drivers reach for the go-kart wheel as young as six years old.

Go-karting, alongside simulation racing, has long acted as a gateway for young people to get involved in Canberra's racing scene.

"We all went through the go-karting stage, that's how you get into the sport. It's the way all the young kids come through," Bates said.

"It's a special part of your life because it's just usually your mum and dad getting a go-kart and going racing — and then it really spirals from there."

Zach Bates says the Canberra community has supported him on his road to he Bathurst 1000. (Supplied: Matt Stone Racing)

He attributes his talent behind the wheel to hard work, sacrifice, and a Canberra community that has backed him along his journey.

"I have an incredible amount of Canberra supporters and sponsors," Bates said.

"What you see on the weekend is years of sacrifice and support from local businesses and some really cool people within Canberra itself and surrounding areas."

He added his team, which includes two mechanics and engineers around his age, worked "incredibly hard".

"We're all just trying our best to make it happen," Bates said.

Zach Bates says his team of mechanics and engineers work incredibly hard. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The 'tricky thing' about Canberra's racing scene

Bates said the lack of a car racing track in Canberra makes it hard for locals to get into racing.

"Of course it's a short trip to Sydney up the road, but it still makes it a little bit difficult for people to get into the sport if they want to," he said.

"Nonetheless, I think we do have some decent talent here."

Rick Bates says he does not think location has a major impact on race car drivers. (ABC News)

But Rick Bates said he did not think being in Canberra, or any particular location, made a noticeable difference to race car drivers.

"Wherever you're based, there's a fair bit of travel involved," he said.

" Canberra is quite central for a base because there are rounds all over Australia. "

The 22-year-old Canberran said he is preparing to face down some "absolute gurus" on the "gnarly track" at the Gold Coast 500 next weekend.

World.title: From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy Jake Niall October 13, 2026 — 7:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Whereas the police investigation into the Pullman hotel incident has conceivably cost Isaac Heeney millions of dollars via loss of sponsors, Nick Blakey has garnered millions from the Pullman imbroglio. It’s a strange economy, the AFL. Nick Blakey dons the North Melbourne guernsey, as his father, John, once did. North Melbourne FC At the least, Blakey will be paid an extra $400,000 or more per season over the next five years by dint of his move south to North. And he has added a further three years on the same kind of remuneration, becoming one of the highest-paid players in the competition, at least until Tasmania arrives. How does a player who found himself in strife – and suspended by the Swans alongside four teammates for breach of standards and professional conduct – end up profiting from his mistake (aside from some sharp work by his agent)?



There are many subplots to North Melbourne’s successful pursuit of Blakey, the father-son recruit whom they’ve landed eight years after he preferred the Swans, where his father John had worked under another Shinboner John Longmire. North has overpaid Blakey in pure dollar terms, at close to $12 million over eight years, although North believes Blakey would have earned the same amount elsewhere. As they acknowledge, North had to go hard to get the player and could not be under-bidders for the first genuine A-grader in his mid-career to join them since the dawn of the millennium. Loading On the draft front, one could argue that North has paid slight unders for Blakey, relative to the asking price for uninjured all-Australians, since future picks are devalued by Tasmania. The caveat is that the Pullman incident is not yet resolved, legally or by the AFL, and North has been willing to take on the risk in the event that their prized recruit is charged. To navigate the Blakey deal and minimise the risks of any fallout or wrinkle, the Kangaroos took the following steps:



1. They asked Blakey for his version of events at the Pullman. From what this column has gathered, they then cross-checked that version with other parties. Related Article AFL 2026 Swans frosty as Blakey departs for North Melbourne with an apology 2. Consulted the AFL about acquiring Blakey, considering the massive outlay and the unusual circumstances of his exit. It is a safe assumption that if the league had misgivings, he would not be headed to his dad’s old team. 3. Chief executive Jenn Watt, head of football Todd Viney and head of strategy Erin Lorenzini addressed the whole AFLW team and fielded questions last Friday when North emerged as the frontrunner. The W players were pleased to have that communication from the hierarchy. 4. Staff, too, were sounded out by the club hierarchy.



Nick Blakey played 173 games in eight seasons for the Swans. Sam Mooy The Blakey camp are privately confident that he will not be stood down by the AFL, irrespective of what transpires in the police investigation and whether charges are laid. Blakey’s desire for a trade – North list boss Brady Rawlings used the word “disgruntlement” on Tuesday after the deal was completed with the Swans – derived from his view that he had not been handled fairly by the red and whites in the aftermath of the Pullman detonation. It was notable that whereas clubs usually make statements about their player being “required” and only available for a ludicrous trade offer, the Swans were largely silent on the Blakey front in the days leading into the trade period and during it. This was read – correctly – as a sign that they were willing to sacrifice him for a fair deal. Heeney and Chad Warner, the other stars facing the investigation, had not explored trades. Warner will be a free agent and target for West Coast and maybe the Wharfie-timers next year.



The difference between Blakey and Heeney is Blakey’s financial gain derives purely from his football skills and availability. Heeney’s losses stem from dents to an exalted image. When the prospect of North chasing Blakey was first mooted post-Pullman, it was speculated in the industry that North’s female leadership of CEO Watt and president Sonja Hood might hold objections to the notion of recruiting a player who had found himself in a police investigation of sexual assault allegations, alongside three teammates (Riley Bice is only a witness for police). View post on X But today one can argue that North’s unique position of having women at the helm has helped them in acquiring Blakey, and in making their case internally for his recruitment. Hood and Watt provide a measure of cultural cover for the club in making the raid. List boss Brady Rawlings was quizzed repeatedly on Tuesday about how North had navigated their Blakey hunt and especially the “what ifs” of a suspension and/or police charges.



The media conference, which had been more about cultural issues and risk assessment than the need for a fast rebounder, concluded following a question that raised the topic of Tarryn Thomas’s termination by the same club in 2024. The club’s media boss terminated the inquisition on that note. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster Marc McGowan Sports reporter The questions underscored how the process of recruiting Nick Blakey was marked by the more complicated considerations that AFL clubs confront, just as the Swans’ decision to suspend the five was heavily skewed by non-football factors, such as their fan base, demographics and position in the Sydney market. Yet for all the changing football mores, the deal came down to one of the AFL’s immutable ways: The gun players are treated differently. Get around our footy coverage

World.title: No consent: Sacked professor loses case after women’s cells used in mice experiment
World.content:
NationalResearch No consent: Sacked professor loses case after women’s cells used in mice experiment Liam Mannix October 13, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The research seemed so promising. Under a microscope, the scientists could see cancerous cells being “completely eradicated” by a cannabis extract. A 2021 announcement trumpeted the results as “groundbreaking”. The research pair-up – the University of Newcastle and ASX-listed hemp grower Ecofibre – seemed convinced they were poised to transform women’s health. “All patients have responded positively,” Ecofibre announced (though the experiments were on patient samples, not on patients themselves). Patents had been filed. Almost five years to the day, the picture is rather different. Fair Work Commission documents reveal the University of Newcastle researcher who led the work has now been terminated for research misconduct. The research centre he directed has shut, with all samples and data from the suspect research destroyed. Staff have lost their jobs, and PhD students have had to abandon their studies. The university has had to repay donors.



Related Article Exclusive

Investigations Dying woman and ethical doubts spark probe into cannabis cancer ‘cure’ A promising beginning Ecofibre is a hemp grower and producer, selling various cannabis-based treatments for pain, including “Endo Relief Cream” and cannabinoid vaginal suppositories known as “Endo Relief Melts”. But the evidence showing cannabis can treat chronic pain is thin on the ground. “Due to a lack of evidence from high-quality research,” the International Association for the Study of Pain said in 2021, it “does not endorse the general use of cannabinoids to treat pain.” Ecofibre and the University of Newcastle hoped to change that. What went wrong from there is chronicled in two Fair Work Commission judgments.



The two organisations entered into a research partnership to test the efficacy of cannabinoids on endometriosis and other gynaecological diseases. Professor Pradeep Tanwar, formerly the director of the Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases at the University of Newcastle. Professor Pradeep Tanwar, director of the University’s Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases, was made chief investigator of those research projects. Tanwar was also the principal investigator in two research projects to study the molecular basis of endometriosis and look for blood markers for the disease being run at three hospitals around Newcastle. By 2023, Ecofibre and the university had been jointly granted patents for hemp treatments for ovarian cancer and endometriosis. “We are well positioned to move to the next stage of our research, which includes full protocol development for eventual human trials,” Tanwar said in an Ecofibre letter to shareholders.



It was then, according to the Fair Work Commission documents, the problems began. Issues with consent In 2023, the university became aware of allegations that patients in Tanwar’s studies had not signed consent forms or were asked to sign them retrospectively. Hospital service investigations concluded that more than 100 patients involved in the research had not signed consent forms for their tissue to be used. This masthead revealed the existence of that investigation in 2025. Nor, the university alleged, were the patients told their tissue would be grafted onto so-called “xenograft mice”.



Related Article Mental health The $300 a week medicine Daniel feels better without Informed consent is sacrosanct in science and covered by strict rules. Fundamentally, research participants must volunteer, and they must understand what they’re signing up to. After investigating, the hospital system pulled its ethical approval for the studies. Ecofibre also terminated its research agreement with the university, which was being used to fund most of the centre’s senior research positions. The company did not return a request for comment. The university suspended Tanwar in April 2024 on full pay.



Without its leader and money to fund ongoing research, the Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases closed in December 2024, and most staff working there lost their jobs. The Fair Work Commission judgment summarises the damage done: “Two students being required to abandon their PhD work and recommence their studies (one of them four years into their PhD), 14 students being disrupted and assigned new supervision, 17 staff having their employment disrupted and career outputs affected and over 1000 mice being expended during the research that will not yield publishable/useable data.” In total, the university spent about $8 million on the research. The commission’s judgment noted that the university had to repay some donors after the scandal broke. The university terminated Tanwar’s employment in August 2025. Speaking on Tuesday, Tanwar said getting patients’ consent was the responsibility of the hospital’s clinicians.



“Under the approved ethics protocols, consent was taken by hospital clinicians,” he said. “Written consent was given in accordance with the legislation. Unfortunately, consent documentation processes at the hospital had shortcomings.” Related Article Exclusive

Legal Cannabis Cannabis sales plummet as regulators crack down on booming industry Tanwar this year appeared before the Fair Work Commission and unsuccessfully argued his dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable. The commission concluded that Tanwar, as chief investigator, “had ultimate responsibility for the ethical conduct of research”, even if it wasn’t his job to directly supervise the doctors who were talking to patients. It found his termination was not unfair. In May, Tanwar appeared before the commission again to appeal the decision, arguing that “all patients provided verbal consent, no patient was harmed, there was no dishonesty or fabrication, and Dr Tanwar did not interact with patients”.



A commission’s full bench, in a judgment published last week, also rejected that claim, finding “the failure to ensure ethical protocols were followed resulted in some women who donated their samples doing so without proper informed consent being obtained in circumstances where they are entitled to expect that the ethical protocols put in place by those researchers will be followed”. Tanwar said he was disappointed. “This outcome is a warning to every lead academic in collaborative research about the length and breadth of ‘ultimate responsibility’. That you can be dismissed for the actions of others in different employment relationships and over which you have no authority,” he said. “This has come at enormous personal and financial cost to me and my family. The commission itself accepted that the dismissal has been extremely difficult for me, both personally and financially.” In a statement, the University of Newcastle said it was “committed to responsible and ethical research”.



“In this case, the Fair Work Commission upheld the outcome of the university’s investigation, finding that the decision to dismiss was sound and that the investigation was reasonable and procedurally fair.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

A Victorian businessman has been charged over his alleged role in a racket involving hundreds of fake qualifications distributed across Big Build sites, potentially endangering the safety of workers and the public. The breakthrough by a police taskforce has prompted the state opposition to commit to expanding the terms of reference of the Carroll government commissioned royal commission into the building industry if it wins government to examine the qualifications scandal and how it may have operated for years without detection by the state’s health and safety regulator WorkSafe or other agencies. Jake Calvert has been charged over the alleged distribution of hundreds of fake certificates. Michael Howard On Tuesday, former AFL prospect-turned construction industry manager Jake Calvert was charged by the Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk with 232 counts of making a false document. The charges come a week after The Age revealed that NSW conman Jack Younes, who also goes by several aliases, has for at least three years been distributing hundreds or even thousands of fake building qualification certificates to Victorian construction firms and workers, including those operating on the Big Build.



This was despite federal regulator, the Australian Skills Quality Authority, being tipped off about Younes’ operation in 2023 and state regulator Worksafe Victoria receiving a further warning about Younes’ operation in July 2025. Jack Younes is suspected of being a key player in the alleged scam. Facebook/NSW Fair Trading Younes — who admitted forging qualification certificates when he was recently confronted by The Age — was still operating freely as recently as last month and has not been arrested. After returning from Queensland, Calvert was confronted by detectives on Tuesday morning over allegations he paid the Younes syndicate to supply traffic management and other building industry qualification certificates to workers across key Big Build and commercial construction sites. The charging of Calvert highlights a far less scrutinised but still systemic alleged corruption and safety issue on the Big Build.



Previously, media and police investigations have focussed on allegations that gangland figures systemically infiltrated the Big Build, including bikies who obtained roles as CFMEU health and safety delegates in a manner that may have also jeopardised worksite safety. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Big Build hit by fake qualifications racket as regulators face questions Calvert, who was recently sacked from his role as an operations manager for Big Build labour hire firm Top Up and who runs his own construction firm, Archer Hire, allegedly sits at the juncture of both scandals. While his charges relate to suspicions he obtained dozens of false certificates for labour hire workers he supplied to Big Build sites, he has been separately raided by police over allegations he sought to give inducements to CFMEU officials in Queensland through a serving Victorian CFMEU official. Detectives have also probed Calvert’s relationship with ex-bikie boss and former CFMEU delegate Tyrone Bell – who is also facing charges of using false qualification certificates.



Prior to entering the construction sector, Calvert was touted as a possible AFL draft pick and played in the VFL. On Tuesday evening, shadow attorney-general James Newbury said the latest police action, along with long-standing concerns about systemic lapses in health and safety on construction sites, needed to be specifically examined by the royal commission. “Organised crime and bikies have been running rampant across government projects. Victorians deserve to know why our workplace safety regulator Worksafe has been missing in action,” Newbury said. “A Liberal and Nationals government will strengthen the terms of reference for the royal commission into the Big Build, to include investigating Worksafe and why it has been sitting on its hands for years.” Newbury also said the chair of Worksafe, former Labor minister Bob Cameron, had presided over the inaction.



In a statement released on Tuesday afternoon, Worksafe said it has been “notified of a number of individuals allegedly seeking to obtain fraudulent qualification certificates, which may have been used to demonstrate competencies they do not have”. “Fraudulent qualifications could pose a health and safety risk if a duty holder relies on them as evidence of skills in a particular area – such as first aid, implementing traffic management plans or working safely at heights – that they do not actually have.” WorkSafe chief health and safety officer Sam Jenkin warned the agency would “take compliance or enforcement action against anyone who puts their co-workers or others in a workplace at risk by working in an area they have knowingly and fraudulently obtained false qualifications for.” But he also said the agency was “limited in the legal action it can take in relation to this type of fraud.” WorkSafe has also issued an industry-wide safety alert about the use of fake certificates, urging employers to verify records.



A Victorian government spokesman said the government thanked the police for uncovering the “rort” and that the royal commission would investigate and make system-wide recommendations. “Every agency has to be vigilant in using its powers when there are reports of grift on government-funded construction sites,” the statement said. In a statement, Taskforce Hawk confirmed the charging of Calvert “as part of an investigation into the production and distribution of false construction and other workplace certifications and qualifications”. “Police will allege the man facilitated false workplace education qualifications. The investigation, which commenced earlier this year, remains ongoing.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

University Admission Centre managing director Kim Paino has a blunt message for school leavers intent on tertiary education and facing a tough time gaining entry to a Sydney university next year. “Take the offer,” said Paino, who joined the chorus warning of the risks involved in the new funding regime, which passed parliament on Tuesday. The University of Sydney said it was forced to end its long-running guaranteed entry scheme because of the changes. Sam Mooy “Students really need to make sure they preference carefully, and if they receive an offer … accept it,” she said. “It doesn’t mean they necessarily have to enrol in that course, but at least it gives them an option.” Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says the new funding package will create an extra 230,000 university places and $3.6 billion in extra funding for tertiary institutions over the next decade, with an emphasis on admitting a higher number of disadvantaged students through specially created places.



It will also tighten numbers at popular metropolitan universities, including the University of Sydney, the University of NSW, Macquarie University and the University of Technology, Sydney, meaning some students may be unable to get a place. This will leave them to either study elsewhere or abandon tertiary education. Related Article Exclusive

University University entry was the hardest it’s ever been this year. Next year will be worse The changes were introduced for a transition period in 2025, before the new regime was enshrined in law. The University of NSW and Macquarie University have said that, as a result, they have been forced to decline prospective students, while the University of Sydney has disbanded its long-running guaranteed-entry scheme and UTS made fewer offers than before. HSC students apply for up to five courses through the UAC. The centre looks at their preferences and will admit students to the first course for which they meet the entry requirements. It conducts two main rounds of offers, in December and January.



Paino urged HSC students to be aspirational but “really try to be realistic” about their results. “That’s always the advice but this year it’ll potentially apply to a wider range of students that won’t have that opportunity to have another crack [at a second round offer] in January,” because of the tightened places, she said. “The traditionally more competitive universities to get into are exactly those that are having to tighten their numbers, so it makes it even harder to get into those particular universities,” she warned. “There still will be places. The government’s saying that overall there’ll be more places available. It’s just not necessarily in the institutions and the courses that are already oversubscribed.” Medicine, which also has additional selection criteria, law and allied health courses such as physiotherapy are historically popular.



Related Article University This plan would put an end to the $50,000 arts degree. It’s also controversial She suggested students who want to study a combined arts/law degree also preference a standalone arts degree, or students aiming for biomedical science also preference a straight science degree. “Look to include a university that isn’t necessarily going to be under the same pressure to manage numbers. Their entry criteria might be a little bit less [stringent],” she said. The federal Department of Education released its semester 1 enrolment data on Tuesday. It shows a 5.3 per cent increase in students commencing a degree compared to 2025. Enrolments are up in teaching (7.7 per cent), health (6.6 per cent), social work (15.7 per cent), engineering (10.5 per cent), clinical psychology (9.8 per cent) and science (6.8 per cent). World.title: Bars look skyward to open in ‘rooftop capital of Australia’
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Bars look skyward to open in ‘rooftop capital of Australia’ Cara Waters October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The rooftop of Garden State hotel used to be unloved and cluttered with air conditioning equipment but a two-year build has transformed it into Melbourne’s newest rooftop bar. The two tiered space overlooking Flinders Lane is dotted with large cream umbrellas shading clusters of bar tables and wicker chairs. Chef James Wilkinson and venue manager Katie Saxton at the new rooftop bar for Garden State. Wayne Taylor It takes time and battling significant red tape to open a rooftop bar in Melbourne, but for many hospitality operators it’s worth the effort. Three new or revamped venues will open in the city in the next month. Garden State is just one of a string of venues looking skyward for expansion; Transit Rooftop Bar is set to reopen in Federation Square next month after a major transformation, along with the Prince Terrace in St Kilda which will open the former Prince deck to the public for the first time.



Paul Waterson, chief executive of Australian Venue Co, owner of Garden State, says opening a rooftop bar in the city centre is not for the faint of heart. Related Article Best of From posh to party, these 10 new rooftop bars and restaurants are built for anything “It’s a really challenging location being in Flinders Lane, so it took a lot of liaison with local stakeholders, nearby neighbours, Melbourne City Council and 101 Collins,” he says. “It was quite an intense planning process and a very intense build as well.” Crane operations were only allowed one day a week, on Saturdays, which slowed construction. Waterson says restricting operating hours and reducing noise levels through acoustic management were key to keeping residents and the council on side.



“I think everyone understands how vibrant Melbourne’s CBD is, and it’s really one of the great things Melbourne is becoming increasingly known for,” he says. “You see all these other states promoting these vibrancy reforms for initiatives that are already in place in Melbourne and I think we sort of undersell that a little bit too.” Transit Rooftop Bar is reopening after a major transformation. Despite the time and expense involved with opening a rooftop bar, Waterson says it made sense to expand the pub upwards creating a four-storey venue and offering an open air outdoor space. “I think Melbourne is the original rooftop capital of Australia,” he says. “We were the first state to really appreciate our great architecture, and we’re a resilient bunch, aren’t we? We’ll go out, sit on a rooftop all year round.”



The two level space holds 300 people and a retractable roof and heating will ensure year round operation. Related Article Coming soon Will this team finally make Fed Square a Melbourne dining hotspot? Garden State has also turned its former function space into a cocktail bar, The Observatory, with plush booths and bespoke cocktails. Garden State venue manager Katie Saxton says she’s expecting to sell plenty of spritzes over summer while food on the rooftop will include prawn rolls with dill mayo and lemon and stracciatella with cucumber, honey and black pepper. “The rooftop market in the CBD is really quite formidable, and everyone loves a rooftop,” she says.



Nearby Transit Rooftop is set to reopen next month following a revamp by Studio Y nearly 20 years after it first opened with a reconfigured layout that opens up city views. The rooftop bar will hold 250 people seated with food by Taxi chef Tony Twitchett and cocktails by Matt Linklater. In St Kilda, after taking the reins of the Prince Hotel DJ and entrepreneur Grant Smillie is opening up the Prince Deck overlooking Acland Street with views across the bay and to the CBD. The Prince’s rooftop will be open to the public for the first time. Kristoffer Paulsen Smillie has taken out the swimming pool which he says was underutilised.



“Uncle Johnny might have ended up in there one night on a wedding, which was a bit embarrassing, but that’s okay,” he says. The deck is licensed for 700 and Smillie says not much red tape was involved because it was an existing function venue. The changes include ensuring there is lots of open outdoor space with tables and chairs for food and drink along with a piano bar. “Rooftop bars are just universal,” Smillie says. “I think there’s nothing better than being outdoors. You can come and dine, drink, and then hang around, watch a little jazz number, or you know, listen to some DJs.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: If the ‘glass cliff’ for women in leadership doesn’t exist, why are men still talking about it?
World.content:
NationalPodcasts If the ‘glass cliff’ for women in leadership doesn’t exist, why are men still talking about it? Tammy Mills October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The academic who coined the term ‘the glass cliff’ says the phenomenon clearly still exists after a scandal involving an Australian partner of global consultancy giant McKinsey & Company. McKinsey senior partner Chris Bradley was dumped from a leadership role at the firm’s research arm after he commented on networking site LinkedIn that the glass cliff was a “very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain”. Professor Michelle Ryan coined the term ‘the glass cliff’ two decades ago. Jamie Kidston/ANU Speaking to host Samantha Selinger- Morris on The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s podcast The Morning Edition, gender equality expert Dr Michelle Ryan says questioning the existence of the glass cliff is an example of discrimination at play. “So here we are, I guess 20-odd years later, and we’ve still got people questioning the phenomenon. So am I surprised? Not at all, it absolutely fits with the research,” Ryan said.



Ryan, now director of the Australian National University’s Global Institute for Women’s Leadership, coined the term with Professor Alexander Haslam in the UK in 2005. The glass cliff, Ryan said, describes a trend of women being appointed to leadership roles only, for example, at a time when a company is in crisis. Related Article Updated

Workplace culture McKinsey strips Australian partner of leadership role after ‘glass cliff’ comments “Therefore their positions are risky and precarious,” Ryan said. She pointed to Sussan Ley as an example. The now-retired MP was the Coalition’s first female leader, appointed to the position after the party’s crushing loss to Labor at the last federal election. She led for nine months.



“So sometimes we know that someone’s got to take the fall or ride out a difficult position, and we put women in those positions,” Ryan said. Ley has rejected the glass cliff had anything to do with her appointment, writing an opinion piece for Women’s Agenda that “all too often women are left to clean up the mess” but she had earned her shot. Click the player above to listen to the full episode, or read on for an edited extract of the conversation below. Samantha Selinger-Morris: Like you said, it’s an established phenomenon, and I know that our mastheads, in addition to others, of course, have covered numerous very high-profile cases, right? We had Vanessa Hudson coming in as Qantas CEO and she had to sort of re-establish the airline’s reputation after it suffered horribly. Amanda Bardwell at Woolworths, Sussan Ley with the Liberal Party. I mean, examples abound. So I wanted to ask you if you were surprised, then, by Chris Bradley’s comments about this. And beyond that, I guess, is there something perhaps unnerving about the fact that Bradley is a leader at a company, McKinsey, that has long sought to advance the particular conversation about challenges that women do face in the workplace? McKinsey published a Women in the Workplace study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In advocacy group, for more than a decade, and a 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare even references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles by women of colour. So what say you, Michelle?



Dr Michelle Ryan: Yeah, so, I mean, I’m not sure it’s really my place to comment on Chris Bradley per se but I’m very happy to sort of talk in more generalities. And in terms of whether I’m surprised that people question the phenomenon, no. It’s part of the phenomenon itself, and it’s also part of the research. So actually, when we first uncovered the phenomenon way back in sort of, you know, 2003, 2004, 2005, when we were really starting to do this, we actually ran a study which was to look at how people responded to it and how they interpreted the phenomenon. So we did a study on the BBC, actually. So we, the BBC, wanted to run an article about the glass cliff. It was the first sort of media article ever about the glass cliff. I think it was 2004 maybe the article came out. And one of the things we did was we added a little survey at the end of it. So when we looked at the responses to this survey, what was really interesting is that for women, it really resonated with them. It either resonated with their own experiences or resonated with what they saw out in the real world. And their interpretations of the phenomenon was very much in terms of how it was discriminatory, how it was problematic. So it might be, “Oh, it looks like women are being set up for failure”, or, “This is a real subtle form of discrimination”. But what was really interesting was that when men interpreted the phenomenon, their response to it was very, very different. So men were much more likely to say, “Oh no, no, it’s a benign phenomenon. It’s really just organisations doing their thing. They’re just looking for the best person for the job, or maybe they’re just trying to signal change, it’s not discrimination.” But what was really interesting was 50 per cent of the respondents, the male respondents, actually said, “I don’t think it exists”. Like, “I actually question the phenomenon itself”. So here we are, I guess 20-odd years later, and we’ve still got people questioning the phenomenon. So am I surprised? Not at all, it absolutely fits with the research. For the story behind the headlines, listen to The Morning Edition, with a new episode live each weekday from 5am.
