World.title: Chalmers warns against sneering at Hanson backers ahead of 12 months of pain
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Chalmers warns against sneering at Hanson backers ahead of 12 months of pain Paul Sakkal and Shane Wright October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has forecast a year of economic turmoil and warned progressives not to sneer at supporters of One Nation, drawing the battlelines with Pauline Hanson as the prime minister assures nervous Labor MPs that the government remains on track to win the next election. Labor will introduce its 30 per cent tax on trusts on Wednesday, a key plank of its ambitious May budget, but uncertainty remains about businesses and families restructuring. The Greens are threatening to launch an inquiry into the proposal, extending scrutiny of the government’s tax agenda. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers. Alex Ellinghausen NSW Right faction Labor MPs vented in a meeting on Monday about potential blowback over impeding trusts changes from tradespeople, among others, following the backlash over the tax office credit card ban and a series of amendments watering down Labor’s budget tax reforms. The government’s economic agenda has been set back by four interest rate hikes this year, persistent inflation, soaring petrol prices driven by the war in Iran and a collapse in consumer confidence, while Pauline Hanson’s support has surged.



“Nobody expects polls to change much any time soon – it would be more surprising if

they did. Same goes for consumer confidence,” Chalmers said, according to a copy of his speech. “If you look at a combination of forecasts from the Reserve Bank and the Treasury, which they’ll update before long in the usual way, there is some cause for some cautious confidence. “They don’t expect things to get a lot better in the next 12 weeks but they do expect things to get a bit better over the next 12 months … We expect the tax reforms will be bedded down and legislated by then, too.” There had been speculation that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese would go to the polls in the back half of 2027 to take advantage of the Coalition’s collapse. But Chalmers’ admission of a year of financial stress and continued global turmoil makes it more likely that Albanese will wait until early 2028, when interest rates may have started to come down. Albanese rejected suggestions of a midterm slump on Tuesday and tried to gee up worried Labor MPs on Tuesday. In a caucus meeting, he said Labor would be “kicking with the wind in the fourth-quarter”, the same line he used last term before defeating Peter Dutton.



Related Article Resolve Political Monitor Voters cool on Hanson as Albanese wears the blame for cost of living “This Liberal Party has abandoned any pretense of being a centre-right party. They withdrew … from the mainstream,” the prime minister said. “The Greens have made a factional decision to go to the fringes at the same time that the Libs, the Nats and One Nation are fighting for the right-wing fringes.” Labor MPs returned to parliament with the latest Resolve Strategic Monitor showing Labor’s primary vote at 29 per cent, One Nation’s at 25 and the Coalition at 23, which would still deliver a victory for Labor. Several MPs, who did not want to be identified, said caucus members discussed Labor’s economic woes in a meeting of the powerful NSW Right faction. MPs lamented yet another backflip on the ATO ban and the repeated anti-business signals being sent by the changes to the capital gains tax discount and now the trusts policy.



One MP said tradespeople were told for years to use trusts and were now being made to feel like the government was coming after them, the latest in a growing list of caucus complaints about Labor’s economic management. In a major speech on the populist threat, Chalmers acknowledged it was a treacherous period for incumbents and told a progressive audience at The Australia Institute: “Hoping the far right goes away or implodes again is not actually a strategy.” Criticism of One Nation’s voter base could not come from a place of “smug moral superiority”, Chalmers warned, but from a place of genuine respect for their concerns, echoing the message of South Australia’s Premier Peter Malinauskas. “When a significant swathe of our fellow Australians find that message of returning to

an idealised version of the good old days appealing – we shouldn’t turn on them,” Chalmers said. “Our role as progressives is not to scold those who see appeal in that message. It’s not to mock them or ‘cancel’ them or talk down to them.”



Liberal and Labor strategists believe One Nation’s support could fade over time, but Chalmers noted that the party would probably have a strong foothold in the next parliament and was being treated favourably by traditional media outlets. One Nation leader Senator Pauline Hanson during a division in the Senate at Parliament House in Canberra this week. Alex Ellinghausen Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has been calling on Chalmers to resign while One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce said on Tuesday on News24 that he would defeat Chalmers. Chalmers said Labor would continue to make economic reforms to counter social and financial anxiety that he said was “fed and fuelled, monetised, politicised and catastrophised by algorithmic rage bait”. “Their superannuation policy would make people much poorer in retirement; their wages policy would eat away at take home pay and living standards; their unfunded commitments would blow a hole in the budget; their migration policy would smash the economy,” he said, setting up Labor’s election framing.



As part of its suite of tax changes contained in the budget, Chalmers unveiled plans to impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts in a bid to align the tax rate on income earned by workers with income moved through trusts. Income funnelled out of trusts often goes to people who declare a taxable income just below changes in tax thresholds – a process called bunching. Related Article Social media Algorithm off-switch to face delay as Coalition, Greens prepare inquiry While the trust changes will sail through the House of Representatives, they will face an inquiry in the Senate with the Greens signalling they may block the proposals if they don’t go far enough to improve the tax system. “We won’t give Labor a free pass on legislation that falls short of that objective,” Greens’ economic justice spokesman Nick McKim said. When originally announced, the government revealed it expected the changes to trusts to raise $4.5 billion in its first full year of operation and $40 billion over a decade.



But Chalmers has been forced into a series of changes after criticisms from accountants, small business operators and charities. There are also concerns that trust operators will face state government stamp duties if they change their tax arrangements to comply with the new laws. In parliament, Chalmers said the government was acting on issues around trusts that had been raised in almost every review of the tax system since the mid-1970s. World.title: What has Tyson Frizell excited about joining the Wests Tigers
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 What has Tyson Frizell excited about joining the Wests Tigers Christian Nicolussi October 13, 2026 — 7:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tyson Frizell revealed Benji Marshall had asked him to join the Wests Tigers on several occasions, and said there was no reason his new club could not enjoy instant success after Newcastle turned a wooden spoon into a grand final within 12 months. Frizell has inked a one-year deal with the Tigers for 2027, which will be the forward’s 17th season in the NRL. Tyson Frizell is excited about leading the way at the Wests Tigers. Steve Siewert/SMH The 35-year-old said a big reason Marshall and the Tigers were eager to sign him was to help lead the young forwards. He said the Tigers 15-year finals drought was not a concern. “I’m pretty good at only worrying about what’s going on in my life and my circle, and we know in rugby league how things can change quickly in 12 months,” Frizell told this masthead.



“People may have been turned off the Knights and where we finished the year before. “A new season brings a whole new range of challenges for every club. What’s happened previously doesn’t matter, and it will be no different with the Tigers. “Guys are coming to the club looking for a fresh start. Kurt Mann has signed, Jayden Brailey has signed; we’ll see where that takes us.” Frizell played with Mann and Brailey at the Knights, he knows skipper Api Koroisau from NSW Origin campaigns, and is getting to know young playmaker Latu Fainu while in camp with Tonga’s World Cup squad. He used to carpool with Marshall from Sydney to Wollongong when the pair played together at St George Illawarra.



Frizell was credited with being a supreme leader who led by his actions at the Knights. “Leadership is something people at the Tigers want me to do – they want me to help with the next crop of players they have there,” he said. The 35-year-old played a key role for the Newcastle Knights’ in their charge to the NRL Grand Final. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I don’t know if leadership comes naturally to me, but it’s come with time in the game. “It’s a younger squad, and I need to earn the respect once I get there. I’m not going to walk in and expect people to listen to me or follow what I do. I need to lead by example, and that needs to be earned through the pre-season.”



Frizell will start with the Tigers in January before preparing for a second successive campaign in Las Vegas when the club plays Melbourne on February 27. Provided he gets through the season well, and the Tigers are happy with him, Frizell refused to automatically shut the door on playing on an 18th season. “Clubs out there can see I’ve got a lot to offer, I feel that way, too; if I get to the point I can’t do it any more, or nobody wants me, I’ll give it up,” Frizell said. “At the end of the day, I need to go out and perform every weekend, and the rest takes care of itself. “You don’t sign anything longer than a one-year deal at my age. I’m only focused on next year.”

World.title: All things considered, better Josh than Pauline
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters All things considered, better Josh than Pauline October 13, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. LEADERSHIP The Liberals have moved to the right since Josh Frydenberg was in parliament. If the party does badly at the 2028 election, he “cannot see the party surviving in its current form” (″⁣Frydenberg: A grateful son or relentless self-promoter?″⁣ 13/10). Against this backdrop, Frydenberg would have a chance to lead his party as a “moderate” by current conservative standards. He is correct that the Libs must reconnect with the political centre. To re-enter politics, difficult tasks await him, firstly against entrenched Liberals competing with One Nation.

Josh Frydenberg will certainly have to be a relentless self-promoter. He will also need centrist policies he can sell to the voters. He could start by checking out the policies of the teal independents, including Monique Ryan, who ousted him. They support action on misogyny, integrity, tax reform and climate.

Josh Frydenberg and the LNP misread the electorate in 2022. He may have a chance now to return to the Liberals with “small l” liberal policies. Better Josh than Pauline.

John Hughes, Mentone Uneasy lies the head that aspires to be

You have to feel for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. With the publication of Josh Frydenberg’s book A Grateful Son, Taylor is now looking over his left shoulder fearing a leadership challenge from Frydenberg.

He has already been looking over his right shoulder, fearing a challenge from Andrew Hastie. And casting a shadow over the Coalition is One Nation. ‘Uneasy lies the head that aspires to be’.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris



Coulda been a contender

It is easier to be a woulda, coulda, shoulda leader than actually take the responsibilities. So many can say what would gave been if they only had the chance, or did the hard work to make it happen.

Josh Fydenberg’s own leadership, in tandem with Scott Morrison’s, the Liberal Party’s values, and their choices in policy, all lost Frydenberg his heartland seat.

The Liberals are being stretched in all directions by the ghosts of Abbott and Howard, trying to align with Canavan, finding Right relevance against a surging One Nation and already have a stronger leader-in-waiting in Hastie.

They don’t need another voice, they need a leader with support and conviction. It’s no time to give an opinion or dip a toe in the water.

It’s time for Frydenberg to take action if he believes he has the answers, and the Liberal Party agrees.

Otherwise, step aside.

Andrew Crane, Richmond No knight in shining armour

Josh Frydenberg was front and centre when the Australian electorate began to fall out of love with the Liberal Party. So any inference by he or anyone else that he could ride in like a knight in shining armour and take the Liberal Party back to the promised land is incomprehensible.

Phil Alexander, Eltham Mixed signals from Wilson campaign

Oh the irony. Economic and financial management identified as a key issue for voters with Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson increasing her popularity in the article “Wilson is gaining economic traction” (13/10) coming the day after the article “Coalition’s flagship policy hit by $880 million budget shortfall” (12/10).

The party of fiscal responsibility? Love it.

Wendy Hinson, Wantirna THE FORUM Learn from the past

Your Letters correspondent’s claims, (“Kirner’s role in dismantling technical education,” 13/10), seem to look longingly at yet another simple solution to complex problems.

ALP Premier Daniel Andrews reintroduced technical schools after coming to power in 2014, but as adjuncts to existing campuses. These are still operating.

The choice of secondary schools is usually strongly influenced by parental choice and in the past, narrow offerings at technical schools cut off many working class students from hopes of a university education. Almost all schools, including expensive private schools, now run VET streams and a broad curriculum so students do have technical subjects available to them. Often students leave school with TAFE certificates already in hand.

As a former teacher in both high and technical schools, I don’t subscribe to the simplistic view that children are either good with their hands or with academic subjects. Good schools have great teachers who create opportunities for everyone.

The person who shut down more than 300 state schools in Victoria was a Liberal, Jeff Kennett.

Jess Wilson is in her first term in parliament and is perhaps unaware how tired teachers are of politicians who seem to know all about education without direct experience.

Helen Hook, Black Rock



Wilson’s Treaty stand

The attributes of a potential leader that your correspondent lists (Letters, ″⁣Jess Wilson’s menagerie of attributes″⁣ 13/10) are about leadership rather than policy. It is policy that should matter and there is one crucial Liberal policy proposal – to repeal the Victorian Statewide Treaty Act 2025 – that I regard as retrograde and a slap in the face for First Nations People.

The Treaty offers First Nations Peoples the possibility that their views on matters that concern them will at last be represented ″⁣inside the tent″⁣ and that the wider community is prepared to listen to their concerns.

Having an agreement with First Nations people is simply the right thing to do. There is already an agreement, which can be honoured, and modified if necessary. To recognise the disadvantage that many Indigenous people have suffered over the decades and the need for us to build good relations, any government after the election should honour the Treaty.

Bruce Henry, Moonee Ponds Preferential treatment

Your front-page article on an impending tight political contest within Victoria was a pertinent reminder that voters must be able to understand the significance of preference flows on polling day.

Unlike the UK’s first-past-the-post system, where the candidate with the greatest number of primary votes wins the seat, here in Australia, a sizeable number of electorates are determined by the cascading preferences that enable a candidate to get over 50 per cent and thus win the seat. This is significant in seats with a considerable number of independents who heavily favour one political party over another in their suggested preferences how-to guide.

The Werribee by-election in February last year was a case in point. Despite there being a whopping 17.5 per cent primary vote swing against the ALP, primary votes were not commensurately directed towards the Liberals and so Labor retained the seat by a thin margin.

Thus, if citizens do truly wish to see change in their electorate, they must give their primary vote to the alternative government and steer away from those independents who plan to highly preference the incumbent party.

Merely launching a protest vote away from the major parties is not good enough if it only guarantees the status quo.

One Nation is now also a main player, so voters need to wisely navigate the unique three-way contest and number every box carefully, lest their vote doesn’t count, is made redundant or is wasted.

Peter Waterhouse, Craigieburn No US opposition

Perhaps the most mystifying aspect of government under Trump in the USA is the lack of apparent organised opposition to his reign. Not a day goes by where the citizens of his country and others are lied to, illegally arrested or detained.

World order is not what it was, and it is primarily his doing. Our economies are floundering largely because of his irrational greed and poor grasp of economic and political fundamentals.

So where is the organised opposition? The Democrats only seem to exist in the lead up to elections. There is no obvious leader of that party, someone who should be publicly challenging inaccuracies and mistruths, and the errors and decisions made.

World leaders step around him frequently, our own prime minister is not an exception. The leaders of Canada and Spain provide some authentic opposition and challenge. Trade unions world wide have been ‘bashed up’, the radical left is not what it was, and revolutionary youth are a distant memory, individualism and survival the cornerstone. Someone, somewhere needs to step forward, history proves it can happen. This bloke is no ordinary human, but he needs to be challenged. He hasn’t been legitimately tested, yet.

Marshall Toohey, Fairfield New American low

In the face of Peter Hegseth’s decision to stage a barbaric, livestreamed execution, put yourself in the place of the American military personnel who are being asked to kill a person in plain view of the entire world.

Humanity reaches a new low in the USA.

Yvonne Trevaskis, Hobart, Tas Last-gasp chance

Well-meaning actions long ago saw baths constructed in the river at Ocean Grove. The resultant silting, forcing Ocean Grove fishermen to instead moor at the Barwon Heads pier is insignificant compared to our government’s wilful continuation of permitting and subsidising fossil fuel extraction for industrial, household use and exportation. Resultant steady increases in land and sea temperatures are accompanied by steady increases in climate events and rising sea levels. During the August 1952 Barwon Heads flood, the river swept through a 1.5m sandbag levee.

After the August 1992 Barwon Heads floods, the levee at the Sheep Wash end of Barwon Heads was found to be full of rabbit burrows. That flood put the Belmont rowing sheds underwater, flooded Connewarre wetlands and closed Wallington Rd on the Ocean Grove side. All it takes is a perfect storm of riverine and/or flash flooding, a high tide, high winds and towns are underwater.

The costs of insecurity, higher house insurance or uninsurable properties on the coast are proof we’re living in a danger zone.

Various forms of council have permitted subdivision and building on river wetlands that extend from Geelong through to Point Lonsdale. Drainage systems are useless if, as with Wye River, sudden rain buckets down on a region. Lowering emissions now, stopping the environmental damage inflicted by fossil fuels, is our last-gasp chance.

Yvonne Parker, Portarlington



Invest in adaptation

As a coastal local, I am struck by the sheer magnitude of the scale of climate impacts on our coastline (“Climate threats increasing as coastal defences crumble”, 12/10). The threat to land and homes, beaches, and wildlife is enormous.

The Climate Council estimates that sea-level rise will cost Australia $855 billion this century. With associated economic losses of more than one per cent of GDP each year, this is the stuff of recessions.

Sea levels in Australia are expected to rise by at least 14cm by 2050 – that’s baked in. Clearly we must invest in adaptation. Yet, if a stitch in time was ever to save nine, now is the time to urgently address climate warming. We can and morally must prevent continued rising of the tide to ensure a safe and stable economy for those to come. Karen Campbell, Geelong Build smaller homes

Housing experts in Melbourne are now talking about smaller homes to overcome the housing shortage (″⁣The hard truth about alternative housing″⁣ 12/10). As a graduate working on commission for AV Jennings out of a display house in the early ’80s in Victoria, people were happy to get into a 10 to 12 square home; and that by pitching the internal ceiling it becomes a very attractive home. Governments could set limits to home size in developments, caveats, if they wanted to. And get obstructive councils out of the way.

John Dobinson, Brisbane, Qld Thanks for the favour

It’s not often nowadays that one reads a newspaper article that induces an early chuckle, and by the end has you giggling in fits. So to writer Margot Saville (“If your child starts year 12 exams today, don’t do what I did”, 13/10), a heartfelt thank you, and to those who missed the piece, ″⁣do yourselves a favour″⁣, as Molly might say.

Dan Happell, Brighton East State sanctioned killing

Your correspondent (13/1) writes there is no moral equivalence between the USA’s judicial executions, and Iran’s wholesale slaughter of its own citizens. There is an old saying ″⁣Whoever saves one life saves the world entire″⁣. The inverse could be ″⁣Whoever takes one life takes the world entire″⁣.

State sanctioned killing is killing, no matter how many or how few.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Long way to go

I’ve always thought the longest word in the English language was ‘smiles’. There’s a mile between the first and last letters.

James Maygothling, Wantirna



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Government

Before we have government-run supermarkets, can we have our government run gas/electricity/water/births, deaths, marriages back?

Peter Rebbech, Kilmore Have I got this right? After performative screams from zombie businesses, they want us taxpayers to pay so they can put their bills on the never-never.

Allan Dowsett, Preston Senator Jacqui Lambie authentically understands, represents and acts for more Australians than any of the major parties, and especially those that posture as standing up for us. To watch her in full flight in the senate is to see the all-to-rare genuine article.

Dale Crisp, Brighton



Frydenberg

Is Josh “A Grateful Son”, or a prodigal son?

Malcolm Cameron, Camberwell I wonder if Josh Frydenberg considered naming his book Just Joshing.

Paul Custance, Highett With the possibility of Josh Frydenberg’s return to federal politics, don’t forget how he tried to undermine Daniel Andrews when he was leading the fight against the COVID pandemic in Victoria.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris Just when the Liberal party has Labor vulnerable over their botched small business policy changes, along comes Josh to steal their oxygen.

Not to mention his one-time staffer, Jess Wilson, who could do without the distraction as the Victorian election approaches.

Rob McCasker, Murdoch WA Trump

What D-chess is President Trump playing this week? His behaviour continues to be truly breathtaking.

Fiona White, Alfredton



Most political leaders would be happy to be characterised as Lincolnian, Churchillian or Ghandian. How will a future leader feel about being called Trumpian?

Bill King, Camberwell Finally

The words adduced by your polysyllabic correspondents have become sesquipedalian.

Arthur Roberts, Elwood The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Crime plague turns up next door to shadow police minister’s office
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Crime plague turns up next door to shadow police minister’s office Fiona Byrne October 13, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Victoria’s plague of vandalism, break-ins and arson attacks has come perilously close to the electoral office of state opposition police spokesman Brad Battin, with an attempted firebombing at the restaurant next door. Talk about an example of what Battin laments is a crime crisis landing practically on his doorstep. Opposition police spokesman Brad Battin with Coalition leader Jess Wilson. Simon Schluter The incident occurred on Monday night at the eatery next to Battin’s electorate office in Berwick in Melbourne’s south-east. We hear that while the crooks fled, an accelerant was left at the scene, and it may not have been the first time the venue has been broken into. Battin’s office did not sustain any damage.



A mobile police camera seen in Wheeler Street, Berwick, on Tuesday afternoon. “Police are investigating an attempted firebombing at a restaurant in Berwick on 12 October,” Victoria Police said in a statement. “It is believed two unknown offenders attended the premises on Wheeler Street just before midnight. Offenders threw an object through the window before they were confronted by a staff member inside and fled. “They were last seen fleeing in a silver vehicle. There were no injuries and the investigation is ongoing.” Police are keen to speak to anyone who witnessed or has CCTV footage of the incident.



We checked in on Battin on Tuesday, figuring that as the opposition’s police spokesman he might have a bit to say about the attempted firebombing. While he was measured, he was clearly concerned. “We have seen the crime crisis escalate across Victoria and in Casey crime continues to rise, and it is these kinds of events that send fear through the community,” he said. We hear a police camera was positioned in Wheeler Street on Tuesday afternoon following the damage the night before. Watch this space. J-Bish’s advisory link to Trump She is already a noted jetsetter, but former foreign minister Julie Bishop is spreading her business wings and has hitched her wagon to a Trump-linked advisory firm in the US.



Bishop revealed on Instagram on Tuesday that she had formed a “strategic alliance” between her Julie Bishop & Partners advisory firm and American Global Strategies, which is chaired by Robert O’Brien, a US national security adviser from 2019 to 2021 and current member of Donald Trump’s President’s Intelligence Advisory Board. Former foreign minister Julie Bishop. Alex Ellinghausen The chief executive of American Global Strategies, which bills itself as advising clients on geopolitical developments, is Alexander Gray, who was previously a director for Oceania security at the White House. Bishop will be among old friends in the connecting of the businesses. Former PM Scott Morrison, her ex-government colleague, is a non-executive vice chairman at American Global Strategies, while Australia’s former top intelligence official Nick Warner is a senior adviser to the company, as is former Australian ambassador to the US Arthur Sinodinos.



“The firms will draw on their respective experience and regional perspectives, with particular relevance for companies operating in strategically important sectors including mining and critical minerals, energy, defence, and technology,” a press blurb explained, as well as providing “senior corporate leaders with strategic guidance”. CBD sought comment from Bishop’s team to find out more about this bonding, asking why she selected this organisation to partner with, if she was a supporter of Donald Trump and if her old mate Morrison had helped connect the parties. We’re waiting to hear back. Bishop stepped down as chancellor of the Australian National University in May after six years in the chair. Meanwhile, she has been keeping those curious up to date with her recent international travels, posting regularly to social media. There was a trip to Italy, a week at the United Nations, and then a couple of days in the south of France to attend the lavish wedding of Australian-born fashion designer Tamara Ralph. Ralph, whose pricey designs are red carpet favourites for celebrities of the calibre of Angelina Jolie and Taylor Swift, married billionaire businessman Bhanu Choudhrie in an extravagant four-day celebration at the Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc this month.



‘Toorak Tom’ returns after suspension “Tom for Toorak”, the pothole-obsessed Stonnington councillor also known as Tom Humphries, is back on deck after serving a four-week suspension from the council and is now calling for changes to the Local Government Act. Humphries, who memorably addressed his constituents as “my fellow Toorakians” when breaking the news online of his suspension, had urged his fellow councillors at a meeting in council chambers last December to support his push to install a menorah at Malvern Town Hall. Stonnington councillor Tom Humphries is back in action. Justin McManus However, his robust presentation and use of words including “antisemitic” and “unlawful” while making his case against an attempt to delay the decision led to him facing arbitration after four fellow councillors – Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr, Deputy Mayor Samantha Choudhury, and councillors Jami Klisaris and Steve Stefanopoulos – claimed his behaviour brought discredit on the council.



Meanwhile, the menorah was approved and installed a week after the heated debate. Related Article City life Toorak councillor banned over ‘obscene’ remarks after heated menorah debate In a report later tabled in council documents, arbiter Diana Price found Humphries was “able to use language that was forceful. However, his statements went well beyond the concept of robust debate in a democracy.” While his suspension, which came into effect in mid-September, ended this week, he can’t seek the mayoralty or deputy mayoralty, which are up for grabs in November, and must apologise to council colleagues. In an Instagram video, he said he would not fight the decision as he reckoned it would cost roughly $250,000 to appeal in the Supreme Court.



Far from taking a back seat on his return to the council front line, Humphries is now planning to push for changes to the Local Government Act, saying his suspension deprived his constituents of representation for a month. “This process has shown me how the Local Government Act works in practice, and it needs to change,” he told CBD on Tuesday. “A complaint by fellow councillors is heard behind closed doors, there’s no right to legal representation, and the result can be that an entire ward loses its elected voice for months. “Toorak Ward has gone a month without the councillor it elected, and I’ll be making up for lost time in delivering the agenda I promised to my residents.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy Jake Niall October 13, 2026 — 7:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Whereas the police investigation into the Pullman hotel incident has conceivably cost Isaac Heeney millions of dollars via loss of sponsors, Nick Blakey has garnered millions from the Pullman imbroglio. It’s a strange economy, the AFL. Nick Blakey dons the North Melbourne guernsey, as his father, John, once did. North Melbourne FC At the least, Blakey will be paid an extra $400,000 or more per season over the next five years by dint of his move south to North. And he has added a further three years on the same kind of remuneration, becoming one of the highest-paid players in the competition, at least until Tasmania arrives. How does a player who found himself in strife – and suspended by the Swans alongside four teammates for breach of standards and professional conduct – end up profiting from his mistake (aside from some sharp work by his agent)?



There are many subplots to North Melbourne’s successful pursuit of Blakey, the father-son recruit whom they’ve landed eight years after he preferred the Swans, where his father John had worked under another Shinboner John Longmire. North has overpaid Blakey in pure dollar terms, at close to $12 million over eight years, although North believes Blakey would have earned the same amount elsewhere. As they acknowledge, North had to go hard to get the player and could not be under-bidders for the first genuine A-grader in his mid-career to join them since the dawn of the millennium. Loading On the draft front, one could argue that North has paid slight unders for Blakey, relative to the asking price for uninjured all-Australians, since future picks are devalued by Tasmania. The caveat is that the Pullman incident is not yet resolved, legally or by the AFL, and North has been willing to take on the risk in the event that their prized recruit is charged. To navigate the Blakey deal and minimise the risks of any fallout or wrinkle, the Kangaroos took the following steps:



1. They asked Blakey for his version of events at the Pullman. From what this column has gathered, they then cross-checked that version with other parties. Related Article AFL 2026 Swans frosty as Blakey departs for North Melbourne with an apology 2. Consulted the AFL about acquiring Blakey, considering the massive outlay and the unusual circumstances of his exit. It is a safe assumption that if the league had misgivings, he would not be headed to his dad’s old team. 3. Chief executive Jenn Watt, head of football Todd Viney and head of strategy Erin Lorenzini addressed the whole AFLW team and fielded questions last Friday when North emerged as the frontrunner. The W players were pleased to have that communication from the hierarchy. 4. Staff, too, were sounded out by the club hierarchy.



Nick Blakey played 173 games in eight seasons for the Swans. Sam Mooy The Blakey camp are privately confident that he will not be stood down by the AFL, irrespective of what transpires in the police investigation and whether charges are laid. Blakey’s desire for a trade – North list boss Brady Rawlings used the word “disgruntlement” on Tuesday after the deal was completed with the Swans – derived from his view that he had not been handled fairly by the red and whites in the aftermath of the Pullman detonation. It was notable that whereas clubs usually make statements about their player being “required” and only available for a ludicrous trade offer, the Swans were largely silent on the Blakey front in the days leading into the trade period and during it. This was read – correctly – as a sign that they were willing to sacrifice him for a fair deal. Heeney and Chad Warner, the other stars facing the investigation, had not explored trades. Warner will be a free agent and target for West Coast and maybe the Wharfie-timers next year.



The difference between Blakey and Heeney is Blakey’s financial gain derives purely from his football skills and availability. Heeney’s losses stem from dents to an exalted image. When the prospect of North chasing Blakey was first mooted post-Pullman, it was speculated in the industry that North’s female leadership of CEO Watt and president Sonja Hood might hold objections to the notion of recruiting a player who had found himself in a police investigation of sexual assault allegations, alongside three teammates (Riley Bice is only a witness for police). View post on X But today one can argue that North’s unique position of having women at the helm has helped them in acquiring Blakey, and in making their case internally for his recruitment. Hood and Watt provide a measure of cultural cover for the club in making the raid. List boss Brady Rawlings was quizzed repeatedly on Tuesday about how North had navigated their Blakey hunt and especially the “what ifs” of a suspension and/or police charges.



The media conference, which had been more about cultural issues and risk assessment than the need for a fast rebounder, concluded following a question that raised the topic of Tarryn Thomas’s termination by the same club in 2024. The club’s media boss terminated the inquisition on that note. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster Marc McGowan Sports reporter The questions underscored how the process of recruiting Nick Blakey was marked by the more complicated considerations that AFL clubs confront, just as the Swans’ decision to suspend the five was heavily skewed by non-football factors, such as their fan base, demographics and position in the Sydney market. Yet for all the changing football mores, the deal came down to one of the AFL’s immutable ways: The gun players are treated differently. Get around our footy coverage

World.title: No consent: Sacked professor loses case after women’s cells used in mice experiment
World.content:
NationalResearch No consent: Sacked professor loses case after women’s cells used in mice experiment Liam Mannix October 13, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The research seemed so promising. Under a microscope, the scientists could see cancerous cells being “completely eradicated” by a cannabis extract. A 2021 announcement trumpeted the results as “groundbreaking”. The research pair-up – the University of Newcastle and ASX-listed hemp grower Ecofibre – seemed convinced they were poised to transform women’s health. “All patients have responded positively,” Ecofibre announced (though the experiments were on patient samples, not on patients themselves). Patents had been filed. Almost five years to the day, the picture is rather different. Fair Work Commission documents reveal the University of Newcastle researcher who led the work has now been terminated for research misconduct. The research centre he directed has shut, with all samples and data from the suspect research destroyed. Staff have lost their jobs, and PhD students have had to abandon their studies. The university has had to repay donors.



Related Article Exclusive

Investigations Dying woman and ethical doubts spark probe into cannabis cancer ‘cure’ A promising beginning Ecofibre is a hemp grower and producer, selling various cannabis-based treatments for pain, including “Endo Relief Cream” and cannabinoid vaginal suppositories known as “Endo Relief Melts”. But the evidence showing cannabis can treat chronic pain is thin on the ground. “Due to a lack of evidence from high-quality research,” the International Association for the Study of Pain said in 2021, it “does not endorse the general use of cannabinoids to treat pain.” Ecofibre and the University of Newcastle hoped to change that. What went wrong from there is chronicled in two Fair Work Commission judgments.



The two organisations entered into a research partnership to test the efficacy of cannabinoids on endometriosis and other gynaecological diseases. Professor Pradeep Tanwar, formerly the director of the Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases at the University of Newcastle. Professor Pradeep Tanwar, director of the University’s Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases, was made chief investigator of those research projects. Tanwar was also the principal investigator in two research projects to study the molecular basis of endometriosis and look for blood markers for the disease being run at three hospitals around Newcastle. By 2023, Ecofibre and the university had been jointly granted patents for hemp treatments for ovarian cancer and endometriosis. “We are well positioned to move to the next stage of our research, which includes full protocol development for eventual human trials,” Tanwar said in an Ecofibre letter to shareholders.



It was then, according to the Fair Work Commission documents, the problems began. Issues with consent In 2023, the university became aware of allegations that patients in Tanwar’s studies had not signed consent forms or were asked to sign them retrospectively. Hospital service investigations concluded that more than 100 patients involved in the research had not signed consent forms for their tissue to be used. This masthead revealed the existence of that investigation in 2025. Nor, the university alleged, were the patients told their tissue would be grafted onto so-called “xenograft mice”.



Related Article Mental health The $300 a week medicine Daniel feels better without Informed consent is sacrosanct in science and covered by strict rules. Fundamentally, research participants must volunteer, and they must understand what they’re signing up to. After investigating, the hospital system pulled its ethical approval for the studies. Ecofibre also terminated its research agreement with the university, which was being used to fund most of the centre’s senior research positions. The company did not return a request for comment. The university suspended Tanwar in April 2024 on full pay.



Without its leader and money to fund ongoing research, the Global Centre for Gynaecological Diseases closed in December 2024, and most staff working there lost their jobs. The Fair Work Commission judgment summarises the damage done: “Two students being required to abandon their PhD work and recommence their studies (one of them four years into their PhD), 14 students being disrupted and assigned new supervision, 17 staff having their employment disrupted and career outputs affected and over 1000 mice being expended during the research that will not yield publishable/useable data.” In total, the university spent about $8 million on the research. The commission’s judgment noted that the university had to repay some donors after the scandal broke. The university terminated Tanwar’s employment in August 2025. Speaking on Tuesday, Tanwar said getting patients’ consent was the responsibility of the hospital’s clinicians.



“Under the approved ethics protocols, consent was taken by hospital clinicians,” he said. “Written consent was given in accordance with the legislation. Unfortunately, consent documentation processes at the hospital had shortcomings.” Related Article Exclusive

Legal Cannabis Cannabis sales plummet as regulators crack down on booming industry Tanwar this year appeared before the Fair Work Commission and unsuccessfully argued his dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable. The commission concluded that Tanwar, as chief investigator, “had ultimate responsibility for the ethical conduct of research”, even if it wasn’t his job to directly supervise the doctors who were talking to patients. It found his termination was not unfair. In May, Tanwar appeared before the commission again to appeal the decision, arguing that “all patients provided verbal consent, no patient was harmed, there was no dishonesty or fabrication, and Dr Tanwar did not interact with patients”.



A commission’s full bench, in a judgment published last week, also rejected that claim, finding “the failure to ensure ethical protocols were followed resulted in some women who donated their samples doing so without proper informed consent being obtained in circumstances where they are entitled to expect that the ethical protocols put in place by those researchers will be followed”. Tanwar said he was disappointed. “This outcome is a warning to every lead academic in collaborative research about the length and breadth of ‘ultimate responsibility’. That you can be dismissed for the actions of others in different employment relationships and over which you have no authority,” he said. “This has come at enormous personal and financial cost to me and my family. The commission itself accepted that the dismissal has been extremely difficult for me, both personally and financially.” In a statement, the University of Newcastle said it was “committed to responsible and ethical research”.



“In this case, the Fair Work Commission upheld the outcome of the university’s investigation, finding that the decision to dismiss was sound and that the investigation was reasonable and procedurally fair.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Charges laid over hundreds of ‘fake’ Big Build qualifications
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaBuilding Bad Charges laid over hundreds of ‘fake’ Big Build qualifications Nick McKenzie October 13, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A Victorian businessman has been charged over his alleged role in a racket involving hundreds of fake qualifications distributed across Big Build sites, potentially endangering the safety of workers and the public. The breakthrough by a police taskforce has prompted the state opposition to commit to expanding the terms of reference of the Carroll government commissioned royal commission into the building industry if it wins government to examine the qualifications scandal and how it may have operated for years without detection by the state’s health and safety regulator WorkSafe or other agencies. Jake Calvert has been charged over the alleged distribution of hundreds of fake certificates. Michael Howard On Tuesday, former AFL prospect-turned construction industry manager Jake Calvert was charged by the Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk with 232 counts of making a false document. The charges come a week after The Age revealed that NSW conman Jack Younes, who also goes by several aliases, has for at least three years been distributing hundreds or even thousands of fake building qualification certificates to Victorian construction firms and workers, including those operating on the Big Build.



This was despite federal regulator, the Australian Skills Quality Authority, being tipped off about Younes’ operation in 2023 and state regulator Worksafe Victoria receiving a further warning about Younes’ operation in July 2025. Jack Younes is suspected of being a key player in the alleged scam. Facebook/NSW Fair Trading Younes — who admitted forging qualification certificates when he was recently confronted by The Age — was still operating freely as recently as last month and has not been arrested. After returning from Queensland, Calvert was confronted by detectives on Tuesday morning over allegations he paid the Younes syndicate to supply traffic management and other building industry qualification certificates to workers across key Big Build and commercial construction sites. The charging of Calvert highlights a far less scrutinised but still systemic alleged corruption and safety issue on the Big Build.



Previously, media and police investigations have focussed on allegations that gangland figures systemically infiltrated the Big Build, including bikies who obtained roles as CFMEU health and safety delegates in a manner that may have also jeopardised worksite safety. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Big Build hit by fake qualifications racket as regulators face questions Calvert, who was recently sacked from his role as an operations manager for Big Build labour hire firm Top Up and who runs his own construction firm, Archer Hire, allegedly sits at the juncture of both scandals. While his charges relate to suspicions he obtained dozens of false certificates for labour hire workers he supplied to Big Build sites, he has been separately raided by police over allegations he sought to give inducements to CFMEU officials in Queensland through a serving Victorian CFMEU official. Detectives have also probed Calvert’s relationship with ex-bikie boss and former CFMEU delegate Tyrone Bell – who is also facing charges of using false qualification certificates.



Prior to entering the construction sector, Calvert was touted as a possible AFL draft pick and played in the VFL. On Tuesday evening, shadow attorney-general James Newbury said the latest police action, along with long-standing concerns about systemic lapses in health and safety on construction sites, needed to be specifically examined by the royal commission. “Organised crime and bikies have been running rampant across government projects. Victorians deserve to know why our workplace safety regulator Worksafe has been missing in action,” Newbury said. “A Liberal and Nationals government will strengthen the terms of reference for the royal commission into the Big Build, to include investigating Worksafe and why it has been sitting on its hands for years.” Newbury also said the chair of Worksafe, former Labor minister Bob Cameron, had presided over the inaction.



In a statement released on Tuesday afternoon, Worksafe said it has been “notified of a number of individuals allegedly seeking to obtain fraudulent qualification certificates, which may have been used to demonstrate competencies they do not have”. “Fraudulent qualifications could pose a health and safety risk if a duty holder relies on them as evidence of skills in a particular area – such as first aid, implementing traffic management plans or working safely at heights – that they do not actually have.” WorkSafe chief health and safety officer Sam Jenkin warned the agency would “take compliance or enforcement action against anyone who puts their co-workers or others in a workplace at risk by working in an area they have knowingly and fraudulently obtained false qualifications for.” But he also said the agency was “limited in the legal action it can take in relation to this type of fraud.” WorkSafe has also issued an industry-wide safety alert about the use of fake certificates, urging employers to verify records.



A Victorian government spokesman said the government thanked the police for uncovering the “rort” and that the royal commission would investigate and make system-wide recommendations. “Every agency has to be vigilant in using its powers when there are reports of grift on government-funded construction sites,” the statement said. In a statement, Taskforce Hawk confirmed the charging of Calvert “as part of an investigation into the production and distribution of false construction and other workplace certifications and qualifications”. “Police will allege the man facilitated false workplace education qualifications. The investigation, which commenced earlier this year, remains ongoing.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: Australian mining’s footy trip mentality to offshore operations must end
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaMining Opinion Australian mining’s footy trip mentality to offshore operations must end The Age's View Editorial October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm

October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Too often, Australian companies operating offshore, particularly in countries with dubious political safeguards, seem to have a footy trip mentality – what happens on tour should stay on tour. Too often, also, a lack of attention is paid to those companies’ offshore pursuits, allowing that culture to persist. In the past week, The Age has published a series of articles scrutinising the push by Hanrine – a company belonging to Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart – into Ecuador. A hillside at La Merced de Buenos Aires showing illegal mining in 2025. James Ross Issues raised include whether the company has appropriately tackled the illegal mining scourge on its concessions in the township of La Merced de Buenos Aires and whether it was complicit with the heavy-handed Ecuadorian security force response to a largely peaceful community protest against Hanrine’s activities. Hanrine not only denied all allegations but attacked the local community leaders as “anti-prosperity activists” in league with the armed illegal miners who have terrorised them. That is an insulting, condescending and inappropriate way to talk about people whose land you claim to want to share to improve their economic position.



It also stands at odds with claims from locals who did work for Hanrine that they were severely mistreated including being fed raw meat and denied communication with their families. So much for being the vanguard of prosperity. Then there’s Llurimagua. As at La Merced de Buenos Aires, Hanrine is keen, along with many other miners, to explore this area for its copper as world demand for the metal reaches fresh records. BHP and South32 are both tipped to bid in the upcoming international tender for Llurimagua. The catch is that the area is internationally renowned for its environmental value, with hundreds of rare or endangered species living in its cloud forests. Unlike the ASX-listed bidders, and probably others, neither Hanrine nor its parent, Hancock Prospecting, is a member of the International Council of Mining and Metals, which seeks to ensure fair treatment and to balance mining’s inevitable environmental impacts.



Hancock is, of course, a private company. It is not subject to the shareholder pressure that has forced so much change on the world’s mining industry in the past two decades. As such if it opts not to sign up to global standards that is its choice, but The Age would argue this is a poor signal to locals that it will conduct itself at world’s-best-practice levels. Hanrine’s response to The Age is laced with indignation at being asked to address the concerns of a community living in effect, in the case of La Merced de Buenos Aires, in a war zone as illegal miners, organised criminals, Colombian revolutionaries and the government fight over the hillsides around the town. Hillsides that, on paper, are Hanrine’s exploration grounds. The statement also chides The Age for reporting on Ecuador during a cost-of-living crisis in Australia. This masthead is more than capable of doing more than one thing at once, and will never resile from the task of holding the powerful to account for their actions.



Hanrine’s chief executive in Ecuador, Carlos de Miguel, whose name the statement is issued under, faces disturbing claims from local workers that he would roam their sites with guard dogs and toting large weapons. Some say, unsurprisingly, they were afraid of him. In his lengthy statement, de Miguel did not address this alleged behaviour. There is no suggestion Rinehart knew of or condoned the behaviour alleged in the articles. Editor's pick Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Exclusive

Investigations McLarens, Mar-a-Lago and machine guns: Introducing Gina Rinehart’s controversial new frontier point man Australian miners in many ways lead the world in technical ability, environmental responsibility and, by and large, governance. Aspiring to those standards, embodied in organisations like the international council, was not enough to prevent BHP’s deadly Samarco disaster in Brazil, or Rio Tinto’s closer-to-home Juukan Gorge disgrace. Neither company was outwardly hostile to the communities they eventually harmed. Both have also sought to make right their damage. It is a marked contrast to Hanrine’s indifferent and dismissive conduct in Ecuador.

World.title: The blunt message to year 12 students aiming for university entry
World.content:
Exclusive NationalUniversity The blunt message to year 12 students aiming for university entry Sally Rawsthorne October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. University Admission Centre managing director Kim Paino has a blunt message for school leavers intent on tertiary education and facing a tough time gaining entry to a Sydney university next year. “Take the offer,” said Paino, who joined the chorus warning of the risks involved in the new funding regime, which passed parliament on Tuesday. The University of Sydney said it was forced to end its long-running guaranteed entry scheme because of the changes. Sam Mooy “Students really need to make sure they preference carefully, and if they receive an offer … accept it,” she said. “It doesn’t mean they necessarily have to enrol in that course, but at least it gives them an option.” Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says the new funding package will create an extra 230,000 university places and $3.6 billion in extra funding for tertiary institutions over the next decade, with an emphasis on admitting a higher number of disadvantaged students through specially created places.



It will also tighten numbers at popular metropolitan universities, including the University of Sydney, the University of NSW, Macquarie University and the University of Technology, Sydney, meaning some students may be unable to get a place. This will leave them to either study elsewhere or abandon tertiary education. Related Article Exclusive

University University entry was the hardest it’s ever been this year. Next year will be worse The changes were introduced for a transition period in 2025, before the new regime was enshrined in law. The University of NSW and Macquarie University have said that, as a result, they have been forced to decline prospective students, while the University of Sydney has disbanded its long-running guaranteed-entry scheme and UTS made fewer offers than before. HSC students apply for up to five courses through the UAC. The centre looks at their preferences and will admit students to the first course for which they meet the entry requirements. It conducts two main rounds of offers, in December and January.



Paino urged HSC students to be aspirational but “really try to be realistic” about their results. “That’s always the advice but this year it’ll potentially apply to a wider range of students that won’t have that opportunity to have another crack [at a second round offer] in January,” because of the tightened places, she said. “The traditionally more competitive universities to get into are exactly those that are having to tighten their numbers, so it makes it even harder to get into those particular universities,” she warned. “There still will be places. The government’s saying that overall there’ll be more places available. It’s just not necessarily in the institutions and the courses that are already oversubscribed.” Medicine, which also has additional selection criteria, law and allied health courses such as physiotherapy are historically popular.



Related Article University This plan would put an end to the $50,000 arts degree. It’s also controversial She suggested students who want to study a combined arts/law degree also preference a standalone arts degree, or students aiming for biomedical science also preference a straight science degree. “Look to include a university that isn’t necessarily going to be under the same pressure to manage numbers. Their entry criteria might be a little bit less [stringent],” she said. The federal Department of Education released its semester 1 enrolment data on Tuesday. It shows a 5.3 per cent increase in students commencing a degree compared to 2025. Enrolments are up in teaching (7.7 per cent), health (6.6 per cent), social work (15.7 per cent), engineering (10.5 per cent), clinical psychology (9.8 per cent) and science (6.8 per cent). World.title: Bars look skyward to open in ‘rooftop capital of Australia’
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Bars look skyward to open in ‘rooftop capital of Australia’ Cara Waters October 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The rooftop of Garden State hotel used to be unloved and cluttered with air conditioning equipment but a two-year build has transformed it into Melbourne’s newest rooftop bar. The two tiered space overlooking Flinders Lane is dotted with large cream umbrellas shading clusters of bar tables and wicker chairs. Chef James Wilkinson and venue manager Katie Saxton at the new rooftop bar for Garden State. Wayne Taylor It takes time and battling significant red tape to open a rooftop bar in Melbourne, but for many hospitality operators it’s worth the effort. Three new or revamped venues will open in the city in the next month. Garden State is just one of a string of venues looking skyward for expansion; Transit Rooftop Bar is set to reopen in Federation Square next month after a major transformation, along with the Prince Terrace in St Kilda which will open the former Prince deck to the public for the first time.



Paul Waterson, chief executive of Australian Venue Co, owner of Garden State, says opening a rooftop bar in the city centre is not for the faint of heart. Related Article Best of From posh to party, these 10 new rooftop bars and restaurants are built for anything “It’s a really challenging location being in Flinders Lane, so it took a lot of liaison with local stakeholders, nearby neighbours, Melbourne City Council and 101 Collins,” he says. “It was quite an intense planning process and a very intense build as well.” Crane operations were only allowed one day a week, on Saturdays, which slowed construction. Waterson says restricting operating hours and reducing noise levels through acoustic management were key to keeping residents and the council on side.



“I think everyone understands how vibrant Melbourne’s CBD is, and it’s really one of the great things Melbourne is becoming increasingly known for,” he says. “You see all these other states promoting these vibrancy reforms for initiatives that are already in place in Melbourne and I think we sort of undersell that a little bit too.” Transit Rooftop Bar is reopening after a major transformation. Despite the time and expense involved with opening a rooftop bar, Waterson says it made sense to expand the pub upwards creating a four-storey venue and offering an open air outdoor space. “I think Melbourne is the original rooftop capital of Australia,” he says. “We were the first state to really appreciate our great architecture, and we’re a resilient bunch, aren’t we? We’ll go out, sit on a rooftop all year round.”



The two level space holds 300 people and a retractable roof and heating will ensure year round operation. Related Article Coming soon Will this team finally make Fed Square a Melbourne dining hotspot? Garden State has also turned its former function space into a cocktail bar, The Observatory, with plush booths and bespoke cocktails. Garden State venue manager Katie Saxton says she’s expecting to sell plenty of spritzes over summer while food on the rooftop will include prawn rolls with dill mayo and lemon and stracciatella with cucumber, honey and black pepper. “The rooftop market in the CBD is really quite formidable, and everyone loves a rooftop,” she says.



Nearby Transit Rooftop is set to reopen next month following a revamp by Studio Y nearly 20 years after it first opened with a reconfigured layout that opens up city views. The rooftop bar will hold 250 people seated with food by Taxi chef Tony Twitchett and cocktails by Matt Linklater. In St Kilda, after taking the reins of the Prince Hotel DJ and entrepreneur Grant Smillie is opening up the Prince Deck overlooking Acland Street with views across the bay and to the CBD. The Prince’s rooftop will be open to the public for the first time. Kristoffer Paulsen Smillie has taken out the swimming pool which he says was underutilised.



“Uncle Johnny might have ended up in there one night on a wedding, which was a bit embarrassing, but that’s okay,” he says. The deck is licensed for 700 and Smillie says not much red tape was involved because it was an existing function venue. The changes include ensuring there is lots of open outdoor space with tables and chairs for food and drink along with a piano bar. “Rooftop bars are just universal,” Smillie says. “I think there’s nothing better than being outdoors. You can come and dine, drink, and then hang around, watch a little jazz number, or you know, listen to some DJs.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: 'Humiliating' - former PM Helen Clark slams NZ abstention on UN pandemic vote
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Helen Clark has slammed New Zealand's abstention on a vote on global pandemic preparedness at the United Nations, describing it as "humiliating".

New Zealand was among five countries that did not vote for a UN declaration designed to strengthen national, regional and international co-operation in the event of a future pandemic.

The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response, while New Zealand and Paraguay abstained.

The other 153 member states of the UN voted for the declaration, which called for "stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year's landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement".

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) said "New Zealand supports the aim of strengthening global health systems and improving pandemic preparedness and response."

But it said: "New Zealand does not support language welcoming the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement…It is very important to New Zealand that its sovereign decision making on health is protected."

The UN said the declaration was "political and non-binding".

Helen Clark - a former UN official - called the vote "humiliating for NZ" in a social media post.

Embedded content removed for printing https://x.com/HelenClarkNZ/status/2109748226123591956

"How low can NZ go?... This results from [New Zealand First]'s courting of the anti-vax vote," she said.

"As New Zealand noted at the time of the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement by the World Health Assembly [2024], any future decision on whether or not to sign and ratify the Pandemic Agreement will be informed by a full National Interest Test under domestic procedures," MFAT said.

The International Health Regulations (IHR) define countries' rights and obligations in handling public health events and emergencies that have the potential to cross borders, a statement on the Ministry of Health website said.

New Zealand was a signatory and had been since its establishment.

But earlier this year, New Zealand told the WHO Director-General it was rejecting the amendments.

Political reaction

In a statement on social media, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said his party "ensured the National Interest Test was included in the coalition agreement to keep our sovereign decision making with New Zealand, not Geneva".

"We believe it is essential to New Zealand that its sovereign decision making on health is protected," Peters said.

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins called the vote "an embarrassment to New Zealand".

"Frankly, I am astounded that New Zealand has shown such cowardice in an important vote before the UN," he said.

It was another example of Christopher Luxon "letting Winston Peters embrace conspiracy theories as New Zealand government positions", Hipkins said.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon initially tried to skirt questions about the vote, saying: "It wasn't a Cabinet decision, you'll need to direct further questions to the foreign minister."

But he then appeared to disagree with Hipkins that it was an "important vote".

"There is literally, every day, a number of declarations that go through the UN - of major and minor significance and importance. Important ones come through a Cabinet decision-making process," Luxon said.

"But in this case, this is one that is up to the Minister of Foreign Affairs to make a call on."

National MP Matt Doocey said National ministers supported voting in favour while formally recording their reservations. However, a Cabinet decision was not required, and Winston Peters made his decision as Foreign Affairs Minister.

World.title: 'Knee jerk response' - Coastguard air volunteers grounded over safety rule changes
World.content:
An air patrol volunteer for Coastguard says he has major safety concerns for boaties in the upper North Island after two teams were grounded.

The volunteer pilots in Auckland and Northland have been immediately benched, due to a change in safety standards which now requires pilots to have commercial licenses.

Coastguard Auckland Air Patrol president Andrew Lamb told Checkpoint the decision came as a total shock.

"We had been having some discussions and then on Friday morning, I got a phone call saying that the board had stood us down for taskings or flight training on the Saturday," he said.

Regulation changes by the Rescue Coordination Centre New Zealand (RCCNZ) had implications for maritime rescue and aviation assets, Lamb said.

"Where we had been flying under one regulation, we no longer would qualify for that and we wouldn't meet the new standards because of being a volunteer organisation effectively," he said.

Lamb said it had not been well thought out as to how search and rescue support gaps would be filled.

"Is Defence Force going to be able to fill that gap? I don't think so," he said.

"We are a search vessel, so we guide the boats… onto the distressed vessel, or it might be a person in water. So we get there a lot quicker. We travel at over 140 knots. So we get there a lot faster than a boat would."

There had been no details shared with grounded volunteers as to how the gap would be filled, Lamb said.

"[From] Ohakea to get an Air Force defense crew up to Auckland and Haraki Gulf… my understanding is it would take about four hours whereas we could probably get there in an hour to an hour and a half. So less than half the time and an awful lot cheaper as well," he said.

"RCCNZ won't task Coastguard in any of these searches because we don't meet their requirements. So there's just a big gap and I my concern is no one has actually thought about this gap. We've made a knee jerk response to something and we haven't backfilled the solution."

Coastguard said the decision was not a reflection on its air patrol volunteers but because Maritime New Zealand's Rescue Coordination Centre introduced new standards for search and rescue operations last year.

World.title: Opportunity still in kingmaker seat in latest 1News Verian poll
World.content:
Opportunity remains kingmaker while the major parties - Labour and National - are tied in the latest 1News Verian Poll.

Party support has remained largely stable, with only small moves up or down.

National has slipped 1 point to 28 percent, tying them with Labour, also on 28 percent.

The Green Party have slipped slightly, falling 1 point to 15 percent.

The ACT Party has gone up 1 point, tying them with New Zealand First who also sits on 10 percent.

Te Pāti Māori is down to just 0.4 percent.

If replicated at the election, that would give National 34 MPs and New Zealand First and ACT 12 - a coalition bloc of 58.

On the left, Labour would get 34 MPs, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori four - depending on how the Māori seats were calculated - and Te Tai Tokerau Party one seat - 57 together.

Opportunity would have 8 seats, meaning they would get to decide who governed.

The previous 1News Verian Poll - released last week - put both major parties neck and neck, with National on 29 percent and Labour on 28.

Meanwhile, the Greens were on 16 percent, New Zealand First on 10 percent and ACT on 9 percent, with Te Pāti Māori on 1 percent and Opportunity on 7 percent.

World.title: Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell one of first at scene of motorcycle crash
World.content:
One person has been injured after a crash in Tauranga on Tuesday afternoon.

National MP and candidate for the Tauranga electorate Sam Uffindell told RNZ he was driving along the harbour bridge when he saw the motorcyclist who had fallen off her bike.

The crash on Te Awanui Drive, between Mirrielees Road on-ramp and Hewletts Road, happened about 3.10pm, police said.

Sam Uffindell Hagen Hopkins

"I just pulled in immediately to see what aid I could give her, make sure she was okay," Uffindell said.

"I just wanted to go in and make sure that she was alright, and to help where she could, make sure an ambulance was called."

Uffindell wanted to give full credit to Brent Warner, the chair of Mount Maunganui Surf Life Saving, who he said pulled in moments later to help out.

"Having him on the scene was great, he's a legend here, and obviously has a huge amount of first aid experience," he said.

Uffindell said he didn't really think about it before going to help.

"You see someone who needs help, you help, that's what you do."

World.title: Radar shines light on unmarked graves of asylum patients
World.content:
Audio player for " Special radar aids search for unmarked graves " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/science-and-technology/1874640%2Fradar-shines-light-on-unmarked-graves-of-asylum-patients

Special radar aids search for unmarked graves Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A special radar is aiding the search for the unmarked graves of patients who died in care in mental asylums near Dunedin.

The region has a long - and often dark - history of large-scale institutional care including Seacliff Lunatic Asylum and Cherry Farm as well as welfare homes and church-run facilities.

Earlier this year, the Dunedin City Council received government funding to help find and honour the patients who were buried in unmarked plots.

On the grassy slope of Waitati Cemetery, amongst the headstones and burial plots, archaeologist Dr Emma St Pierre was searching for unmarked graves.

Waitati Cemetery. Tess Brunton

It did not take her long.

She found four people buried in unmarked graves in the shadow of a monument.

Using historical records, she estimated roughly 6500 deaths were registered in the Seacliff group of asylums over about 100 years to 1969.

Archaeologist Dr Emma St Pierre said finding unmarked graves was not uncommon in cemeteries in her experience. Tess Brunton

She said Waitati cemetery was a sensible place to start - it was close to some of the asylums, had a higher proportion of patients buried here and had plenty of unmarked graves.

She created grids to survey before wheeling a ground-penetrating radar over the top that could reach up to 2 metres in depth.

"A lot of people think that you're finding bones. It's only in very rare cases that you would find bones with (ground-penetrating radar) if that was all that was left," she said.

"Often what you're looking for is the coffin or the grave cuts. You can see disturbance in the soil so it's basically reflections off contrasting materials in the ground."

The radar finds an unmarked grave a Waitati Cemetery. Tess Brunton

Cemetery records showed two to three patients were buried in some plots - but St Pierre was also checking if the records matched up with what the radar found.

"That's sort of the goal here is to see whether the (ground-penetrating radar) data marries up with the historical research or whether there were people being buried en masse or more people buried than what has been recorded in the historical data," St Pierre said.

While pushing along the radar, she pointed at the many dents in the ground, saying they likely marked unmarked graves where the ground had subsided after air pockets escaped and soil settled.

She hoped the mahi would be helpful.

"Whānau or former patients may either get some closure or find some kind of resolution or peace from it."

Project lead, council parks planning manager John Brenkley said the project was about acknowledging people who died in care.

Project Lead, council parks planning manager John Brenkley would like to create a database of all the people buried in Dunedin cemeteries including unmarked graves. Tess Brunton

"Where we're standing at the moment is just grass and you would never know that there's any graves here but we know from the plans that there is a grid of graves below us and around us," he said.

"We know that where the Seacliff people are in that grid and so we're just going through and verifying that from positions that we know."

The council invited people to provide relevant information to help them piece together the stories with about 50 people getting in touch.
