Tech.title: Smart ring maker Ultrahuman to roll out biological-age model across UAE
Tech.content:
Ultrahuman, a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates.

On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process.

The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview.

“If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?”

Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company.

Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said.

Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline.

The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted.

Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups.

The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns.

Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program.

Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk.

Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi.

The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games.

What Is Google Workspace Individual, and How Does It Work? Google is making changes to its productivity suite again, and some of it may cost you money. Here's what you need to know.

What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Tech.title: Microsoft President Says AI Has Fewer Regulations Than Milk. So Now What?
Tech.content:
The next time you pick up a carton of milk, consider this: It has likely passed through more safety inspections than the AI system writing your emails, screening your job application or negotiating with your bank. That, according to Microsoft President Brad Smith, is the problem.

In an interview with ITV last week, Smith said that AI is less regulated than milk and washing machines. He proposed that governments adopt established production safety practices and that AI companies build “kill switches,” a kind of emergency brake that would allow operators to shut down a system that begins behaving in an unsafe or unintended way.

Smith’s comments come amid growing public concern that voluntary industry commitments to safety — a form of toothless self-regulation — are not enough to manage systems that can influence decisions, handle sensitive data and, in the wrong hands, enable cyberattacks. Recent cases of so-called “rogue AI agents” escaping their environments, such as the summer’s infamous Hugging Face hack and attempted breaches of Australian and US government websites, have drawn scrutiny to AI’s alleged “existential risk” and sparked calls for a pause.

More from CNET

On Saturday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed Smith’s sentiments in a lengthy X post, saying that the biggest companies lack a “mechanistic understanding” of the tools they deploy. Nadella also argued for slower development, incident reporting and independent review.

“We must build contained systems whose behavior we can observe, limits we can test and actions we can always contain,” Nadella wrote.

Microsoft’s statements come less than two weeks after top AI executives, including Nadella, met with President Donald Trump, who announced his proposal to rename AI as “super intelligence.“

Several Silicon Valley leaders — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk — signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, pledging to establish internal committees to oversee development and to work with independent auditors. (Though Microsoft doesn’t appear to have signed Trump’s voluntary accord, Nadella notably uses the term “super intelligence” in his recent X post.)

Smith’s and Nadella’s comments place Microsoft closer to Anthropic’s camp of “caution,” which calls for stronger AI oversight. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s Altman said that we should all just “accept some bad things happening” for the benefit of AI, whereas Zuckerberg and Huang continue to double down on their rejection of an industry-wide, coordinated slowdown in AI development.

Wherever they stand on the regulation debate, AI leaders all stand to benefit in some way from engaging in the discussion on safety guardrails. For example, Microsoft recently released Microsoft Execution Containers, an enterprise security feature that protects devices by restricting the files and programs AI models can access and providing a built-in kill switch to instantly shut them down if needed.

A Microsoft representative declined to make any further comment.

The “rogue AI” narrative and Trump’s “super intelligence” rebrand serve as implicit marketing for the biggest AI companies — making them wealthier and more powerful. Cheng Xin/Getty Images

The ‘rogue AI’ narrative and Big Tech regulation

Despite increasingly public safety threats, it’s unlikely that the Trump administration will back regulation across the entire AI industry. The president has declared AI safety concerns a hoax, even as insiders report that more nuanced debates are unfolding behind closed doors. Last month, Trump posted on Truth Social that the only guardrail the AI industry needs is a “strong and smart president.”

In December 2025, Trump issued an executive order designed to prevent states from passing “cumbersome legislation” regulating AI model development, passing the buck to his own administration. The president continues to post online about maintaining a low-regulation environment for the biggest AI companies.

Many prominent AI critics argue that the entire regulatory framework is flawed from the start because it lets AI companies define the security threats and respond on their own terms. Distributed AI Research Institute founder Timnit Gebru has argued that the “rogue AI” narrative surrounding incidents like Hugging Face and access to government websites shifts attention away from basic corporate failures.

“This is not models going rogue,” Gebru told Democracy Now during an interview on Oct. 1. “This is gross incompetence and negligence by a particular company.”

Gebru said that people need to understand that these fallible machines don’t act autonomously with their own agency. “We need to hold corporations liable for unleashing these kinds of error-prone models into the world,” she said.

According to Gebru, the focus on so-called runaway AI and the push for voluntary self-regulation are ways for the industry to avoid accountability under existing law. Rather than face liability for unsafe security practices occurring now, AI companies redirect the conversation to an unprecedented danger likely to occur in the future.

The real danger is regulatory capture, where AI companies shape the rules that are supposed to constrain them. In this way, the public is asked to trust the morality of the very companies that build and profit from AI.

Tech.title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder AI Models to Play Catch-Up With Rivals
Tech.content:
Tech giant Meta debuted its new Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full premium AI models on Monday, continuing a push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently called the “AI frontier,” where the heavy hitters in the artificial intelligence space have dominated.

The models build upon the Muse Spark AI model, launched earlier this year. Meta calls the new paid tiers its “most capable models to date,” reporting the models can perform personal and professional agentic tasks ranging from handling insurance claims to helping renters understand a lease agreement to building entire working apps.

Meta says its new models, the fruits of billions of dollars invested over the last year, leapfrog the competition. But it’s playing catch-up with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google in the AI race.

More from CNET

“Meta is making up for lost time with lots of new AI tools,” Katelyn Chedraoui, CNET’s expert reporter on artificial intelligence, told me. “But this new frontier model comes amid serious safety concerns in the AI industry. Safeguards will be essential to any new launch.”

Many researchers and experts are advocating for external evaluation and regulation of the technology, with some AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, making high-profile calls to slow AI development. Meanwhile, Zuckerberg has been vocal in his belief that labs can and should self-police to stave off the worst effects of AI.

“I’m much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI, which is that it is just going to go do its own thing,” Zuckerberg told Financial Times in an interview this week.

Meta recently announced the Muse Charm AI hardware, which looks like a keychain or pendant. Meta/CNET

Muse Wonder and Wonder Full

Muse Wonder is the “state-of-the-art” premium-tier AI model from Meta. It is available first to coders who pay for access to the Meta Model API, via the Power Plan at $20 per month or the Maximum Plan at $100 per month. However, Meta’s announcement says it “will soon power experiences in Muse” with more flexible per-million-token pricing.

Meta says Muse Wonder builds on the core capabilities of its Muse Spark AI model with more advanced features, greater processing power and improved capability in law, finance and health applications. Meta gives the example of Muse parsing a leasing agreement or handling an insurance claim. (To be clear, do not rely on AI for healthcare or mental health.) Muse Wonder’s new “frontier coding performance” will also enable the agent to assist in building games and apps.

Muse Wonder introduces two new features: Active Memory and Active Focus.

The first, Active Memory, enables the model to remember and carry information across conversations. Storing potentially sensitive data immediately sets my privacy-conscious Spidey Sense on edge. That said, Meta says it has trained its Muse Wonder model to avoid sharing private information without permission and has hardened it against cyberattacks. The company even says that “developers and security teams can use models like Muse Wonder to find flaws in their own code and strengthen their systems,” which — I gotta be honest — sounds to me like the peak tech hubris.

Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, has been vocal in his belief that labs can and should self-police to stave off the worst effects of AI. James Martin/CNET

The second new feature, Active Focus, keeps the AI agent working when it runs into technical dead ends. With Active Focus, Muse Wonder is said to be capable of alternative approaches, recovering from errors and asking the user for clarification. That should let the model handle more complex tasks than Spark and encounter fewer roadblocks, which we’ve seen firsthand in our testing.

But boasting that your AI model can more effectively circumnavigate what may be blocks put in place (perhaps for a reason) sounds eerily familiar. Recently, Anthropic revoked access to its AI models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5, after the US government imposed sweeping restrictions on who could use them.

Muse Wonder Full is said to be an even more powerful version of the premium Wonder model with all of the same new features, but with a shift in focus toward businesses and power users. Basically, Wonder Full unlocks more flexible reasoning, a tweaked base model and access to more behind-the-scenes processing power, making it a better fit for unfamiliar tasks, engineering and professional workflows.

Tech.title: Smartphone Shipments Just Hit a New Low. Thanks, RAMageddon
Tech.content:
If you’re holding on to your phone despite a wave of new, high-powered options, you’re not alone. Hitting the lowest mark since 2012, smartphone shipments worldwide continued a months-long skid, slumping 20% in the third quarter of 2026 due to the RAMageddon memory shortage, according to a new analysis by Counterpoint Research.

Counterpoint said that the cost of DRAM and NAND — the two main memory chips used in smartphones, computers and data centers — continues to rise, forcing manufacturers to raise phone prices, which are up 20% overall this year. Memory costs more because there’s less of it to go around, thanks to the massive AI infrastructure buildup and its voracious appetite for chips.

It was the second consecutive quarter to take “the full brunt of the memory crisis,” Shilpi Jain, a senior analyst at Counterpoint, said in a statement Monday.

More from CNET

Research firm Gartner has estimated that companies will spend $1.4 trillion on AI infrastructure this year and $2.6 trillion overall. More than 70% of global memory chip production will go toward AI investment, TrendForce said. Global fears about rising inflation for most products and services are also likely suppressing phone sales.

Some manufacturers fared all right during the third quarter, according to Counterpoint. Samsung’s market share was 23%, up from 19% in 2025, thanks in part to “robust initial demand” for the Galaxy Fold 8. Apple’s third-quarter market share was 22%, the first time the company has surpassed 20% in that three-month period. But both companies saw a year-over-year decline in shipments.

Things aren’t looking rosy for customers’ wallets, either. Earlier this month, Samsung hiked prices by $100 for its Galaxy S26 phones, and Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched last month with prices set $100 above the previous generation.

How are consumers responding?

The third quarter saw a number of notable smartphone introductions, including Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, the Google Pixel 11 and, in the period’s waning days, the iPhone 18 Pro line and Apple’s first foldable, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Friday.

Shoppers will be cautious about buying the latest and greatest in smartphones because of higher prices, says TMT analyst Paolo Pescatore.

“New design features, including foldables, may generate excitement and appeal, but their steep price premiums remain hard to justify when most people want a device that delivers robust, reliable connectivity,” Pescatore told CNET via email. “For many, the question is straightforward: why replace a perfectly functioning smartphone that continues to meet their everyday needs?”

Counterpoint Research found in a recent survey that half of respondents — spanning the US, UK, India, China and Germany — would wait until holiday sales to buy a new phone. That number rises to 56% among Gen Z consumers. Counterpoint’s Jain said consumers are increasingly shopping for “refurbished devices and prioritizing higher-value devices.”

With sales down, phonemakers might resort to different strategies for customers, including refurbished handsets, repairs and trade-in schemes, Pescatore said. Cellphone carriers like T-Mobile, Verizon Wireless and AT&T could also use financing plans and bundled services as enticements.

As AI investment continues to devour memory supply, phone prices won’t be falling anytime soon. And with companies focusing more on premium devices, there could be fewer budget alternatives available for customers, Counterpoint Research said.

Tech.title: This Cheap Roller Is a Must for Dog and Cat Owners Battling Pet Hair
Tech.content:
Pets are family, but family can be messy. Managing pet hair from animals is a daily struggle for owners and during shedding season, things get especially dire. The same goes for cat owners with litter boxes: those tiny bits of clay end up in the darndest of places, including between the sheets. Ick.

No matter what I’ve tried, litter and pet hair end up on furniture or in your bed almost constantly. Vacuums work well for keeping floors free of pet hair, but they’re less effective in other parts of the home.

The inexpensive SandBar does things even the best pet hair vacuums can’t. John Carlsen/CNET

I recently spotted an inexpensive tool that promises to collect hair, sand, and pieces of litter. It doesn’t rely on a cord or battery and costs just $30. I took a chance and tested the SandBar, a dual-roll lint roller, to see if it can make it easier to keep stray hair and litter at bay. I also wanted to see how it would fare with other lint-roller-adjacent tasks like dusting and cleaning floors.

More from CNET

How SandBar Roller differs from other lint rollers

The SandBar Roller Starter Kit I tested included the roller head, an extendable handle and two preinstalled lint rolls. John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar Roller’s appeal lies in its two large lint rollers instead of one. While the idea doesn’t seem like much of a departure from a typical large lint roller, I couldn’t find any other dual-roller designs intended for use between bedsheets like SandBar. By arranging the rollers this way, SandBar can clean the top and bottom sheets at the same time without getting stuck.

The Best Handheld Vacuums, Tested by CNET See at CNET

While SandBar markets its proprietary lint rolls as stronger than normal rolls, they’re not much different from the extra-large pet-hair version of the Scotch-Brite lint roller. Both are 8 inches wide, with an inner diameter of 1.5 inches. Much to SandBar’s credit, its six-pack of refill rolls is just $20, which is very competitive with other lint roll refills I found on Amazon, with the optional subscription price dropping to just $16 for each one-, two- or three-month delivery.

Testing the SandBar Roller

The extendable handle is very practical. John Carlsen/CNET

Ostensibly, this design targets coastal homes, where sand gets everywhere — hence the SandBar name. While I don’t live on the coast, I’ve experienced sand in my bed while traveling, or after day trips to the desert, and cat litter is a near-daily occurrence. With that in mind, I conducted a series of informal tests to see how the SandBar Roller holds up.

When I put the SandBar between the sheets, it moved fairly smoothly, at least until it snagged on some sheets that were too loose. It didn’t jam, but that means it works better for beds with the sheet firmly tucked at the foot — something I don’t do for various sleep-friendly reasons. Still, it worked well after tightening the sheets a bit, even snagging a few cat hairs and litter fragments. It’s a nice alternative to washing the sheets as frequently as I have to now.

I like the stickiness of the rolls, which is satisfyingly tacky without leaving residue or making used strips hard to pull off. John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar removed cat fur from hard-to-reach places

Next, I wanted to see how it handled cleaning smart window shades and curtains, which often collect fur as my cat patrols windows a few times a day. It was a little more awkward, but taking the handle off proved effective, and the sticky roller collected a substantial amount of fur. I had to peel off multiple sheets because of the amount of fur, but it took only a few passes to clean the curtain. The SandBar Roller was very useful on furniture and pet beds, but I noticed that being too aggressive can occasionally dislodge a roll.

The SandBar Roller left a fairly clean surface when I dusted off a TV cabinet and soundbar. Still, I wouldn’t trade it out for the duster and handheld vacuum I usually use. Likewise, it did well on the linoleum floor and carpet near my cat’s litter box, but still, I prefer the cleaner result I get from vacuuming.

Should you buy the SandBar Roller?

The specialized design does its job well, but is probably too niche for people who aren’t pet parents or near vast swathes of sand. John Carlsen/CNET

At $30, the SandBar Roller is unlikely to break anyone’s budget, especially when you can find similarly large bed lint rollers for the same price. In that context alone, including the cost of refill rolls, it’s probably as good as any other option. Still, the dual-roll design’s ability to get between sheets is a compelling reason to consider the SandBar Roller over the competition. The design suits households that typically deal with a lot of sand and litter in the beds. I could even see myself taking it camping for quick dirt cleanup in a sleeping bag.

However, I wouldn’t recommend it for short-term beach house rentals because it cuts corners — new guests expect clean sheets when they arrive. That said, making a SandBar Roller available during a guest’s visit could improve their experience, as long as you leave instructions explaining what it’s for and how it works.

If you don’t need the second roll — and mainly deal with pet hair on furniture — the ChomChom Roller doesn’t need refill rolls, making it a much better option for $25. Likewise, a handheld vacuum can do the same job with a bit more flexibility around the house — though it’s not quiet enough to use when others are sleeping. While it’s nice to have so many options, it’s always worth going with what works best for your needs and situation.

Tech.title: Beats Teases Upcoming Pokemon Portable Pill Speaker: Gotta Hear ‘Em All
Tech.content:
Put a Pokemon character, especially Pikachu, on just about anything — including a $100 Polaroid camera — and fans will take notice. On Monday, Beats by Dre teased an upcoming collaboration where the colorful characters seem to be coming to decorate Beats Pill Bluetooth speakers.

Beats by Dre didn’t share a lot of information, but the caption “Time to catch something new” plays off the classic Pokemon tagline, “Gotta catch ’em all!” The 6-second video shows electrical charges in yellow and purple flashing over a shadowed Beats Pill speaker. It ends with a screen showing the Pokemon Poke Ball logo and the Beats by Dre “b” logo, with an X between them, teasing a product collaboration.

Time to catch something new. pic.twitter.com/Rt0IfTKENC — Beats by Dre (@beatsbydre) October 12, 2026

The inclusion of yellow sparks in the video seems to hint that the Beats speaker will be themed around the popular yellow Pokemon, Pikachu. Tech site 9to5Toys suggests that the purple flashes might mean another Beats speaker could be themed around a purple character, such as Mewtwo, Gengar or Ditto.

More from CNET

Beats’ teaser did not announce a release date for a Pokemon-themed Pill speaker, but Apple’s Welcome Home event, expected to focus on new smart home devices, is scheduled for Tuesday. Apple bought Beats by Dre for $3 billion back in 2014.

The speaker isn’t a brand-new revelation for those who stay up to date on all things Pokemon. Last week, a Pokemon fan who goes by BritBrattv posted a photo to Facebook showing a bright yellow Pikachu-themed Beats Pill speaker in what appears to be a Target shopping cart, though that photo hasn’t been confirmed as official.

And former Apple CEO Tim Cook shared a video on X in August showing Pikachu visiting Apple Park.

“Today’s agenda at Apple Park,” Cook wrote. “Introduce the @Pokemon team to John, talk gaming, and politely ask Pikachu to stay out of the pond. Two out of three were accomplished.” By “John,” he presumably means John Ternus, the new Apple CEO.

Representatives for Beats by Dre and Pokemon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Beats Pill speaker, in non-Pokemon designs, is priced at $129 at Target and Amazon as of Monday. In a 2024 review, CNET executive reviews editor David Carnoy called the Pill “a very good compact Bluetooth speaker,” praising its sound quality and strong battery life.

Tech.title: Cyberattack Targets French Supermarket Refrigerators, Forcing Mass Food Disposal
Tech.content:
Hundreds of supermarkets in France were the subject of a coordinated hack early Monday morning that turned up the heat on fridges and freezers, causing food to spoil and, in some cases, fires to break out.

According to reports from AFP, three major grocery chains in the country — E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U — reported that hackers forced connected fridges and freezers at hundreds of stores to go into defrost mode for several hours, raising their temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). Paris authorities told the news agency that other grocery chains were also hit.

While it’s unclear who is responsible for the attacks or the exact exploit chain used, the hackers targeted software on two Danfoss system controllers. The company told the industry publication Cooling Post that the affected systems, AK-SM800 and AK-SC355, were running outdated firmware. “We are working with affected customers to implement appropriate mitigation measures, including firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable,” Danfoss told Cooling Post.

More from CNET

On a web page for its AK-SM800 controllers, Danfoss says the company “takes security seriously” and that “new measures are being implemented” to improve security.

A representative for Danfoss didn’t immediately return a request for comment.

The incidents are alarming for several reasons. In addition to proving yet again that network-connected devices, especially older ones, can be targets of attack, the French supermarket attack highlights vulnerabilities in global food supplies that can be quickly and dangerously exploited.

Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Cooperative U, said in a post on X that an investigation into the attack is underway. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he posted (translated from French).

Je confirme qu’une cyberattaque touche depuis cette nuit les installations de production de froid de plusieurs magasins de notre réseau @CooperativeU.

Nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées, en lien avec les frigoristes, pour rétablir la situation au plus vite. Une enquête devra… — Dominique Schelcher (@schelcher) October 12, 2026

The ‘internet of things’ is being attacked

The attack on a French supermarket underscores the growing risk of attacks on operational technology and cold-chain infrastructure. Though the fridges and freezer units weren’t consumer smart fridges with app controls and touch screens, the controllers were connected to the internet to remotely manage defrost cycles, temperatures and alarms across many stores.

Companies may have many reasons for using these kinds of OT devices. They can log temperatures to ensure they’re meeting food safety standards, deploy firmware updates to prevent security incidents like this one and get alerts if a fridge or freezer is malfunctioning. Some devices like this also monitor inventory or even update prices for digital shelf displays.

But just as appliances from companies such as Samsung can be affected by a hack or even software glitches — like a recent incident in Korea that bricked some smart fridges — these industrial devices rely on imperfect software and internet connections, which expose them to the outside world.

Older IT and operational systems that are incorporated into connected systems may be especially difficult to defend, said Nathaniel Jones, senior vice president of global threat intelligence at Darktrace. “A cyber incident no longer affects only data or business systems; it can manipulate physical equipment and cause real-world damage.”



That damage can scale quickly if those systems are spread across many locations, all of which are exposed to the internet. “If it is connected, it can be targeted,” Jones said in a statement to CNET via email.

If that’s not scary enough, these are the same types of vulnerabilities that can make utilities such as power grids, water suppliers and even nuclear power plants vulnerable to attack.

Tech.title: More Indigenous Languages Come to iPhone and iPad Keyboards in New Apple Update
Tech.content:
When Apple released iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 in September, much of the buzz centered on the update’s revamped Siri AI. However, the update also brought a handful of new indigenous languages to the device’s keyboard, allowing users to type and send messages in Blackfoot and other languages. In the US, Monday is Indigenous Peoples’ Day, a federally recognized holiday honoring Native American heritage, culture and sovereignty.

Some of the supported languages have only a couple of thousand speakers. Consider Cherokee, which has only about 1,500 fluent speakers in the entire world. Cherokee was the first Native American language Apple added to iOS back in 2010, and its inclusion has been seen by some as a welcome development.

“The technology that we utilize with Apple has allowed us to take everything that we really are trying to achieve here, which is the perpetuation and the revitalization of Cherokee language and culture, and use that same technology to make it relevant to the young people that are learning here,” Chuck Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, said, according to Apple.

More from CNET

Teachers in Oklahoma are also using these tools in their classrooms to help more students engage with Native American languages. These tools can help students practice their pronunciation by allowing them to record themselves to revisit later.

“In Cherokee language, every sound is so important,” Erlinda “Daksi” Soap, a fifth-grade teacher at Oklahoma’s Cherokee Immersion School, told Apple. “One sound off, and you’re saying a completely different word.”

The Cherokee keyboard can be accessed and used across iOS devices. Apple/CNET

There are 85 characters, originally 86, in the written Cherokee language used to represent the sounds — or syllables — in the spoken language. Cherokee artist Roy Boney Jr. worked with Apple engineers to bring the Cherokee syllabary to Apple devices.

“A big part of being Cherokee is you ensuring things like language and culture survive and continue,” he told Apple.

High-schooler Olivia Daugherty graduated from the immersion school in 2024. She said she remembers her father teaching her to count and name animals in Cherokee as a child, and that she was nervous about losing her language and culture. Now, younger generations are helping to secure the language’s future.

“I was worried about my language and culture, and the way I might lose my community, and I might lose my language,” Daugherty told Apple. “My niece, she’s a first-language speaker in our language … She’s one of the first in a very long time.”
